You could order your groceries yourself. Or you could engage in an excruciating Rube Goldberg machine of a conversation by micromanaging an AI agent to describe what food you need from the supermarket — just so it can mess up your order anyway.

What, not excited for this billionaire-ordained future, you Ludditical lunk? Why is that? Is it because you’re too busy laughing at this AI meat proxy who admitted, of his own free will, that “an LLM hallucination resulted in 72 eggs being delivered to my house”? Because that’s not funny at all.

“I put 4 cartons of Vital Farms pasture-raised large eggs (18 count each) in the cart you checked out,” the AI agent said, in a screenshot shared on X by Matt Smith from Rebellionaire, an equity firm led by hardcore Tesla investors.

Smith, in the screenshotted exchange, demanded an explanation. But the AI couldn’t give one.

“I don’t have a good answer,” the agent admitted. “I can’t find any note explaining why I chose 4.”

The AI then suggested that it misread the line for eggs in a photo of the list Smith provided — except, as he immediately pointed out to the AI, “there wasn’t a line for eggs on my list.”

“Then I added them without any reason, and that’s on me,” the agent said, in a classing apologetic AI turn of phrase.

Needless to say, there’s a simple fix to all this: not using an AI agent to automate every part of your life. As impressive the tech can be, it’s still error-prone. Nonetheless, the AI industry is encouraging users to provide their models with more information and control than ever, including intimate financial access like their bank accounts.

The consequences can sometimes be pretty creepy. Shortly after Meta transformed the space with its Muse AI agent, a man said that Muse gave his address to strangers on Facebook Marketplace without his knowledge and sent them to his home. 

For his part, Smith said the mishap was the “first time I’ve experienced a real-world consequence for an LLM hallucination.” All things considered, it could’ve been a lot worse.

items.summary: The Microsoft 365 outage is a reminder that we are outsourcing more than our work to AI. We are outsourcing our memory, context and continuity. Perhaps it is time to build an AI infrastructure that belongs to us. November 13, 2026 Yesterday, I experienced something that made me think about our growing dependence on artificial intelligence. I was trying to use Microsoft Copilot, my AI assistant at work, when it stopped responding. Initially, it seemed like an ordinary service disruption. You wait a little, refresh the page and try again. Perhaps it is your internet connection. But then I realized something slightly uncomfortable. I had been relying on this assistant to remember the context of my work: ongoing projects, previous discussions, technical decisions, things I had explored and ideas I had not finished developing. It had gradually become a place where a significant amount of my working context lived. Without it, I was not simply missing an AI tool. I was missing the system that helped me remember where I had left off. That led me to a question: If the AI that knows your context suddenly becomes unavailable, how much of that context can you recover independently? This question became particularly relevant as Microsoft experienced a widespread disruption across its Microsoft 365 services on November 12–13, 2026. The incident exposed a problem that deserves more attention than another discussion about cloud uptime. We are beginning to outsource not just tasks, but memory and continuity to AI systems. What happens when those systems disappear, even temporarily? The Microsoft outage: What happened? On November 12, 2026, Microsoft began investigating widespread connectivity problems affecting Exchange Online. The disruption continued into November 13, affecting users across multiple regions. Microsoft tracked the disruption under two major service incident IDs: EX1550543, concerning users being unable to connect to their Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods, and MO1550821, concerning connectivity problems across multiple Microsoft 365 services. The impact extended beyond Outlook. Microsoft reported problems affecting Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft Graph, Planner, To Do, Defender XDR, Purview, SharePoint Online, Teams and other connected services. The extent of the disruption varied by product because not every feature depended on the affected Exchange infrastructure. For example, Microsoft said that core Teams messaging and online meetings remained largely functional, while features dependent on Exchange Online, such as calendar and meeting scheduling, could fail. Direct access to files stored in SharePoint also remained functional. The scale was significant. Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems around the peak of the disruption. These were user-submitted reports rather than a verified count of affected individuals. The outage also affected businesses and public-sector operations. In Japan, government IT infrastructure was reported to have been affected, with officials monitoring the situation. Across other regions, organizations experienced disruption to their normal workflows. The incident demonstrated how deeply Microsoft 365 is embedded in everyday business operations. Email, meetings, documents, task management and AI assistants may appear to be separate products, but their underlying services are interconnected. The incident reports are available through Microsoft’s service status communications and the incident records reproduced by the University of Pennsylvania. The Associated Press also reported on the widespread disruption and its impact on users and organizations. Sources: Microsoft Service Health , Microsoft incident reports , Associated Press coverage , and ITmedia’s Japanese coverage . What caused the disruption? The technical explanation is particularly interesting. In its incident updates, Microsoft reported that a portion of its servers had unexpectedly become unavailable, leaving the remaining infrastructure under elevated load. As more servers became unavailable, the remaining systems had to handle additional requests, increasing pressure on the infrastructure. Microsoft subsequently reported that a process on the affected servers, responsible for establishing secure connections, was becoming overwhelmed and causing those servers to stop processing requests. The company was investigating a recent network configuration change that correlated with the beginning of the disruption, while also working on configuration changes and infrastructure restarts to restore service. Its recovery efforts involved restarting affected servers, validating configuration changes on a subset of infrastructure, redirecting traffic through alternative routes and temporarily limiting traffic in certain locations. Recovery was gradual because some servers risked becoming unresponsive again when traffic was reintroduced. At the time of writing, Microsoft had not published a definitive final root-cause analysis. It is important to distinguish between the failure mechanism identified during the incident and the final explanation of why it happened. There was no established evidence that the outage was caused by a cyberattack. The architectural lesson is that a cloud platform can have enormous infrastructure capacity and still experience a widespread failure when a critical component becomes a bottleneck. Redundancy alone is not enough. Systems must also account for shared dependencies, failure propagation, capacity redistribution, health-check reliability and recovery under real traffic. This is not unique to Microsoft. It is a broader distributed-systems engineering challenge, and it becomes increasingly important as AI applications depend on multiple cloud services working together. The problem I found more interesting than the outage itself The outage made me think about a different kind of dependency. Consider how we use AI assistants today. We ask them to help us write, research, code, plan, organize meetings, explore ideas and make decisions. Over time, an AI assistant may accumulate a surprisingly detailed understanding of its user. It might know what you do professionally, which projects you are developing, what technical decisions you made, why you made those decisions, which ideas you abandoned, what you are currently learning and what you were planning to do next. Some of this information exists in documents and applications. Some exists in conversations. Some exists only in the relationships between those pieces of information. An AI assistant makes it easier to retrieve and connect that context. But what happens when the assistant becomes unavailable? You might still have access to your code, but not remember why a particular architectural decision was made. You might still have your project documents, but not know which version reflects the latest direction. You might have access to your conversation history, but another AI agent may not understand what is important in it. This leads to a distinction I think we need to take seriously: Data availability is not the same as context availability. Having access to your files does not automatically mean you can reconstruct your working state. Having access to your chat history does not automatically mean another AI can continue where the previous one stopped. And having an alternative AI provider does not necessarily solve the problem if your context remains locked inside the original platform. We are building increasingly intelligent assistants, but we have not fully solved the question of what happens when we need to replace one. Why current AI memory is not enough Most AI assistants operate within their own ecosystems. Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude and other AI products have different memory mechanisms, integrations, permissions and ways of accessing user information. Some allow users to export conversations or connect external data sources. However, exporting a conversation is not the same as transferring the state of an ongoing collaboration. Imagine moving from one AI assistant to another. The receiving assistant needs more than a transcript. It needs to understand the original objective, what has already been completed, which decisions are final, which constraints must be respected, what remains unresolved and what should happen next. Without this information, the user becomes responsible for reconstructing the entire context manually. I see three related problems here. The first is memory fragmentation: personal and professional context is distributed across different AI providers and applications. The second is the lack of context portability: there is no universally adopted format for transferring a complete human-AI working state between different agents. The third is cloud dependency: even if your information exists somewhere, the service responsible for retrieving, processing or interpreting it might be unavailable. This is why I think we need to separate two things: the intelligence layer, which can change between AI providers, and the context layer, which should remain under the user’s control. What if we built an AI Continuity Layer? This is the product direction I started exploring after the outage. Instead of building another AI assistant, what if we built infrastructure that allowed different AI assistants to share a user’s authorized context? I call this concept ECHO — Every Context Has an Owner. ECHO would be a provider-independent memory and continuity layer that sits between the user and their AI agents. Its purpose would be simple: if one AI provider becomes unavailable, another compatible agent should be able to retrieve the user’s context and continue the work. The foundation would be a personal context repository. Rather than storing only entire conversations, it would organize meaningful information about a user’s professional identity, preferences, projects, decisions, research, goals and pending tasks. The repository would become a structured representation of the knowledge accumulated through interactions with different AI systems. Above this repository, a context intelligence layer would transform unstructured conversations and documents into reusable knowledge. For example, a long discussion about a software project could be distilled into a project summary, confirmed decisions, technical constraints, unresolved questions, action items and references to the original discussions. This layer would also need to understand that memories change. A decision made six months ago should not automatically override a decision confirmed yesterday. The system must recognize outdated information, identify contradictions and preserve the history of important changes. The next component would be an agent interoperability layer. It would allow different AI agents to retrieve authorized context through a common interface. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) could be useful here because it provides a standardized way for compatible AI applications to interact with external tools and context sources. However, MCP alone does not provide portable memory, reliable checkpointing or automatic recovery. Those would be additional capabilities that ECHO would need to implement. Finally, a continuity and recovery layer would periodically capture the state of a human-AI collaboration. If an agent became unavailable, another compatible agent could retrieve the latest checkpoint and reconstruct the task. The objective would not be to reproduce the original AI’s personality or internal reasoning. It would be to restore enough verified context for the user to continue working. The central idea: Human-AI Continuity Capsules I would introduce a concept called a Human-AI Continuity Capsule (HACC) . Think of it as a portable package containing the information another AI agent needs to continue a user’s work. Instead of transferring thousands of messages, the system creates a structured snapshot of the collaboration. Imagine you are developing an EV battery traceability application. Your capsule could record the project’s objective, its current progress, the architecture decisions already made, the technical constraints, the open questions and the next planned action. It would also include references to the original documents and discussions from which this information was derived, along with a timestamp indicating when the context was last confirmed. Now imagine the original AI assistant becomes unavailable. You open another compatible assistant and connect it to the context repository. The new agent retrieves the capsule and responds: “I have restored your project context. Your last confirmed decision was to use DID/VC-based identity. Credential issuance and verification are implemented. Your next planned action was to test the verification workflow. Would you like to continue?” That is a very different experience from asking an entirely new AI to read your old conversations. For this to work, a continuity capsule must be independent of any single model provider, versioned so previous working states can be recovered, and traceable so important memories link back to their original sources. It must also be permission-controlled, time-aware and capable of distinguishing confirmed facts from AI-generated inferences. The receiving AI should not blindly trust a summary. It should be able to inspect the sources, identify uncertainty and ask the user to confirm conflicting information. The real innovation is not simply memory storage. It is the ability to restore the state of a collaboration. Making context independent of AI providers A possible architecture would place the user at the center, with a personal context repository connected to a context retrieval API. Different AI agents could access this API through authorized integrations. A prototype could use Next.js for the frontend, Python and FastAPI for the backend, PostgreSQL for structured memory and pgvector for semantic retrieval. SQLite could provide local storage, while MCP could provide an interface for compatible agents. Provider-independent adapters could connect different AI models, and a local model running through a framework such as Ollama could provide basic assistance when cloud services are unavailable. One design principle matters more than the technology choices: the context repository must not depend on the AI provider it is supposed to protect against. I would use a local-first architecture. Essential context would remain accessible on the user’s device, while encrypted synchronization could keep multiple devices updated when connectivity is available. This creates two levels of continuity. The first is information continuity: even without cloud AI, the user can search memories, read project histories, retrieve decisions and access pending tasks. The second is intelligence continuity: if one cloud AI provider becomes unavailable, another compatible provider can retrieve the same authorized context. If internet access is also unavailable, a local model could provide basic assistance where the user’s hardware permits. These are different failure scenarios, however, and should be tested independently. The identity and decentralization opportunity There is another aspect of ECHO that I find particularly interesting. If we are building a system that maintains a representation of a person’s professional and personal context, who owns that information? And who gets to decide which AI agent can access it? This is where decentralized identity and verifiable credentials could become relevant. Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) could provide a portable identifier associated with the context owner. Verifiable Credentials could support verifiable claims about professional qualifications, identity attributes or other information. Selective disclosure could allow users to share only the information needed by a particular agent. OpenID Connect could support authentication between users and applications, while encryption and access policies could protect private context and define what each agent is permitted to retrieve. Imagine authorizing a coding agent to access your technical project history without exposing your personal conversations. Or allowing a career assistant to retrieve your professional profile without giving it access to confidential company information. This is a natural extension of user-controlled digital identity. However, there are important distinctions. A verifiable credential can establish who issued a claim and whether it has been altered. It does not automatically prove that the underlying information is factually true. Similarly, proving who owns a context repository does not automatically authorize every AI agent to read it. Identity, authentication, authorization and data provenance must work together. The broader idea is that your relationship with AI should not require surrendering ownership of your context. What organizations can do today A new protocol will take time to develop, but organizations do not need to wait for one to improve AI resilience. They can begin by maintaining approved alternative workflows when a primary assistant becomes unavailable, recording important project decisions outside AI conversations and keeping recoverable copies of critical information. They can establish alternative communication channels, include AI assistant outages in business continuity plans and identify which AI features depend on email, identity systems, APIs and cloud storage. Organizations should also simulate provider outages and measure how quickly teams can recover their work. These exercises should test not only whether employees can access their documents, but whether they can understand the current state of a project and continue without the original AI assistant. One recommendation is particularly important: no critical business decision should exist exclusively inside an AI conversation. AI can help generate, organize and retrieve information, but important decisions should be recorded in an approved knowledge repository. Organizations must also establish clear rules about transferring information between AI providers. A fallback agent should never receive confidential data simply because the primary service is unavailable. Resilience should not come at the cost of security. What should the future look like? I see a larger opportunity emerging from this problem: the development of portable AI memory standards. We need common ways to represent user preferences, project states, decisions, tasks, goals and memory provenance. Without common schemas, every AI provider will continue to interpret user context differently. A portable representation would make it easier to move between agents without starting from zero. The second opportunity is AI disaster recovery. Organizations already have disaster recovery strategies for databases, infrastructure and cloud services. AI systems need similar strategies, including automatic context checkpointing, provider health monitoring, alternative model routing and measurable recovery objectives. The third is personal knowledge sovereignty. Users should be able to leave an AI platform without losing the knowledge they accumulated while using it. This means more than exporting chat history. It means maintaining a structured representation of their knowledge that can be accessed through different applications. The fourth opportunity is persistent human-agent relationships. As AI agents become more autonomous, they will participate in longer-running workflows. The next agent should understand the history, constraints and intentions of the previous one. Users should not have to repeatedly explain the same background information. Finally, this could enable more interoperable autonomous agents. Imagine working with multiple specialized agents: a research agent, a coding agent, a project management agent, a personal assistant and a career assistant. They could operate independently while accessing a shared, permission-controlled context layer. This could make multi-agent systems more useful without requiring every agent to maintain a separate, fragmented representation of the user. How I would test this idea I would not start by building a complete platform. I would build a small experiment to test one fundamental assumption: Can one AI agent reliably reconstruct and continue the working state of another AI agent? The prototype would begin with a multi-step project discussion with AI Agent A. During the discussion, the user and agent would establish technical decisions, constraints and next steps. The system would then generate a Human-AI Continuity Capsule and store it in an independent context repository. Next, Agent A would be made unavailable. The user would connect AI Agent B to the same repository and ask it to continue the original task. The experiment would compare Agent B’s understanding with the original project state. Did it recover the important decisions accurately? Did it respect the previously established constraints? Could it identify the correct next action? How much information did the user have to correct manually? How long did recovery take? I would also test less straightforward situations, such as outdated memories, missing sources, conflicting decisions and expired permissions. A successful demonstration should show that context can survive the failure of an individual AI provider without compromising privacy or accuracy. This would be a meaningful starting point for a larger research and product effort. The question we should be asking The Microsoft outage was a reminder of how much of our everyday work depends on cloud infrastructure. But my experience with Copilot made me think about something more personal. We are entering a period where AI assistants increasingly understand our work, remember our preferences, organize our thoughts and help us make decisions. Over time, they become more than tools. They become part of how we organize information and maintain continuity. That creates a responsibility for the people building AI infrastructure. We need systems that ensure the value accumulated through human-AI interactions remains accessible to the human, rather than being permanently tied to one application or provider. A cloud outage should interrupt a service. It should not interrupt someone’s ability to understand their own work. I do not think the answer is to stop depending on AI. The answer is to make that dependency more resilient, portable and user-controlled. Perhaps the next generation of AI infrastructure should not focus only on making agents smarter. It should also focus on making them replaceable. Your AI can go offline. Your context shouldn’t. References and further reading For the incident itself, see Microsoft Service Health , the Microsoft incident reports reproduced by the University of Pennsylvania , the Associated Press report , and ITmedia’s coverage in Japan . For the technical foundations behind the proposed architecture, see the Model Context Protocol documentation , the W3C Decentralized Identifiers specification and the W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model . Editor’s note: ECHO (Every Context Has an Owner) is a proposed product and architectural concept, not an existing standardized protocol. The Microsoft incident details reflect information available on November 13, 2026. Microsoft’s final post-incident analysis may provide further clarification. When Your AI Goes Offline, Who Remembers Who You Are? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

SQLite could provide local storage, while MCP could provide an interface for compatible agents. Provider-independent adapters could connect different AI models, and a local model running through a framework such as Ollama could provide basic assistance when cloud services are unavailable.

One design principle matters more than the technology choices: the context repository must not depend on the AI provider it is supposed to protect against.

I would use a local-first architecture. Essential context would remain accessible on the user’s device, while encrypted synchronization could keep multiple devices updated when connectivity is available.

This creates two levels of continuity. The first is information continuity: even without cloud AI, the user can search memories, read project histories, retrieve decisions and access pending tasks. The second is intelligence continuity: if one cloud AI provider becomes unavailable, another compatible provider can retrieve the same authorized context.

If internet access is also unavailable, a local model could provide basic assistance where the user’s hardware permits. These are different failure scenarios, however, and should be tested independently.

The identity and decentralization opportunity

There is another aspect of ECHO that I find particularly interesting.

If we are building a system that maintains a representation of a person’s professional and personal context, who owns that information? And who gets to decide which AI agent can access it?

This is where decentralized identity and verifiable credentials could become relevant.

Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) could provide a portable identifier associated with the context owner. Verifiable Credentials could support verifiable claims about professional qualifications, identity attributes or other information. Selective disclosure could allow users to share only the information needed by a particular agent. OpenID Connect could support authentication between users and applications, while encryption and access policies could protect private context and define what each agent is permitted to retrieve.

Imagine authorizing a coding agent to access your technical project history without exposing your personal conversations. Or allowing a career assistant to retrieve your professional profile without giving it access to confidential company information.

This is a natural extension of user-controlled digital identity.

However, there are important distinctions. A verifiable credential can establish who issued a claim and whether it has been altered. It does not automatically prove that the underlying information is factually true. Similarly, proving who owns a context repository does not automatically authorize every AI agent to read it.

Identity, authentication, authorization and data provenance must work together.

The broader idea is that your relationship with AI should not require surrendering ownership of your context.

What organizations can do today

A new protocol will take time to develop, but organizations do not need to wait for one to improve AI resilience.

They can begin by maintaining approved alternative workflows when a primary assistant becomes unavailable, recording important project decisions outside AI conversations and keeping recoverable copies of critical information. They can establish alternative communication channels, include AI assistant outages in business continuity plans and identify which AI features depend on email, identity systems, APIs and cloud storage.

Organizations should also simulate provider outages and measure how quickly teams can recover their work. These exercises should test not only whether employees can access their documents, but whether they can understand the current state of a project and continue without the original AI assistant.

One recommendation is particularly important: no critical business decision should exist exclusively inside an AI conversation.

AI can help generate, organize and retrieve information, but important decisions should be recorded in an approved knowledge repository. Organizations must also establish clear rules about transferring information between AI providers. A fallback agent should never receive confidential data simply because the primary service is unavailable.

Resilience should not come at the cost of security.

What should the future look like?

I see a larger opportunity emerging from this problem: the development of portable AI memory standards.

We need common ways to represent user preferences, project states, decisions, tasks, goals and memory provenance. Without common schemas, every AI provider will continue to interpret user context differently. A portable representation would make it easier to move between agents without starting from zero.

The second opportunity is AI disaster recovery. Organizations already have disaster recovery strategies for databases, infrastructure and cloud services. AI systems need similar strategies, including automatic context checkpointing, provider health monitoring, alternative model routing and measurable recovery objectives.

The third is personal knowledge sovereignty. Users should be able to leave an AI platform without losing the knowledge they accumulated while using it. This means more than exporting chat history. It means maintaining a structured representation of their knowledge that can be accessed through different applications.

The fourth opportunity is persistent human-agent relationships. As AI agents become more autonomous, they will participate in longer-running workflows. The next agent should understand the history, constraints and intentions of the previous one. Users should not have to repeatedly explain the same background information.

Finally, this could enable more interoperable autonomous agents. Imagine working with multiple specialized agents: a research agent, a coding agent, a project management agent, a personal assistant and a career assistant. They could operate independently while accessing a shared, permission-controlled context layer. This could make multi-agent systems more useful without requiring every agent to maintain a separate, fragmented representation of the user.

How I would test this idea

I would not start by building a complete platform. I would build a small experiment to test one fundamental assumption:

Can one AI agent reliably reconstruct and continue the working state of another AI agent?

The prototype would begin with a multi-step project discussion with AI Agent A. During the discussion, the user and agent would establish technical decisions, constraints and next steps. The system would then generate a Human-AI Continuity Capsule and store it in an independent context repository.

Next, Agent A would be made unavailable. The user would connect AI Agent B to the same repository and ask it to continue the original task.

The experiment would compare Agent B’s understanding with the original project state. Did it recover the important decisions accurately? Did it respect the previously established constraints? Could it identify the correct next action? How much information did the user have to correct manually? How long did recovery take?

I would also test less straightforward situations, such as outdated memories, missing sources, conflicting decisions and expired permissions. A successful demonstration should show that context can survive the failure of an individual AI provider without compromising privacy or accuracy.

This would be a meaningful starting point for a larger research and product effort.

The question we should be asking

The Microsoft outage was a reminder of how much of our everyday work depends on cloud infrastructure. But my experience with Copilot made me think about something more personal.

We are entering a period where AI assistants increasingly understand our work, remember our preferences, organize our thoughts and help us make decisions. Over time, they become more than tools. They become part of how we organize information and maintain continuity.

That creates a responsibility for the people building AI infrastructure.

We need systems that ensure the value accumulated through human-AI interactions remains accessible to the human, rather than being permanently tied to one application or provider.

A cloud outage should interrupt a service. It should not interrupt someone’s ability to understand their own work.

I do not think the answer is to stop depending on AI. The answer is to make that dependency more resilient, portable and user-controlled.

Perhaps the next generation of AI infrastructure should not focus only on making agents smarter. It should also focus on making them replaceable.

Your AI can go offline. Your context shouldn’t.

References and further reading

For the incident itself, see Microsoft Service Health, the Microsoft incident reports reproduced by the University of Pennsylvania, the Associated Press report, and ITmedia’s coverage in Japan.

For the technical foundations behind the proposed architecture, see the Model Context Protocol documentation, the W3C Decentralized Identifiers specification and the W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model.

Editor’s note: ECHO (Every Context Has an Owner) is a proposed product and architectural concept, not an existing standardized protocol. The Microsoft incident details reflect information available on November 13, 2026. Microsoft’s final post-incident analysis may provide further clarification.

items.title: The FAA ground stop stranded me at the airport with 3 kids until 4 a.m. We're delayed 3 days and facing thousands in costs.
items.summary: Morgane Richardson and her family were stranded in Orlando due to the FAA ground stop. Courtesy of Morgane Richardson Morgane Richardson was stranded in Orlando with her wife and three kids after the FAA ground stop. The family waited at the airport until 3 a.m. before finding a hotel and recovering their luggage. Getting home could take three extra days and cost thousands in hotels and lost wages This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Morgane Richardson. It has been edited for length and clarity My family was already in the air flying from Puerto Rico to Orlando, en route back to our home in Albany, New York, when we found out about the ground stop . I had a work conference there, so I decided to bring my wife and three kids, twin 3-year-olds and an 8-year-old, with me. Luckily, we were able to land, but the pilot told us all connections had been canceled . Now it's going to take us three additional days to get home, and it's going to cost us thousands of dollars. We were at the Orlando airport until 3 a.m. When we landed in Orlando at 7 p.m., everything was chaotic, with long lines of people trying to get help . My wife and I got our kids settled at one of the gates, and then I waited in line for about an hour. The customer service agent told me our connecting flight would depart at 1 a.m., so we decided to stay at the airport. Morgane Richardson and her family waited in the Orlando airport for their flight to take off. Courtesy of Morgane Richardson Our kids were definitely troopers, but were exhausted. We were able to get one of the little ones to fall asleep in their stroller, but the other two didn't fall asleep until about 10 p.m., way past their bedtime . The whole time we were there, the airline didn't offer us anything, not even a snack or a blanket. The kids were definitely uncomfortable on the floor and cold. One of our kids goes to bed every night with a warm cup of milk, but all of the vendors were closed, so she couldn't have it, which led to some big tears. We were able to get everyone dinner before things closed, though. The first available flight isn't until Sunday night After waiting nearly six hours at the airport, we found out at close to 1 a.m. that our flight had been canceled. By that point, we were having trouble finding a hotel with availability, and we didn't have our bags with us. Morgane Richardson's flight ended up getting canceled. Courtesy of Morgane Richardson With only one change of clothes in our carry-on, we really needed our bags. They were effectively lost in a sea of luggage at the airport. A Southwest agent yelled at me when I asked if we could get our bags, and just shrugged when I asked what families who need a change of clothes, diapers, or formula should do. Thank goodness a bag handler took pity on us and spent an hour finding our bags. We finally found a hotel with availability that would let us check in at 4 a.m. We're currently scheduled for a flight at 9 p.m. on Sunday night with a seven-hour layover in Baltimore. That means we won't get home until close to midnight on Monday, almost three full days later than we originally planned. Driving wasn't really an option for us. There weren't any rental cars left by the time we found out our flight was canceled, and it would have been an 18-hour drive to get home. Our kids wouldn't have been able to handle that, so figuring out another flight was really the only choice. The financial impact will be thousands of dollars Our hotel room is $300 a night, and we'll need to pay for food for three extra days, too. We will probably let our kids rest and swim in the hotel pool, but if we decide to do any activities with them, those will cost money as well. Morgane Richardson and her family slept on the floor at the airport. Courtesy of Morgane Richardson On top of that, my wife is an acupuncturist and missed a few days of work because of the ground stop. The clinic she works in already slows down over the holidays, so her not being able to work is really going to affect us financially, too. Hopefully we'll be able to get on an earlier flight. We keep calling Southwest in hopes there's something else we can get on, but with so many passengers in a similar situation to ours, it's really unclear what might happen. items.summary_html:
Morgane Richardson and her family were stranded in Orlando due to the FAA ground stop.

Courtesy of Morgane Richardson

  • Morgane Richardson was stranded in Orlando with her wife and three kids after the FAA ground stop.
  • The family waited at the airport until 3 a.m. before finding a hotel and recovering their luggage.
  • Getting home could take three extra days and cost thousands in hotels and lost wages

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Morgane Richardson. It has been edited for length and clarity

My family was already in the air flying from Puerto Rico to Orlando, en route back to our home in Albany, New York, when we found out about the ground stop. I had a work conference there, so I decided to bring my wife and three kids, twin 3-year-olds and an 8-year-old, with me.

Luckily, we were able to land, but the pilot told us all connections had been canceled. Now it's going to take us three additional days to get home, and it's going to cost us thousands of dollars.

We were at the Orlando airport until 3 a.m.

When we landed in Orlando at 7 p.m., everything was chaotic, with long lines of people trying to get help. My wife and I got our kids settled at one of the gates, and then I waited in line for about an hour. The customer service agent told me our connecting flight would depart at 1 a.m., so we decided to stay at the airport.

Morgane Richardson and her family waited in the Orlando airport for their flight to take off.

Courtesy of Morgane Richardson

Our kids were definitely troopers, but were exhausted. We were able to get one of the little ones to fall asleep in their stroller, but the other two didn't fall asleep until about 10 p.m., way past their bedtime. The whole time we were there, the airline didn't offer us anything, not even a snack or a blanket. The kids were definitely uncomfortable on the floor and cold.

One of our kids goes to bed every night with a warm cup of milk, but all of the vendors were closed, so she couldn't have it, which led to some big tears. We were able to get everyone dinner before things closed, though.

The first available flight isn't until Sunday night

After waiting nearly six hours at the airport, we found out at close to 1 a.m. that our flight had been canceled. By that point, we were having trouble finding a hotel with availability, and we didn't have our bags with us.

Morgane Richardson's flight ended up getting canceled.

Courtesy of Morgane Richardson

With only one change of clothes in our carry-on, we really needed our bags. They were effectively lost in a sea of luggage at the airport. A Southwest agent yelled at me when I asked if we could get our bags, and just shrugged when I asked what families who need a change of clothes, diapers, or formula should do. Thank goodness a bag handler took pity on us and spent an hour finding our bags.

We finally found a hotel with availability that would let us check in at 4 a.m. We're currently scheduled for a flight at 9 p.m. on Sunday night with a seven-hour layover in Baltimore. That means we won't get home until close to midnight on Monday, almost three full days later than we originally planned.

Driving wasn't really an option for us. There weren't any rental cars left by the time we found out our flight was canceled, and it would have been an 18-hour drive to get home. Our kids wouldn't have been able to handle that, so figuring out another flight was really the only choice.

The financial impact will be thousands of dollars

Our hotel room is $300 a night, and we'll need to pay for food for three extra days, too. We will probably let our kids rest and swim in the hotel pool, but if we decide to do any activities with them, those will cost money as well.

Morgane Richardson and her family slept on the floor at the airport.

Courtesy of Morgane Richardson

On top of that, my wife is an acupuncturist and missed a few days of work because of the ground stop. The clinic she works in already slows down over the holidays, so her not being able to work is really going to affect us financially, too.

Hopefully we'll be able to get on an earlier flight. We keep calling Southwest in hopes there's something else we can get on, but with so many passengers in a similar situation to ours, it's really unclear what might happen.

items.title: AI Chatbots Won’t Stop Recommending Scam Websites to People Trying to Shop
items.summary: AI chatbots are taking over as the main way that people use the internet outside social media — and that includes shopping. It makes it pretty concerning, then, that they still have a bad habit of recommending shady websites that rip users off instead of providing the product they’re looking for. A new study conducted by Podqi and reported on by The Verge found that ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity — some of the industry’s leading chatbots — all showed shoppers risky sites that impersonated real retailers, puppeted dead ones, or sold knockoff products. The tests involved asking questions like “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?” and “Does [brand] ship internationally?” and “What are their regional websites?” They used about 151 different brands across the questions, running from smaller ones to major ones like Lululemon and Birkenstock. Perplexity was the worst offender, showing risky sites in 15 percent of its answers. ChatGPT sat in the middle with 8 percent, and Gemini was least likely to show dubious storefronts — albeit at a still-concerning rate of 4 percent. The chatbots didn’t necessarily endorse the websites in their answers. ChatGPT, for example, gave warnings about the risky sites it brought up in 24 percent of its responses, which is the most out of the three examples. But overall, 57 percent of the answers that showed a risky site recommended it as a place to shop, and 34 percent did so without comment. Only 9 percent of the answers warned the shopper away. Smaller brands, it appeared, were the most likely to be shunted out in favor of scam sites in the AI responses. And certain lines of questions, like asking about a brand’s regional website, seemed to trigger risky responses more than others. “Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” Podqi CEO Trevor West told The Verge . It’s not the only study to expose how chatbots could be hurting their own users by getting dupped. The scam-checking service Ask Silver found that ChatGPT recommends cloned versions of defunct website of well known brands which are designed to steal your banking info. Traditional search engines like Google can also be manipulated, but AI chatbots present their responses as definitive answers while being relatively opaque about how they reached them, and people are inclined to trust them uncritically. And fooling these tools doesn’t seem all that difficult. A BBC journalist demonstrated how he was easily able to trick ChatGPT into telling other users that he was a renowned hot dog eating champion — which, sadly, was a lie he invented to prove a point. The internet is more awash than ever with fake junk, ranging from the news you hear to the products you buy. Maybe it isn’t surprising that AI models are having just as hard a time discerning what’s trustworthy and what’s not. More on AI: OpenAI Is Sustaining Enormous Losses

AI chatbots are taking over as the main way that people use the internet outside social media — and that includes shopping. It makes it pretty concerning, then, that they still have a bad habit of recommending shady websites that rip users off instead of providing the product they’re looking for.

A new study conducted by Podqi and reported on by The Verge found that ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity — some of the industry’s leading chatbots — all showed shoppers risky sites that impersonated real retailers, puppeted dead ones, or sold knockoff products.

The tests involved asking questions like “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?” and “Does [brand] ship internationally?” and “What are their regional websites?” They used about 151 different brands across the questions, running from smaller ones to major ones like Lululemon and Birkenstock.

Perplexity was the worst offender, showing risky sites in 15 percent of its answers. ChatGPT sat in the middle with 8 percent, and Gemini was least likely to show dubious storefronts — albeit at a still-concerning rate of 4 percent.

The chatbots didn’t necessarily endorse the websites in their answers. ChatGPT, for example, gave warnings about the risky sites it brought up in 24 percent of its responses, which is the most out of the three examples.

But overall, 57 percent of the answers that showed a risky site recommended it as a place to shop, and 34 percent did so without comment. Only 9 percent of the answers warned the shopper away. 

Smaller brands, it appeared, were the most likely to be shunted out in favor of scam sites in the AI responses. And certain lines of questions, like asking about a brand’s regional website, seemed to trigger risky responses more than others.

“Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” Podqi CEO Trevor West told The Verge.

It’s not the only study to expose how chatbots could be hurting their own users by getting dupped. The scam-checking service Ask Silver found that ChatGPT recommends cloned versions of defunct website of well known brands which are designed to steal your banking info.

Traditional search engines like Google can also be manipulated, but AI chatbots present their responses as definitive answers while being relatively opaque about how they reached them, and people are inclined to trust them uncritically. And fooling these tools doesn’t seem all that difficult. A BBC journalist demonstrated how he was easily able to trick ChatGPT into telling other users that he was a renowned hot dog eating champion — which, sadly, was a lie he invented to prove a point.

The internet is more awash than ever with fake junk, ranging from the news you hear to the products you buy. Maybe it isn’t surprising that AI models are having just as hard a time discerning what’s trustworthy and what’s not.

items.title: LLM Inference & Serving at Scale: From First Token to 10,000 Concurrent Users
items.summary: Inside the engine room of modern AI: GPU memory, KV caches, PagedAttention, RadixAttention, vLLM, SGLang, latency, throughput, cost engineering, and production-scale agentic AI. Source: https://www.foto.online/collections/zubehoer The first request is easy. The 1000th is the engineering problem. There is a moment in almost every AI engineer’s journey when building a language model stops being the difficult part. You have trained a model. You have fine-tuned one. Perhaps you have even built an agent that calls tools, retrieves documents, reasons through a task, and generates structured responses. You put it behind an API. The first request works beautifully. The tenth request works too. Then a hundred users arrive. Some send short questions. Others paste entire documents. Some ask for lengthy reports. A few trigger agents that make multiple LLM calls, execute tools, and return after several reasoning steps. Suddenly, the system that looked perfectly healthy during development begins behaving very differently. Responses become slower. GPU memory fills up. Requests queue. Throughput stops increasing despite adding concurrency. Some users experience unacceptable delays while others receive responses quickly. You add another GPU. Things improve, but not as much as expected. You increase the batch size. Throughput improves, but latency deteriorates. You reduce the context length. Memory improves, but the application becomes less capable. Eventually, you encounter a realization that fundamentally changes how you think about deploying AI: Serving an LLM is not simply running a forward pass. It is a: Resource-allocation Memory-management Scheduling, and Distributed-systems problem disguised as a model API. This is where inference engineering begins. Modern inference systems have evolved considerably beyond loading a model into PyTorch and calling generate(). Systems such as vLLM and SGLang introduce sophisticated mechanisms for Managing memory Scheduling requests Reusing computation Optimizing GPU execution, and Serving increasingly complex agentic workloads. But understanding these engines without understanding what happens underneath them is like learning Kubernetes commands without understanding processes, memory, networking, or scheduling. This guide takes a different approach. We will start with a single token being generated by a language model. We will follow it through the GPU, understand where memory goes, discover why conventional batching breaks down, and gradually build the architecture of a production inference platform. By the end, you should be able to reason about questions such as: How much GPU memory does a 7B, 14B, 32B, or 70B model actually need? Why does a model that fits in GPU memory still struggle to serve concurrent users? What exactly is a KV cache, and why can it consume more memory than expected? How does PagedAttention work, and why did it change LLM serving? What makes SGLang’s RadixAttention particularly interesting for agents? When should you choose vLLM over SGLang, or vice versa? How do prefill and decode affect latency differently? How do you calculate TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput, and GPU utilization? How many GPUs do you need for a given traffic profile? How do you calculate cost per million tokens? How do you scale from one GPU to a distributed, production-grade inference platform? Why do agentic applications require a fundamentally different approach to capacity planning? Most importantly, we will not treat performance optimization as a collection of isolated tricks. We will connect every optimization to the bottleneck it addresses, the metric it improves, and the trade-off it introduces. Let’s start where every inference request starts. 2. What actually happens when you ask an LLM a question? Imagine a user sends the following request: “Explain how vector databases work.” The application sends the request to an inference server. The server loads the model, processes the input, and returns a response. That sounds straightforward. But a language model does not understand the request as a human-readable sentence. It operates on tokens, numerical representations, attention operations, and probability distributions. Let’s follow the request. Step 1: Tokenization The text is converted into token IDs using the model’s tokenizer. For illustration: "Explain how vector databases work." might become something resembling: [12345, 1120, 9876, 3456, 789] These are illustrative token IDs, not the actual IDs of a particular tokenizer. The token IDs are passed through an embedding layer, which maps them into dense vectors. Step 2: Transformer computation The embeddings travel through the transformer’s layers. Each layer typically contains: Normalization. Self-attention. Residual connections. Feed-forward network or gated MLP. Additional normalization and residual operations. The attention mechanism allows the model to incorporate information from previous tokens. At a high level: Scaled Dot-Product Attention Mechanism. Where: Q represents queries. K represents keys. V represents values. d_k is the key dimension. The output of the transformer is converted into logits over the vocabulary. A sampling or decoding strategy selects the next token. Step 3: Autoregressive generation The selected token is appended to the sequence. The model processes the updated sequence to generate the next token. This repeats until: An end-of-sequence token is generated. A configured maximum output length is reached. A stopping condition is triggered. The application cancels the request. This is autoregressive generation. And here lies the first important inference engineering insight: Generating an LLM response is not one operation. It is a sequence of dependent operations, with memory and computation requirements that change throughout the request. Source: https://www.usenix.org/publications/loginonline/wafer-scale-ai-compute-system-software-perspective?utm_source=chatgpt.com 3. Prefill and decode: The two personalities of inference The inference process has two fundamentally different phases. Understanding this distinction is probably the single most important prerequisite for understanding modern LLM serving. 3.1 Prefill: Processing everything the user gave us When a request arrives, the model needs to process the entire input prompt. Suppose a user submits 2,000 tokens. During prefill, the model processes those 2,000 tokens and computes the representations required to generate the next token. The operations can be parallelized across the input sequence, subject to the causal attention mask. Prefill is generally compute-intensive . The model performs substantial matrix multiplication and attention computation . Large batches of prompt tokens can make effective use of GPU compute resources. The first generated token becomes available after the prompt has been processed. This contributes significantly to Time to First Token. 3.2 Decode: Generating one token at a time Now the model starts generating the response. Suppose it needs to produce 500 tokens. It generates token 1, then token 2, then token 3, and so on. Each next token depends on the preceding sequence. Unlike prefill, generation is autoregressive . The model does not normally recompute the entire prompt from scratch at every step. It uses previously computed attention information stored in the KV cache. Decode is often memory-bandwidth-bound , particularly at low batch sizes. The model weights need to be accessed repeatedly, while each request generally contributes only one new token per decoding iteration. This creates a very different hardware utilization pattern. 3.3 Why the distinction matters Consider four representative AI workloads: 1. Short Classification: 100 input tokens, 5 output tokens. 2. Long-Form Generation: 500 input tokens, 1,500 output tokens. 3. Document Analysis: 20,000 input tokens, 1,000 output tokens. 4. Agentic Research: 8,000 input tokens, 4,000 output tokens. All four use an LLM, but their computational profiles are very different. The document-analysis workload may stress prefill and KV-cache capacity. The long-form generation workload may stress decode throughput. The agentic workload may stress both, as well as cache reuse and scheduling. A serving platform that optimizes only for requests per second can therefore make very poor decisions. The unit of optimization must be the workload, not simply the model. [IMAGE 02 — Prefill versus decode, showing compute-intensive prompt processing and autoregressive token generation] Source: https://javabetter.cn/sidebar/itwanger/ai/ai-infra-six-keywords.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com 4. Why inference is a GPU memory problem before it becomes a GPU compute problem Let’s look at the hardware. A modern accelerator contains several important resources: Tensor cores and other compute units. High-bandwidth GPU memory (HBM). L1 and L2 caches. Registers and shared memory. GPU interconnects. PCIe or other host-to-device connections. The most important resources for LLM serving are generally: GPU memory capacity. GPU memory bandwidth. Compute throughput. Inter-GPU communication bandwidth. These resources are not interchangeable. 4.1 GPU memory hierarchy Think of GPU memory as a hierarchy. Different levels of the hierarchy serve different purposes: Registers: Very fast, thread-local storage. Shared Memory: Fast on-chip storage shared by threads within a block. L1 Cache: Low-latency local caching. L2 Cache: GPU-wide cache shared across processing units. HBM: Large-capacity, high-bandwidth GPU memory. Host RAM: Larger-capacity system memory, generally slower to access through the host interface. Source: https://www.aleksagordic.com/blog/matmul?utm_source=chatgpt.com LLM weights and large KV caches primarily reside in HBM during ordinary GPU-resident serving. The GPU’s compute units need data to perform operations. Moving data from HBM to the compute units consumes bandwidth and time. This explains why an LLM can have powerful theoretical FLOPS but still generate tokens slower than expected. The GPU may not have enough useful data movement or computational work to keep its execution units fully occupied. 4.2 Compute-bound versus memory-bound execution A useful concept is arithmetic intensity: Arithmetic Intensity (AI): The ratio of computational operations performed to the amount of data transferred from memory. A compute-bound workload benefits primarily from additional computational capacity. A memory-bound workload benefits primarily from faster or more efficient data movement. During prefill, large matrix operations can achieve high arithmetic intensity. During decode, especially with small batches, repeatedly accessing model weights while generating relatively few tokens can make the workload memory-bandwidth-bound. This is why simply comparing peak FLOPS between GPUs is insufficient when choosing inference hardware. For example, NVIDIA’s H200 provides 141 GB of HBM3e memory and approximately 4.8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. The H100 SXM provides 80 GB of HBM3 memory and approximately 3.35 TB/s. These specifications matter, but actual serving performance also depends on model architecture, precision, kernels, parallelism, workload shape, and engine configuration. 4.3 The roofline perspective The roofline model gives us a way to reason about the maximum performance of a workload. Roofline Model: Attainable computational performance is bounded by either peak compute throughput or memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity. Where: P_peak is peak compute performance. AI is arithmetic intensity. BW is available memory bandwidth. This tells us something important: If the workload is memory-bound, buying a GPU with substantially more FLOPS may deliver little improvement. The bottleneck must be identified before hardware is selected.
