Model weights: How much memory does a model need? Let’s begin with the simplest memory calculation. A model contains parameters, and each parameter occupies a certain number of bytes depending on its numerical precision. The approximate weight memory is: For common formats: FP32: 4 bytes per parameter FP16: 2 bytes per parameter BF16: 2 bytes per parameter FP8: 1 byte per parameter INT8: 1 byte per parameter INT4: 0.5 bytes per parameter These are storage estimates. Actual quantized checkpoints can have additional scale, zero-point, metadata, and alignment overhead. 5.1 Worked example: A 7B model For a 7-billion-parameter model in BF16: That is approximately 14 GB in decimal units, or 13.0 GiB. In INT4: Approximately 3.5 GB before quantization metadata and runtime overhead. 5.2 Memory estimates across model sizes 7B model BF16: 14 GB INT8: 7 GB INT4: 3.5 GB 8B model BF16: 16 GB INT8: 8 GB INT4: 4 GB 14B model BF16: 28 GB INT8: 14 GB INT4: 7 GB 32B model BF16: 64 GB INT8: 32 GB INT4: 16 GB 70B model BF16: 140 GB INT8: 70 GB INT4: 35 GB Note: These are theoretical weight-storage estimates using 2 bytes per BF16 parameter, 1 byte per INT8 parameter, and 0.5 bytes per INT4 parameter. Actual GPU memory requirements may be higher due to quantization metadata, KV cache, activations, temporary buffers, and runtime overhead. A model that needs 14 GB for weights cannot necessarily be served safely on a 16 GB GPU. Why? Because weights are only one component of the memory budget. You also need: KV cache. Activations and temporary tensors. CUDA graphs and execution buffers. Attention and GEMM workspaces. Communication buffers. Allocator and runtime overhead. Additional memory for adapters or other loaded models, where applicable. This brings us to the most important memory component in inference. 6. The KV cache: The memory that grows with every conversation Remember that the transformer uses attention to incorporate information from previous tokens. During prefill, the model computes keys and values for the prompt. Rather than recomputing these for every generated token, the model retains them in memory. These retained tensors form the Key-Value cache , commonly called the KV cache. Every newly generated token contributes additional key and value entries. This is what makes autoregressive generation efficient, but it also creates a memory problem. The longer the sequence, the larger the cache. The more concurrent requests, the more cache capacity the server needs. 6.1 Deriving KV-cache memory For a standard transformer with conventional attention caching: KV Cache Memory Estimation: The memory required to store Key and Value tensors across all transformer layers, attention heads, sequence positions, and batch elements. Where: L: number of transformer layers. H_KV: number of key/value heads. D_H: dimension of each attention head. T: number of tokens retained per sequence. B: number of concurrent sequences. S: bytes per KV element. The factor 2 accounts for keys and values. This formula assumes uniform layers with standard K/V storage. Architectures using sliding-window attention, MLA, hybrid attention, or cross-layer sharing require architecture-specific adjustments. 6.2 A real numerical example Consider an illustrative 8B-class architecture with: 32 transformer layers. 8 KV heads. 128 dimensions per head. BF16 KV cache. 8,192 tokens per sequence. The cache memory per token is: That is 128 KiB per token. For an 8,192-token sequence: One sequence can therefore consume approximately 1 GiB of KV cache. Now imagine 32 concurrent sequences, each retaining 8,192 tokens. Thirty-two GiB of KV cache. And this is before accounting for model weights and other runtime allocations. This is why memory planning cannot stop at model parameter count. 6.3 Why GQA and MQA matter The number of KV heads is important. Traditional Multi-Head Attention (MHA) generally has one KV head per query head. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares KV heads across groups of query heads. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) uses a single KV head. Reducing the number of KV heads can substantially reduce KV-cache memory. For example, reducing from 32 KV heads to 8 KV heads reduces the corresponding cache requirement by a factor of four, assuming other dimensions remain constant. This is one reason modern model architectures can be much more practical to serve than parameter count alone might suggest. 6.4 Your memory budget is a sum, not a single number A useful planning equation is: Total GPU Memory Requirement: The combined memory footprint of model weights, KV cache, runtime overhead, computational workspace, and communication buffers during inference. The actual serving engine determines the precise allocation and may reserve memory for future KV-cache growth. A useful initial approximation is: Available KV Cache Memory: The GPU memory remaining for KV cache allocation after accounting for model weights and memory reserved for runtime operations and other overheads. Then: Approximate KV Cache-Based Concurrency: The maximum number of sequences that can be accommodated concurrently, determined by the available KV cache memory divided by the memory required per sequence. This is only a first-order estimate. Real capacity also depends on block granularity, maximum sequence lengths, scheduling, cache sharing, preemption, and the mix of prompt and generation lengths. The key lesson: model size determines whether you can load the model. KV-cache capacity determines how much concurrent work you can sustain. Source: https://cdn.analyticsvidhya.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/KV-Caching.webp 7. Why conventional batching is not enough Suppose you have four users. User A needs 100 output tokens. User B needs 500 output tokens. User C needs 50 output tokens. User D needs 1,000 output tokens. A conventional static batch processes requests together. But what happens when User C finishes much earlier than User D? The batch may have to wait for the longest-running request or otherwise manage partially occupied batch slots. This is inefficient. LLM generation is particularly awkward because requests finish at different times and have different sequence lengths . 7.1 Static batching Static batching groups a fixed set of requests into a batch. Advantages: Simple execution model. Predictable batch composition. Useful for offline workloads with known input shapes. Limitations: Requests have different generation lengths. Finished requests can leave unused batch capacity. New requests may wait for an existing batch to finish. Memory requirements vary across requests. 7.2 Dynamic batching Dynamic batching collects requests arriving within a batching window. It can improve GPU utilization by combining requests. However, conventional request-level dynamic batching still struggles with the autoregressive nature of LLM generation. 7.3 Continuous batching Continuous batching changes the scheduling unit. Instead of treating an entire generation request as one indivisible batch member, the engine schedules work at individual generation iterations. When a request finishes, its resources can be released and another request can enter the active batch. Conceptually: Iteration 1: A, B, C, D Iteration 2: A, B, C, D Iteration 3: A, B, D, E Iteration 4: A, B, D, E Iteration 5: B, D, E, F Here, E and F enter as earlier requests complete. The GPU remains better occupied, and the scheduler can adapt to changing request lengths. This is one of the defining characteristics of modern LLM serving. The important insight is that continuous batching is not simply putting more prompts together. It is continuously managing a changing population of active decoding sequences. The seminal ORCA work introduced iteration-level scheduling as a way to improve transformer serving. Modern inference engines build on this broader scheduling philosophy. Source: HRDbjYSbsAEq5Q6.png 8. PagedAttention: What if GPU memory behaved like virtual memory? We now understand two things: KV cache grows as requests generate tokens. Different requests have different sequence lengths and memory lifetimes. Traditional contiguous memory allocation can become inefficient under these conditions. Imagine allocating one large contiguous memory region for every conversation. Some conversations finish early. Others grow longer. Some need additional memory. This creates fragmentation and makes it difficult to reuse free regions efficiently. The vLLM research team approached this problem with an idea inspired by operating-system virtual memory. What if KV-cache memory were managed in fixed-size blocks instead of requiring one contiguous allocation per request? That is the central intuition behind PagedAttention. 8.1 Logical blocks and physical blocks Imagine that each sequence has a logical sequence of KV-cache blocks. The physical blocks do not need to be contiguous in GPU memory. A block table maps logical blocks to physical blocks. For example: Request A: Logical blocks: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 Physical blocks: 7 → 2 → 9 → 4 Request B: Logical blocks: 0 → 1 → 2 Physical blocks: 1 → 6 → 8 The attention implementation uses the mapping to access the relevant KV entries. This provides several advantages: Less fragmentation. Flexible allocation. Better memory utilization. Easier reclamation of completed requests. Sharing of common KV blocks where supported. More effective batching. 8.2 Why paging matters Without efficient KV-cache management, memory fragmentation can limit how many sequences fit into the GPU. PagedAttention makes the cache allocation more flexible . The original PagedAttention paper introduced vLLM and demonstrated substantial serving-throughput improvements over earlier systems under its evaluated workloads. It is important not to interpret the original paper’s speedup as a universal performance guarantee. Modern engine versions, hardware, model architectures, and workload distributions all change the comparison. 8.3 The virtual-memory analogy PagedAttention applies virtual-memory concepts to GPU KV cache management: Virtual Address Space → Logical Token Positions Physical Memory Pages → Physical KV Blocks Page Table → Block Table Page Allocation → KV-Block Allocation Memory Reclamation → KV-Block Release Shared Pages → Shared KV Prefixes The analogy is useful, although the underlying implementation and access semantics are not identical to a general-purpose operating system. Source: https://medium.com/red-buffer/private-scalable-llm-inference-for-data-compliance-vllm-sglang-539ad81af04f 8.4 What about prefix sharing? Suppose 100 users interact with the same application. Every request starts with an identical system prompt. A conventional approach may independently compute and retain the same prefix KV state for every request. That is redundant. If the serving engine can safely reuse the KV state corresponding to the common prefix, it avoids repeating part of the computation. vLLM supports Automatic Prefix Caching, which can reuse KV-cache blocks for shared prefixes. This becomes particularly valuable for: Long system prompts. Repeated document context. Shared few-shot examples. Multi-turn conversations. Repeated application templates. The exact benefit depends on cache hit rates, prefix lengths, request locality, and cache eviction. And this leads us naturally to SGLang. 9. SGLang and RadixAttention: When the workload is more than a chatbot vLLM’s PagedAttention changed how we think about KV-cache allocation. SGLang takes cache reuse into another interesting direction. Consider a customer-support agent. Every conversation may include: A shared system prompt. A set of application instructions. Customer-specific information. Conversation history. A new user query. A research agent may repeatedly execute: A planning prompt. A search operation. A tool-result interpretation. A second planning operation. Another search. A final synthesis. These workflows create overlapping prefixes and repeated model calls. What if the runtime could organize reusable KV states around shared token prefixes? This is where RadixAttention comes in. 9.1 The radix-tree intuition A radix tree is a tree structure that represents shared prefixes efficiently. Consider these sequences: A: SYSTEM → POLICY → USER_A → QUERY_A B: SYSTEM → POLICY → USER_B → QUERY_B C: SYSTEM → POLICY → USER_C → QUERY_C The first two segments are shared. Instead of treating all three as entirely independent sequences, a radix-tree-based cache can represent the common prefix once and branch into request-specific continuations. Conceptually: SYSTEM | POLICY / | \ USER_A USER_B USER_C | | | QUERY_A QUERY_B QUERY_C SGLang’s RadixAttention uses this idea to support automatic KV-cache reuse across multiple generation calls. 9.2 Why agents benefit Agents frequently repeat structured prompt components. A tool-using agent might repeatedly include: System instructions. Tool schemas. Planning templates. Previous execution results. Shared context. The more overlap between requests, the more opportunity exists for cache reuse. However, reuse is not guaranteed simply because two requests come from the same application. The token prefixes must match under the runtime’s cache semantics. Changes in tokenization, formatting, tool schemas, and prompt construction can reduce cache hits. Cache capacity, eviction, and request routing also matter. 9.3 RadixAttention versus PagedAttention It is important to understand that these technologies address related but different aspects of serving. 1. Main Idea PagedAttention: Block-based KV cache memory management. RadixAttention: Prefix-aware KV cache reuse. 2. Core Benefit PagedAttention: Efficient memory allocation and reduced fragmentation. RadixAttention: Avoiding repeated computation of shared prefixes. 3. Mental Model PagedAttention: Virtual memory pages. RadixAttention: Shared-prefix tree. 4. Particularly Useful For PagedAttention: General concurrent LLM serving. RadixAttention: Repeated and structured LLM calls. 5. Key Consideration PagedAttention: Block allocation and cache capacity. RadixAttention: Prefix locality and cache residency. They should not be treated as mutually exclusive concepts. Both engines have broader memory-management and caching implementations that evolve over time. 9.4 The SGLang architecture SGLang combines a programming interface for structured LLM applications with a high-performance runtime. Its original research introduced: A structured generation language. RadixAttention. Efficient execution of multiple generation calls. Structured output decoding using compressed finite-state machines. The NeurIPS 2024 paper reported improvements of up to 6.4× on its evaluated workloads compared with the systems used in those experiments. That result is especially interesting because the evaluated workloads included agent control, reasoning, JSON generation, and retrieval-augmented generation. Again, it is a paper-specific result, not a promise that every application will experience that speedup. Source: https://note.com/humble_bobcat51/n/n79aec7cef370?utm_source=chatgpt.com 10. vLLM versus SGLang: Which inference engine should you choose? Both are serious inference-serving systems. Both support high-performance serving, continuous batching, KV-cache management, and advanced execution optimizations. The choice should not be made based on a single benchmark chart. It should be made based on the workload. 10.1 vLLM vLLM is an excellent general-purpose choice for high-throughput LLM serving. Its ecosystem includes: PagedAttention-based memory management. Continuous batching. Automatic Prefix Caching. Chunked prefill. Quantization support. Tensor, pipeline, data, and expert parallelism options. Speculative decoding. OpenAI-compatible serving APIs. Monitoring and deployment integrations. A typical starting point: pip install vllm vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 8000 \ --dtype auto \ --max-model-len 8192 The exact flags and supported configurations depend on the installed vLLM version and hardware. You can then interact with the OpenAI-compatible endpoint. from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY" ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B", messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": "Explain continuous batching." } ], max_tokens=256 ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) 10.2 SGLang SGLang is particularly interesting when your application consists of structured, repeated, multi-step LLM interactions. Its strengths include: RadixAttention. Prefix-aware KV-cache reuse. Structured generation. Efficient constrained decoding. Continuous batching. Multi-model and multimodal serving capabilities. Optimizations for complex LLM programs. A basic server launch looks like: pip install "sglang[all]" python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --host 0.0.0.0 \ --port 30000 As with vLLM, consult the current version’s documentation for hardware-specific options and supported features. 10.3 The practical comparison Source: https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D5610AQFCLcRB6SF7BA/image-shrink_800/B56aEkUXwnG0Ak-/0/1791610683055?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=6Mlj-2p1DJxtIieDLGGGs32ZFPLqqE-cYOSI6uWLQS8 1. General-Purpose Serving vLLM: Strong choice. SGLang: Strong choice. 2. KV-Cache Management vLLM: PagedAttention-based design. SGLang: RadixAttention-based reuse. 3. Prefix Reuse vLLM: Automatic Prefix Caching. SGLang: RadixAttention. 4. Structured Generation vLLM: Supported. SGLang: A major design focus. 5. Agentic Workloads vLLM: Strong. SGLang: Particularly interesting. 6. OpenAI-Compatible APIs vLLM: Yes. SGLang: Yes. 7. Distributed Serving vLLM: Yes. SGLang: Yes. 8. Production Monitoring vLLM: Supported. SGLang: Supported. My recommendation: Start with vLLM when you need a broadly applicable serving engine and a straightforward deployment path. Evaluate SGLang early when your application repeatedly invokes the model with overlapping prefixes, uses structured generation extensively, or executes complex multi-step LLM programs. But do not select either engine based on theoretical superiority. Benchmark both with the same model, hardware, request distribution, concurrency, prompt lengths, output lengths, and latency targets. The winning inference engine is the one that delivers the best quality-adjusted goodput at your required service level and cost. 11. Understanding latency: The user does not experience your tokens per second An inference server can generate thousands of tokens per second across all users and still deliver a terrible user experience. Why? Because aggregate throughput and individual request latency measure different things. Let’s define the important metrics. 11.1 Time to First Token (TTFT) TTFT measures how long a user waits before receiving the first generated token. Time to First Token (TTFT): The total time from request arrival until the first generated token is delivered, including queueing, prompt processing (prefill), and system overhead. Depending on the measurement boundary, overhead may include tokenization, networking, and request handling. TTFT matters enormously in interactive applications. A user waiting two seconds for the first response experiences something very different from a user waiting 200 milliseconds. 11.2 Time Per Output Token (TPOT) TPOT measures the average time required to generate each output token after the first token. Time Per Output Token (TPOT): The average time required to generate each subsequent output token after the first token, excluding the initial time-to-first-token. For a simplified example, suppose a request produces 100 tokens after its first token and takes 5 seconds to generate them. That is 50 milliseconds per token. 11.3 Inter-Token Latency (ITL) ITL measures the time between consecutive output tokens. Unlike an average TPOT, ITL can expose irregular pauses and spikes during streaming. A system might have a reasonable average but still occasionally pause for several hundred milliseconds. Those pauses are important for interactive user experience. 11.4 End-to-end latency A simplified approximation is: End-to-End Latency: The approximate total response time, calculated as the time to first token plus the time required to generate the remaining output tokens. Actual measurement must account for the exact definition of TTFT, streaming behavior, networking, and completion boundaries. 11.5 Throughput Two common throughput measurements are: Request throughput Requests Per Second (RPS): The number of successfully completed inference requests per second, measuring the request-processing throughput of an LLM serving system. Token throughput Tokens Per Second (TPS): The number of tokens generated per second, measuring the token-generation throughput of an LLM inference system. Always clarify whether TPS means output tokens per second, input tokens per second, or combined token throughput. These are not interchangeable. 11.6 Goodput This is where production engineering becomes more interesting. Imagine a server processes 1,000 requests. But 300 violate the latency requirements. Should we call the system successful because it completed 1,000 requests? Not necessarily. Goodput measures useful completed work that satisfies the application’s service-level requirements. A simplified definition is: Goodput: The rate of successfully completed requests that meet predefined Service Level Objectives (SLOs), measuring useful throughput rather than raw request throughput. You can also define token-based goodput for applications where generated tokens are the relevant unit of successful work. This is why maximizing raw throughput is not always the right objective. Source: https://www.bentoml.com/blog/the-shift-to-distributed-llm-inference 11.7 Percentiles matter Never rely exclusively on average latency. Measure: p50: Median experience. p90: Experience of the slower 10%. p95: Experience of the slower 5%. p99: Experience of the slower 1%. For production applications, p95 and p99 are particularly important. A system with 500 ms average TTFT and 8-second p99 TTFT may be unacceptable for an interactive application. 12. The inference performance triangle Inference optimization involves three competing objectives: Latency. Throughput. Cost. Increasing batch size often improves aggregate throughput because model weights and other data can be reused across more active sequences. But larger batches can also increase: Queueing delay. Scheduling complexity. KV-cache pressure. Memory requirements. Tail latency. Similarly, reducing precision can reduce memory requirements and increase performance, but it may affect model quality. Increasing the context length improves application flexibility, but increases cache requirements and prefill computation. There is no universal configuration that simultaneously maximizes all three objectives. The engineering task is to find the operating point that satisfies the application’s SLOs at an acceptable cost. 13. Continuous batching is only the beginning: Chunked prefill We previously saw that prefill and decode behave differently. Now imagine a system with several active users generating responses. Suddenly, a new request arrives with a 30,000-token prompt. The GPU begins processing that long prompt. While it is doing so, active decode requests may experience delays. This is called prefill-decode interference. The system must balance two competing needs: Process new prompts efficiently. Keep existing users generating tokens smoothly. 13.1 Chunked prefill Instead of processing an entire long prompt in one large operation, the engine divides it into smaller chunks. For example: Original prompt: 12,000 tokens Chunk 1: 2,048 tokens Chunk 2: 2,048 tokens Chunk 3: 2,048 tokens Chunk 4: 2,048 tokens Chunk 5: 2,048 tokens Chunk 6: 1,760 tokens The scheduler can interleave these chunks with ongoing decode work. Conceptually: Iteration 1: Decode A + Decode B + Prefill chunk 1 Iteration 2: Decode A + Decode B + Prefill chunk 2 Iteration 3: Decode A + Decode C + Prefill chunk 3 Iteration 4: Decode B + Decode C + Prefill chunk 4 This reduces the risk that one long prompt monopolizes execution. The SARATHI research line is particularly relevant here. It explores chunked prefills and decode-maximal batching to improve the throughput-latency trade-off. 13.2 When chunked prefill helps Mixed workloads with short and long prompts. Interactive applications. Long-context document processing. Concurrent chat and retrieval workloads. Systems where decode latency must remain stable. 13.3 The trade-off Chunking introduces scheduling decisions and potentially additional overhead. A chunk size that works for one model and GPU may not work for another. The correct value must be benchmarked against the actual prompt-length distribution and latency objectives. 14. Disaggregated serving: Separate prefill and decode when their needs diverge What if prefill and decode require different hardware allocation strategies? Prefill is generally more compute-intensive. Decode is often more memory-bandwidth-sensitive. If both phases share the same GPU pool, they compete for resources. Disaggregated serving addresses this by separating the two phases into distinct resource pools. 14.1 The architecture Incoming requests | API Gateway | Router / Scheduler | +--------+--------+ | | PREFILL POOL DECODE POOL | | Prompt processing Token generation | | KV-cache creation ----> KV-cache transfer | Streaming response The prefill pool processes the prompt and produces the required KV state. That state is transferred to the decode pool, where generation continues. 14.2 Why it helps You can allocate resources independently. For example: More compute capacity for prefill. More memory bandwidth or KV capacity for decode. Different tensor-parallel configurations. Different scaling policies. Better isolation between long prompts and active generation. DistServe is an important research contribution in this area. Its OSDI 2024 paper explored how separating prefill and decode can improve goodput under latency constraints. 14.3 Why you should not automatically disaggregate There is a price. You now need to move KV state between resource pools. This introduces: Network communication. Transfer latency. Additional infrastructure. Coordination between pools. More complex scheduling. Failure-handling requirements. If the workload is small or the network is insufficient, disaggregation may make performance worse. Start with a well-tuned colocated serving architecture. Disaggregate when measured evidence shows that phase interference or resource imbalance justifies the additional complexity. Source: https://www.infoq.cn/article/QJAPI0RrIrKCY2fN3KTL 15. Quantization: More than fitting a model onto a smaller GPU Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent model weights or other tensors. It is one of the most important techniques for inference optimization. Consider a 32B model. At BF16: A 32-billion-parameter model stored in BF16 requires approximately 64 GB of memory for its weights alone. At an idealized 4-bit representation: A 32-billion-parameter model stored in INT4 requires approximately 16 GB of memory for its weights alone. This is a substantial reduction. But quantization is not free. 15.1 Weight quantization Common options include: FP8 INT8 INT4 AWQ GPTQ FP8 or other low-precision checkpoint formats supported by the relevant engine Each format has different calibration, kernel, hardware, and quality characteristics. 15.2 KV-cache quantization Weights are not the only tensors that can be compressed. KV caches can also be stored at lower precision in supported configurations. This can increase effective context capacity or concurrent sequence capacity. However, the accuracy and latency trade-offs depend on the model and cache implementation. 15.3 A useful way to think about quantization OptimizationPrimary targetWeight quantizationModel weight memoryKV-cache quantizationPer-token cache memoryActivation quantizationIntermediate tensor representationQuantized kernelsEfficient low-precision execution A common mistake is to assume that reducing weight precision automatically doubles serving capacity. Not necessarily. If KV cache is the limiting resource, weight quantization may free some capacity but the ultimate concurrency limit may still be determined by cache requirements or runtime constraints. 15.4 The correct validation strategy For every quantized model, measure: Weight memory. KV-cache capacity. TTFT. TPOT. Output quality. Structured-output reliability. Task-specific accuracy. Throughput at the target latency. An INT4 model that runs faster but fails important financial calculations or structured extraction tasks is not a successful optimization. 16. Speculative decoding: Let a smaller model help a larger model Autoregressive generation has an inherent sequential dependency. Can we generate multiple candidate tokens before invoking the main model? Speculative decoding attempts to do exactly that. A smaller draft model proposes several tokens. The larger target model verifies the proposed tokens in a more parallel fashion. Compatible tokens are accepted, while rejected portions are corrected through the target model’s decoding process. Conceptually: Input prompt | Draft model | Candidate tokens T1 T2 T3 T4 | Target model | Verification | Accept compatible tokens | Continue generation 16.1 Why it works The draft model is cheaper to execute. If it predicts several tokens that the target model accepts, the system can generate multiple output tokens with fewer expensive target-model iterations. Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/blog/posts/from-research-to-production-accelerate-oss-llm-with-eagle-3-on-vertex 16.2 The important caveat Speculative decoding does not guarantee a speedup. Performance depends on: Draft-model quality. Acceptance rate. Draft-model overhead. Target-model architecture. Batch size. Memory bandwidth. Verification implementation. It is particularly attractive for workloads where the target model’s autoregressive generation is a significant bottleneck. It is less attractive when the draft model introduces more overhead than the accepted tokens justify. 17. Parallelism: When one GPU is no longer enough Eventually, model weights or serving requirements exceed the practical capacity of a single accelerator. Now we need distributed inference. There are several forms of parallelism. 17.1 Data parallelism (DP) Multiple replicas of the model process independent requests. Load Balancer | +-----------+-----------+ | | | Replica 1 Replica 2 Replica 3 | | | GPU(s) GPU(s) GPU(s) Data parallelism increases serving capacity by distributing requests across replicas. It is particularly useful when a model fits within the memory of an individual replica. 17.2 Tensor parallelism (TP) Tensor parallelism splits portions of model operations across GPUs. For example, different GPUs hold portions of a large weight matrix. They collaborate during computation. Benefits: Reduces per-GPU weight memory. Enables larger models. Can increase effective compute capacity. Trade-offs: Collective communication. Synchronization overhead. Dependence on interconnect bandwidth. More complex deployment. Tensor parallelism is particularly sensitive to GPU interconnect topology. NVLink-connected GPUs can behave very differently from GPUs communicating through a slower interconnect. 17.3 Pipeline parallelism (PP) Pipeline parallelism distributes different transformer layers across GPUs. GPU 1: Layers 1–20 | GPU 2: Layers 21–40 | GPU 3: Layers 41–60 | GPU 4: Layers 61–80 This reduces the model memory required on each GPU. However, pipeline execution introduces scheduling and pipeline-bubble considerations. 17.4 Expert parallelism (EP) For Mixture-of-Experts models, different expert networks can be distributed across devices. Tokens are routed to selected experts. This introduces additional communication and load-balancing requirements. 17.5 Choosing the right strategy StrategyMain objectiveImportant considerationDPMore independent replicasReplication costTPSplit model operationsCommunicationPPSplit transformer layersPipeline utilizationEPDistribute expertsRouting and all-to-all communication These strategies can be combined. The correct configuration depends on model architecture, hardware topology, memory requirements, and workload. A distributed model is not automatically a faster model. It is a model that can use distributed resources effectively. Capacity planning: How many GPUs do you actually need? Let’s now move from individual inference requests to infrastructure planning. Suppose a product has 10,000 registered users. Does it need 10,000 simultaneous inference slots? No. Registered users, active users, concurrent requests, and active decoding sequences are different quantities. Capacity planning must begin with the actual traffic profile. 18.1 Start with traffic assumptions Consider this illustrative application: Registered users: 10,000. Peak active users: 1,000. Concurrent inference requests: 200. Average input length: 2,000 tokens. Average output length: 500 tokens. Average request duration: 10 seconds. These are assumptions for the example, not benchmark measurements. 18.2 Calculate request throughput Using Little’s Law: Little’s Law: The average number of requests in a system equals the request arrival rate multiplied by the average time spent in the system. Where: L is the average number of requests in the system. lambda is the arrival rate. W is the average time spent in the system. If the average number of concurrent requests is 200 and the average request duration is 10 seconds: Request Arrival Rate: An average of 20 requests arrive per second when 200 requests are received over a 10-second interval. 18.3 Calculate token demand Average input tokens per second: Input Token Throughput: At an arrival rate of 20 requests per second and an average input length of 2,000 tokens per request, the system must process 40,000 input tokens per second. Average output tokens per second: Output Token Throughput: At an arrival rate of 20 requests per second and an average output length of 500 tokens per request, the system must generate 10,000 output tokens per second. Total token processing demand: Total Token Throughput: The system must process 50,000 tokens per second, comprising 40,000 input tokens and 10,000 output tokens. The system needs to process approximately 40,000 input tokens and generate 10,000 output tokens per second under these assumptions. Do not treat the combined 50,000 figure as equivalent to 50,000 generated tokens per second. Prefill and decode have different computational profiles. 18.4 Why this matters Suppose a benchmark reports that one GPU sustains: 8,000 input tokens per second. 2,500 output tokens per second. These are hypothetical values for demonstrating the calculation. The output requirement alone implies: GPU Capacity Estimation: A requirement of 10,000 output tokens per second, with each GPU delivering 2,500 tokens per second, necessitates approximately 4 GPUs. The input requirement implies: Prefill Capacity Estimation: A requirement of 40,000 input tokens per second, with each GPU processing 8,000 input tokens per second, necessitates approximately 5 GPUs. A simplistic estimate would therefore require at least five GPU-equivalents. But real deployment needs additional capacity for: Latency constraints. Request variability. KV-cache capacity. Queueing. Failures. Deployment overhead. Traffic bursts. Redundancy. A more realistic planning equation is: GPU Provisioning Formula: The required GPU count is determined by peak demand, sustainable per-GPU capacity, target utilization, and additional redundancy to maintain availability and handle failures. Here, U_target represents the intended operating margin, not simply GPU utilization. The exact calculation should be performed separately for prefill, decode, memory capacity, and latency constraints. 18.5 The biggest capacity-planning mistake Do not size infrastructure using average traffic alone. If peak traffic is five times average traffic, infrastructure sized only for average demand will either violate SLOs or require aggressive admission control during spikes. Use: Average demand. Peak demand. Burst duration. Request arrival distribution. Input/output token distributions. Concurrent sequence counts. Maximum context requirements. And benchmark realistic traffic, not just synthetic requests with identical lengths. 19. Cost engineering: How much does one million tokens really cost? Now we arrive at the question every production AI team eventually asks. How much does inference cost? The answer is not simply the price of a GPU. It is the cost of operating that GPU relative to the amount of useful work it delivers. 19.1 Cost per million output tokens Let: C_h = hourly cost of one GPU. T = sustainable output tokens per second. Then: Cost per Million Tokens: The estimated inference cost of processing one million tokens, calculated from the hourly GPU cost and token throughput per second. Suppose: GPU cost = $3 per hour. Sustainable output throughput = 2,000 tokens per second. Then: Inference Cost Calculation: At an hourly GPU cost of $3 and a throughput of 2,000 tokens per second, the estimated cost is approximately $0.417 per million tokens. This is an illustrative GPU-only cost estimate. It excludes: CPU and RAM. Storage. Networking. Platform overhead. Idle capacity. Replication. Monitoring. Engineering and operational costs. 19.2 What if the GPU is only 40% utilized? Suppose the effective useful throughput falls to 800 tokens per second. Inference Cost Calculation: At an hourly GPU cost of $3 and a throughput of 800 tokens per second, the estimated cost is approximately $1.042 per million tokens. The same GPU now costs approximately 2.5 times as much per million generated tokens. This is why utilization and scheduling matter. 19.3 Input and output costs should be separated Prefill and decode have different performance characteristics. Therefore, a better cost model is: Total Inference Cost: The combined cost of prompt processing (prefill), output generation (decode), and supporting infrastructure. For example: Phase-Wise Inference Cost: Prefill and decode costs are estimated separately based on their respective token counts, processing times, and GPU-second pricing. These are simplified allocation models. If prefill and decode share the same GPU pool, allocate cost using measured resource consumption or a defensible accounting policy rather than counting the same GPU time twice. 19.4 Monthly infrastructure cost A basic estimate: Monthly GPU Infrastructure Cost: The estimated monthly compute expenditure, calculated using the number of provisioned GPUs, hourly cost per GPU, and an assumed 730 operating hours per month. For five GPUs at $3 per hour: Monthly Infrastructure Cost: Provisioning 5 GPUs at $3 per GPU-hour for 730 hours results in an estimated monthly cost of $10,950. This is the approximate monthly accelerator rental cost under continuous operation. The real bill will depend on instance type, commitment discounts, utilization, regional pricing, and infrastructure overhead. 19.5 The cost optimization hierarchy My recommended order: Remove redundant model calls. Reduce unnecessary prompt tokens. Introduce prefix caching. Use efficient batching. Optimize KV-cache utilization. Benchmark quantization. Improve decode throughput. Improve GPU utilization. Evaluate speculative decoding. Reconsider model size and hardware placement. The cheapest token is often the token you never had to compute. 20. Agentic inference: The problem changes when the model becomes a worker Traditional chat applications generally involve one request and one response. Agentic systems are different. An agent may: Receive a task. Generate a plan. Call a search tool. Read the result. Generate another plan. Call an API. Inspect the response. Retry an operation. Generate a final answer. A single user request can therefore trigger multiple inference requests. 20.1 The agentic amplification factor Define: Agentic Amplification Factor: The average number of LLM calls triggered per user request, indicating how much additional inference activity agentic workflows introduce. If 100 users each trigger an average of 6 model calls: Agentic Workload Expansion: 100 user requests, with an average of 6 LLM calls per request, generate 600 total LLM calls. But call count alone is insufficient. Some calls may contain large conversation histories, tool schemas, or retrieved documents. A more useful token-demand model is: Agentic Token Demand: The expected total token-processing demand per second, calculated by multiplying the user request arrival rate by the expected cumulative input and output tokens consumed across all LLM calls within each request. Where: lambda_user is the user request arrival rate. N is the number of LLM calls per task. Each call has its own input and output token demand. 20.2 Why SGLang becomes interesting Agentic workloads often repeat prompt structures. The system prompt, instructions, tool descriptions, and parts of the conversation may remain unchanged across calls. RadixAttention’s prefix-reuse capabilities can reduce repeated computation when the workload has reusable token prefixes. vLLM’s Automatic Prefix Caching can also help with suitable repeated-prefix workloads. 20.3 The bigger architecture A production agent platform should not simply send every operation to one shared LLM endpoint. Consider routing requests according to task characteristics. User Request | Agent Runtime | Task Classification | +----------+----------+ | | | Simple Reasoning Complex Tasks Tasks Agents | | | Small Larger Specialized Model Model Model | | | +----------+----------+ | Tool Execution | Result Evaluation | Final Generation This introduces model routing, workload isolation, and specialized serving pools. 20.4 Agentic systems require more than GPU optimization Other important engineering concerns include: Maximum tool-call budgets. Request deadlines. Cancellation propagation. Idempotency. Retry limits. Tool execution timeouts. Context compaction. Prompt growth control. Per-tenant quotas. Distributed tracing. Model fallback. Circuit breakers. An agent that loops indefinitely is not merely an application bug. It can become a runaway inference-cost problem. In the agentic era, inference engineering and agent orchestration are increasingly inseparable. Source: https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/article/introduction-to-mcp-understanding-how-clients-servers-and-llms-work-together 21. Benchmarking: Stop trusting single-number performance claims A benchmark that says “ Model X generates 5,000 tokens per second ” is almost meaningless without additional information. You need to know: Which GPU? Which model? Which precision? Which inference engine? What was the input length? What was the output length? What was the concurrency? Was prefix caching enabled? Was speculative decoding enabled? Was the measurement aggregate or per user? What latency did the system achieve? A benchmark without workload information is not a capacity-planning result. 21.1 Build a realistic workload matrix 1. Short Chat Input length: 256 tokens Output length: 128 tokens Concurrency: 16 2. Medium Chat Input length: 1,024 tokens Output length: 512 tokens Concurrency: 32 3. Document Analysis Input length: 8,192 tokens Output length: 1,024 tokens Concurrency: 16 4. Long Context Input length: 32,768 tokens Output length: 2,048 tokens Concurrency: 8 5. Agentic Workload Input length: Variable Output length: Variable Concurrency: 32 These are example test scenarios, not recommended universal values. 21.2 Benchmark metrics Capture: TTFT p50/p95/p99. TPOT p50/p95/p99. ITL distribution. End-to-end latency. Input tokens per second. Output tokens per second. Requests per second. KV-cache utilization. GPU memory utilization. GPU compute utilization. Queue length. Preemption count. Cache hit rate. Error and timeout rates. 21.3 Benchmarking vLLM vLLM provides serving benchmarks through its benchmarking tooling. A representative command pattern is: vllm bench serve \ --backend openai \ --base-url http://localhost:8000 \ --endpoint /v1/completions \ --model YOUR_MODEL \ --dataset-name random \ --num-prompts 1000 \ --request-rate 10 The exact flags vary across releases. Check the installed version’s help output and use the appropriate chat or completion workload. 21.4 Benchmarking SGLang SGLang provides benchmarking utilities for serving workloads. A typical approach is to use its serving benchmark tooling against the deployed endpoint, varying: Request rate. Concurrency. Input length. Output length. Dataset. Streaming mode. Use the same request corpus for both engines. 21.5 Open-loop versus closed-loop testing This distinction is important. In closed-loop testing, clients send a new request after the previous request completes. As the server slows down, the arrival rate naturally falls. This can hide overload. In open-loop testing, requests arrive at a specified rate regardless of previous completion. This better exposes queue buildup and overload behavior. A robust evaluation should include both types of testing. 21.6 A disciplined benchmark protocol Fix the model checkpoint. Fix the hardware. Fix the numerical precision. Fix the engine version. Warm up the system. Use identical input/output distributions. Run several concurrency levels. Record latency percentiles. Monitor GPU and KV-cache utilization. Repeat the test. Compare quality and cost. Publish the configuration alongside the results. Do not report the highest observed throughput while ignoring latency violations. The useful number is the sustainable throughput at the required SLO. 22. Production architecture: From a model server to an inference platform A model server is not a production platform. A production platform must handle traffic, authentication, model routing, resource allocation, monitoring, deployment, failure recovery, and cost controls. Here is a reference architecture. CLIENT APPLICATIONS | API GATEWAY | Authentication / Rate Limits | INFERENCE GATEWAY | Routing / Load Balancing | Request Classification | +--------------+--------------+ | | | MODEL A MODEL B MODEL C | | | vLLM SGLang vLLM | | | GPU POOL GPU POOL GPU POOL | | | +--------------+--------------+ | OBSERVABILITY | Metrics / Logs / Traces / Costs | AUTOSCALING | GPU INFRASTRUCTURE Let’s examine the components. 22.1 API gateway Responsibilities: Authentication. Authorization. Rate limiting. Request validation. Tenant identification. Request-size limits. API versioning. Never expose unrestricted model-serving endpoints to the public internet. 22.2 Inference gateway The inference gateway is more specialized. It understands model-serving characteristics. It can route requests based on: Model identifier. Available replicas. Queue length. Prefix-cache locality. Input length. Workload class. Latency objectives. Tenant priority. A prefix-aware routing strategy can improve cache reuse by sending requests to replicas that already retain relevant prefixes. However, routing to a cache-hot replica must be balanced against queue pressure and availability. 22.3 Model-serving layer Each model replica should have an explicit resource and performance profile. For example: Model: Qwen 8B Precision: BF16 Engine: vLLM GPU: H100 Max context: Configured limit KV cache: GPU resident Parallelism: TP=1 API: OpenAI compatible The configuration must be validated against the hardware and model architecture. 22.4 Containerization Package the inference runtime into a reproducible container. Pin: Engine version. CUDA runtime. PyTorch version. Model revision. Python dependencies. Quantization configuration. Startup parameters. This reduces deployment drift. 22.5 Kubernetes orchestration Kubernetes can manage: Model-serving pods. GPU resource allocation. Service discovery. Rolling deployments. Health checks. Replication. Autoscaling. Failure recovery. However, GPU autoscaling is not equivalent to ordinary CPU autoscaling. Model loading can take time. GPU availability may be constrained. A new replica may need to download large model weights and warm up before serving traffic. Therefore, scaling decisions should consider both current demand and startup delay. 22.6 Autoscaling Useful signals include: Pending request count. Queue waiting time. Active sequences. KV-cache utilization. Input-token rate. Output-token rate. TTFT violations. GPU memory pressure. CPU utilization alone is generally insufficient. Queue-based scaling is particularly useful because queue growth directly indicates that demand is exceeding currently available service capacity. Google Cloud’s GKE inference guidance discusses queue-size and batch-size signals for GPU inference autoscaling. 22.7 Rolling deployments A model deployment should not simply terminate the old server and start the new one. A safer pattern: Launch new replicas. Load the model. Run health checks. Warm up kernels and execution paths. Run smoke tests. Add the replicas to routing. Gradually shift traffic. Drain existing requests from old replicas. Retire the old deployment. This reduces the risk of user-facing outages. Source: https://woonyee.org/projects/ml-inference-sys-review 23. Observability: If you cannot see the bottleneck, you cannot optimize it A production inference platform needs visibility into both application behavior and GPU execution. Source: https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/large-language-models/1.2.0/observability.html I recommend four observability layers. Layer 1: Request metrics Requests per second. Successful requests. Failed requests. Timeouts. Request queue duration. End-to-end latency. Token counts. Layer 2: Inference metrics TTFT. TPOT. ITL. Prefill throughput. Decode throughput. Active sequences. KV-cache utilization. Prefix-cache hit rate. Preemption count. Layer 3: Infrastructure metrics GPU utilization. GPU memory utilization. GPU power. Memory bandwidth, where measurable. CPU utilization. Host memory. Network throughput. Inter-GPU communication. Layer 4: Business metrics Cost per successful request. Cost per million input tokens. Cost per million output tokens. Cost per completed agent task. Requests per tenant. Model quality. SLO compliance. 23.1 Prometheus and Grafana A common architecture uses: Prometheus for metrics collection. Grafana for dashboards. OpenTelemetry for traces. Centralized log aggregation. vLLM exposes production metrics through its metrics endpoint. SGLang also supports Prometheus-oriented metrics. Useful dashboards should make it possible to answer questions such as: Is TTFT increasing because of queueing or prefill? Is decode throughput falling because of memory pressure? Is the KV cache approaching capacity? Are requests being preempted? Are prefix-cache hit rates deteriorating? Is one replica receiving disproportionately more traffic? Is GPU utilization high while useful token throughput remains low? A good dashboard should help an engineer move from symptom to cause. 23.2 Distributed tracing For agentic applications, tracing is essential. One user request might trigger: User request | +-- Agent planning call | +-- Search tool | +-- Summarization call | +-- Database query | +-- Verification call | +-- Final generation Without distributed traces, you may see a 30-second response but have no idea which stage consumed the time. Trace every stage with a shared request or task identifier. 24. Production reliability: The engineering that benchmarks do not reveal A benchmark usually assumes a relatively controlled environment. Production does not. Real traffic contains: Unexpectedly long prompts. Malformed requests. Client disconnections. Bursty traffic. Slow tool calls. GPU failures. Model loading delays. Memory exhaustion. Network interruptions. Repeated retries. Your inference platform must handle these conditions. 24.1 Admission control Not every request should be accepted immediately. The server should reject, defer, or degrade requests when accepting them would violate the SLOs of already-running workloads. Admission decisions can consider: Estimated prompt length. Maximum output tokens. Available KV capacity. Queue depth. Tenant quotas. Request deadline. 24.2 Backpressure If downstream model capacity is saturated, upstream components must receive that information. Otherwise, queues grow without limit. Use bounded queues, explicit timeouts, and appropriate overload responses. 24.3 Cancellation When a client disconnects or cancels a request, the serving system should stop unnecessary generation and release resources. This is especially important when agents abandon tasks or execute retries. 24.4 Retries Retries can improve resilience but can also amplify overload. Use: Bounded retries. Exponential backoff. Jitter. Idempotency where relevant. Retry budgets. Do not blindly retry requests that have already consumed substantial GPU resources. 24.5 Multi-tenancy In a shared inference platform, different tenants may have different requirements. Consider: Request quotas. Token quotas. Priority classes. Per-tenant concurrency. Model access policies. Cost attribution. Isolation of sensitive workloads. A platform serving several enterprise customers must not allow one tenant’s traffic spike to degrade everyone else’s experience. 25. Advanced optimization: Where serious inference engineering begins Once the basic serving platform is stable, there are additional optimization opportunities. 25.1 Prefix-aware routing Route requests to replicas with reusable KV prefixes when the benefit outweighs the additional queueing or load imbalance. 25.2 KV-cache offloading Move selected cache data from GPU memory to host memory or other supported storage tiers. This can increase effective cache capacity, but introduces transfer and retrieval latency. 25.3 Cache eviction policies Cache capacity is finite. The serving system needs to decide which entries to retain and which to evict. Good policies depend on: Reuse probability. Prefix popularity. Recency. Memory pressure. Request locality. Expected future demand. 25.4 Kernel optimization Attention and matrix-multiplication kernels have a substantial influence on inference speed. Technologies such as FlashAttention and FlashInfer improve aspects of attention execution and memory access. Kernel selection must match the model architecture, GPU generation, tensor shape, and numerical format. 25.5 CUDA graphs CUDA graphs can reduce CPU launch overhead by capturing and replaying sequences of GPU operations. This is useful when execution patterns are sufficiently compatible with graph capture. However, graph capture introduces constraints around shapes, memory allocation, and execution behavior. 25.6 Continuous profiling Use GPU profilers and runtime instrumentation to identify: Kernel launch overhead. Poor occupancy. Memory stalls. Communication overhead. Kernel inefficiency. Synchronization bottlenecks. Never assume that an optimization helped simply because it sounds theoretically attractive. Measure it. 26. Putting everything together: A practical inference engineering playbook Let’s convert the concepts into a repeatable engineering process. The production inference journey. Imagine you are asked to serve an open-source 32B model for an enterprise application. You have been given a GPU budget and must support interactive traffic. How do you approach the problem? Phase 1: Understand the workload Collect: Peak requests per second. Average and peak concurrency. Input-token distribution. Output-token distribution. Context-length requirements. Agentic call amplification. Streaming requirements. Latency SLOs. Tenant distribution. Do not start with a GPU purchase. Start with demand. Phase 2: Understand the model Inspect: Parameter count. Number of transformer layers. Attention architecture. KV-head count. Head dimension. Context length. Precision. Quantization compatibility. Model-specific execution requirements. Calculate approximate weight and KV-cache memory. Phase 3: Select hardware Compare available accelerators based on: HBM capacity. Memory bandwidth. Compute capability. Interconnect. GPU availability. Hourly cost. Regional availability. Check whether the model fits within a single GPU or requires parallelism. Phase 4: Select the inference engine Deploy both vLLM and SGLang when practical. Use identical model revisions and hardware. Benchmark representative workloads. Evaluate cache reuse, structured generation, latency, throughput, and operational complexity. Phase 5: Tune the runtime Experiment systematically with: Maximum model length. Maximum active sequences. KV-cache capacity. Chunked prefill. Prefix caching. Quantization. Tensor parallelism. Speculative decoding. Change one major variable at a time. Phase 6: Build the platform Introduce: API gateway. Inference gateway. Authentication. Request routing. Bounded queues. Model-serving replicas. Kubernetes orchestration. Prometheus. Grafana. OpenTelemetry. Phase 7: Load test Test: Normal traffic. Peak traffic. Burst traffic. Long-context requests. Mixed prompt lengths. Long generations. Cache-hit and cache-miss scenarios. Agentic workflows. Phase 8: Optimize cost and goodput Calculate: Cost per million input tokens. Cost per million output tokens. Cost per successful request. Cost per completed agent task. SLO-compliant throughput. Keep optimizing until the system meets its quality, latency, reliability, and cost objectives. 27. A worked production design: Serving 10,000 users Let’s finish the engineering journey with a hypothetical deployment. Suppose an enterprise application has: Registered Users: 10,000 Peak Active Users: 1,000 Peak Concurrent LLM Requests: 200 Average Input Length: 2,000 tokens Average Output Length: 500 tokens Average Request Duration: 10 seconds Target TTFT (p95): 1.5 seconds Target TPOT (p95): 60 milliseconds These are design assumptions, not guarantees or measured performance. Step 1: Calculate demand Request throughput Input demand: Output demand: Peak Inference Demand Estimation: At 20 requests per second, with an average of 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens per request, the serving system must sustain 40,000 input tokens/sec and 10,000 output tokens/sec. Step 2: Estimate KV-cache pressure Assume an illustrative model with 128 KiB of KV cache per token. If the 200 active sequences each retain an average of 4,000 tokens: Estimated KV Cache Requirement: For 200 concurrent requests, each with 4,000 tokens, at 128 KiB per token, the total KV cache requirement is approximately 97.66 GiB. This is the aggregate logical KV-cache requirement before accounting for prefix sharing, cache implementation overhead, block allocation, and any distributed cache strategy. The actual memory required depends on how sequences are distributed across replicas and GPUs. Step 3: Choose an architecture A reasonable first design would be: Multiple model-serving replicas. vLLM as the initial general-purpose serving engine. SGLang evaluated against representative agentic traffic. A routing layer distributing requests. A queue-aware scaling policy. Prometheus and Grafana. OpenTelemetry tracing. Explicit per-tenant limits. Step 4: Validate GPU count Do not decide the GPU count from the 200 concurrent users alone. Benchmark each candidate GPU configuration. Measure: Sustainable prefill throughput. Sustainable decode throughput. KV-cache capacity. TTFT at the target concurrency. TPOT at the target concurrency. p95 and p99 latency. Failure and preemption behavior. Then calculate the GPU count independently for compute, memory, and latency constraints. Step 5: Introduce agent-aware routing If the application has several agent workflows, route: Short classification tasks to smaller models. General conversation to the standard model pool. Long-context reasoning to a specialized pool. Repeated structured agent calls to a cache-aware serving pool. Step 6: Establish an operating envelope Define the maximum sustainable request rate at which: TTFT remains within target. TPOT remains within target. KV-cache pressure remains manageable. Error rates remain acceptable. Cost remains within budget. This is the platform’s sustainable operating envelope. It is far more valuable than knowing that a GPU once achieved a particular peak token throughput. 28. The future of inference engineering Inference is evolving from a relatively simple model-execution problem into a sophisticated distributed-computing discipline. Several trends are particularly important. 28.1 Agentic inference Models are increasingly becoming components in larger systems that plan, execute, retrieve, verify, and interact with external tools. This increases the importance of scheduling, cache reuse, workload routing, and cost controls. 28.2 Disaggregated architectures Separating prefill, decode, and potentially other stages enables more specialized resource allocation. 28.3 More sophisticated KV-cache systems KV caches are becoming first-class infrastructure resources. Caching, offloading, compression, sharing, and eviction policies will increasingly influence platform economics. 28.4 Hardware-aware serving The best serving configuration will increasingly depend on hardware topology, memory bandwidth, numerical precision, and specialized execution kernels. 28.5 Multi-model inference platforms Production systems will not always use one large model for everything. They will route requests across specialized models based on task complexity, quality requirements, latency, and cost. 28.6 Quality-adjusted inference economics The objective will not simply be to generate more tokens. It will be to generate useful, correct outputs at the lowest sustainable cost while meeting latency and reliability requirements. That is a much more meaningful engineering objective. 29. Final thoughts: Inference is where AI meets systems engineering We began with a simple user request. We followed it through tokenization, prefill, decode, attention, KV-cache allocation, GPU memory, and scheduling. We then explored how PagedAttention and RadixAttention address different aspects of the memory problem. We examined continuous batching, chunked prefill, disaggregated serving, quantization, speculative decoding, and distributed parallelism. Finally, we moved beyond the inference engine itself and designed a production platform involving gateways, routing, Kubernetes, autoscaling, observability, reliability, and cost controls. There is one idea I want you to take away from this entire journey: The objective of inference engineering is not to make a model generate tokens as quickly as possible. It is to maximize useful, quality-preserving, SLO-compliant work per unit of compute and cost. That distinction separates someone who can deploy a model from someone who can architect an inference platform. A fast model is useful. A memory-efficient model is better. A well-scheduled model is better still. But a system that can serve thousands of users predictably, economically, and reliably, while supporting complex agentic workflows, is where real inference engineering begins. And that is the engineering challenge worth mastering. 30. Your inference engineering learning roadmap If you have reached this point, here is the sequence I recommend for turning the concepts into practical expertise. LLM Inference and Serving: 11 Stages to Master Transformer Inference, Prefill and Decode — Understand how tokens are processed and generated. GPU Architecture and Memory — Estimate compute, memory, and bandwidth requirements. KV Cache and Attention Architectures — Calculate memory consumption and concurrency limits. PagedAttention and RadixAttention — Understand KV-cache memory efficiency and prefix reuse. vLLM and SGLang — Deploy, configure, and compare inference engines. Benchmarking and SLOs — Quantify throughput, latency, and serving performance. Quantization and Speculative Decoding — Optimize inference speed, memory consumption, and execution efficiency. Tensor, Pipeline and Data Parallelism — Serve larger models across multiple GPUs and nodes. Kubernetes and Inference Gateways — Build and orchestrate distributed inference platforms. Observability and Cost Engineering — Monitor production infrastructure, reliability, utilization, and inference costs. Agentic Inference — Optimize multi-step AI workloads, tool calls, and cumulative token consumption. A useful exercise is to take one open-source model and serve it through both vLLM and SGLang. Keep the hardware, model revision, precision, and request distribution identical. Then measure: TTFT. TPOT. Throughput. KV-cache utilization. GPU memory. Cost per million generated tokens. Repeat with a shared-prefix workload and a long-context workload. You will learn more from a disciplined comparison like this than from memorizing dozens of inference-engine configuration flags.
