Inside the engine room of modern AI: GPU memory, KV caches, PagedAttention, RadixAttention, vLLM, SGLang, latency, throughput, cost engineering, and production-scale agentic AI.Source: https://www.foto.online/collections/zubehoer

The first request is easy. The 1000th is the engineering problem.

There is a moment in almost every AI engineer’s journey when building a language model stops being the difficult part.

You have trained a model. You have fine-tuned one. Perhaps you have even built an agent that calls tools, retrieves documents, reasons through a task, and generates structured responses.

You put it behind an API.

The first request works beautifully.

The tenth request works too.

Then a hundred users arrive. Some send short questions. Others paste entire documents. Some ask for lengthy reports. A few trigger agents that make multiple LLM calls, execute tools, and return after several reasoning steps.

Suddenly, the system that looked perfectly healthy during development begins behaving very differently.

Responses become slower. GPU memory fills up. Requests queue. Throughput stops increasing despite adding concurrency. Some users experience unacceptable delays while others receive responses quickly.

You add another GPU. Things improve, but not as much as expected.

You increase the batch size. Throughput improves, but latency deteriorates.

You reduce the context length. Memory improves, but the application becomes less capable.

Eventually, you encounter a realization that fundamentally changes how you think about deploying AI:

Serving an LLM is not simply running a forward pass. It is a:

  1. Resource-allocation
  2. Memory-management
  3. Scheduling, and
  4. Distributed-systems problem

disguised as a model API.

This is where inference engineering begins.

Modern inference systems have evolved considerably beyond loading a model into PyTorch and calling generate().

Systems such as vLLM and SGLang introduce sophisticated mechanisms for

  1. Managing memory
  2. Scheduling requests
  3. Reusing computation
  4. Optimizing GPU execution, and
  5. Serving increasingly complex agentic workloads.

But understanding these engines without understanding what happens underneath them is like learning Kubernetes commands without understanding processes, memory, networking, or scheduling.

This guide takes a different approach.

We will start with a single token being generated by a language model. We will follow it through the GPU, understand where memory goes, discover why conventional batching breaks down, and gradually build the architecture of a production inference platform.

By the end, you should be able to reason about questions such as:

  • How much GPU memory does a 7B, 14B, 32B, or 70B model actually need?
  • Why does a model that fits in GPU memory still struggle to serve concurrent users?
  • What exactly is a KV cache, and why can it consume more memory than expected?
  • How does PagedAttention work, and why did it change LLM serving?
  • What makes SGLang’s RadixAttention particularly interesting for agents?
  • When should you choose vLLM over SGLang, or vice versa?
  • How do prefill and decode affect latency differently?
  • How do you calculate TTFT, TPOT, throughput, goodput, and GPU utilization?
  • How many GPUs do you need for a given traffic profile?
  • How do you calculate cost per million tokens?
  • How do you scale from one GPU to a distributed, production-grade inference platform?
  • Why do agentic applications require a fundamentally different approach to capacity planning?

Most importantly, we will not treat performance optimization as a collection of isolated tricks. We will connect every optimization to the bottleneck it addresses, the metric it improves, and the trade-off it introduces.

Let’s start where every inference request starts.

2. What actually happens when you ask an LLM a question?

Imagine a user sends the following request:

“Explain how vector databases work.”

The application sends the request to an inference server. The server loads the model, processes the input, and returns a response.

That sounds straightforward.

But a language model does not understand the request as a human-readable sentence. It operates on tokens, numerical representations, attention operations, and probability distributions.

Let’s follow the request.

Step 1: Tokenization

The text is converted into token IDs using the model’s tokenizer.

For illustration:

"Explain how vector databases work."

might become something resembling:

[12345, 1120, 9876, 3456, 789]

These are illustrative token IDs, not the actual IDs of a particular tokenizer.

The token IDs are passed through an embedding layer, which maps them into dense vectors.

Step 2: Transformer computation

The embeddings travel through the transformer’s layers.

Each layer typically contains:

  1. Normalization.
  2. Self-attention.
  3. Residual connections.
  4. Feed-forward network or gated MLP.
  5. Additional normalization and residual operations.

The attention mechanism allows the model to incorporate information from previous tokens.

At a high level:

Scaled Dot-Product Attention Mechanism.

Where:

  • Q represents queries.
  • K represents keys.
  • V represents values.
  • d_k is the key dimension.

The output of the transformer is converted into logits over the vocabulary.

A sampling or decoding strategy selects the next token.

Step 3: Autoregressive generation

The selected token is appended to the sequence.

The model processes the updated sequence to generate the next token.

This repeats until:

  • An end-of-sequence token is generated.
  • A configured maximum output length is reached.
  • A stopping condition is triggered.
  • The application cancels the request.

This is autoregressive generation.

And here lies the first important inference engineering insight:

Generating an LLM response is not one operation. It is a sequence of dependent operations, with memory and computation requirements that change throughout the request.

Source: https://www.usenix.org/publications/loginonline/wafer-scale-ai-compute-system-software-perspective?utm_source=chatgpt.com3. Prefill and decode: The two personalities of inference

The inference process has two fundamentally different phases.

Understanding this distinction is probably the single most important prerequisite for understanding modern LLM serving.

3.1 Prefill: Processing everything the user gave us

When a request arrives, the model needs to process the entire input prompt.

Suppose a user submits 2,000 tokens.

During prefill, the model processes those 2,000 tokens and computes the representations required to generate the next token.

The operations can be parallelized across the input sequence, subject to the causal attention mask.

Prefill is generally compute-intensive.

The model performs substantial matrix multiplication and attention computation. Large batches of prompt tokens can make effective use of GPU compute resources.

The first generated token becomes available after the prompt has been processed.

This contributes significantly to Time to First Token.

3.2 Decode: Generating one token at a time

Now the model starts generating the response.

Suppose it needs to produce 500 tokens.

It generates token 1, then token 2, then token 3, and so on.

Each next token depends on the preceding sequence.

Unlike prefill, generation is autoregressive.

The model does not normally recompute the entire prompt from scratch at every step. It uses previously computed attention information stored in the KV cache.

Decode is often memory-bandwidth-bound, particularly at low batch sizes.

The model weights need to be accessed repeatedly, while each request generally contributes only one new token per decoding iteration.

This creates a very different hardware utilization pattern.

3.3 Why the distinction matters

Consider four representative AI workloads:

1. Short Classification: 100 input tokens, 5 output tokens.

2. Long-Form Generation: 500 input tokens, 1,500 output tokens.

3. Document Analysis: 20,000 input tokens, 1,000 output tokens.

4. Agentic Research: 8,000 input tokens, 4,000 output tokens.

All four use an LLM, but their computational profiles are very different.

The document-analysis workload may stress prefill and KV-cache capacity.

The long-form generation workload may stress decode throughput.

The agentic workload may stress both, as well as cache reuse and scheduling.

A serving platform that optimizes only for requests per second can therefore make very poor decisions.

The unit of optimization must be the workload, not simply the model.

[IMAGE 02 — Prefill versus decode, showing compute-intensive prompt processing and autoregressive token generation]

Source: https://javabetter.cn/sidebar/itwanger/ai/ai-infra-six-keywords.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com4. Why inference is a GPU memory problem before it becomes a GPU compute problem

Let’s look at the hardware.

A modern accelerator contains several important resources:

  • Tensor cores and other compute units.
  • High-bandwidth GPU memory (HBM).
  • L1 and L2 caches.
  • Registers and shared memory.
  • GPU interconnects.
  • PCIe or other host-to-device connections.

The most important resources for LLM serving are generally:

  1. GPU memory capacity.
  2. GPU memory bandwidth.
  3. Compute throughput.
  4. Inter-GPU communication bandwidth.

These resources are not interchangeable.

4.1 GPU memory hierarchy

Think of GPU memory as a hierarchy. Different levels of the hierarchy serve different purposes:

  • Registers: Very fast, thread-local storage.
  • Shared Memory: Fast on-chip storage shared by threads within a block.
  • L1 Cache: Low-latency local caching.
  • L2 Cache: GPU-wide cache shared across processing units.
  • HBM: Large-capacity, high-bandwidth GPU memory.
  • Host RAM: Larger-capacity system memory, generally slower to access through the host interface.
Source: https://www.aleksagordic.com/blog/matmul?utm_source=chatgpt.com

LLM weights and large KV caches primarily reside in HBM during ordinary GPU-resident serving.

The GPU’s compute units need data to perform operations. Moving data from HBM to the compute units consumes bandwidth and time.

This explains why an LLM can have powerful theoretical FLOPS but still generate tokens slower than expected.

The GPU may not have enough useful data movement or computational work to keep its execution units fully occupied.

4.2 Compute-bound versus memory-bound execution

A useful concept is arithmetic intensity:

Arithmetic Intensity (AI): The ratio of computational operations performed to the amount of data transferred from memory.

A compute-bound workload benefits primarily from additional computational capacity.

A memory-bound workload benefits primarily from faster or more efficient data movement.

During prefill, large matrix operations can achieve high arithmetic intensity.

During decode, especially with small batches, repeatedly accessing model weights while generating relatively few tokens can make the workload memory-bandwidth-bound.

This is why simply comparing peak FLOPS between GPUs is insufficient when choosing inference hardware.

For example, NVIDIA’s H200 provides 141 GB of HBM3e memory and approximately 4.8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. The H100 SXM provides 80 GB of HBM3 memory and approximately 3.35 TB/s.

These specifications matter, but actual serving performance also depends on model architecture, precision, kernels, parallelism, workload shape, and engine configuration.

4.3 The roofline perspective

The roofline model gives us a way to reason about the maximum performance of a workload.

Roofline Model: Attainable computational performance is bounded by either peak compute throughput or memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity.

Where:

  • P_peak is peak compute performance.
  • AI is arithmetic intensity.
  • BW is available memory bandwidth.

This tells us something important:

If the workload is memory-bound, buying a GPU with substantially more FLOPS may deliver little improvement.

The bottleneck must be identified before hardware is selected.

[IMAGE 03 — GPU memory hierarchy and roofline model]

Source: https://www.qualcomm.com/news/onq/2026/07/hbc-hbm-sram-ai-inference-workload-analysis?utm_source=chatgpt.com5. Model weights: How much memory does a model need?

Let’s begin with the simplest memory calculation.

A model contains parameters, and each parameter occupies a certain number of bytes depending on its numerical precision.

The approximate weight memory is:

For common formats:

  • FP32: 4 bytes per parameter
  • FP16: 2 bytes per parameter
  • BF16: 2 bytes per parameter
  • FP8: 1 byte per parameter
  • INT8: 1 byte per parameter
  • INT4: 0.5 bytes per parameter

These are storage estimates. Actual quantized checkpoints can have additional scale, zero-point, metadata, and alignment overhead.

5.1 Worked example: A 7B model

For a 7-billion-parameter model in BF16:

That is approximately 14 GB in decimal units, or 13.0 GiB.

In INT4:

Approximately 3.5 GB before quantization metadata and runtime overhead.

5.2 Memory estimates across model sizes

7B model

  • BF16: 14 GB
  • INT8: 7 GB
  • INT4: 3.5 GB

8B model

  • BF16: 16 GB
  • INT8: 8 GB
  • INT4: 4 GB

14B model

  • BF16: 28 GB
  • INT8: 14 GB
  • INT4: 7 GB

32B model

  • BF16: 64 GB
  • INT8: 32 GB
  • INT4: 16 GB

70B model

  • BF16: 140 GB
  • INT8: 70 GB
  • INT4: 35 GB

Note: These are theoretical weight-storage estimates using 2 bytes per BF16 parameter, 1 byte per INT8 parameter, and 0.5 bytes per INT4 parameter. Actual GPU memory requirements may be higher due to quantization metadata, KV cache, activations, temporary buffers, and runtime overhead.

A model that needs 14 GB for weights cannot necessarily be served safely on a 16 GB GPU.

Why?

Because weights are only one component of the memory budget.

You also need:

  • KV cache.
  • Activations and temporary tensors.
  • CUDA graphs and execution buffers.
  • Attention and GEMM workspaces.
  • Communication buffers.
  • Allocator and runtime overhead.
  • Additional memory for adapters or other loaded models, where applicable.

This brings us to the most important memory component in inference.

6. The KV cache: The memory that grows with every conversation

Remember that the transformer uses attention to incorporate information from previous tokens.

During prefill, the model computes keys and values for the prompt.

Rather than recomputing these for every generated token, the model retains them in memory.

These retained tensors form the Key-Value cache, commonly called the KV cache.

Every newly generated token contributes additional key and value entries.

This is what makes autoregressive generation efficient, but it also creates a memory problem.

The longer the sequence, the larger the cache.

The more concurrent requests, the more cache capacity the server needs.

6.1 Deriving KV-cache memory

For a standard transformer with conventional attention caching:

KV Cache Memory Estimation: The memory required to store Key and Value tensors across all transformer layers, attention heads, sequence positions, and batch elements.

Where:

  • L: number of transformer layers.
  • H_KV: number of key/value heads.
  • D_H: dimension of each attention head.
  • T: number of tokens retained per sequence.
  • B: number of concurrent sequences.
  • S: bytes per KV element.
  • The factor 2 accounts for keys and values.

This formula assumes uniform layers with standard K/V storage. Architectures using sliding-window attention, MLA, hybrid attention, or cross-layer sharing require architecture-specific adjustments.

6.2 A real numerical example

Consider an illustrative 8B-class architecture with:

  • 32 transformer layers.
  • 8 KV heads.
  • 128 dimensions per head.
  • BF16 KV cache.
  • 8,192 tokens per sequence.

The cache memory per token is:

That is 128 KiB per token.

For an 8,192-token sequence:

One sequence can therefore consume approximately 1 GiB of KV cache.

Now imagine 32 concurrent sequences, each retaining 8,192 tokens.

Thirty-two GiB of KV cache.

And this is before accounting for model weights and other runtime allocations.

This is why memory planning cannot stop at model parameter count.

6.3 Why GQA and MQA matter

The number of KV heads is important.

Traditional Multi-Head Attention (MHA) generally has one KV head per query head.

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares KV heads across groups of query heads.

Multi-Query Attention (MQA) uses a single KV head.

Reducing the number of KV heads can substantially reduce KV-cache memory.

For example, reducing from 32 KV heads to 8 KV heads reduces the corresponding cache requirement by a factor of four, assuming other dimensions remain constant.

This is one reason modern model architectures can be much more practical to serve than parameter count alone might suggest.

6.4 Your memory budget is a sum, not a single number

A useful planning equation is:

Total GPU Memory Requirement: The combined memory footprint of model weights, KV cache, runtime overhead, computational workspace, and communication buffers during inference.

The actual serving engine determines the precise allocation and may reserve memory for future KV-cache growth.

A useful initial approximation is:

Available KV Cache Memory: The GPU memory remaining for KV cache allocation after accounting for model weights and memory reserved for runtime operations and other overheads.

Then:

Approximate KV Cache-Based Concurrency: The maximum number of sequences that can be accommodated concurrently, determined by the available KV cache memory divided by the memory required per sequence.

This is only a first-order estimate. Real capacity also depends on block granularity, maximum sequence lengths, scheduling, cache sharing, preemption, and the mix of prompt and generation lengths.

The key lesson: model size determines whether you can load the model. KV-cache capacity determines how much concurrent work you can sustain.

Source: https://cdn.analyticsvidhya.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/KV-Caching.webp7. Why conventional batching is not enough

Suppose you have four users.

  • User A needs 100 output tokens.
  • User B needs 500 output tokens.
  • User C needs 50 output tokens.
  • User D needs 1,000 output tokens.

A conventional static batch processes requests together.

But what happens when User C finishes much earlier than User D?

The batch may have to wait for the longest-running request or otherwise manage partially occupied batch slots.

This is inefficient.

LLM generation is particularly awkward because requests finish at different times and have different sequence lengths.
7.1 Static batching

Static batching groups a fixed set of requests into a batch.

Advantages:

  • Simple execution model.
  • Predictable batch composition.
  • Useful for offline workloads with known input shapes.

Limitations:

  • Requests have different generation lengths.
  • Finished requests can leave unused batch capacity.
  • New requests may wait for an existing batch to finish.
  • Memory requirements vary across requests.
7.2 Dynamic batching

Dynamic batching collects requests arriving within a batching window.

It can improve GPU utilization by combining requests.

However, conventional request-level dynamic batching still struggles with the autoregressive nature of LLM generation.

7.3 Continuous batching

Continuous batching changes the scheduling unit.

Instead of treating an entire generation request as one indivisible batch member, the engine schedules work at individual generation iterations.

When a request finishes, its resources can be released and another request can enter the active batch.

Conceptually:

Iteration 1: A, B, C, D
Iteration 2: A, B, C, D
Iteration 3: A, B, D, E
Iteration 4: A, B, D, E
Iteration 5: B, D, E, F

Here, E and F enter as earlier requests complete.

The GPU remains better occupied, and the scheduler can adapt to changing request lengths.

This is one of the defining characteristics of modern LLM serving.

The important insight is that continuous batching is not simply putting more prompts together. It is continuously managing a changing population of active decoding sequences.

The seminal ORCA work introduced iteration-level scheduling as a way to improve transformer serving. Modern inference engines build on this broader scheduling philosophy.

Source: HRDbjYSbsAEq5Q6.png8. PagedAttention: What if GPU memory behaved like virtual memory?

We now understand two things:

  1. KV cache grows as requests generate tokens.
  2. Different requests have different sequence lengths and memory lifetimes.

Traditional contiguous memory allocation can become inefficient under these conditions.

Imagine allocating one large contiguous memory region for every conversation.

Some conversations finish early. Others grow longer. Some need additional memory.

This creates fragmentation and makes it difficult to reuse free regions efficiently.

The vLLM research team approached this problem with an idea inspired by operating-system virtual memory.

What if KV-cache memory were managed in fixed-size blocks instead of requiring one contiguous allocation per request?

That is the central intuition behind PagedAttention.

8.1 Logical blocks and physical blocks

Imagine that each sequence has a logical sequence of KV-cache blocks.

The physical blocks do not need to be contiguous in GPU memory.

A block table maps logical blocks to physical blocks.

For example:

Request A:
Logical blocks:  0 → 1 → 2 → 3
Physical blocks: 7 → 2 → 9 → 4
Request B:
Logical blocks:  0 → 1 → 2
Physical blocks: 1 → 6 → 8

The attention implementation uses the mapping to access the relevant KV entries.

This provides several advantages:

  • Less fragmentation.
  • Flexible allocation.
  • Better memory utilization.
  • Easier reclamation of completed requests.
  • Sharing of common KV blocks where supported.
  • More effective batching.
8.2 Why paging matters

Without efficient KV-cache management, memory fragmentation can limit how many sequences fit into the GPU.

PagedAttention makes the cache allocation more flexible.

The original PagedAttention paper introduced vLLM and demonstrated substantial serving-throughput improvements over earlier systems under its evaluated workloads.

It is important not to interpret the original paper’s speedup as a universal performance guarantee. Modern engine versions, hardware, model architectures, and workload distributions all change the comparison.

8.3 The virtual-memory analogy

PagedAttention applies virtual-memory concepts to GPU KV cache management:

  • Virtual Address Space → Logical Token Positions
  • Physical Memory Pages → Physical KV Blocks
  • Page Table → Block Table
  • Page Allocation → KV-Block Allocation
  • Memory Reclamation → KV-Block Release
  • Shared Pages → Shared KV Prefixes

The analogy is useful, although the underlying implementation and access semantics are not identical to a general-purpose operating system.

Source: https://medium.com/red-buffer/private-scalable-llm-inference-for-data-compliance-vllm-sglang-539ad81af04f8.4 What about prefix sharing?

Suppose 100 users interact with the same application.

Every request starts with an identical system prompt.

A conventional approach may independently compute and retain the same prefix KV state for every request.

That is redundant.

If the serving engine can safely reuse the KV state corresponding to the common prefix, it avoids repeating part of the computation.

vLLM supports Automatic Prefix Caching, which can reuse KV-cache blocks for shared prefixes.

This becomes particularly valuable for:

  • Long system prompts.
  • Repeated document context.
  • Shared few-shot examples.
  • Multi-turn conversations.
  • Repeated application templates.

The exact benefit depends on cache hit rates, prefix lengths, request locality, and cache eviction.

And this leads us naturally to SGLang.

9. SGLang and RadixAttention: When the workload is more than a chatbot

vLLM’s PagedAttention changed how we think about KV-cache allocation.

SGLang takes cache reuse into another interesting direction.

Consider a customer-support agent.

Every conversation may include:

  1. A shared system prompt.
  2. A set of application instructions.
  3. Customer-specific information.
  4. Conversation history.
  5. A new user query.

A research agent may repeatedly execute:

  1. A planning prompt.
  2. A search operation.
  3. A tool-result interpretation.
  4. A second planning operation.
  5. Another search.
  6. A final synthesis.

These workflows create overlapping prefixes and repeated model calls.

What if the runtime could organize reusable KV states around shared token prefixes?

This is where RadixAttention comes in.

9.1 The radix-tree intuition

A radix tree is a tree structure that represents shared prefixes efficiently.

Consider these sequences:

A: SYSTEM → POLICY → USER_A → QUERY_A
B: SYSTEM → POLICY → USER_B → QUERY_B
C: SYSTEM → POLICY → USER_C → QUERY_C

The first two segments are shared.

Instead of treating all three as entirely independent sequences, a radix-tree-based cache can represent the common prefix once and branch into request-specific continuations.

Conceptually:

SYSTEM
                    |
                  POLICY
               /     |     \
           USER_A  USER_B  USER_C
              |       |       |
           QUERY_A QUERY_B QUERY_C

SGLang’s RadixAttention uses this idea to support automatic KV-cache reuse across multiple generation calls.

9.2 Why agents benefit

Agents frequently repeat structured prompt components.

A tool-using agent might repeatedly include:

  • System instructions.
  • Tool schemas.
  • Planning templates.
  • Previous execution results.
  • Shared context.

The more overlap between requests, the more opportunity exists for cache reuse.

However, reuse is not guaranteed simply because two requests come from the same application.

The token prefixes must match under the runtime’s cache semantics. Changes in tokenization, formatting, tool schemas, and prompt construction can reduce cache hits.

Cache capacity, eviction, and request routing also matter.

9.3 RadixAttention versus PagedAttention

It is important to understand that these technologies address related but different aspects of serving.

1. Main Idea

  • PagedAttention: Block-based KV cache memory management.
  • RadixAttention: Prefix-aware KV cache reuse.

2. Core Benefit

  • PagedAttention: Efficient memory allocation and reduced fragmentation.
  • RadixAttention: Avoiding repeated computation of shared prefixes.

3. Mental Model

  • PagedAttention: Virtual memory pages.
  • RadixAttention: Shared-prefix tree.

4. Particularly Useful For

  • PagedAttention: General concurrent LLM serving.
  • RadixAttention: Repeated and structured LLM calls.

5. Key Consideration

  • PagedAttention: Block allocation and cache capacity.
  • RadixAttention: Prefix locality and cache residency.

They should not be treated as mutually exclusive concepts. Both engines have broader memory-management and caching implementations that evolve over time.

9.4 The SGLang architecture

SGLang combines a programming interface for structured LLM applications with a high-performance runtime.

Its original research introduced:

  • A structured generation language.
  • RadixAttention.
  • Efficient execution of multiple generation calls.
  • Structured output decoding using compressed finite-state machines.

The NeurIPS 2024 paper reported improvements of up to 6.4× on its evaluated workloads compared with the systems used in those experiments.

That result is especially interesting because the evaluated workloads included agent control, reasoning, JSON generation, and retrieval-augmented generation.

Again, it is a paper-specific result, not a promise that every application will experience that speedup.

Source: https://note.com/humble_bobcat51/n/n79aec7cef370?utm_source=chatgpt.com10. vLLM versus SGLang: Which inference engine should you choose?

Both are serious inference-serving systems.

Both support high-performance serving, continuous batching, KV-cache management, and advanced execution optimizations.

The choice should not be made based on a single benchmark chart.

It should be made based on the workload.

10.1 vLLM

vLLM is an excellent general-purpose choice for high-throughput LLM serving.

Its ecosystem includes:

  • PagedAttention-based memory management.
  • Continuous batching.
  • Automatic Prefix Caching.
  • Chunked prefill.
  • Quantization support.
  • Tensor, pipeline, data, and expert parallelism options.
  • Speculative decoding.
  • OpenAI-compatible serving APIs.
  • Monitoring and deployment integrations.

A typical starting point:

pip install vllm
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  --dtype auto \
  --max-model-len 8192

The exact flags and supported configurations depend on the installed vLLM version and hardware.

You can then interact with the OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",
    api_key="EMPTY"
)
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Explain continuous batching."
        }
    ],
    max_tokens=256
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
10.2 SGLang

SGLang is particularly interesting when your application consists of structured, repeated, multi-step LLM interactions.

Its strengths include:

  • RadixAttention.
  • Prefix-aware KV-cache reuse.
  • Structured generation.
  • Efficient constrained decoding.
  • Continuous batching.
  • Multi-model and multimodal serving capabilities.
  • Optimizations for complex LLM programs.

A basic server launch looks like:

pip install "sglang[all]"
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30000

As with vLLM, consult the current version’s documentation for hardware-specific options and supported features.

  • SGLang: RadixAttention.

4. Structured Generation

  • vLLM: Supported.
  • SGLang: A major design focus.

5. Agentic Workloads

  • vLLM: Strong.
  • SGLang: Particularly interesting.

6. OpenAI-Compatible APIs

  • vLLM: Yes.
  • SGLang: Yes.

7. Distributed Serving

  • vLLM: Yes.
  • SGLang: Yes.

8. Production Monitoring

  • vLLM: Supported.
  • SGLang: Supported.

My recommendation:

Start with vLLM when you need a broadly applicable serving engine and a straightforward deployment path.

Evaluate SGLang early when your application repeatedly invokes the model with overlapping prefixes, uses structured generation extensively, or executes complex multi-step LLM programs.

But do not select either engine based on theoretical superiority.

Benchmark both with the same model, hardware, request distribution, concurrency, prompt lengths, output lengths, and latency targets.

The winning inference engine is the one that delivers the best quality-adjusted goodput at your required service level and cost.
11. Understanding latency: The user does not experience your tokens per second

An inference server can generate thousands of tokens per second across all users and still deliver a terrible user experience.

Why?

Because aggregate throughput and individual request latency measure different things.

Let’s define the important metrics.

11.1 Time to First Token (TTFT)
TTFT measures how long a user waits before receiving the first generated token.
Time to First Token (TTFT): The total time from request arrival until the first generated token is delivered, including queueing, prompt processing (prefill), and system overhead.

Depending on the measurement boundary, overhead may include tokenization, networking, and request handling.

TTFT matters enormously in interactive applications.

A user waiting two seconds for the first response experiences something very different from a user waiting 200 milliseconds.

11.2 Time Per Output Token (TPOT)
TPOT measures the average time required to generate each output token after the first token.
Time Per Output Token (TPOT): The average time required to generate each subsequent output token after the first token, excluding the initial time-to-first-token.

For a simplified example, suppose a request produces 100 tokens after its first token and takes 5 seconds to generate them.

That is 50 milliseconds per token.

11.3 Inter-Token Latency (ITL)
ITL measures the time between consecutive output tokens.

Unlike an average TPOT, ITL can expose irregular pauses and spikes during streaming.

A system might have a reasonable average but still occasionally pause for several hundred milliseconds.

Those pauses are important for interactive user experience.

11.4 End-to-end latency

A simplified approximation is:

End-to-End Latency: The approximate total response time, calculated as the time to first token plus the time required to generate the remaining output tokens.

Actual measurement must account for the exact definition of TTFT, streaming behavior, networking, and completion boundaries.

11.5 Throughput

Two common throughput measurements are:

Request throughput

Requests Per Second (RPS): The number of successfully completed inference requests per second, measuring the request-processing throughput of an LLM serving system.

Token throughput

Tokens Per Second (TPS): The number of tokens generated per second, measuring the token-generation throughput of an LLM inference system.

Always clarify whether TPS means output tokens per second, input tokens per second, or combined token throughput.

These are not interchangeable.

11.6 Goodput

This is where production engineering becomes more interesting.

Imagine a server processes 1,000 requests.

But 300 violate the latency requirements.

Should we call the system successful because it completed 1,000 requests?

Not necessarily.

Goodput measures useful completed work that satisfies the application’s service-level requirements.

A simplified definition is:

Goodput: The rate of successfully completed requests that meet predefined Service Level Objectives (SLOs), measuring useful throughput rather than raw request throughput.

You can also define token-based goodput for applications where generated tokens are the relevant unit of successful work.

This is why maximizing raw throughput is not always the right objective.

Source: https://www.bentoml.com/blog/the-shift-to-distributed-llm-inference11.7 Percentiles matter

Never rely exclusively on average latency.

Measure:

  • p50: Median experience.
  • p90: Experience of the slower 10%.
  • p95: Experience of the slower 5%.
  • p99: Experience of the slower 1%.

For production applications, p95 and p99 are particularly important.

A system with 500 ms average TTFT and 8-second p99 TTFT may be unacceptable for an interactive application.

12. The inference performance triangle

Inference optimization involves three competing objectives:

  1. Latency.
  2. Throughput.
  3. Cost.

Increasing batch size often improves aggregate throughput because model weights and other data can be reused across more active sequences.

But larger batches can also increase:

  • Queueing delay.
  • Scheduling complexity.
  • KV-cache pressure.
  • Memory requirements.
  • Tail latency.

Similarly, reducing precision can reduce memory requirements and increase performance, but it may affect model quality.

Increasing the context length improves application flexibility, but increases cache requirements and prefill computation.

There is no universal configuration that simultaneously maximizes all three objectives.

The engineering task is to find the operating point that satisfies the application’s SLOs at an acceptable cost.

13. Continuous batching is only the beginning: Chunked prefill

We previously saw that prefill and decode behave differently.

Now imagine a system with several active users generating responses.

Suddenly, a new request arrives with a 30,000-token prompt.

The GPU begins processing that long prompt.

While it is doing so, active decode requests may experience delays.

This is called prefill-decode interference.

The system must balance two competing needs:

  • Process new prompts efficiently.
  • Keep existing users generating tokens smoothly.
13.1 Chunked prefill

Instead of processing an entire long prompt in one large operation, the engine divides it into smaller chunks.

For example:

Original prompt: 12,000 tokens
Chunk 1: 2,048 tokens
Chunk 2: 2,048 tokens
Chunk 3: 2,048 tokens
Chunk 4: 2,048 tokens
Chunk 5: 2,048 tokens
Chunk 6: 1,760 tokens

The scheduler can interleave these chunks with ongoing decode work.

Conceptually:

Iteration 1: Decode A + Decode B + Prefill chunk 1
Iteration 2: Decode A + Decode B + Prefill chunk 2
Iteration 3: Decode A + Decode C + Prefill chunk 3
Iteration 4: Decode B + Decode C + Prefill chunk 4

This reduces the risk that one long prompt monopolizes execution.

The SARATHI research line is particularly relevant here. It explores chunked prefills and decode-maximal batching to improve the throughput-latency trade-off.

13.2 When chunked prefill helps
  • Mixed workloads with short and long prompts.
  • Interactive applications.
  • Long-context document processing.
  • Concurrent chat and retrieval workloads.
  • Systems where decode latency must remain stable.
13.3 The trade-off

Chunking introduces scheduling decisions and potentially additional overhead.

A chunk size that works for one model and GPU may not work for another.

The correct value must be benchmarked against the actual prompt-length distribution and latency objectives.

14. Disaggregated serving: Separate prefill and decode when their needs diverge

What if prefill and decode require different hardware allocation strategies?

Prefill is generally more compute-intensive.

Decode is often more memory-bandwidth-sensitive.

If both phases share the same GPU pool, they compete for resources.

Disaggregated serving addresses this by separating the two phases into distinct resource pools.

14.1 The architecture
Incoming requests
                         |
                   API Gateway
                         |
                   Router / Scheduler
                         |
                +--------+--------+
                |                 |
          PREFILL POOL       DECODE POOL
                |                 |
         Prompt processing   Token generation
                |                 |
          KV-cache creation ----> KV-cache transfer
                                  |
                           Streaming response

The prefill pool processes the prompt and produces the required KV state.

That state is transferred to the decode pool, where generation continues.

14.2 Why it helps

You can allocate resources independently.

For example:

  • More compute capacity for prefill.
  • More memory bandwidth or KV capacity for decode.
  • Different tensor-parallel configurations.
  • Different scaling policies.
  • Better isolation between long prompts and active generation.

DistServe is an important research contribution in this area.

Its OSDI 2024 paper explored how separating prefill and decode can improve goodput under latency constraints.

14.3 Why you should not automatically disaggregate

There is a price.

You now need to move KV state between resource pools.

This introduces:

  • Network communication.
  • Transfer latency.
  • Additional infrastructure.
  • Coordination between pools.
  • More complex scheduling.
  • Failure-handling requirements.

If the workload is small or the network is insufficient, disaggregation may make performance worse.

Start with a well-tuned colocated serving architecture. Disaggregate when measured evidence shows that phase interference or resource imbalance justifies the additional complexity.

Source: https://www.infoq.cn/article/QJAPI0RrIrKCY2fN3KTL15. Quantization: More than fitting a model onto a smaller GPU

Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent model weights or other tensors.

It is one of the most important techniques for inference optimization.

Consider a 32B model.

At BF16:

A 32-billion-parameter model stored in BF16 requires approximately 64 GB of memory for its weights alone.

At an idealized 4-bit representation:

A 32-billion-parameter model stored in INT4 requires approximately 16 GB of memory for its weights alone.

This is a substantial reduction.

But quantization is not free.

15.1 Weight quantization

Common options include:

  • FP8
  • INT8
  • INT4
  • AWQ
  • GPTQ
  • FP8 or other low-precision checkpoint formats supported by the relevant engine

Each format has different calibration, kernel, hardware, and quality characteristics.

15.2 KV-cache quantization

Weights are not the only tensors that can be compressed.

KV caches can also be stored at lower precision in supported configurations.

This can increase effective context capacity or concurrent sequence capacity.

However, the accuracy and latency trade-offs depend on the model and cache implementation.

15.3 A useful way to think about quantization

OptimizationPrimary targetWeight quantizationModel weight memoryKV-cache quantizationPer-token cache memoryActivation quantizationIntermediate tensor representationQuantized kernelsEfficient low-precision execution

A common mistake is to assume that reducing weight precision automatically doubles serving capacity.

Not necessarily.

If KV cache is the limiting resource, weight quantization may free some capacity but the ultimate concurrency limit may still be determined by cache requirements or runtime constraints.

15.4 The correct validation strategy

For every quantized model, measure:

  1. Weight memory.
  2. KV-cache capacity.
  3. TTFT.
  4. TPOT.
  5. Output quality.
  6. Structured-output reliability.
  7. Task-specific accuracy.
  8. Throughput at the target latency.

An INT4 model that runs faster but fails important financial calculations or structured extraction tasks is not a successful optimization.

16. Speculative decoding: Let a smaller model help a larger model

Autoregressive generation has an inherent sequential dependency.

Can we generate multiple candidate tokens before invoking the main model?

Speculative decoding attempts to do exactly that.

A smaller draft model proposes several tokens.

The larger target model verifies the proposed tokens in a more parallel fashion.

Compatible tokens are accepted, while rejected portions are corrected through the target model’s decoding process.

Conceptually:

Input prompt
                       |
                 Draft model
                       |
              Candidate tokens
                T1 T2 T3 T4
                       |
                 Target model
                       |
                Verification
                       |
             Accept compatible tokens
                       |
              Continue generation
16.1 Why it works

The draft model is cheaper to execute.

If it predicts several tokens that the target model accepts, the system can generate multiple output tokens with fewer expensive target-model iterations.

Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/blog/posts/from-research-to-production-accelerate-oss-llm-with-eagle-3-on-vertex16.2 The important caveat

Speculative decoding does not guarantee a speedup.

Performance depends on:

  • Draft-model quality.
  • Acceptance rate.
  • Draft-model overhead.
  • Target-model architecture.
  • Batch size.
  • Memory bandwidth.
  • Verification implementation.

It is particularly attractive for workloads where the target model’s autoregressive generation is a significant bottleneck.

It is less attractive when the draft model introduces more overhead than the accepted tokens justify.

17. Parallelism: When one GPU is no longer enough

Eventually, model weights or serving requirements exceed the practical capacity of a single accelerator.

Now we need distributed inference.

There are several forms of parallelism.

17.1 Data parallelism (DP)

Multiple replicas of the model process independent requests.

Load Balancer
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |           |           |
       Replica 1   Replica 2   Replica 3
          |           |           |
        GPU(s)      GPU(s)      GPU(s)

Data parallelism increases serving capacity by distributing requests across replicas.

It is particularly useful when a model fits within the memory of an individual replica.

17.2 Tensor parallelism (TP)

Tensor parallelism splits portions of model operations across GPUs.

For example, different GPUs hold portions of a large weight matrix.

They collaborate during computation.

Benefits:

  • Reduces per-GPU weight memory.
  • Enables larger models.
  • Can increase effective compute capacity.

Trade-offs:

  • Collective communication.
  • Synchronization overhead.
  • Dependence on interconnect bandwidth.
  • More complex deployment.

Tensor parallelism is particularly sensitive to GPU interconnect topology.

NVLink-connected GPUs can behave very differently from GPUs communicating through a slower interconnect.

17.3 Pipeline parallelism (PP)

Pipeline parallelism distributes different transformer layers across GPUs.

GPU 1: Layers 1–20
       |
GPU 2: Layers 21–40
       |
GPU 3: Layers 41–60
       |
GPU 4: Layers 61–80

This reduces the model memory required on each GPU.

However, pipeline execution introduces scheduling and pipeline-bubble considerations.

17.4 Expert parallelism (EP)

For Mixture-of-Experts models, different expert networks can be distributed across devices.

Tokens are routed to selected experts.

This introduces additional communication and load-balancing requirements.

17.5 Choosing the right strategy

StrategyMain objectiveImportant considerationDPMore independent replicasReplication costTPSplit model operationsCommunicationPPSplit transformer layersPipeline utilizationEPDistribute expertsRouting and all-to-all communication

These strategies can be combined.

The correct configuration depends on model architecture, hardware topology, memory requirements, and workload.

A distributed model is not automatically a faster model. It is a model that can use distributed resources effectively.

Source: https://cai-jianfeng.github.io/posts/2023/12/blog-code-pytorch-distributed/18. Capacity planning: How many GPUs do you actually need?

Let’s now move from individual inference requests to infrastructure planning.

Suppose a product has 10,000 registered users.

Does it need 10,000 simultaneous inference slots?

No.

Registered users, active users, concurrent requests, and active decoding sequences are different quantities.

Capacity planning must begin with the actual traffic profile.

18.1 Start with traffic assumptions

Consider this illustrative application:

  • Registered users: 10,000.
  • Peak active users: 1,000.
  • Concurrent inference requests: 200.
  • Average input length: 2,000 tokens.
  • Average output length: 500 tokens.
  • Average request duration: 10 seconds.

These are assumptions for the example, not benchmark measurements.

18.2 Calculate request throughput

Using Little’s Law:

Little’s Law: The average number of requests in a system equals the request arrival rate multiplied by the average time spent in the system.

Where:

  • L is the average number of requests in the system.
  • lambda is the arrival rate.
  • W is the average time spent in the system.

If the average number of concurrent requests is 200 and the average request duration is 10 seconds:

Request Arrival Rate: An average of 20 requests arrive per second when 200 requests are received over a 10-second interval.18.3 Calculate token demand

Average input tokens per second:

Input Token Throughput: At an arrival rate of 20 requests per second and an average input length of 2,000 tokens per request, the system must process 40,000 input tokens per second.

Average output tokens per second:

Output Token Throughput: At an arrival rate of 20 requests per second and an average output length of 500 tokens per request, the system must generate 10,000 output tokens per second.

Total token processing demand:

Total Token Throughput: The system must process 50,000 tokens per second, comprising 40,000 input tokens and 10,000 output tokens.

The system needs to process approximately 40,000 input tokens and generate 10,000 output tokens per second under these assumptions.

Do not treat the combined 50,000 figure as equivalent to 50,000 generated tokens per second. Prefill and decode have different computational profiles.

18.4 Why this matters

Suppose a benchmark reports that one GPU sustains:

  • 8,000 input tokens per second.
  • 2,500 output tokens per second.

These are hypothetical values for demonstrating the calculation.

The output requirement alone implies:

GPU Capacity Estimation: A requirement of 10,000 output tokens per second, with each GPU delivering 2,500 tokens per second, necessitates approximately 4 GPUs.

The input requirement implies:

Prefill Capacity Estimation: A requirement of 40,000 input tokens per second, with each GPU processing 8,000 input tokens per second, necessitates approximately 5 GPUs.

A simplistic estimate would therefore require at least five GPU-equivalents.

But real deployment needs additional capacity for:

  • Latency constraints.
  • Request variability.
  • KV-cache capacity.
  • Queueing.
  • Failures.
  • Deployment overhead.
  • Traffic bursts.
  • Redundancy.

A more realistic planning equation is:

GPU Provisioning Formula: The required GPU count is determined by peak demand, sustainable per-GPU capacity, target utilization, and additional redundancy to maintain availability and handle failures.

Here, U_target represents the intended operating margin, not simply GPU utilization.

The exact calculation should be performed separately for prefill, decode, memory capacity, and latency constraints.

18.5 The biggest capacity-planning mistake

Do not size infrastructure using average traffic alone.

If peak traffic is five times average traffic, infrastructure sized only for average demand will either violate SLOs or require aggressive admission control during spikes.

Use:

  • Average demand.
  • Peak demand.
  • Burst duration.
  • Request arrival distribution.
  • Input/output token distributions.
  • Concurrent sequence counts.
  • Maximum context requirements.

And benchmark realistic traffic, not just synthetic requests with identical lengths.

19. Cost engineering: How much does one million tokens really cost?

Now we arrive at the question every production AI team eventually asks.

How much does inference cost?

The answer is not simply the price of a GPU.

It is the cost of operating that GPU relative to the amount of useful work it delivers.

19.1 Cost per million output tokens

Let:

  • C_h = hourly cost of one GPU.
  • T = sustainable output tokens per second.

Then:

Cost per Million Tokens: The estimated inference cost of processing one million tokens, calculated from the hourly GPU cost and token throughput per second.

Suppose:

  • GPU cost = $3 per hour.
  • Sustainable output throughput = 2,000 tokens per second.

Then:

Inference Cost Calculation: At an hourly GPU cost of $3 and a throughput of 2,000 tokens per second, the estimated cost is approximately $0.417 per million tokens.

This is an illustrative GPU-only cost estimate.

It excludes:

  • CPU and RAM.
  • Storage.
  • Networking.
  • Platform overhead.
  • Idle capacity.
  • Replication.
  • Monitoring.
  • Engineering and operational costs.
19.2 What if the GPU is only 40% utilized?

Suppose the effective useful throughput falls to 800 tokens per second.

Inference Cost Calculation: At an hourly GPU cost of $3 and a throughput of 800 tokens per second, the estimated cost is approximately $1.042 per million tokens.

The same GPU now costs approximately 2.5 times as much per million generated tokens.

This is why utilization and scheduling matter.

19.3 Input and output costs should be separated

Prefill and decode have different performance characteristics.

Therefore, a better cost model is:

Total Inference Cost: The combined cost of prompt processing (prefill), output generation (decode), and supporting infrastructure.

For example:

Phase-Wise Inference Cost: Prefill and decode costs are estimated separately based on their respective token counts, processing times, and GPU-second pricing.

These are simplified allocation models. If prefill and decode share the same GPU pool, allocate cost using measured resource consumption or a defensible accounting policy rather than counting the same GPU time twice.

19.4 Monthly infrastructure cost

A basic estimate:

Monthly GPU Infrastructure Cost: The estimated monthly compute expenditure, calculated using the number of provisioned GPUs, hourly cost per GPU, and an assumed 730 operating hours per month.

For five GPUs at $3 per hour:

Monthly Infrastructure Cost: Provisioning 5 GPUs at $3 per GPU-hour for 730 hours results in an estimated monthly cost of $10,950.

This is the approximate monthly accelerator rental cost under continuous operation.

The real bill will depend on instance type, commitment discounts, utilization, regional pricing, and infrastructure overhead.

19.5 The cost optimization hierarchy

My recommended order:

  1. Remove redundant model calls.
  2. Reduce unnecessary prompt tokens.
  3. Introduce prefix caching.
  4. Use efficient batching.
  5. Optimize KV-cache utilization.
  6. Benchmark quantization.
  7. Improve decode throughput.
  8. Improve GPU utilization.
  9. Evaluate speculative decoding.
  10. Reconsider model size and hardware placement.

The cheapest token is often the token you never had to compute.

20. Agentic inference: The problem changes when the model becomes a worker

Traditional chat applications generally involve one request and one response.

Agentic systems are different.

An agent may:

  1. Receive a task.
  2. Generate a plan.
  3. Call a search tool.
  4. Read the result.
  5. Generate another plan.
  6. Call an API.
  7. Inspect the response.
  8. Retry an operation.
  9. Generate a final answer.

A single user request can therefore trigger multiple inference requests.

20.1 The agentic amplification factor

Define:

Agentic Amplification Factor: The average number of LLM calls triggered per user request, indicating how much additional inference activity agentic workflows introduce.

If 100 users each trigger an average of 6 model calls:

Agentic Workload Expansion: 100 user requests, with an average of 6 LLM calls per request, generate 600 total LLM calls.

But call count alone is insufficient.

Some calls may contain large conversation histories, tool schemas, or retrieved documents.

A more useful token-demand model is:

Agentic Token Demand: The expected total token-processing demand per second, calculated by multiplying the user request arrival rate by the expected cumulative input and output tokens consumed across all LLM calls within each request.

Where:

  • lambda_user is the user request arrival rate.
  • N is the number of LLM calls per task.
  • Each call has its own input and output token demand.
20.2 Why SGLang becomes interesting

Agentic workloads often repeat prompt structures.

The system prompt, instructions, tool descriptions, and parts of the conversation may remain unchanged across calls.

RadixAttention’s prefix-reuse capabilities can reduce repeated computation when the workload has reusable token prefixes.

vLLM’s Automatic Prefix Caching can also help with suitable repeated-prefix workloads.

20.3 The bigger architecture

A production agent platform should not simply send every operation to one shared LLM endpoint.

Consider routing requests according to task characteristics.

User Request
                         |
                    Agent Runtime
                         |
                 Task Classification
                         |
              +----------+----------+
              |          |          |
           Simple     Reasoning    Complex
           Tasks       Tasks       Agents
              |          |          |
           Small       Larger      Specialized
           Model       Model       Model
              |          |          |
              +----------+----------+
                         |
                   Tool Execution
                         |
                 Result Evaluation
                         |
                 Final Generation

This introduces model routing, workload isolation, and specialized serving pools.

20.4 Agentic systems require more than GPU optimization

Other important engineering concerns include:

  • Maximum tool-call budgets.
  • Request deadlines.
  • Cancellation propagation.
  • Idempotency.
  • Retry limits.
  • Tool execution timeouts.
  • Context compaction.
  • Prompt growth control.
  • Per-tenant quotas.
  • Distributed tracing.
  • Model fallback.
  • Circuit breakers.

An agent that loops indefinitely is not merely an application bug. It can become a runaway inference-cost problem.

In the agentic era, inference engineering and agent orchestration are increasingly inseparable.

Source: https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/article/introduction-to-mcp-understanding-how-clients-servers-and-llms-work-together21. Benchmarking: Stop trusting single-number performance claims

A benchmark that says “Model X generates 5,000 tokens per second” is almost meaningless without additional information.

You need to know:

  • Which GPU?
  • Which model?
  • Which precision?
  • Which inference engine?
  • What was the input length?
  • What was the output length?
  • What was the concurrency?
  • Was prefix caching enabled?
  • Was speculative decoding enabled?
  • Was the measurement aggregate or per user?
  • What latency did the system achieve?

A benchmark without workload information is not a capacity-planning result.

21.1 Build a realistic workload matrix

1. Short Chat

  • Input length: 256 tokens
  • Output length: 128 tokens
  • Concurrency: 16

2. Medium Chat

  • Input length: 1,024 tokens
  • Output length: 512 tokens
  • Concurrency: 32

3. Document Analysis

  • Input length: 8,192 tokens
  • Output length: 1,024 tokens
  • Concurrency: 16

4. Long Context

  • Input length: 32,768 tokens
  • Output length: 2,048 tokens
  • Concurrency: 8

5. Agentic Workload

  • Input length: Variable
  • Output length: Variable
  • Concurrency: 32

These are example test scenarios, not recommended universal values.

21.2 Benchmark metrics

Capture:

  • TTFT p50/p95/p99.
  • TPOT p50/p95/p99.
  • ITL distribution.
  • End-to-end latency.
  • Input tokens per second.
  • Output tokens per second.
  • Requests per second.
  • KV-cache utilization.
  • GPU memory utilization.
  • GPU compute utilization.
  • Queue length.
  • Preemption count.
  • Cache hit rate.
  • Error and timeout rates.
21.3 Benchmarking vLLM

vLLM provides serving benchmarks through its benchmarking tooling.

A representative command pattern is:

vllm bench serve \
  --backend openai \
  --base-url http://localhost:8000 \
  --endpoint /v1/completions \
  --model YOUR_MODEL \
  --dataset-name random \
  --num-prompts 1000 \
  --request-rate 10

The exact flags vary across releases. Check the installed version’s help output and use the appropriate chat or completion workload.

21.4 Benchmarking SGLang

SGLang provides benchmarking utilities for serving workloads.

A typical approach is to use its serving benchmark tooling against the deployed endpoint, varying:

  • Request rate.
  • Concurrency.
  • Input length.
  • Output length.
  • Dataset.
  • Streaming mode.

Use the same request corpus for both engines.

21.5 Open-loop versus closed-loop testing

This distinction is important.

In closed-loop testing, clients send a new request after the previous request completes.

As the server slows down, the arrival rate naturally falls.

This can hide overload.

In open-loop testing, requests arrive at a specified rate regardless of previous completion.

This better exposes queue buildup and overload behavior.

A robust evaluation should include both types of testing.

21.6 A disciplined benchmark protocol
  1. Fix the model checkpoint.
  2. Fix the hardware.
  3. Fix the numerical precision.
  4. Fix the engine version.
  5. Warm up the system.
  6. Use identical input/output distributions.
  7. Run several concurrency levels.
  8. Record latency percentiles.
  9. Monitor GPU and KV-cache utilization.
  10. Repeat the test.
  11. Compare quality and cost.
  12. Publish the configuration alongside the results.

Do not report the highest observed throughput while ignoring latency violations.

The useful number is the sustainable throughput at the required SLO.

22. Production architecture: From a model server to an inference platform

A model server is not a production platform.

A production platform must handle traffic, authentication, model routing, resource allocation, monitoring, deployment, failure recovery, and cost controls.
