Let’s examine the components.

22.1 API gateway

Responsibilities:

  • Authentication.
  • Authorization.
  • Rate limiting.
  • Request validation.
  • Tenant identification.
  • Request-size limits.
  • API versioning.

Never expose unrestricted model-serving endpoints to the public internet.

22.2 Inference gateway

The inference gateway is more specialized.

It understands model-serving characteristics.

It can route requests based on:

  • Model identifier.
  • Available replicas.
  • Queue length.
  • Prefix-cache locality.
  • Input length.
  • Workload class.
  • Latency objectives.
  • Tenant priority.

A prefix-aware routing strategy can improve cache reuse by sending requests to replicas that already retain relevant prefixes.

However, routing to a cache-hot replica must be balanced against queue pressure and availability.

22.3 Model-serving layer

Each model replica should have an explicit resource and performance profile.

For example:

Model: Qwen 8B
Precision: BF16
Engine: vLLM
GPU: H100
Max context: Configured limit
KV cache: GPU resident
Parallelism: TP=1
API: OpenAI compatible

The configuration must be validated against the hardware and model architecture.

22.4 Containerization

Package the inference runtime into a reproducible container.

Pin:

  • Engine version.
  • CUDA runtime.
  • PyTorch version.
  • Model revision.
  • Python dependencies.
  • Quantization configuration.
  • Startup parameters.

This reduces deployment drift.

22.5 Kubernetes orchestration

Kubernetes can manage:

  • Model-serving pods.
  • GPU resource allocation.
  • Service discovery.
  • Rolling deployments.
  • Health checks.
  • Replication.
  • Autoscaling.
  • Failure recovery.

However, GPU autoscaling is not equivalent to ordinary CPU autoscaling.

Model loading can take time. GPU availability may be constrained. A new replica may need to download large model weights and warm up before serving traffic.

Therefore, scaling decisions should consider both current demand and startup delay.

22.6 Autoscaling

Useful signals include:

  • Pending request count.
  • Queue waiting time.
  • Active sequences.
  • KV-cache utilization.
  • Input-token rate.
  • Output-token rate.
  • TTFT violations.
  • GPU memory pressure.

CPU utilization alone is generally insufficient.

Queue-based scaling is particularly useful because queue growth directly indicates that demand is exceeding currently available service capacity.

Google Cloud’s GKE inference guidance discusses queue-size and batch-size signals for GPU inference autoscaling.

22.7 Rolling deployments

A model deployment should not simply terminate the old server and start the new one.

A safer pattern:

  1. Launch new replicas.
  2. Load the model.
  3. Run health checks.
  4. Warm up kernels and execution paths.
  5. Run smoke tests.
  6. Add the replicas to routing.
  7. Gradually shift traffic.
  8. Drain existing requests from old replicas.
  9. Retire the old deployment.

This reduces the risk of user-facing outages.

Source: https://woonyee.org/projects/ml-inference-sys-review23. Observability: If you cannot see the bottleneck, you cannot optimize it

A production inference platform needs visibility into both application behavior and GPU execution.

Source: https://docs.nvidia.com/nim/large-language-models/1.2.0/observability.html

I recommend four observability layers.

Layer 1: Request metrics
  • Requests per second.
  • Successful requests.
  • Failed requests.
  • Timeouts.
  • Request queue duration.
  • End-to-end latency.
  • Token counts.
Layer 2: Inference metrics
  • TTFT.
  • TPOT.
  • ITL.
  • Prefill throughput.
  • Decode throughput.
  • Active sequences.
  • KV-cache utilization.
  • Prefix-cache hit rate.
  • Preemption count.
Layer 3: Infrastructure metrics
  • GPU utilization.
  • GPU memory utilization.
  • GPU power.
  • Memory bandwidth, where measurable.
  • CPU utilization.
  • Host memory.
  • Network throughput.
  • Inter-GPU communication.
Layer 4: Business metrics
  • Cost per successful request.
  • Cost per million input tokens.
  • Cost per million output tokens.
  • Cost per completed agent task.
  • Requests per tenant.
  • Model quality.
  • SLO compliance.
23.1 Prometheus and Grafana

A common architecture uses:

  • Prometheus for metrics collection.
  • Grafana for dashboards.
  • OpenTelemetry for traces.
  • Centralized log aggregation.

vLLM exposes production metrics through its metrics endpoint.

SGLang also supports Prometheus-oriented metrics.

Useful dashboards should make it possible to answer questions such as:

  • Is TTFT increasing because of queueing or prefill?
  • Is decode throughput falling because of memory pressure?
  • Is the KV cache approaching capacity?
  • Are requests being preempted?
  • Are prefix-cache hit rates deteriorating?
  • Is one replica receiving disproportionately more traffic?
  • Is GPU utilization high while useful token throughput remains low?

A good dashboard should help an engineer move from symptom to cause.

23.2 Distributed tracing

For agentic applications, tracing is essential.

One user request might trigger:

User request
  |
  +-- Agent planning call
  |
  +-- Search tool
  |
  +-- Summarization call
  |
  +-- Database query
  |
  +-- Verification call
  |
  +-- Final generation

Without distributed traces, you may see a 30-second response but have no idea which stage consumed the time.

Trace every stage with a shared request or task identifier.

24. Production reliability: The engineering that benchmarks do not reveal

A benchmark usually assumes a relatively controlled environment.

Production does not.

Real traffic contains:

  • Unexpectedly long prompts.
  • Malformed requests.
  • Client disconnections.
  • Bursty traffic.
  • Slow tool calls.
  • GPU failures.
  • Model loading delays.
  • Memory exhaustion.
  • Network interruptions.
  • Repeated retries.

Your inference platform must handle these conditions.

24.1 Admission control

Not every request should be accepted immediately.

The server should reject, defer, or degrade requests when accepting them would violate the SLOs of already-running workloads.

Admission decisions can consider:

  • Estimated prompt length.
  • Maximum output tokens.
  • Available KV capacity.
  • Queue depth.
  • Tenant quotas.
  • Request deadline.
24.2 Backpressure

If downstream model capacity is saturated, upstream components must receive that information.

Otherwise, queues grow without limit.

Use bounded queues, explicit timeouts, and appropriate overload responses.

24.3 Cancellation

When a client disconnects or cancels a request, the serving system should stop unnecessary generation and release resources.

This is especially important when agents abandon tasks or execute retries.

24.4 Retries

Retries can improve resilience but can also amplify overload.

Use:

  • Bounded retries.
  • Exponential backoff.
  • Jitter.
  • Idempotency where relevant.
  • Retry budgets.

Do not blindly retry requests that have already consumed substantial GPU resources.

24.5 Multi-tenancy

In a shared inference platform, different tenants may have different requirements.

Consider:

  • Request quotas.
  • Token quotas.
  • Priority classes.
  • Per-tenant concurrency.
  • Model access policies.
  • Cost attribution.
  • Isolation of sensitive workloads.

A platform serving several enterprise customers must not allow one tenant’s traffic spike to degrade everyone else’s experience.

25. Advanced optimization: Where serious inference engineering begins

Once the basic serving platform is stable, there are additional optimization opportunities.

25.1 Prefix-aware routing

Route requests to replicas with reusable KV prefixes when the benefit outweighs the additional queueing or load imbalance.

25.2 KV-cache offloading

Move selected cache data from GPU memory to host memory or other supported storage tiers.

This can increase effective cache capacity, but introduces transfer and retrieval latency.

25.3 Cache eviction policies

Cache capacity is finite.

The serving system needs to decide which entries to retain and which to evict.

Good policies depend on:

  • Reuse probability.
  • Prefix popularity.
  • Recency.
  • Memory pressure.
  • Request locality.
  • Expected future demand.
25.4 Kernel optimization

Attention and matrix-multiplication kernels have a substantial influence on inference speed.

Technologies such as FlashAttention and FlashInfer improve aspects of attention execution and memory access.

Kernel selection must match the model architecture, GPU generation, tensor shape, and numerical format.

25.5 CUDA graphs

CUDA graphs can reduce CPU launch overhead by capturing and replaying sequences of GPU operations.

This is useful when execution patterns are sufficiently compatible with graph capture.

However, graph capture introduces constraints around shapes, memory allocation, and execution behavior.

25.6 Continuous profiling

Use GPU profilers and runtime instrumentation to identify:

  • Kernel launch overhead.
  • Poor occupancy.
  • Memory stalls.
  • Communication overhead.
  • Kernel inefficiency.
  • Synchronization bottlenecks.

Never assume that an optimization helped simply because it sounds theoretically attractive.

Measure it.

26. Putting everything together: A practical inference engineering playbook

Let’s convert the concepts into a repeatable engineering process.

The production inference journey.

Imagine you are asked to serve an open-source 32B model for an enterprise application.

You have been given a GPU budget and must support interactive traffic.

How do you approach the problem?

Phase 1: Understand the workload

Collect:

  • Peak requests per second.
  • Average and peak concurrency.
  • Input-token distribution.
  • Output-token distribution.
  • Context-length requirements.
  • Agentic call amplification.
  • Streaming requirements.
  • Latency SLOs.
  • Tenant distribution.

Do not start with a GPU purchase.

Start with demand.

Phase 2: Understand the model

Inspect:

  • Parameter count.
  • Number of transformer layers.
  • Attention architecture.
  • KV-head count.
  • Head dimension.
  • Context length.
  • Precision.
  • Quantization compatibility.
  • Model-specific execution requirements.

Calculate approximate weight and KV-cache memory.

Phase 3: Select hardware

Compare available accelerators based on:

  • HBM capacity.
  • Memory bandwidth.
  • Compute capability.
  • Interconnect.
  • GPU availability.
  • Hourly cost.
  • Regional availability.

Check whether the model fits within a single GPU or requires parallelism.

Phase 4: Select the inference engine

Deploy both vLLM and SGLang when practical.

Use identical model revisions and hardware.

Benchmark representative workloads.

Evaluate cache reuse, structured generation, latency, throughput, and operational complexity.

Phase 5: Tune the runtime

Experiment systematically with:

  • Maximum model length.
  • Maximum active sequences.
  • KV-cache capacity.
  • Chunked prefill.
  • Prefix caching.
  • Quantization.
  • Tensor parallelism.
  • Speculative decoding.

Change one major variable at a time.

Phase 6: Build the platform

Introduce:

  • API gateway.
  • Inference gateway.
  • Authentication.
  • Request routing.
  • Bounded queues.
  • Model-serving replicas.
  • Kubernetes orchestration.
  • Prometheus.
  • Grafana.
  • OpenTelemetry.
Phase 7: Load test

Test:

  • Normal traffic.
  • Peak traffic.
  • Burst traffic.
  • Long-context requests.
  • Mixed prompt lengths.
  • Long generations.
  • Cache-hit and cache-miss scenarios.
  • Agentic workflows.
Phase 8: Optimize cost and goodput

Calculate:

  • Cost per million input tokens.
  • Cost per million output tokens.
  • Cost per successful request.
  • Cost per completed agent task.
  • SLO-compliant throughput.

Keep optimizing until the system meets its quality, latency, reliability, and cost objectives.

27. A worked production design: Serving 10,000 users

Let’s finish the engineering journey with a hypothetical deployment.

Suppose an enterprise application has:

  • Registered Users: 10,000
  • Peak Active Users: 1,000
  • Peak Concurrent LLM Requests: 200
  • Average Input Length: 2,000 tokens
  • Average Output Length: 500 tokens
  • Average Request Duration: 10 seconds
  • Target TTFT (p95): 1.5 seconds
  • Target TPOT (p95): 60 milliseconds

These are design assumptions, not guarantees or measured performance.

Step 1: Calculate demand

Request throughput

Input demand:

Output demand:

Peak Inference Demand Estimation: At 20 requests per second, with an average of 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens per request, the serving system must sustain 40,000 input tokens/sec and 10,000 output tokens/sec.
Step 2: Estimate KV-cache pressure

Assume an illustrative model with 128 KiB of KV cache per token.

If the 200 active sequences each retain an average of 4,000 tokens:

Estimated KV Cache Requirement: For 200 concurrent requests, each with 4,000 tokens, at 128 KiB per token, the total KV cache requirement is approximately 97.66 GiB.

This is the aggregate logical KV-cache requirement before accounting for prefix sharing, cache implementation overhead, block allocation, and any distributed cache strategy.

The actual memory required depends on how sequences are distributed across replicas and GPUs.

Step 3: Choose an architecture

A reasonable first design would be:

  • Multiple model-serving replicas.
  • vLLM as the initial general-purpose serving engine.
  • SGLang evaluated against representative agentic traffic.
  • A routing layer distributing requests.
  • A queue-aware scaling policy.
  • Prometheus and Grafana.
  • OpenTelemetry tracing.
  • Explicit per-tenant limits.
Step 4: Validate GPU count

Do not decide the GPU count from the 200 concurrent users alone.

Benchmark each candidate GPU configuration.

Measure:

  • Sustainable prefill throughput.
  • Sustainable decode throughput.
  • KV-cache capacity.
  • TTFT at the target concurrency.
  • TPOT at the target concurrency.
  • p95 and p99 latency.
  • Failure and preemption behavior.

Then calculate the GPU count independently for compute, memory, and latency constraints.

Step 5: Introduce agent-aware routing

If the application has several agent workflows, route:

  • Short classification tasks to smaller models.
  • General conversation to the standard model pool.
  • Long-context reasoning to a specialized pool.
  • Repeated structured agent calls to a cache-aware serving pool.
Step 6: Establish an operating envelope

Define the maximum sustainable request rate at which:

  • TTFT remains within target.
  • TPOT remains within target.
  • KV-cache pressure remains manageable.
  • Error rates remain acceptable.
  • Cost remains within budget.

This is the platform’s sustainable operating envelope.

It is far more valuable than knowing that a GPU once achieved a particular peak token throughput.

28. The future of inference engineering

Inference is evolving from a relatively simple model-execution problem into a sophisticated distributed-computing discipline.

Several trends are particularly important.

28.1 Agentic inference

Models are increasingly becoming components in larger systems that plan, execute, retrieve, verify, and interact with external tools.

This increases the importance of scheduling, cache reuse, workload routing, and cost controls.

28.2 Disaggregated architectures

Separating prefill, decode, and potentially other stages enables more specialized resource allocation.

28.3 More sophisticated KV-cache systems

KV caches are becoming first-class infrastructure resources.

Caching, offloading, compression, sharing, and eviction policies will increasingly influence platform economics.

28.4 Hardware-aware serving

The best serving configuration will increasingly depend on hardware topology, memory bandwidth, numerical precision, and specialized execution kernels.

28.5 Multi-model inference platforms

Production systems will not always use one large model for everything.

They will route requests across specialized models based on task complexity, quality requirements, latency, and cost.

28.6 Quality-adjusted inference economics

The objective will not simply be to generate more tokens.

It will be to generate useful, correct outputs at the lowest sustainable cost while meeting latency and reliability requirements.

That is a much more meaningful engineering objective.

29. Final thoughts: Inference is where AI meets systems engineering

We began with a simple user request.

We followed it through tokenization, prefill, decode, attention, KV-cache allocation, GPU memory, and scheduling.

We then explored how PagedAttention and RadixAttention address different aspects of the memory problem.

We examined continuous batching, chunked prefill, disaggregated serving, quantization, speculative decoding, and distributed parallelism.

Finally, we moved beyond the inference engine itself and designed a production platform involving gateways, routing, Kubernetes, autoscaling, observability, reliability, and cost controls.

There is one idea I want you to take away from this entire journey:

The objective of inference engineering is not to make a model generate tokens as quickly as possible. It is to maximize useful, quality-preserving, SLO-compliant work per unit of compute and cost.

That distinction separates someone who can deploy a model from someone who can architect an inference platform.

A fast model is useful.

A memory-efficient model is better.

A well-scheduled model is better still.

But a system that can serve thousands of users predictably, economically, and reliably, while supporting complex agentic workflows, is where real inference engineering begins.

And that is the engineering challenge worth mastering.

30. Your inference engineering learning roadmap

If you have reached this point, here is the sequence I recommend for turning the concepts into practical expertise.

LLM Inference and Serving: 11 Stages to Master

  1. Transformer Inference, Prefill and Decode — Understand how tokens are processed and generated.
  2. GPU Architecture and Memory — Estimate compute, memory, and bandwidth requirements.
  3. KV Cache and Attention Architectures — Calculate memory consumption and concurrency limits.
  4. PagedAttention and RadixAttention — Understand KV-cache memory efficiency and prefix reuse.
  5. vLLM and SGLang — Deploy, configure, and compare inference engines.
  6. Benchmarking and SLOs — Quantify throughput, latency, and serving performance.
  7. Quantization and Speculative Decoding — Optimize inference speed, memory consumption, and execution efficiency.
  8. Tensor, Pipeline and Data Parallelism — Serve larger models across multiple GPUs and nodes.
  9. Kubernetes and Inference Gateways — Build and orchestrate distributed inference platforms.
  10. Observability and Cost Engineering — Monitor production infrastructure, reliability, utilization, and inference costs.
  11. Agentic Inference — Optimize multi-step AI workloads, tool calls, and cumulative token consumption.

A useful exercise is to take one open-source model and serve it through both vLLM and SGLang.

Keep the hardware, model revision, precision, and request distribution identical.

Then measure:

  • TTFT.
  • TPOT.
  • Throughput.
  • KV-cache utilization.
  • GPU memory.
  • Cost per million generated tokens.

Repeat with a shared-prefix workload and a long-context workload.

You will learn more from a disciplined comparison like this than from memorizing dozens of inference-engine configuration flags.

Resources and references

This article draws on foundational research, official inference-engine documentation, GPU architecture references, benchmarking guidance, and the learning resources listed below. Documentation and CLI interfaces evolve, so always consult the current version before reproducing a configuration.

B. Foundational research papers

C. Inference engine documentation

items.title: AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part.
items.summary: This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It covers more than 200 AWS services and was written entirely by agents. The most useful part of the launch is a story Swami Sivasubramanian tells in the announcement. About 20 years ago, Sivasubramanian helped build the replication engine inside Alf, a Paxos-based lock service that still powers AWS systems such as S3 and DynamoDB. The first build took about four months. When he later asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to rebuild it, he supervised the agent for four nights before he saw the problem: The agent had no way to check its own results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours. Same agent, same task. Four nights became two hours because the feedback loop changed. “An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against.” As Sivasubramanian puts it, distributed systems are hard to test. That matches what I see across teams running coding agents on production systems. An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against. AWS Emulator solves that for the AWS APIs your code calls. It does not solve it for the services your team owns, and that is where most agent-written changes break. AWS puts infrastructure inside the agent’s loop A coding agent works in a loop. It writes code, runs it, reads the result, and decides what to change next. Sivasubramanian’s point is that in distributed systems, that loop runs inside infrastructure. If the services the code calls do not behave like the real ones, the agent learns the wrong lesson and keeps going. AWS Emulator puts AWS into that loop on a laptop. Point existing AWS tools and code at it with one environment variable, and tests run against emulated services without changes. Autonomous agents wrote every line of the emulator, working from AWS’s public API models. Each behavior is pinned by a fidelity test that first passes against real AWS, then against the emulator, and every change passes a merge gate where security agents review it. Sivasubramanian’s conclusion is that when agents write the code, the engineer’s job is to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when the work is correct. The first reactions on Hacker News went straight to trust. One commenter counted roughly 30,000 commits in three weeks and questioned the quality. That is a fair question aimed at the wrong thing. Who wrote the code tells you little. What it was verified against tells you a lot, and AWS’s answer is real AWS. “Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.” What changed is who runs the loop. A developer checks a change a few times a day, and an agent checks it on every iteration. Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all. Every loop runs against mocks, an emulator, or the running system An agent can verify its work against one of three things, and each has a different weakness. Mocks are the weakest option, and AI has made them cheap. One Hacker News commenter argued that it is now faster to have AI mock your APIs , adding that “AI has been a boon for test coverage.” But an agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not. Emulators are a real step up. AWS Emulator is checked against real AWS, so its behavior comes from the service rather than from the agent. An emulator is still a model, though, and AWS is open about that. The repository keeps a folder of behaviors the agents found that do not match real AWS yet, and operations that are not implemented return an error instead of a fake success. An IDC analyst noted that at launch the emulator does not simulate throttling, outages, or per-Region availability, which is where retry and failover logic gets exercised. “An agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.” Sivasubramanian says as much about his own work on Alf. Simulation ironed out most of its concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing on real servers then turned up different problems, because “the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.” You can’t emulate your own system the way AWS emulated its own In the same HN thread, a self-described Amazonian outlined the approach most teams take with agents today: Close off as much of the system as possible, mock or simulate the dependencies that cannot be closed off, then let the agent loose. That works when the part you cannot close off is a cloud API with a published spec. It breaks down when that part is your own system. AWS Emulator works because AWS had two things most teams will never have for their own software: a complete, machine-readable spec of every operation and a stable reference to check against in real AWS. Now picture a payments platform with 60 microservices. The contracts between those services live in code, in a few OpenAPI files that drifted months ago and in the heads of the engineers who wrote them. There is no single spec, and the reference implementation is the running system itself, which changes every time someone merges. With agents opening pull requests (PRs) multiple times a day, it changes faster than any model of it could keep up with. That is also where agent-written application code tends to break. The failures are rarely about how a managed queue handles a visibility timeout. They are a field renamed in one service that a consumer two teams away still reads, an event payload a downstream service does not expect, a query that is fast on fixtures and slow on production-sized data, or configuration, feature flags and secrets that only exist in the cluster. No emulator of a cloud provider will ever see them. The environment belongs on the engineer’s list Sivasubramanian lists specs, tests, and merge gates as the engineer’s job now. I would add the environment, because it decides what the agent can catch. A realistic loop has six properties. The change runs in a production-like environment , next to the services, data, and configuration it will ship into. Each change gets its own isolated environment, so 10 agents working in parallel do not step on each other. The environment starts in seconds, because an agent that waits 20 minutes stops using it and the loop collapses back to unit tests. And the agent creates the environment and reads results itself, without filing a ticket. The loop also runs the integration and end-to-end suites the team already trusts, not tests the agent wrote to agree with itself. And it produces evidence a reviewer or merge gate can act on before the change merges. The hard part is getting production-like fidelity and fast startup at the same time. Cloning a full stack for every change buys fidelity and loses on speed and cost. A team of 10 engineers running multiple parallel agent sessions might produce 100 PRs a day or more that need to be verified. No team can justify the cost of 100+ full copies of the system. Emulate what you don’t own, and run what you own for real Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop. For managed cloud services with published contracts, an emulator gives agents fast, free feedback on a laptop. If a service writes to S3 and reads from a queue, AWS Emulator catches API misuse in seconds without touching an AWS account. “Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.” For the system you own, deploy only what the change modifies instead of cloning the stack. Requests and messages tagged for that change’s environment reach the new versions, and everything else is served by the shared stable environment that is already running. Databases and queues get lightweight per-environment schemas or topics only where the change needs data isolation. That is how an environment starts in seconds and still behaves like production. Uber and Lyft built internal systems on this model for the same reason. Then make the merge gate ask for both. A PR that passed against an emulator and against the system it is joining is one a reviewer can trust. Every agent will have a loop, and realism is what separates them Sivasubramanian’s agent went from four nights to two hours once it could check its own work. For application teams, the next jump depends on what it checks against. An emulator covers the cloud APIs you call, and only the running system covers the services you own. Having a verification loop is now expected. The realism of that loop is what decides how much you can trust the code that comes out of it. If you want your agents verifying every change in a production-like environment before merge, we built Signadot to make that the default.
items.summary_html:
This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It covers more than 200 AWS services and was written entirely by agents. The most useful part of the launch is a story Swami Sivasubramanian tells in the announcement.

About 20 years ago, Sivasubramanian helped build the replication engine inside Alf, a Paxos-based lock service that still powers AWS systems such as S3 and DynamoDB. The first build took about four months. When he later asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to rebuild it, he supervised the agent for four nights before he saw the problem: The agent had no way to check its own results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

Same agent, same task. Four nights became two hours because the feedback loop changed.

“An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against.”

As Sivasubramanian puts it, distributed systems are hard to test. That matches what I see across teams running coding agents on production systems. An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against. AWS Emulator solves that for the AWS APIs your code calls. It does not solve it for the services your team owns, and that is where most agent-written changes break.

AWS puts infrastructure inside the agent’s loop

A coding agent works in a loop. It writes code, runs it, reads the result, and decides what to change next. Sivasubramanian’s point is that in distributed systems, that loop runs inside infrastructure. If the services the code calls do not behave like the real ones, the agent learns the wrong lesson and keeps going.

AWS Emulator puts AWS into that loop on a laptop. Point existing AWS tools and code at it with one environment variable, and tests run against emulated services without changes.

Autonomous agents wrote every line of the emulator, working from AWS’s public API models. Each behavior is pinned by a fidelity test that first passes against real AWS, then against the emulator, and every change passes a merge gate where security agents review it. Sivasubramanian’s conclusion is that when agents write the code, the engineer’s job is to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when the work is correct.

The first reactions on Hacker News went straight to trust. One commenter counted roughly 30,000 commits in three weeks and questioned the quality. That is a fair question aimed at the wrong thing. Who wrote the code tells you little. What it was verified against tells you a lot, and AWS’s answer is real AWS.

“Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.”

What changed is who runs the loop. A developer checks a change a few times a day, and an agent checks it on every iteration. Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.

Every loop runs against mocks, an emulator, or the running system

An agent can verify its work against one of three things, and each has a different weakness.

Mocks are the weakest option, and AI has made them cheap. One Hacker News commenter argued that it is now faster to have AI mock your APIs, adding that “AI has been a boon for test coverage.” But an agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.

Emulators are a real step up. AWS Emulator is checked against real AWS, so its behavior comes from the service rather than from the agent.

An emulator is still a model, though, and AWS is open about that. The repository keeps a folder of behaviors the agents found that do not match real AWS yet, and operations that are not implemented return an error instead of a fake success. An IDC analyst noted that at launch the emulator does not simulate throttling, outages, or per-Region availability, which is where retry and failover logic gets exercised.

“An agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.”

Sivasubramanian says as much about his own work on Alf. Simulation ironed out most of its concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing on real servers then turned up different problems, because “the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.”

You can’t emulate your own system the way AWS emulated its own

In the same HN thread, a self-described Amazonian outlined the approach most teams take with agents today: Close off as much of the system as possible, mock or simulate the dependencies that cannot be closed off, then let the agent loose. That works when the part you cannot close off is a cloud API with a published spec. It breaks down when that part is your own system.

AWS Emulator works because AWS had two things most teams will never have for their own software: a complete, machine-readable spec of every operation and a stable reference to check against in real AWS.

Now picture a payments platform with 60 microservices. The contracts between those services live in code, in a few OpenAPI files that drifted months ago and in the heads of the engineers who wrote them. There is no single spec, and the reference implementation is the running system itself, which changes every time someone merges. With agents opening pull requests (PRs) multiple times a day, it changes faster than any model of it could keep up with.

That is also where agent-written application code tends to break. The failures are rarely about how a managed queue handles a visibility timeout. They are a field renamed in one service that a consumer two teams away still reads, an event payload a downstream service does not expect, a query that is fast on fixtures and slow on production-sized data, or configuration, feature flags and secrets that only exist in the cluster. No emulator of a cloud provider will ever see them.

The environment belongs on the engineer’s list

Sivasubramanian lists specs, tests, and merge gates as the engineer’s job now. I would add the environment, because it decides what the agent can catch.

A realistic loop has six properties. The change runs in a production-like environment, next to the services, data, and configuration it will ship into. Each change gets its own isolated environment, so 10 agents working in parallel do not step on each other. The environment starts in seconds, because an agent that waits 20 minutes stops using it and the loop collapses back to unit tests. And the agent creates the environment and reads results itself, without filing a ticket.

The loop also runs the integration and end-to-end suites the team already trusts, not tests the agent wrote to agree with itself. And it produces evidence a reviewer or merge gate can act on before the change merges.

The hard part is getting production-like fidelity and fast startup at the same time. Cloning a full stack for every change buys fidelity and loses on speed and cost. A team of 10 engineers running multiple parallel agent sessions might produce 100 PRs a day or more that need to be verified. No team can justify the cost of 100+ full copies of the system.

Emulate what you don’t own, and run what you own for real

Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.

For managed cloud services with published contracts, an emulator gives agents fast, free feedback on a laptop. If a service writes to S3 and reads from a queue, AWS Emulator catches API misuse in seconds without touching an AWS account.

“Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.”

For the system you own, deploy only what the change modifies instead of cloning the stack. Requests and messages tagged for that change’s environment reach the new versions, and everything else is served by the shared stable environment that is already running. Databases and queues get lightweight per-environment schemas or topics only where the change needs data isolation. That is how an environment starts in seconds and still behaves like production. Uber and Lyft built internal systems on this model for the same reason.

Then make the merge gate ask for both. A PR that passed against an emulator and against the system it is joining is one a reviewer can trust.

Every agent will have a loop, and realism is what separates them

Sivasubramanian’s agent went from four nights to two hours once it could check its own work. For application teams, the next jump depends on what it checks against. An emulator covers the cloud APIs you call, and only the running system covers the services you own.

Having a verification loop is now expected. The realism of that loop is what decides how much you can trust the code that comes out of it. If you want your agents verifying every change in a production-like environment before merge, we built Signadot to make that the default.

The post AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part. appeared first on The New Stack.

items.title: Onboarding UI Design for AI Builders and Vibe Coders: 12 Real App Examples With Copy-Paste Prompts
items.summary: Welcome screens, sign-up choices and permission asks from 64 popular apps, scored on 10 details, and turned into prompts for Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Cursor. Cover with the words Onboarding UI, 12 real app examples, and app icons from Arc Search, Bevel, Headspace, Grab, Walmart, Duolingo, Monzo, Public, Strava, Instagram, Zomato and Spotify as stickers Most AI-built apps open the same way: a logo, a sign-up form, and then the system asking for notifications before anyone knows what the app does. Each of those is a moment people leave, and it's the part of an app that AI builders almost never design on purpose. This guide is for people who build: AI builders shipping with Lovable, Bolt or v0, mobile developers in Expo or React Native, and founders vibe-coding in Cursor or Claude Code who want their first minute to feel as considered as the rest of the app. We went through 141 welcome, sign-up and permission screens from 64 popular apps and scored every app on 10 details. Here are the numbers, the 12 screens worth copying, and a prompt for each that you can paste into your AI builder. How to use the prompts Lovable, Bolt or v0: build the welcome screen first, then sign-up, then each permission ask as its own message. Say where each one appears ("after the first saved item"). Cursor or Claude Code: ask it to wire the permission prompts to the real APIs (expo-notifications, expo-location, the Notification API on web), so the pre-ask triggers the system dialog. Replace the [brackets] with real examples from your app. A sample notification about your own product beats any generic copy. Keep your brand. The prompts describe layout and behaviour, not colours. Add "use my existing theme" if the tool starts restyling things. What 64 real onboarding flows do Scored from 141 welcome, sign-up and permission screens in 64 iOS apps, captured in 2026. An app counts once if any of its screens shows the detail. Permission asks have grown up. Most apps now explain why before the system prompt appears (38 of 64), and 25 show their own notification screen first, the pattern that protects your one chance to get a "yes" from iOS. Welcome screens haven't caught up. Only 11 apps show the real product on their first screen, and only 9 let you look around before making an account. For an AI-built app nobody has heard of yet, those two are the biggest levers in this post: show what it does, then let people try it. If you build only one thing from this post, build this kit. Seven pieces, how many of the 64 apps use each, and the app to copy: Each of these is one prompt in the examples below or in the starter prompt at the end. 1. The welcome screen: show, don't tell The first screen has one job: make it obvious what the app does. The best ones show the product itself. Arc Search: the welcome screen is a demo Arc Search screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Arc doesn't describe its AI search. It shows you the exact thing to tap. "Let Arc search and summarize for you" with the key words in italics. One sentence, one promise. A phone showing the real search screen with "Try it!" and a hand-drawn arrow. Real example searches, each with a "Browse for Me" button: the feature you'll use, already explained. The keyboard is up. It looks ready to use, because it nearly is. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Make the first onboarding screen of my app a live demo. Full-bleed [brand gradient] background, a two-line headline "Let [App] [do the main job] for you" with the key verbs in italics. Below, a phone frame containing a real screenshot or live component of [the main feature], with a handwritten "Try it!" label and a curved arrow pointing at [the key button]. Show 4–5 realistic example rows inside the frame. A primary "Next" button sits at the bottom; on web, render the frame as a scaled real component instead of an image. Bevel: one feature per slide, shown as real cards Bevel screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Bevel's onboarding carousel uses its actual UI components as the illustrations. "Sleep" in big type, with one line on what it does: "Discover your sleep patterns to achieve consistent rest." Real sleep cards from the app: Optimized rest, Deep sleep 1h 21m, Daily sleep report. You see exactly what you'll get. Five dots show how many slides there are. One "Continue" button, the same on every slide. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Create a 4–5 slide onboarding carousel for my app. Each slide: a large feature name ("[Sleep]"), one grey line on the benefit, and a cluster of 2–3 real UI cards from my app rendered as components with sample data (not illustrations), slightly overlapping with soft shadows. Page dots above a full-width dark "Continue" button that advances the slide; swiping also works. On the last slide, the button changes to "Get started". Add a "Skip" link in the top right. Headspace: every sign-in option, one tap each Headspace screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Headspace's account screen offers five ways in and makes them all look equally easy. Friendly brand shapes instead of a logo, so the screen feels like the app. "Create an account" as the only heading. Continue with Apple, Google, Facebook or Email, each a full-width outlined button with its logo. "Continue with SSO" for people signing in through work. "Already have an account? Log in" at the bottom. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Build my sign-up screen: a brand illustration at the top, the heading "Create an account", then full-width outlined buttons with logos, in this order: "Continue with Apple", "Continue with Google", "Continue with Email" (opens an email form). Add "Continue with SSO" only if [I support workplace login]. Under them, "Already have an account? Log in". Use [Supabase Auth] for the providers and send new users straight into the app, not to a profile form. 2. Let people in before you ask for an account An account is a commitment. These apps make it easy to look around first. Grab: the app first, the account later Grab screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Grab opens straight into its real home screen, and the sign-up sits at the bottom like a welcome mat. The real home screen, working: search, Transport, Bike, Food, Mart. You can see the whole app. "Claim your free welcome perks" with discount cards. A reason to sign up, not a demand. "Sign Up" and "Log In" side by side in a panel at the bottom. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Let new users into my app without an account. Show the real home screen with [browseable content] immediately, and overlay a bottom panel (not blocking scrolling above it) with a welcome banner "[Claim your welcome offer]", 3–4 small offer cards, and two buttons side by side: "Sign up" (primary) and "Log in". Only require sign-in when the user tries to [order/save/post], and then bring them back to exactly what they were doing. Walmart: say what an account is for, then offer guest Walmart screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Walmart lists what signing in gets you, and puts "Continue as guest" right under it. A bright illustration of what you can do: pay, track, pick up. Four page dots, so you know this is a short tour. "Welcome to Walmart. Sign in to track orders and earn Walmart Cash…" Each reason is a real benefit. A small "Sign in" button, not a giant one. "Continue as guest". The way around is on the same screen. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: On my welcome screen, show a brand illustration, a short page indicator, the heading "Welcome to [App]", and one sentence listing 2–3 concrete benefits of an account ("Sign in to [track orders], [earn rewards] and [get faster checkout]."). Under it, a primary "Sign in" pill button and a text link "Continue as guest" that drops the user into the app with a temporary local session that can be upgraded to an account later without losing data. Duolingo: start learning, sign up later Duolingo screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Duolingo's welcome screen has three words that do all the work: "Learn for free. Forever." Duo and the wordmark, centred, on white. "Learn for free. Forever." The one objection people have, answered on the first screen. "GET STARTED" in the brand green. It goes straight into a lesson, not a form. "I ALREADY HAVE AN ACCOUNT" as an outlined second button. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Design my first screen with my logo and name centred, and under it a one-line promise that removes the biggest objection ("[Learn for free. Forever.]"). At the bottom: a primary "Get started" button that starts [the core experience] immediately without an account, and an outlined "I already have an account" button. After the user finishes [their first task], show a "Save your progress" screen that asks them to create an account. 3. Asking for notifications iOS only lets you ask once. These apps earn the yes on their own screen before the system dialog appears. Monzo: show the notification you'll get Monzo screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Instead of describing notifications, Monzo shows one, written for you. "£20 at EE. This is £3 more than last month" as a real-looking notification, plus a second one stacked behind it. "Notifications keep you up to date on money coming into and going out of your account." Why it matters, in one sentence. "Turn Notifications On" as the main button. This is what triggers the iOS prompt. "I don't want notifications". Honest wording, and just as easy to tap. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Before requesting push permission, show a screen with the title "Notifications" and two stacked mock notification cards from my app with real-looking, personal content (app icon, app name, "[£20 at EE]", "[This is £3 more than last month]"). Under them, one sentence on what notifications help with. Buttons: primary "Turn notifications on" that calls the real permission request (expo-notifications or the web Notification API), and a secondary "I don't want notifications" that continues without asking. Never call the system prompt before this screen. Public: one example, one list, one skip Public screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Public's notification ask sits inside the sign-up progress bar, so it feels like a step, not a pop-up. "About you" with a progress bar, so this is clearly part of setting up. "AAPL Earnings. Reports robust Q2 earnings." One real-looking notification on a soft card. "Enable investing notifications" and a list of exactly what you'll hear about: price moves, income payments, earnings, transfers. A dark "Enable notifications" button at the bottom. "Skip for now". "For now" means you'll be asked again later. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Add a notification step to my sign-up flow, shown with the same progress bar as the other steps. Centre: a soft card holding one realistic notification from my app ([icon], "[AAPL Earnings]", "[Reports robust Q2 earnings.]"). Below: the heading "Enable [investing] notifications" and one sentence listing the specific alerts users get. Buttons: dark full-width "Enable notifications" (triggers the system prompt) and a text "Skip for now" that moves to the next step and schedules a re-ask after [the user's first trade]. Strava: tell people what the next tap is Strava screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Strava knows the system dialog comes next, and it says so. A bell icon above the headline. "Don't miss a thing. Allow notifications so you can track each step of your journey." The benefit before the ask. A Strava notification over an orange swoosh: "Way to go. Kudos for an activity in the books!" A friendly, real example. "Make sure you select 'Allow' on the next step…" Small text that prepares people for the iOS dialog. "Choose permissions" as the button, honest about what happens next. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Create a notification pre-permission screen: a bell icon, the headline "Don't miss a thing", one line on the benefit, and a sample notification card from my app on a brand-coloured shape ("[Way to go 👏] [Kudos for your activity]"). Above the button, small grey text: "Make sure you select 'Allow' on the next step to receive notifications from [App]." Primary button "Choose permissions" triggers the real system prompt and then continues onboarding whatever the answer. 4. Other permissions: say why, and offer a way around Camera, photos, location and Bluetooth asks work best with a reason and an alternative. Instagram: three questions answered before the camera roll Instagram screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Photo access is personal. Instagram answers how, why and what if before asking. "Allow Instagram to access your photos and videos" as a plain headline. "How you'll use this": add photos and videos and apply effects. "How we'll use this": to let you share and suggest photos. The company's side, said out loud. "How these settings work": you can change it anytime in device settings. One "Continue" button. No pressure, no trick wording. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Before requesting [photo library] access, show a sheet with an icon, the headline "Allow [App] to access your [photos and videos]", and three short sections, each with an icon: "How you'll use this" ([what the user can do]), "How we'll use this" ([what the app does with it, honestly]) and "How these settings work" ("You can change your choice at any time in your device settings."). One primary "Continue" button that calls the real permission API, and limited access handled gracefully if the user picks only some photos. Zomato: always offer the manual way Zomato screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Location makes food delivery work, but Zomato never makes it the only option. "Set your location to start exploring restaurants near you". The reason is in the headline. A 3D city illustration with a pin and restaurants around it. "Enable Device Location" as the main button. "Enter Your Location Manually". Saying no to the permission doesn't mean leaving the app. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: Build a location step for my app: a headline that includes the reason ("Set your location to [find X near you]"), a friendly map illustration, a primary "Enable device location" button that requests permission (expo-location or navigator.geolocation), and an outlined "Enter your location manually" button that opens an address search with autocomplete. If permission is denied, go straight to the manual search instead of showing an error. Spotify: why, and who's in control Spotify screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below. Bluetooth and local network access sound technical. Spotify translates them into one short reason. Speakers, phones, laptops and TVs floating together. The illustration shows the benefit: play anywhere. "Allow Spotify to access Bluetooth and your local network". The headline says exactly what's being asked. "Why do you need this? To find and play on all your devices." The reason, as a question and answer. "You're in control. Change permissions at any time in Settings." Reassurance. A green "Continue" pill. The system prompt comes next. Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor: For technical permissions like [Bluetooth or local network], show a dark screen with an illustration of the benefit, a headline that names the permission plainly ("Allow [App] to access [Bluetooth and your local network]"), and two short rows with icons: "Why do you need this?" with a one-line answer, and "You're in control" with "Change permissions at any time in Settings." One "Continue" button triggers the system prompt; if it's denied, the related feature shows an inline "Turn on in Settings" link later instead of blocking. The onboarding checklist Show the real product on the first screen, not a mascot and a slogan. Answer the biggest objection in one line ("Free. Forever.", "No card needed"). Let people try before signing up, and ask for an account when there's something to save. Offer Apple and Google sign-in first, then email. Never trigger a system permission prompt cold. Show your own screen first. Use a real example of the notification people will get. Say why for every permission, in the headline or one line under it. Give a real alternative: "Enter location manually", "Skip for now". Ask at the moment it matters, such as notifications after the first order, not on launch. Keep it short: a progress bar if there are more than three steps. Copy the starter prompt: a complete onboarding flow: Build my app's onboarding flow using my existing theme and [Supabase Auth]. 1) Welcome: one screen (or a 3–4 slide carousel) that shows real UI components of [the main feature] with sample data, a one-line promise, "Get started" and "I already have an account". 2) Let users into [the core experience] without an account; store their work locally. 3) Ask for an account when they first [save/order/share]: Continue with Apple, Continue with Google, Continue with email, then migrate their local data into the new account. 4) Notifications: after the first [success moment], show my own pre-ask screen with two realistic sample notifications, "Turn notifications on" (calls the real permission API) and "Not now" (re-ask after 7 days, at most twice). 5) For location, camera or photos: a screen or sheet that names the permission, explains why in one line, says it can be changed in Settings, and offers a manual alternative if denied. 6) Show a progress bar if there are more than three steps, and never trigger a system prompt without my own screen first. Onboarding UI FAQ What should the first onboarding screen show? What the app does, ideally by showing the real product. Only 11 of the 64 apps we studied show actual UI on their welcome screen; Arc Search and Bevel are the best examples, using real components as the illustration. Should users sign up before using the app? Not if you can avoid it. Only 9 of 64 apps let people look around first, and the ones that do, like Grab, Walmart and Duolingo, ask for an account when there's something to save or buy. How do I ask for push notification permission? Show your own screen before the system dialog, with a real example notification and a "Not now" option. 25 of 64 apps use their own pre-ask; the best, like Monzo and Public, show exactly what a notification from them looks like. Should I offer Sign in with Apple and Google? Yes. 27 of 64 apps offer one-tap sign-in with Apple or Google, and Apple requires Sign in with Apple if you offer other third-party logins in an iOS app. How do I build onboarding with Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor? Build it in order: welcome, try-first, sign-up, then each permission ask, and tell the AI to wire the asks to real permission APIs. Each example above has a prompt for one screen, and the starter prompt builds the whole flow. How we did this We looked at 141 screens tagged as welcome, get-started or permission screens in 64 iOS apps, captured in 2026, and scored each app once per detail if any of its screens showed it. All product names belong to their owners. The screens are shown to discuss design; no app on this page endorses this article. Onboarding UI Design for AI Builders and Vibe Coders: 12 Real App Examples With Copy-Paste Prompts was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Welcome screens haven't caught up. Only 11 apps show the real product on their first screen, and only 9 let you look around before making an account. For an AI-built app nobody has heard of yet, those two are the biggest levers in this post: show what it does, then let people try it.

If you build only one thing from this post, build this kit. Seven pieces, how many of the 64 apps use each, and the app to copy:

Each of these is one prompt in the examples below or in the starter prompt at the end.1. The welcome screen: show, don't tell

The first screen has one job: make it obvious what the app does. The best ones show the product itself.

Arc Search: the welcome screen is a demoArc Search screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Arc doesn't describe its AI search. It shows you the exact thing to tap.

  1. "Let Arc search and summarize for you" with the key words in italics. One sentence, one promise.
  2. A phone showing the real search screen with "Try it!" and a hand-drawn arrow.
  3. Real example searches, each with a "Browse for Me" button: the feature you'll use, already explained.
  4. The keyboard is up. It looks ready to use, because it nearly is.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Make the first onboarding screen of my app a live demo. Full-bleed [brand gradient] background, a two-line headline "Let [App] [do the main job] for you" with the key verbs in italics. Below, a phone frame containing a real screenshot or live component of [the main feature], with a handwritten "Try it!" label and a curved arrow pointing at [the key button]. Show 4–5 realistic example rows inside the frame. A primary "Next" button sits at the bottom; on web, render the frame as a scaled real component instead of an image.
Bevel: one feature per slide, shown as real cardsBevel screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Bevel's onboarding carousel uses its actual UI components as the illustrations.

  1. "Sleep" in big type, with one line on what it does: "Discover your sleep patterns to achieve consistent rest."
  2. Real sleep cards from the app: Optimized rest, Deep sleep 1h 21m, Daily sleep report. You see exactly what you'll get.
  3. Five dots show how many slides there are.
  4. One "Continue" button, the same on every slide.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Create a 4–5 slide onboarding carousel for my app. Each slide: a large feature name ("[Sleep]"), one grey line on the benefit, and a cluster of 2–3 real UI cards from my app rendered as components with sample data (not illustrations), slightly overlapping with soft shadows. Page dots above a full-width dark "Continue" button that advances the slide; swiping also works. On the last slide, the button changes to "Get started". Add a "Skip" link in the top right.
Headspace: every sign-in option, one tap eachHeadspace screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Headspace's account screen offers five ways in and makes them all look equally easy.

  1. Friendly brand shapes instead of a logo, so the screen feels like the app.
  2. "Create an account" as the only heading.
  3. Continue with Apple, Google, Facebook or Email, each a full-width outlined button with its logo.
  4. "Continue with SSO" for people signing in through work.
  5. "Already have an account? Log in" at the bottom.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Build my sign-up screen: a brand illustration at the top, the heading "Create an account", then full-width outlined buttons with logos, in this order: "Continue with Apple", "Continue with Google", "Continue with Email" (opens an email form). Add "Continue with SSO" only if [I support workplace login]. Under them, "Already have an account? Log in". Use [Supabase Auth] for the providers and send new users straight into the app, not to a profile form.
2. Let people in before you ask for an account

An account is a commitment. These apps make it easy to look around first.

Grab: the app first, the account laterGrab screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Grab opens straight into its real home screen, and the sign-up sits at the bottom like a welcome mat.

  1. The real home screen, working: search, Transport, Bike, Food, Mart. You can see the whole app.
  2. "Claim your free welcome perks" with discount cards. A reason to sign up, not a demand.
  3. "Sign Up" and "Log In" side by side in a panel at the bottom.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Let new users into my app without an account. Show the real home screen with [browseable content] immediately, and overlay a bottom panel (not blocking scrolling above it) with a welcome banner "[Claim your welcome offer]", 3–4 small offer cards, and two buttons side by side: "Sign up" (primary) and "Log in". Only require sign-in when the user tries to [order/save/post], and then bring them back to exactly what they were doing.
Walmart: say what an account is for, then offer guestWalmart screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Walmart lists what signing in gets you, and puts "Continue as guest" right under it.

  1. A bright illustration of what you can do: pay, track, pick up.
  2. Four page dots, so you know this is a short tour.
  3. "Welcome to Walmart. Sign in to track orders and earn Walmart Cash…" Each reason is a real benefit.
  4. A small "Sign in" button, not a giant one.
  5. "Continue as guest". The way around is on the same screen.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

On my welcome screen, show a brand illustration, a short page indicator, the heading "Welcome to [App]", and one sentence listing 2–3 concrete benefits of an account ("Sign in to [track orders], [earn rewards] and [get faster checkout]."). Under it, a primary "Sign in" pill button and a text link "Continue as guest" that drops the user into the app with a temporary local session that can be upgraded to an account later without losing data.
Duolingo: start learning, sign up laterDuolingo screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Duolingo's welcome screen has three words that do all the work: "Learn for free. Forever."

  1. Duo and the wordmark, centred, on white.
  2. "Learn for free. Forever." The one objection people have, answered on the first screen.
  3. "GET STARTED" in the brand green. It goes straight into a lesson, not a form.
  4. "I ALREADY HAVE AN ACCOUNT" as an outlined second button.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Design my first screen with my logo and name centred, and under it a one-line promise that removes the biggest objection ("[Learn for free. Forever.]"). At the bottom: a primary "Get started" button that starts [the core experience] immediately without an account, and an outlined "I already have an account" button. After the user finishes [their first task], show a "Save your progress" screen that asks them to create an account.
3. Asking for notifications

iOS only lets you ask once. These apps earn the yes on their own screen before the system dialog appears.

Monzo: show the notification you'll getMonzo screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Instead of describing notifications, Monzo shows one, written for you.

  1. "£20 at EE. This is £3 more than last month" as a real-looking notification, plus a second one stacked behind it.
  2. "Notifications keep you up to date on money coming into and going out of your account." Why it matters, in one sentence.
  3. "Turn Notifications On" as the main button. This is what triggers the iOS prompt.
  4. "I don't want notifications". Honest wording, and just as easy to tap.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Before requesting push permission, show a screen with the title "Notifications" and two stacked mock notification cards from my app with real-looking, personal content (app icon, app name, "[£20 at EE]", "[This is £3 more than last month]"). Under them, one sentence on what notifications help with. Buttons: primary "Turn notifications on" that calls the real permission request (expo-notifications or the web Notification API), and a secondary "I don't want notifications" that continues without asking. Never call the system prompt before this screen.
Public: one example, one list, one skipPublic screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Public's notification ask sits inside the sign-up progress bar, so it feels like a step, not a pop-up.

  1. "About you" with a progress bar, so this is clearly part of setting up.
  2. "AAPL Earnings. Reports robust Q2 earnings." One real-looking notification on a soft card.
  3. "Enable investing notifications" and a list of exactly what you'll hear about: price moves, income payments, earnings, transfers.
  4. A dark "Enable notifications" button at the bottom.
  5. "Skip for now". "For now" means you'll be asked again later.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Add a notification step to my sign-up flow, shown with the same progress bar as the other steps. Centre: a soft card holding one realistic notification from my app ([icon], "[AAPL Earnings]", "[Reports robust Q2 earnings.]"). Below: the heading "Enable [investing] notifications" and one sentence listing the specific alerts users get. Buttons: dark full-width "Enable notifications" (triggers the system prompt) and a text "Skip for now" that moves to the next step and schedules a re-ask after [the user's first trade].
Strava: tell people what the next tap isStrava screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Strava knows the system dialog comes next, and it says so.

  1. A bell icon above the headline.
  2. "Don't miss a thing. Allow notifications so you can track each step of your journey." The benefit before the ask.
  3. A Strava notification over an orange swoosh: "Way to go. Kudos for an activity in the books!" A friendly, real example.
  4. "Make sure you select 'Allow' on the next step…" Small text that prepares people for the iOS dialog.
  5. "Choose permissions" as the button, honest about what happens next.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Create a notification pre-permission screen: a bell icon, the headline "Don't miss a thing", one line on the benefit, and a sample notification card from my app on a brand-coloured shape ("[Way to go 👏] [Kudos for your activity]"). Above the button, small grey text: "Make sure you select 'Allow' on the next step to receive notifications from [App]." Primary button "Choose permissions" triggers the real system prompt and then continues onboarding whatever the answer.
4. Other permissions: say why, and offer a way around

Camera, photos, location and Bluetooth asks work best with a reason and an alternative.

Instagram: three questions answered before the camera rollInstagram screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Photo access is personal. Instagram answers how, why and what if before asking.

  1. "Allow Instagram to access your photos and videos" as a plain headline.
  2. "How you'll use this": add photos and videos and apply effects.
  3. "How we'll use this": to let you share and suggest photos. The company's side, said out loud.
  4. "How these settings work": you can change it anytime in device settings.
  5. One "Continue" button. No pressure, no trick wording.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Before requesting [photo library] access, show a sheet with an icon, the headline "Allow [App] to access your [photos and videos]", and three short sections, each with an icon: "How you'll use this" ([what the user can do]), "How we'll use this" ([what the app does with it, honestly]) and "How these settings work" ("You can change your choice at any time in your device settings."). One primary "Continue" button that calls the real permission API, and limited access handled gracefully if the user picks only some photos.
Zomato: always offer the manual wayZomato screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Location makes food delivery work, but Zomato never makes it the only option.

  1. "Set your location to start exploring restaurants near you". The reason is in the headline.
  2. A 3D city illustration with a pin and restaurants around it.
  3. "Enable Device Location" as the main button.
  4. "Enter Your Location Manually". Saying no to the permission doesn't mean leaving the app.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

Build a location step for my app: a headline that includes the reason ("Set your location to [find X near you]"), a friendly map illustration, a primary "Enable device location" button that requests permission (expo-location or navigator.geolocation), and an outlined "Enter your location manually" button that opens an address search with autocomplete. If permission is denied, go straight to the manual search instead of showing an error.
Spotify: why, and who's in controlSpotify screen, captured on iOS in 2026. The numbers match the notes below.

Bluetooth and local network access sound technical. Spotify translates them into one short reason.

  1. Speakers, phones, laptops and TVs floating together. The illustration shows the benefit: play anywhere.
  2. "Allow Spotify to access Bluetooth and your local network". The headline says exactly what's being asked.
  3. "Why do you need this? To find and play on all your devices." The reason, as a question and answer.
  4. "You're in control. Change permissions at any time in Settings." Reassurance.
  5. A green "Continue" pill. The system prompt comes next.

Prompt for Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor:

For technical permissions like [Bluetooth or local network], show a dark screen with an illustration of the benefit, a headline that names the permission plainly ("Allow [App] to access [Bluetooth and your local network]"), and two short rows with icons: "Why do you need this?" with a one-line answer, and "You're in control" with "Change permissions at any time in Settings." One "Continue" button triggers the system prompt; if it's denied, the related feature shows an inline "Turn on in Settings" link later instead of blocking.
The onboarding checklist
  • Show the real product on the first screen, not a mascot and a slogan.
  • Answer the biggest objection in one line ("Free. Forever.", "No card needed").
  • Let people try before signing up, and ask for an account when there's something to save.
  • Offer Apple and Google sign-in first, then email.
  • Never trigger a system permission prompt cold. Show your own screen first.
  • Use a real example of the notification people will get.
  • Say why for every permission, in the headline or one line under it.
  • Give a real alternative: "Enter location manually", "Skip for now".
  • Ask at the moment it matters, such as notifications after the first order, not on launch.
  • Keep it short: a progress bar if there are more than three steps.

Copy the starter prompt: a complete onboarding flow:

Build my app's onboarding flow using my existing theme and [Supabase Auth]. 1) Welcome: one screen (or a 3–4 slide carousel) that shows real UI components of [the main feature] with sample data, a one-line promise, "Get started" and "I already have an account". 2) Let users into [the core experience] without an account; store their work locally. 3) Ask for an account when they first [save/order/share]: Continue with Apple, Continue with Google, Continue with email, then migrate their local data into the new account. 4) Notifications: after the first [success moment], show my own pre-ask screen with two realistic sample notifications, "Turn notifications on" (calls the real permission API) and "Not now" (re-ask after 7 days, at most twice). 5) For location, camera or photos: a screen or sheet that names the permission, explains why in one line, says it can be changed in Settings, and offers a manual alternative if denied. 6) Show a progress bar if there are more than three steps, and never trigger a system prompt without my own screen first.
Onboarding UI FAQWhat should the first onboarding screen show?

What the app does, ideally by showing the real product. Only 11 of the 64 apps we studied show actual UI on their welcome screen; Arc Search and Bevel are the best examples, using real components as the illustration.

Should users sign up before using the app?

Not if you can avoid it. Only 9 of 64 apps let people look around first, and the ones that do, like Grab, Walmart and Duolingo, ask for an account when there's something to save or buy.

How do I ask for push notification permission?

Show your own screen before the system dialog, with a real example notification and a "Not now" option. 25 of 64 apps use their own pre-ask; the best, like Monzo and Public, show exactly what a notification from them looks like.

Should I offer Sign in with Apple and Google?

Yes. 27 of 64 apps offer one-tap sign-in with Apple or Google, and Apple requires Sign in with Apple if you offer other third-party logins in an iOS app.

How do I build onboarding with Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Cursor?

Build it in order: welcome, try-first, sign-up, then each permission ask, and tell the AI to wire the asks to real permission APIs. Each example above has a prompt for one screen, and the starter prompt builds the whole flow.

How we did this

We looked at 141 screens tagged as welcome, get-started or permission screens in 64 iOS apps, captured in 2026, and scored each app once per detail if any of its screens showed it.

All product names belong to their owners. The screens are shown to discuss design; no app on this page endorses this article.
