items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix
items.summary: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our head-to-head coding comparisons. Anthropic compared Fable 5.2 with its predecessor, Fable 5.1 , on safeguard blocks, output speed, and API pricing. The company states that Fable 5.2 triggered about 55% fewer safeguard blocks than Fable 5.1 overall and about 60% fewer in cybersecurity in early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork. It also says Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster and lists standard API rates of $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Both rates are 20% lower than Fable 5.1’s $10 and $50. I compared Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1 on three developer tasks and tracked refusals, accuracy, tokens, estimated cost, and elapsed time. The comparison uses one run per model for each task or version, including the October Fable 5.1 webhook result. That’s a small sample, and the API runs used a different setup from Anthropic’s safeguard testing. The tests For the new runs, I used Anthropic’s API with the default effort setting of High for both models, with no turn cap or fallback model. A script graded every run against an answer key I created for the tests. The dollar figures are estimated API costs. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately . Webhook chat : I reused a 50-turn scripted chat that I first ran on Fable 5.1 in October. It simulates a dev lead building a small webhook relay. The chat contains 25 project rules, eight of which change later and three of which are only implied. At the end, the model writes the config and code and then takes an eight-question recall quiz. Signature checker : I gave each model a written spec for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders, and then sent a change request. A hidden suite of 50 tests graded the final code output. Login repo fix : Each model worked as an agent in a small login library with interacting bugs in passwords, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit. Webhook chat In the October Fable 5.1 run I’m using for comparison, the API refused 34 of 50 turns. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. In that October run, I kept my prompts in the chat history and discarded refused model responses. Fable 5.1 also refused the final code and the quiz, so it scored zero on both. The task was to build an ordinary backend relay. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. Fable 5.2 finished the same script without a refusal. That gave me a complete run to grade for long-conversation recall. Its code used the most recent version of all eight rules, which changed midway, and on the quiz it answered “unknown” to the three questions that had no answer. Fable 5.2 didn’t fill gaps with guesses. The numbers: • Fable 5.2 : 50 turns, 298,709 in, 41,828 out (28,550 reasoning), $4.06, 427 s. • Fable 5.1 (October) : 34 of 50 turns refused, with no code or quiz answers. Signature checker Fable 5.1 refused both turns of this test in under a second each, and the API labeled both refusals “cyber.” The spec asked for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders. The API returned no output on either turn. Anthropic says benign security work can trigger its cyber classifier . Fable 5.2 took the same spec, handled the change request, and passed all 50 hidden tests, including the edge cases on timestamps, rotated secrets, and replays. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 2 turns, 21,299 in, 26,167 out (18,407 reasoning), $1.22, 253 s. Fable 5.1 : 2 turns, both refused, 3,206 reported input tokens, 0 output tokens, $0.00 under Anthropic’s billing rules for cyber refusals before output , 2 s. Login repo fix This was the one test where both models completed the work, showing how they compare once refusals are out of the picture. The models kept getting perfect scores, so I made the tests harder and reran them twice. Here’s what differed between the tests: Version 1 : The library had bugs in four modules that handle password hashing, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. It also had one wrong test. Version 2 : I added a one-time-code module with its own bugs and tightened the rules in the existing modules. Usernames had to match across Unicode forms, and sessions had to handle a clock that runs backward. Version 3 : I added an audit log that must redact secrets and a rate limiter. Neither module came with any tests. The models tied on all three versions of the login repo fix. Both scored 50/50 on each version, fixing the bugs the grader covered and reporting the wrong test without editing it. Fable 5.1 never refused on the login repo fix, even though the task covered passwords, lockouts, and reset tokens. Across the three versions, dividing total output tokens (including reasoning) by total elapsed time gives about 107 tokens per second for Fable 5.2 and 82 for Fable 5.1. The elapsed time includes the entire task run. Fable 5.2 took four turns on each version, while Fable 5.1 took 7, 21, and 25. Fable 5.2 also produced more reasoning tokens on each version. Fable 5.2 finished the first two versions faster and at a lower estimated cost. It took longer and cost more on the third. The numbers: Version 1 Fable 5.2 : 4 turns, 16,149 in, 4,502 out (1,178 reasoning), $0.27, 43 s. Fable 5.1 : 7 turns, 33,935 in, 4,761 out (1,149 reasoning), $0.36, 52 s. Version 2 Fable 5.2 : 4 turns, 24,081 in, 10,024 out (4,887 reasoning), $0.56, 95 s. Fable 5.1 : 21 turns, 139,189 in, 9,475 out (4,018 reasoning), $0.68, 118 s. Version 3 Fable 5.2 : 4 turns, 34,269 in, 17,964 out (10,578 reasoning), $0.96, 166 s. Fable 5.1 : 25 turns, 208,826 in, 10,638 out (4,342 reasoning), $0.79, 132 s. Results The token, cost, and time totals below cover the signature checker and all three login repo versions. Fable 5.1 produced no output on the signature checker, while Fable 5.2 spent 253 seconds and an estimated $1.22 completing it. Across the three login versions that both models completed, elapsed time and estimated cost were close. The combined totals include the work only Fable 5.2 completed on the signature checker. Test Claude Fable 5.2 Claude Fable 5.1 Webhook chat refusals (of 50) 0 34 (October) Webhook chat code and quiz 25 of 25, 8 of 8 0 of 25, 0 of 8 (October) Signature checker (of 50) 50 0, both turns refused Login repo fix, 3 versions (of 150) 150 150 Tokens in / out, signature checker and login fix 95,798 / 58,657 385,156 / 24,874 Estimated cost, signature checker and login fix (sum of displayed estimates) $3.01 $1.83 Total time, signature checker and login fix (sum of displayed times) 557 s 304 s What do I think? In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals. Fable 5.1 blocked ordinary webhook and signature-checking work, and Fable 5.2 completed both without a single refusal. Anthropic says the newer model still uses cyber safeguards . In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals. Across the three login repo versions, Fable 5.2 produced about 30% more output tokens per second of elapsed time, including reasoning, while taking about the same total time. The runs took 304 seconds in total on Fable 5.2 and 302 seconds on Fable 5.1. The displayed cost estimates add up to $1.79 and $1.83, respectively, a savings of about 2% for these runs. Anthropic’s 20% price cut applies to its standard per-token rates. I ran each version once per model, so I’d try both on your own workload to see what the numbers look like for you.

The elapsed time includes the entire task run. Fable 5.2 took four turns on each version, while Fable 5.1 took 7, 21, and 25. Fable 5.2 also produced more reasoning tokens on each version. 

Fable 5.2 finished the first two versions faster and at a lower estimated cost. It took longer and cost more on the third.

Results

The token, cost, and time totals below cover the signature checker and all three login repo versions. Fable 5.1 produced no output on the signature checker, while Fable 5.2 spent 253 seconds and an estimated $1.22 completing it. Across the three login versions that both models completed, elapsed time and estimated cost were close. The combined totals include the work only Fable 5.2 completed on the signature checker.

What do I think?

In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals. Fable 5.1 blocked ordinary webhook and signature-checking work, and Fable 5.2 completed both without a single refusal. Anthropic says the newer model still uses cyber safeguards.

items.title: Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy
items.summary:
Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer ( WeightSpace ) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp , needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull: Prompt optimization (DSPy’s MIPROv2, GEPA ) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change. Fine-tuning (DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside BetterTogether ) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU. The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly. What did the original research show? The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking: Reading weights: Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone. Fixing a broken policy: A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes. Writing from zero: On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps. Fixing an LLM: Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability. How does dspy-wsp work? dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer. The GitHub Repo describes 3 actors: The student: the small model your DSPy program runs on. Its weights load into a local Python process. The writer: a frontier LLM, recommended as gpt-6-astra at maximum reasoning effort. The sandbox: a kernel where the writer runs code. macOS uses built-in sandbox-exec ; Linux uses bubblewrap. Forward passes come from a fixed budget ( max_passes=25 in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. The repo is explicit about data separation: trainset is the writer’s practice set. holdout moves a fraction (0.25 in the example) of training data into a check set. The writer can score edits on it but never sees the examples. valset stays hidden and runs once at the end. Metrics can return dspy.Prediction(score=..., feedback=...) . The feedback text is visible to the writer. What did the writer actually change? The results write-up lists every edit. "> How well does it work? Typed Decisions benchmark results Cmpnd tested on Typed Decisions , a benchmark for typed probabilistic decisions. A model reads 1 piece of unstructured state and answers 5 typed questions at once. Each answer is a probability distribution. The test split has 400 cases and 2,000 decisions. Each model got 25 forward passes from GPT-6-Astra. Gains are paired, with a standard error of ±0.7 to 1.4 points. Model Unoptimized ReAnchor WeightSpace WeightSpace + ReAnchor d1-omni-600M 50.9% 60.2% (+9.3) 66.9% (+16.1) 69.1% (+18.3) NanoJev (Qwen3-0.6B) 39.2% 50.7% (+11.6) 52.4% (+13.3) 56.4% (+17.3) d1-2B 60.6% 70.1% (+9.5) 74.0% (+13.4) 77.9% (+17.3) Clef-Flash (9B) 68.8% 70.3% (+1.5) 70.7% (+1.9) 75.3% (+6.5) Sources: Cmpnd blog chart for d1-omni-600M, d1-2B and Clef-Flash; results README for NanoJev. ReAnchor is an earlier Cmpnd optimizer. Decision models output probabilities, and thresholds turn those into answers. ReAnchor refits each question’s thresholds with no LLM calls. WeightSpace changes the model; ReAnchor recalibrates its output. The 2 stack well. Three patterns stand out: WeightSpace beat ReAnchor alone on every model shown. On d1-omni-600M, it added +16.1 versus +9.3. The largest model gained least. The 9B Clef-Flash gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. The combination matters most at 9B. Clef-Flash jumped to +6.5 when both optimizers ran. Does the writer model matter? The answer is yes. With gpt-6.1-sol as the writer, WeightSpace alone gave +5.8 on d1-omni-600M, +12.1 on NanoJev and −0.6 on d1-2B. Astra produced +16.1, +13.3 and +13.4 on the same models. Did dspy-wsp bend the original paper’s rules? Slightly, and Cmpnd says so. By default, the writer can recompute the decision head inside its kernel. Setting simulate_head=False enforces the paper’s stricter rule. Under that rule, d1-omni-600M gained only +2.8 ± 0.7 points. Adding ReAnchor brought it to +9.3, no better than ReAnchor alone. How do you deploy an edited model? Each run writes a patch to run_dir . The patch holds manifest.json and edit.npz , with only the changed entries. It also stores sha256 hashes of every base and edited tensor. Anyone with the public base model can rebuild the edited weights exactly. Decision models: compiled.wsp_patch.write_checkpoint(backend.weights_dir, "edited-d1/") Text LLMs: dspy-wsp apply / , then serve with vLLM. Programs: compiled.save("program.json") and reload with allow_unsafe_lm_state=True . The edited model runs locally. On Apple silicon it uses MLX. On Linux it uses PyTorch, on an NVIDIA GPU if present. What models does dspy-wsp support? A GEPASearch option, contributed by Michael Isaac, adds population search for decision models. How does WeightSpace compare with other DSPy optimizers? Gains fall at 9B, and the package is explicitly experimental. Check out the Cmpnd blog post , the GitHub repo , the full results and the original Weight-Space Programming research . items.summary_html:
Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp, a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy. Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace, an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

TL;DR
  • What it is: A DSPy optimizer (WeightSpace) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp, needs DSPy 3.5.
  • Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head.
  • Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU).
  • Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points.
  • Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor.
  • Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8.
  • Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models.
What is weight-space programming?

Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming.

A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out.

How is it different from fine-tuning or prompt optimization?

It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull:

  • Prompt optimization (DSPy’s MIPROv2, GEPA) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change.
  • Fine-tuning (DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside BetterTogether) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU.
  • Weight-space programming changes weights by reasoning. The editor forms a hypothesis (“these neurons over-score option B”), writes code to patch them, and checks the result with a few forward passes.

The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly.

What did the original research show?

The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking:

  • Reading weights: Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone.
  • Fixing a broken policy: A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes.
  • Writing from zero: On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps.
  • Fixing an LLM: Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%.

The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability.

How does dspy-wsp work?

dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer. The GitHub Repo describes 3 actors:

  1. The student: the small model your DSPy program runs on. Its weights load into a local Python process.
  2. The writer: a frontier LLM, recommended as gpt-6-astra at maximum reasoning effort.
  3. The sandbox: a kernel where the writer runs code. macOS uses built-in sandbox-exec; Linux uses bubblewrap.

The writer works in turns. Each turn has a short explanation, then 1 code block. That block is either:

  • a Python block that reads or edits weights inside the sandbox, or
  • a forward block that runs your DSPy program on practice examples.

Forward passes come from a fixed budget (max_passes=25 in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. A hidden validation set then compares original and edited weights on the same examples and seeds.

What data does the writer see?

The repo is explicit about data separation:

  • trainset is the writer’s practice set.
  • holdout moves a fraction (0.25 in the example) of training data into a check set. The writer can score edits on it but never sees the examples.
  • valset stays hidden and runs once at the end.
  • Metrics can return dspy.Prediction(score=..., feedback=...). The feedback text is visible to the writer.
What did the writer actually change?

The results write-up lists every edit. The edits are small and targeted:

ModelTensor editedScopeTimeWriter costd1-omni-600Mhead.scorer.1.weight (+ bias, scorer.3.weight)112,640 of 1,048,576 entries, plus 22078 min$7.63NanoJev (Qwen3-0.6B)scalar.weight1,024 entries167 min$6.92d1-2Blayers.23.feed_forward.w2.weightAll 15.7M entries, rank-9 change83 min$5.42

d1-2B has no decision head, so the writer edited its backbone at layer 23. On d1-omni-600M, the writer rewrote part of the decision head’s scorer.

What does the code look like?

The Repo example triages support tickets. The signature uses only decision-type outputs:

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
import dspy
from typing import Literal
from dspy_wsp import WeightSpace, load_decision_backend

class Triage(dspy.Signature):
    """Triage a support ticket."""
    ticket: str = dspy.InputField()
    urgent: bool = dspy.OutputField(desc="Does this ticket need a reply today?")
    team: Literal["billing", "technical", "account"] = dspy.OutputField(desc="Which team should handle it?")

backend = load_decision_backend("d1")   # d1-omni-600M
optimizer = WeightSpace(
    metric=metric,
    writer_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-6-astra", model_type="responses", reasoning_effort="max"),
    backend=backend,
    max_passes=25,
    holdout=0.25,
    run_dir="runs/triage",
)
compiled = optimizer.compile(dspy.Predict(Triage), trainset=train, valset=test)
compiled(ticket="I was charged twice this month.")   # runs on the edited weights

After compile, the program calls the edited local model instead of a hosted API. compiled.wsp_patch.summary() shows what changed.

How well does it work? Typed Decisions benchmark results

Cmpnd tested on Typed Decisions, a benchmark for typed probabilistic decisions. A model reads 1 piece of unstructured state and answers 5 typed questions at once. Each answer is a probability distribution. The test split has 400 cases and 2,000 decisions.

Each model got 25 forward passes from GPT-6-Astra. Gains are paired, with a standard error of ±0.7 to 1.4 points.

ModelUnoptimizedReAnchorWeightSpaceWeightSpace + ReAnchord1-omni-600M50.9%60.2% (+9.3)66.9% (+16.1)69.1% (+18.3)NanoJev (Qwen3-0.6B)39.2%50.7% (+11.6)52.4% (+13.3)56.4% (+17.3)d1-2B60.6%70.1% (+9.5)74.0% (+13.4)77.9% (+17.3)Clef-Flash (9B)68.8%70.3% (+1.5)70.7% (+1.9)75.3% (+6.5)

Sources: Cmpnd blog chart for d1-omni-600M, d1-2B and Clef-Flash; results README for NanoJev.

ReAnchor is an earlier Cmpnd optimizer. Decision models output probabilities, and thresholds turn those into answers. ReAnchor refits each question’s thresholds with no LLM calls. WeightSpace changes the model; ReAnchor recalibrates its output. The 2 stack well.

Three patterns stand out:

  • WeightSpace beat ReAnchor alone on every model shown. On d1-omni-600M, it added +16.1 versus +9.3.
  • The largest model gained least. The 9B Clef-Flash gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone.
  • The combination matters most at 9B. Clef-Flash jumped to +6.5 when both optimizers ran.
Does the writer model matter?

The answer is yes. With gpt-6.1-sol as the writer, WeightSpace alone gave +5.8 on d1-omni-600M, +12.1 on NanoJev and −0.6 on d1-2B. Astra produced +16.1, +13.3 and +13.4 on the same models.

Did dspy-wsp bend the original paper’s rules?

Slightly, and Cmpnd says so. By default, the writer can recompute the decision head inside its kernel. Setting simulate_head=False enforces the paper’s stricter rule. Under that rule, d1-omni-600M gained only +2.8 ± 0.7 points. Adding ReAnchor brought it to +9.3, no better than ReAnchor alone.

How do you deploy an edited model?

Each run writes a patch to run_dir. The patch holds manifest.json and edit.npz, with only the changed entries. It also stores sha256 hashes of every base and edited tensor. Anyone with the public base model can rebuild the edited weights exactly.

  • Decision models: compiled.wsp_patch.write_checkpoint(backend.weights_dir, "edited-d1/")
  • Text LLMs: dspy-wsp apply /, then serve with vLLM.
  • Programs: compiled.save("program.json") and reload with allow_unsafe_lm_state=True.

The edited model runs locally. On Apple silicon it uses MLX. On Linux it uses PyTorch, on an NVIDIA GPU if present.

What models does dspy-wsp support? BackendModelAliasArchitectureD1BackendLiquid AI d1-omni (text path)"d1"Encoder with decision headNanoJevBackendNanoJev"nanojev"Qwen3 backbone with decision headD1LMBackendLiquid AI d1 on LFM3"d1-2b"LM answering at question positions

Text-generating LLMs work through VLLMBackend (NVIDIA), HFBackend (CUDA, MPS or CPU) and MLXBackend (Apple silicon). A GEPASearch option, contributed by Michael Isaac, adds population search for decision models.

How does WeightSpace compare with other DSPy optimizers?   • Weight-space programming lets a frontier LLM edit weights directly, without gradients or training data.
  • dspy-wsp wraps it as a DSPy optimizer: pip install dspy-wsp, MIT license.
  • 25 writer passes cost $5.42 to $7.63 and took 78 to 167 minutes.
  • d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% with WeightSpace + ReAnchor.
  • Gains fall at 9B, and the package is explicitly experimental.

Check out the Cmpnd blog post, the GitHub repo, the full results and the original Weight-Space Programming research. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

items.title: Nvidia's new CEO search is on. Here are the top candidates to replace Jensen Huang.
items.summary: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Wednesday. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia is on the hunt for a new CEO after Jensen Huang resigned. The board of directors appointed Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. Arm CEO Rene Haas, former Apple CEO Tim Cook, and Nvidia VP Ian Buck are among potential candidates. The search for Nvidia's new CEO is officially underway. The company's board of directors announced that CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigned "effective immediately" in a statement on Wednesday. The board tapped Colette Kress , executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO until a permanent successor is found. Huang resigned three days after he admitted to having an affair, and Nvidia's board opened an investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." As the fallout around Nvidia continues, analysts, investors, and prediction market bettors have begun to wonder who could helm the company next. Here's who they're pitching. Rene Haas Rene Haas, chief executive officer of Arm Holdings Plc, holds the AGI CPU chip during the Arm Everywhere event in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, March 24, 2026. Arm Holdings will begin selling its own chips, called AGI CPUs, for the first time, aiming to claim a bigger piece of the massive spending on AI gear. Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images The CEO of Arm Holdings, a semiconductor manufacturing company, is one name that's been bandied about. On Wednesday, The Financial Times reported that Nvidia has approached Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Sources told the outlet that it's not guaranteed Haas will be offered the role or accept it. Haas previously served as vice president and general manager of Nvidia's computing products business unit for 7 years. Ian Buck Ian Buck, vice president of accelerated computing at Nvidia Corp., holds the Groq 3 LPU chip during the Nvidia GTC conference in San Jose, California, US, on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the company is firing up manufacturing of H200 AI accelerators for customers in China, a sign of progress in the chipmaker's effort to reenter the vital market. Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Reuters reported that analysts and investors view Ian Buck , Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, as a possible candidate for the top job. "The permanent job is a different story, though, because Nvidia's edge comes from its technology, and the board would likely want an engineer in the chair, Josh Gilbert, a lead analyst at eToro, told Reuters. "Someone like Ian Buck, who led the software platform that keeps developers tied to Nvidia's chips, is the sort of internal name you'd expect to come up." Prediction market users are also banking on Buck. He's at the top of the list on both Kalshi and Polymarket. Colette Kress Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia Nvidia Reuters reported that analysts and investors also view interim CEO Colette Kress as someone who could do the job long-term. Armina Rosenberg, a cofounder at Minotaur Capital, which owns Nvidia stock, told Reuters that finding a new permanent CEO won't be quick. "The more realistic route is an interim leader from the long-serving inner circle, possibly as a co-CEO structure: one leader to steady the business and the finances, such as Colette Kress, alongside a product and technology leader, such as Ian Buck," Rosenberg told the outlet. Tim Cook VALERIE MACON / AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump also weighed in on the search for Nvidia's new CEO, recommending former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Cook stepped down as CEO in September, but remains executive chairman. "NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday. Thomas Kurian Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of cloud services at Google LLC, speaks during the Google Cloud Next '19 event in San Francisco, California, U.S., on Tuesday, April 9, 2019. The conference brings together industry experts to discuss the future of cloud computing. Photographer: Michael Short/Bloomberg via Getty Images Michael Short/Bloomberg via Getty Images Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., had a few ideas of his own. During an interview with Fortune, Ives named Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian as a promising candidate. Kurian joined Google in 2019 after working at Oracle and McKinsey. Nikesh Arora Nikesh Arora, chief executive officer at Palo Alto Networks Inc., arrives for a meeting on artificial intelligence with tech executives at the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. The gathering follows a surge in concern about AI potentially posing a threat to humans. Photographer: Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora is getting swept up in the speculation, too. An Nvidia shareholder told The Economic Times that Arora is among his top picks to replace Huang. Ives also said Arora is on his list. Johny Srouji Johny Srouji, senior vice president of hardware technologies at Apple Inc., speaks during the Apple Worldwide Developers Conference seen on a laptop computer in Arlington, Virginia, U.S., on Monday, June 22, 2020. Apple will walk into its annual development conference facing one of the biggest backlashes from its giant community of creators since the App Store started almost 12 years ago. Photographer: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Johny Srouji, the senior vice president of hardware technology at Apple, is another name popping up in conversations. A person familiar with the matter told Semafor that Srouji is being considered for the CEO role. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Wednesday.

Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images

  • Nvidia is on the hunt for a new CEO after Jensen Huang resigned.
  • The board of directors appointed Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO.
  • Arm CEO Rene Haas, former Apple CEO Tim Cook, and Nvidia VP Ian Buck are among potential candidates.

The search for Nvidia's new CEO is officially underway.

The company's board of directors announced that CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigned "effective immediately" in a statement on Wednesday. The board tapped Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO until a permanent successor is found.

Huang resigned three days after he admitted to having an affair, and Nvidia's board opened an investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."

As the fallout around Nvidia continues, analysts, investors, and prediction market bettors have begun to wonder who could helm the company next. Here's who they're pitching.

Rene Haas
Rene Haas, chief executive officer of Arm Holdings Plc, holds the AGI CPU chip during the Arm Everywhere event in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, March 24, 2026. Arm Holdings will begin selling its own chips, called AGI CPUs, for the first time, aiming to claim a bigger piece of the massive spending on AI gear. Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The CEO of Arm Holdings, a semiconductor manufacturing company, is one name that's been bandied about. On Wednesday, The Financial Times reported that Nvidia has approached Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Sources told the outlet that it's not guaranteed Haas will be offered the role or accept it.

Haas previously served as vice president and general manager of Nvidia's computing products business unit for 7 years.

Ian Buck
Ian Buck, vice president of accelerated computing at Nvidia Corp., holds the Groq 3 LPU chip during the Nvidia GTC conference in San Jose, California, US, on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the company is firing up manufacturing of H200 AI accelerators for customers in China, a sign of progress in the chipmaker's effort to reenter the vital market. Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Reuters reported that analysts and investors view Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, as a possible candidate for the top job.

"The permanent job is a different story, though, because Nvidia's edge comes from its technology, and the board would likely want an engineer in the chair, Josh Gilbert, a lead analyst at eToro, told Reuters. "Someone like Ian Buck, who led the software platform that keeps developers tied to Nvidia's chips, is the sort of internal name you'd expect to come up."

Prediction market users are also banking on Buck. He's at the top of the list on both Kalshi and Polymarket.

Colette Kress
Colette Kress, chief financial officer of Nvidia

Nvidia

Reuters reported that analysts and investors also view interim CEO Colette Kress as someone who could do the job long-term. Armina Rosenberg, a cofounder at Minotaur Capital, which owns Nvidia stock, told Reuters that finding a new permanent CEO won't be quick.

"The more realistic route is an interim leader from the long-serving inner circle, possibly as a co-CEO structure: one leader to steady the business and the finances, such as Colette Kress, alongside a product and technology leader, such as Ian Buck," Rosenberg told the outlet.

Tim Cook

VALERIE MACON / AFP via Getty Images

President Donald Trump also weighed in on the search for Nvidia's new CEO, recommending former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Cook stepped down as CEO in September, but remains executive chairman.

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday.

Thomas Kurian
Thomas Kurian, chief executive officer of cloud services at Google LLC, speaks during the Google Cloud Next '19 event in San Francisco, California, U.S., on Tuesday, April 9, 2019. The conference brings together industry experts to discuss the future of cloud computing. Photographer: Michael Short/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Michael Short/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., had a few ideas of his own. During an interview with Fortune, Ives named Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian as a promising candidate.

Kurian joined Google in 2019 after working at Oracle and McKinsey.

Nikesh Arora
Nikesh Arora, chief executive officer at Palo Alto Networks Inc., arrives for a meeting on artificial intelligence with tech executives at the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. The gathering follows a surge in concern about AI potentially posing a threat to humans. Photographer: Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora is getting swept up in the speculation, too. An Nvidia shareholder told The Economic Times that Arora is among his top picks to replace Huang. Ives also said Arora is on his list.

Johny Srouji
Johny Srouji, senior vice president of hardware technologies at Apple Inc., speaks during the Apple Worldwide Developers Conference seen on a laptop computer in Arlington, Virginia, U.S., on Monday, June 22, 2020. Apple will walk into its annual development conference facing one of the biggest backlashes from its giant community of creators since the App Store started almost 12 years ago. Photographer: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Johny Srouji, the senior vice president of hardware technology at Apple, is another name popping up in conversations. A person familiar with the matter told Semafor that Srouji is being considered for the CEO role.

items.title: The Fallout from Jensen’s Downfall
items.summary: Welcome, Weekenders! Jexit, as I’d like to christen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, is an ugly matter, an implosion with fallout across continents and several different industries. No one irradiated by it walks away a picture of good health. Huang obfuscated the truth, promising senior executives at his company that he’d had just the one affair, with Alice Huang, the former executive at Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. But that wasn’t the case. He reportedly had at least two others, including one with a direct report. Nvidia’s board almost didn’t act and only did so on the insistence of the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter. I’m not surprised. The board is dominated by people who’ve known Huang for decades. And there was not even a board chair. The friendships Huang thought he had in Washington weren’t nearly enough to save him, a reminder of the fickleness of politics as Silicon Valley goes through the necessary course correction to win influence with the ascendant left. (Alex Karp is a Democrat again, did you hear ?) Indeed, it looks pretty obvious that some factions within Trump-led Washington worked against Huang. Many of the reporters who have been most active in the last week are in Washington. Some U.S. authorities say the former Megaspeed executive was a spy. Was she? More reports in recent days cast doubt on whether she really was. No matter. The mere implication was a useful weapon to wield against Huang. The spy-who-loved-him situation was catnip for reporters, but I don’t want to hand out laurels to the media. Huang’s bullying tendencies went underhighlighted for years—first because Nvidia was too complex and confusing to cover, and then because of Huang’s presentation of himself as a nerdish, articulate poster boy for the AI age. It makes me wonder who else is escaping close coverage as the tech landscape continues to widen and morph. Throughout Jexit, Huang has maintained a sizable base of support in Silicon Valley. A host of prominent names rushed to his defense—from venture capitalists Vinod Khosla and Ron Conway to Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney . Huang still has a legion of allies within Nvidia. On Thursday evening, a petition from Nvidia employees circulated online advocating for his reinstatement. I wonder how misguided that hero worship might later seem. Congressional investigations into Huang and Nvidia loom—he has agreed to testify before Thanksgiving—and already we’re starting to see reports about how he really ran Nvidia, a place where he was comfortable steamrolling over more cautious executives. Stephen Witt, who wrote a 2025 biography of Huang, “The Thinking Machine,” describes him in a new essay for The New York Times as a person energized “by arrogance and toxic self-regard.” Witt also makes it clear how willfully blind everyone was to Huang’s behavior. When Nvidia began in the early ’90s, its corporate mascot was Dawn, an “underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie” that was “memory-holed in 2020 around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company.” The title of Witt’s book refers to both the technology Huang sold and Huang himself. As Witt has contemplated Jexit, he has mulled whether he might return to covering Huang: “I should write a sequel: ‘The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine.’” —Abram Brown ( abe@theinformation.com ) The Information’s Must-Read Stories Sex, Lies and AI Chips: Jensen Huang’s Last Days as Nvidia CEO Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets Alice Huang’s Companies Invested in DeepSeek, Promising Nvidia Chips Commerce Department Finalizing Long-Awaited AI Remote Access Rule Listening: “ Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny ” Let’s acknowledge the Horta in the room—so to speak. With Patrick Stewart’s death last week, more than a few of us have been feeling nostalgic about “Star Trek,” myself included, and it pushed me toward a welcome discovery: Brent Spiner (aka Data) and Jonathan Frakes (aka Commander Riker) have spent the last few months together debuting a podcast! And it is utterly delightful. The conceit behind “Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny” is simple: Guests from across the entertainment firmament join Spiner and Frakes to talk about their careers and how they’ve intersected with other famous people. (A bell dings each time someone drops a name.) It’s a nod to just how far the “Star Trek” acting universe extends, and some of their guests beam in direct from Trek land. William Shatner (Captain Kirk) and LeVar Burton (Chief Engineer Geordi La Forge) have both appeared—as have Michael Dorn (Worf) and Seth MacFarlane (the “Family Guy” creator, who has a major Trek obsession). But the show is not a total Trekkie con: Noah Wyle and Ron Perlman have stopped by, too. Another recent guest was Margo Martindale, the beloved character actress (and Frakes’ former Harvard University classmate). I especially enjoyed that conversation. Frequently, “Dropping Names” is a window into B-list Hollywood, an existence beneath the industry’s shiniest tier. It is not an entirely unexplored new world, but it is a strange one filled with what-ifs and missed connections. Stewart escaped from it—Spiner and Frakes never did. Now well into their 70s, both actors seem charmingly comfortable at their place within it.— Abram Brown Reading: “ Ladies’ Man ” by Laurence Leamer A question we’ve all been asking ourselves this week: Why would someone with great wealth and power risk it all for sex ? Well, at least in the case of John F. Kennedy Jr., his lifelong randiness was seemingly an effort to prove to himself that he wasn’t the weak, chronically ill fellow he in fact was. “Sex was an assertion of health—a way to defy his ailments,” Laurence Leamer writes in “Ladies’ Man,” a new biography of JFK told chiefly via his many romances. (Leamer’s 2012 bestseller “Capote’s Women” was turned into FX’s “Feud: Capote vs. the Swans.”) Leamer’s retelling of the president’s life is gossiply enveloping, though it never applies a gimlet-eyed gaze to its handsome, oft-idolized subject. Leamer portrays Kennedy as shallow and callow, with a self-professed “slam, bam, thank-you-ma’am” motto toward women. By Kennedy’s own count, he slept with well over 1,000 women, an estimate he offered casually to a friend without compunction. Lovesickness may never have troubled Kennedy, but he did suffer from a number of other ailments, including his famous bad back, as well as Addison’s disease, which affects the adrenal glands. In accounting these maladies, “Ladies’ Man” doubles as an unsettling look at midcentury medicine: Among many procedures and treatments, Kennedy underwent four back surgeries and relied on small, steroid-filled pellets inserted under his skin. As Leamer dryly notes in an observation as true of the Kennedys’ era as of our own, “the wealthy sometimes pursue experimental cures that most other people would never consider.” “Ladies’ Man” broadly charts the Kennedy clan’s rise to prominence, an ascendance marked by the dalliances of JFK’s sister Kathleen, a London socialite who later attached herself to “one of the great roués” of British nobility, and those of his millionaire father. The paterfamilias had his own bravado thinking on fornication—“I want to get the most out of life, including sex”—and was known to labor over hiring a new secretary, sometimes interviewing several dozen applicants. In several chapters, Leamer shows the extent to which elites like the Kennedys will go to keep their misdeeds hidden. That was never more important to JFK than it became in cloaking his affair with Marilyn Monroe. When gossip spread about the president’s relationship with the actress, Kennedy coerced friend William Haddad, a former journalist turned Peace Corps inspector general, to dispel the rumors among the media even though they were true. “He lied to me,” Haddad recalled. “He used my credibility.” —A.B. Watching: “ Primetime ” The film from director Lance Oppenheim that has lately sucked up so much of the oxygen within pop culture is his joint production with Nathan Fielder—yes, that would be “You Can See Everything,” the Elizabeth Holmes documentary. Perhaps I could also direct your attention to the other Oppenheim movie that came out this fall, “Primetime,” which is newly available for streaming rental. Like “You Can See Everything,” “Primetime” is a movie about complicated deceptions, exploitation and false identities—a fictionalized biopic of NBC journalist Chris Hansen, host of “To Catch a Predator,” the short-lived, hidden-camera show from the 2000s that set up sting operations to capture men who wanted child sex. Hansen is portrayed by Robert Pattinson, who brings a reptilian carnivorousness to a star turn that will probably nab him an Oscar nomination. The supporting performances are also excellent, with Emmy winner Merritt Wever as “To Catch a Predator” producer Andie Bender and Skyler Gisondo as Decoy Dan, a youthful, almost androgynous actor who assumes the role of onscreen bait. Oppenheim keeps “Primetime”’s focus narrow, and it unfolds over the first few months of Hansen’s frantic campaign to turn his ickfest into a hit NBC program that could compete against ABC’s “Lost.” Oppenheim’s camerawork and shot selection in “Primetime” feels like a somewhat unfamiliar style for a feature film—a reflection of his decade-plus career in documentaries. (His “Ren Faire,” which examined the drama around a Renaissance fair in Texas, was a 2024 HBO standout.) Oppenheim likes shadows and grimy soft focus, and what he ends up with is a vérité-esque haunted house picture. (The climax comes as a fierce rainstorm lashes a tidy suburban home, calling to mind “Poltergeist”’s finale.) The most obvious ghouls in “Primetime” are the sex perverts, who are summoned and duly exorcised in quick order. They’re not the only dark souls, though: Hansen is another, scheming to seize fame and snare increasingly prominent men on camera. And thus emerges a further thematic link between “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything”: Both feature protagonists wearing masks of attractive ambition over their monstrous tendencies. Still, it’s sparse camouflage.— A.B.

Welcome, Weekenders! 

Jexit, as I’d like to christen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, is an ugly matter, an implosion with fallout across continents and several different industries. No one irradiated by it walks away a picture of good health. 

Huang obfuscated the truth, promising senior executives at his company that he’d had just the one affair, with Alice Huang, the former executive at Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. But that wasn’t the case. He reportedly had at least two others, including one with a direct report. 

Nvidia’s board almost didn’t act and only did so on the insistence of the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter. I’m not surprised. The board is dominated by people who’ve known Huang for decades. And there was not even a board chair. 

The friendships Huang thought he had in Washington weren’t nearly enough to save him, a reminder of the fickleness of politics as Silicon Valley goes through the necessary course correction to win influence with the ascendant left. (Alex Karp is a Democrat again, did you hear?) Indeed, it looks pretty obvious that some factions within Trump-led Washington worked against Huang. Many of the reporters who have been most active in the last week are in Washington.

Some U.S. authorities say the former Megaspeed executive was a spy. Was she? More reports in recent days cast doubt on whether she really was. No matter. The mere implication was a useful weapon to wield against Huang. 

The spy-who-loved-him situation was catnip for reporters, but I don’t want to hand out laurels to the media. Huang’s bullying tendencies went underhighlighted for years—first because Nvidia was too complex and confusing to cover, and then because of Huang’s presentation of himself as a nerdish, articulate poster boy for the AI age. It makes me wonder who else is escaping close coverage as the tech landscape continues to widen and morph. 

Throughout Jexit, Huang has maintained a sizable base of support in Silicon Valley. A host of prominent names rushed to his defense—from venture capitalists Vinod Khosla and Ron Conway to Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. Huang still has a legion of allies within Nvidia. On Thursday evening, a petition from Nvidia employees circulated online advocating for his reinstatement.

I wonder how misguided that hero worship might later seem. Congressional investigations into Huang and Nvidia loom—he has agreed to testify before Thanksgiving—and already we’re starting to see reports about how he really ran Nvidia, a place where he was comfortable steamrolling over more cautious executives. 

Stephen Witt, who wrote a 2025 biography of Huang, “The Thinking Machine,” describes him in a new essay for The New York Times as a person energized “by arrogance and toxic self-regard.” Witt also makes it clear how willfully blind everyone was to Huang’s behavior. When Nvidia began in the early ’90s, its corporate mascot was Dawn, an “underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie” that was “memory-holed in 2020 around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company.”

The title of Witt’s book refers to both the technology Huang sold and Huang himself. As Witt has contemplated Jexit, he has mulled whether he might return to covering Huang: “I should write a sequel: ‘The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine.’”—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny”

Let’s acknowledge the Horta in the room—so to speak. With Patrick Stewart’s death last week, more than a few of us have been feeling nostalgic about “Star Trek,” myself included, and it pushed me toward a welcome discovery: Brent Spiner (aka Data) and Jonathan Frakes (aka Commander Riker) have spent the last few months together debuting a podcast! And it is utterly delightful. 

The conceit behind “Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny” is simple: Guests from across the entertainment firmament join Spiner and Frakes to talk about their careers and how they’ve intersected with other famous people. (A bell dings each time someone drops a name.) It’s a nod to just how far the “Star Trek” acting universe extends, and some of their guests beam in direct from Trek land. William Shatner (Captain Kirk) and LeVar Burton (Chief Engineer Geordi La Forge) have both appeared—as have Michael Dorn (Worf) and Seth MacFarlane (the “Family Guy” creator, who has a major Trek obsession). But the show is not a total Trekkie con: Noah Wyle and Ron Perlman have stopped by, too. 

Another recent guest was Margo Martindale, the beloved character actress (and Frakes’ former Harvard University classmate). I especially enjoyed that conversation. Frequently, “Dropping Names” is a window into B-list Hollywood, an existence beneath the industry’s shiniest tier. It is not an entirely unexplored new world, but it is a strange one filled with what-ifs and missed connections. Stewart escaped from it—Spiner and Frakes never did. Now well into their 70s, both actors seem charmingly comfortable at their place within it.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Ladies’ Man” by Laurence Leamer

A question we’ve all been asking ourselves this week: Why would someone with great wealth and power risk it all for sex?

Well, at least in the case of John F. Kennedy Jr., his lifelong randiness was seemingly an effort to prove to himself that he wasn’t the weak, chronically ill fellow he in fact was. “Sex was an assertion of health—a way to defy his ailments,” Laurence Leamer writes in “Ladies’ Man,” a new biography of JFK told chiefly via his many romances. By Kennedy’s own count, he slept with well over 1,000 women, an estimate he offered casually to a friend without compunction. 

Lovesickness may never have troubled Kennedy, but he did suffer from a number of other ailments, including his famous bad back, as well as Addison’s disease, which affects the adrenal glands. In accounting these maladies, “Ladies’ Man” doubles as an unsettling look at midcentury medicine: Among many procedures and treatments, Kennedy underwent four back surgeries and relied on small, steroid-filled pellets inserted under his skin. As Leamer dryly notes in an observation as true of the Kennedys’ era as of our own, “the wealthy sometimes pursue experimental cures that most other people would never consider.”

“Ladies’ Man” broadly charts the Kennedy clan’s rise to prominence, an ascendance marked by the dalliances of JFK’s sister Kathleen, a London socialite who later attached herself to “one of the great roués” of British nobility, and those of his millionaire father. The paterfamilias had his own bravado thinking on fornication—“I want to get the most out of life, including sex”—and was known to labor over hiring a new secretary, sometimes interviewing several dozen applicants.

In several chapters, Leamer shows the extent to which elites like the Kennedys will go to keep their misdeeds hidden. That was never more important to JFK than it became in cloaking his affair with Marilyn Monroe. When gossip spread about the president’s relationship with the actress, Kennedy coerced friend William Haddad, a former journalist turned Peace Corps inspector general, to dispel the rumors among the media even though they were true. “He lied to me,” Haddad recalled. “He used my credibility.”—A.B.

Watching: “Primetime”

The film from director Lance Oppenheim that has lately sucked up so much of the oxygen within pop culture is his joint production with Nathan Fielder—yes, that would be “You Can See Everything,” the Elizabeth Holmes documentary. Perhaps I could also direct your attention to the other Oppenheim movie that came out this fall, “Primetime,” which is newly available for streaming rental. 

Like “You Can See Everything,” “Primetime” is a movie about complicated deceptions, exploitation and false identities—a fictionalized biopic of NBC journalist Chris Hansen, host of “To Catch a Predator,” the short-lived, hidden-camera show from the 2000s that set up sting operations to capture men who wanted child sex. Hansen is portrayed by Robert Pattinson, who brings a reptilian carnivorousness to a star turn that will probably nab him an Oscar nomination. The supporting performances are also excellent, with Emmy winner Merritt Wever as “To Catch a Predator” producer Andie Bender and Skyler Gisondo as Decoy Dan, a youthful, almost androgynous actor who assumes the role of onscreen bait. 

Oppenheim keeps “Primetime”’s focus narrow, and it unfolds over the first few months of Hansen’s frantic campaign to turn his ickfest into a hit NBC program that could compete against ABC’s “Lost.” Oppenheim’s camerawork and shot selection in “Primetime” feels like a somewhat unfamiliar style for a feature film—a reflection of his decade-plus career in documentaries. (His “Ren Faire,” which examined the drama around a Renaissance fair in Texas, was a 2024 HBO standout.) Oppenheim likes shadows and grimy soft focus, and what he ends up with is a vérité-esque haunted house picture. (The climax comes as a fierce rainstorm lashes a tidy suburban home, calling to mind “Poltergeist”’s finale.) The most obvious ghouls in “Primetime” are the sex perverts, who are summoned and duly exorcised in quick order. They’re not the only dark souls, though: Hansen is another, scheming to seize fame and snare increasingly prominent men on camera. And thus emerges a further thematic link between “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything”: Both feature protagonists wearing masks of attractive ambition over their monstrous tendencies. Still, it’s sparse camouflage.—A.B.

items.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
items.summary: AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth , try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training. “Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.” Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess. This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer. The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools. Web results Internal data Freshness Often hours or days old Can be months out of date without anyone noticing Quality Uneven: official docs next to forum threads Curated, but written for a past state of the product Structure Mostly unstructured text Mix of text, metadata and structured records Authority Has to be inferred from the source Known, but rarely stored as a field Access control Public Per customer, region, contract or role The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it? Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available. Why concatenating results breaks in production The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways: Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither. Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date. Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones. Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers. A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does. “A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does.” Clarm, a Y Combinator company that builds sales and support agents for open-source software companies, hit this early . Its founder, Marcus Storm-Mollard, said the team realized “search, not generation, was the real problem to solve.” Generating an answer was the easy part. Finding the right information to ground it in was the hard part, which is why Clarm runs text search, vector similarity, and structured filters through a single query instead of stitching separate stores together. What changes when agents search across sources When agents combine live web results with internal data, they need to account for different retrieval methods, metadata, permissions, and ranking signals. Four design considerations stand out. 1. Retrieve across methods in one query Keyword matching catches exact product names, error codes, and version strings, which embeddings are notoriously bad at. Vector search catches paraphrases and intent. Structured filters enforce hard constraints like customer, version, and entitlement. Within a single indexed collection, hybrid retrieval can combine keyword matching, vector similarity, and structured filters. That does not, by itself, fuse results from an external web search API with results from an internal index. The two-source integration requires a separate design decision. select * from evidence where ({targetHits: 200}nearestNeighbor(embedding, q) or userQuery()) and visibility contains "customer" and product_version contains "4.2" The broader lesson is that retrieval systems need to handle lexical matching, semantic similarity, and filtering together. These requirements matter regardless of the search platform chosen. Perplexity hit this wall when it set out to build search in-house for its answer engine. Its CEO, Aravind Srinivas, has summed up the company’s approach as “first solve search, then solve everything else.” But when the team evaluated existing tools , it found that vector databases couldn’t reliably support even simple Boolean filters, while traditional search backends offered only primitive semantic ranking. It needed lexical retrieval, semantic retrieval, and filtering in one engine, at consumer scale, and chose Vespa to build it. 2. Rank on more than similarity Relevance to the query is only one signal. Agents also need to weigh freshness, source authority, and business rules together: official documentation over forum threads, last week’s changelog over last year’s wiki page, the customer’s contracted version over the latest release. Multiphase ranking is a practical way to do this. A cheap first phase scores thousands of candidates on a blend of signals, and a more expensive learned model reorders the few that remain: rank-profile agent_evidence { inputs { query(q) tensor<float>(x[384]) } rank-properties { freshness(published_at).maxAge: 7776000 } first-phase { expression: bm25(body) + closeness(field, embedding) + 0.5 * freshness(published_at) + attribute(source_authority) } second-phase { rerank-count: 100 expression: xgboost("evidence-ranker.json") } } The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text. (The maxAge setting controls how quickly freshness decays ; here it’s 90 days.) “The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text.” Metal AI , which builds an intelligence platform for private equity firms, runs into this with due diligence questionnaires. Firms answer thousands of them from investors, and a model can’t freely generate the answers. They have to come from a bank of responses that legal has already approved, and that bank changes over time and lives in documents and spreadsheets. Similarity alone could easily surface an approved answer that’s been replaced. So Metal indexes the answer bank with recency in mind and ranks freshness alongside semantic similarity, so the agent pulls the current approved answer, not just the closest match. 3. Treat web results as candidates, not answers Web search and internal retrieval often return separate result sets, each with its own relevance signals. Simply passing both sets to the model leaves it to reconcile differences in freshness, authority, and relevance. A more deliberate approach is to evaluate evidence from both sources against a consistent set of criteria before selecting what goes into the prompt. Vespa’s flexible ranking capabilities can support this approach, but the implementation depends on how the external results are integrated into the retrieval pipeline. Depending on provider terms and system constraints, teams might index permitted external content into a shared search collection or retrieve from separate systems and apply a subsequent fusion or reranking step. There is no universal fusion method. Each option has trade-offs in latency, freshness, score comparability, and operational complexity. 4. Hold up at agent call volume This isn’t a hypothetical load pattern. At Metal, AI agents handle 95% of retrieval , not people. When someone asks for a portfolio company’s EBITDA, an agent decides which entity types to query (documents, companies, metrics, activities), applies recency and workflow filters, runs the query, and then keeps going, paginating or pulling related entities until it has enough context to answer. Clarm sees something similar from the other direction: developers working alongside its agents send thousands of queries a day, in sessions that have run as long as 22 hours. “They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.” Every one of those calls sits on the critical path to the agent’s answer. Retrieval and ranking need to stay predictable under that load, which favors running inference where the data already lives instead of shipping large candidate sets across the network to a separate ranking service. Every network hop you remove is latency you get back on every call, multiplied by every step of the task. Jon Bratseth, Vespa’s CEO, describes this as the central engineering challenge with agents: They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search. A worked example: the support agent and the changelog Here’s a scenario most support teams will recognize. A customer upgrades a payments SDK from 4.1 to 4.2, their checkout integration stops working, and they open a ticket. The agent does what you’d want and searches the web first. It finds the SDK’s changelog from four days ago, which deprecates the authentication call the integration relies on, and a forum thread where another developer posted a workaround. Then it searches internally, returning a March knowledge base article that still tells customers to use the old call, the customer’s account record showing they’re on 4.2, and a restricted engineering ticket about the same bug. Handed to the model as one long list, this is a trap. The knowledge base article matches the customer’s wording almost exactly, so it ranks well on similarity. The forum workaround reads confidently. The engineering ticket contains notes the customer should never see. When the retrieval layer is doing its job, both sets of evidence go through the same pipeline. In this example, the team uses a shared collection: web results are indexed into Vespa as short-lived documents alongside internal data, retrieved with one query and scored by rank profiles aligned with the same business rules: For this ticket, that means: The visibility filter excludes the internal ticket at query time, so it never reaches the prompt. The version filter keeps only material that applies to the library version on the customer’s account. Ranking boosts the changelog for authority and recency, demotes the older knowledge base article, and keeps the forum thread as supporting evidence. The model receives three or four well-ordered passages instead of twenty, each with its source. In this illustrative outcome, the answer cites the changelog, explains the change, and points to the supported fix. The search API helps find fresh evidence, and the retrieval design determines which evidence the agent receives. Before you wire web search into an agent Store dates and source types on everything. Internal or external, every document needs a publication date and a source type you can rank on. Write signals into the documents themselves. Keep freshness, authority, and source type on each document instead of in a separate feature store. That way they shape ranking from the first phase, not just when reranking the top results. Always include lexical signals. Even when your embeddings are strong, keyword matching is what catches the exact version numbers, error codes, and product names agents depend on. Filter in the query. Apply permissions at retrieval time, not in post-processing. Send passages, not pages. Rank the chunks within each retrieved document and pass only the most relevant spans to the model, sized to what it actually needs per call. Measure retrieval on its own. Build a test set of real agent questions and track whether the right evidence lands in the top results, separately from how the model phrases the answer. Load-test at agent volume. Benchmark with the number of retrieval calls a typical task actually makes, not one query per request. Final thoughts Managed web search for agents removes a real, frustrating failure mode, and more teams will adopt it as it leaves beta. That makes the next question more pressing. When an agent can see the open web and your private data at the same time, the quality of its work depends on how well it chooses between them. Bratseth puts it more simply: Relevance is your moat . As models get more capable and more widely available, most companies end up with access to roughly the same intelligence. What sets them apart is their own information and how well their systems use it. He breaks relevance into four parts: comprehensiveness, freshness, recall accuracy, and ranking quality. Live web search helps with the first two. The last two are still yours to build. The model shouldn’t improvise that choice on every call. It belongs in a retrieval layer you can inspect, test, and tune, where you weigh freshness, authority, permissions, and relevance together. Web search helps agents find evidence. Ranking is how they decide what to believe. For teams building agents, the practical next step is to evaluate retrieval quality separately from answer generation: test whether the right evidence appears, whether permissions are enforced before context assembly, and whether fresh and authoritative sources are prioritized when documents conflict. If you want to try this pattern, Vespa combines lexical, vector, and structured retrieval with multi-phase ranking in one pipeline, and it’s available as open source or as a managed service on Vespa Cloud. The RAG Blueprint walks through how to design the schema, retrieval strategy, and ranking phases step by step, and you can start a free trial to build it yourself.

items.title: Runtime: AWS rolls out a Nitro boost
items.summary: Welcome to Runtime! Today on Product Saturday: AWS has a new option for sandbox shoppers, Databricks lets the Genie out, and more. Please forward this email to a friend or colleague! If it was forwarded to you, sign up here to get Runtime for free every week, or level up here . Ship it Sand dollars : It's been roughly ten years since enterprise tech decided to embrace the container as the preferred vehicle for their applications. Lightweight and flexible, containers allowed companies to launch and close applications much faster than virtual machines, and their popularity led to all kinds of managed container services at the hyperscalers. At AWS, customers can choose to run containerized applications on EKS (which gets Kubernetes involved) or ECS, but those applications (or agents) need to share resources with other apps running on a tenant and that might not be a great idea for sensitive workloads. This week the cloud provider shaved five minutes off CEO Matt Garman's upcoming re:Invent keynote speech by announcing AWS Nitro Sandboxes, which can run on either managed container service or the flagship EC2 compute service. The new service was designed to give "each container the boundary of a hardware-isolated virtual machine (VM). Each sandbox gets the security properties of the Nitro System (strong isolation, zero operator access to customer data, and attestation) while keeping the familiar container experience," AWS said in a blog post . This would allow companies to run sensitive apps or agents on managed container services as if they were running on their own VM, boosting the productivity of their instances. The strategic importance of sandboxes is pretty clear to most IT organizations working with AI agents at this point, and the new service challenges similar ones from companies like Vercel. But managing costs could be tricky. Delivery, continued Shift left: Containers became so popular that companies who wanted or needed to manage their own data centers wanted to get in on the action without having to manage public cloud apps and on-premises apps separately. Red Hat's OpenShift became one of the more popular ways to do that over the years, and this week it introduced OpenShift 5 at KubeCon North America. The new version "enables IT teams to deploy AI workloads, virtual machines (VMs) and containerized workloads side-by-side through a simple, in-place update from Red Hat OpenShift 4," Red Hat said in a press release . It now supports MCP, and comes with several agents that can help operations teams diagnose and fix issues as they come up. Wishcasting : If the personal agent is going to catch on across enterprises, it seems more likely that they'll bet on a system that's already managing their corporate data over one managed by Meta. This week Databricks introduced the second generation of its Genie enterprise assistant, which now runs autonomously on behalf of its users. The idea is that Genie can monitor ongoing projects and take on work as needed, emailing the human user when a decision comes up that requires their input. "Since it runs within a company's existing Databricks environment, Genie is governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway, so every action stays within the controls companies already have in place," Databricks said in a blog post . Reset button : Even companies with the strongest operations teams and security tools can be hit by catastrophic errors or ransomware attacks that hijack data, which makes having a backup and recovery system absolutely essential. This week Commvault rolled out a new service that promises to recover business context and application logic as well as data in the event something goes wrong. Commvault Recovery Studio "will orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow to help organizations resume business operations fast," the company said in a press release .
