DictReader ( f ) : ts = datetime . fromisoformat ( row [ "changed_at" ] ) edits [ row [ "record_id" ] ] . append ( ( ts , row [ "changed_by" ] , row [ "field" ] ) ) report = [ ] for rid , rows in edits . items ( ) : rows . sort ( ) fields = defaultdict ( int ) people = set ( ) for _ , who , field in rows : fields [ field ] += 1 people . add ( who ) repeated = { k : v for k , v in fields . items ( ) if v > 1 } if repeated : report . append ( ( rid , len ( rows ) , len ( people ) , repeated ) ) report . sort ( key = lambda r : r [ 1 ] , reverse = True ) for rid , total , people , repeated in report [ : 20 ] : print ( f "{rid}: {total} edits by {people} people; repeated fields: {repeated}" ) Reading the output The same field edited by different people usually means two people think they own it. items.summary_html:
When a small team says "this process is slow", the cause is often not speed. It is rework: the same order, quote or ticket gets touched again and again because a rule is unclear.

You can measure that before you spend anything on AI. It is one of the most useful numbers when you audit a business workflow ahead of an AI purchase, and you only need an exported change log.

The input

Most tools can export an activity or change history. Shape it into a CSV like this:

record_id,changed_at,changed_by,field
ORD-101,2026-10-05T10:02,asha,status
ORD-101,2026-10-05T10:40,ravi,delivery_date
ORD-101,2026-10-06T09:15,asha,delivery_date
ORD-102,2026-10-05T11:00,asha,status
The script 
import csv
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

edits = defaultdict(list)
with open("changes.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(row["changed_at"])
        edits[row["record_id"]].append((ts, row["changed_by"], row["field"]))

report = []
for rid, rows in edits.items():
    rows.sort()
    fields = defaultdict(int)
    people = set()
    for _, who, field in rows:
        fields[field] += 1
        people.add(who)
    repeated = {k: v for k, v in fields.items() if v > 1}
    if repeated:
        report.append((rid, len(rows), len(people), repeated))

report.sort(key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)
for rid, total, people, repeated in report[:20]:
    print(f"{rid}: {total} edits by {people} people; repeated fields: {repeated}")
Reading the output
  • The same field edited by different people usually means two people think they own it. Fix ownership first.
  • A date field edited many times often means customers change plans and there is no rule for how far ahead changes are allowed.
  • A status field that flips back and forth means the steps are not clear, or one step is being skipped and caught later.

None of these are solved by adding a model. Write the rule, agree who owns the field, then check the log again.

When to bring in automation

If the rework drops once rules are written down, the remaining work is often predictable enough to automate with a person approving the risky actions. That is the point where a build makes sense.

I work on this at NxFlowAI (our first step with clients is a 72-hour audit). If you want to see how we explain our own scoring logic in public, the Vibe Checker methodology write-up is open.

items.title: Stanford NCM: The New Way of Generating Text 31x Faster

items.summary_html:
Image by author.

Every LLM you use today writes the same way: one token, then the next, then the next. A 1,000-token answer means about 1,000 steps in a line, and step 501 cannot start until step 500 is done. Your GPU can do a lot of work in parallel, but text generation keeps it waiting in a queue. That’s a big reason long answers feel slow.

Stanford’s new Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) tries a different route. It sketches the whole answer roughly first, then adds detail level by level, like a blurry WhatsApp photo that gets sharper as it loads. On OpenWebText it writes 1,024 tokens in 32 passes instead of 1,024.

The paper headline is “31x faster”. That number is real, but most people read it wrong, and I’ll come to that.

The first half of this post explains the idea in plain words. The second half is what I actually ran on an RTX 4060 laptop GPU with Stanford’s released checkpoints: a BBC article summarized level by level, ten more articles checked against BBC’s own summaries, two inputs that broke it, a Sudoku score, and a diffusion model for comparison.

I also made a video on this, you can watch it right here:

https://medium.com/media/914efbefcc86d06ea48f4c4f116a087a/hrefTwo ways models write today

Autoregressive LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama) predict one token at a time. Each new token depends on everything before it, so the steps can’t run side by side. More output means more steps, always.

Diffusion language models came in to remove that queue. Think of a fill-in-the-blanks exam paper. The model starts with the whole answer as blanks, and in every round it fills many blanks at once and fixes the ones it got wrong earlier. No waiting in line, so it can be fast: Google DeepMind’s experimental Gemini Diffusion samples at about 1,479 tokens per second.

The cost is that diffusion needs many rounds, and every round looks at the whole answer again. Cut the rounds to save time and quality drops. I show that with a real diffusion model later in this post.

NCM is a third way.

Source: Next-Concept Modeling paper (arXiv 2610.14162), Figure 2How NCM works

NCM is really two models working together.

1. The compressor. It takes a piece of text and squeezes it into a list of numbers called codes. A code is just a position in a list, like ordering by item number in a restaurant with 4,096 dishes on the menu. If token IDs feel familiar, codes are the same kind of thing: not human-readable on their own.

The key part is that the codes come in levels. The first level has only a few codes and carries the rough gist. Every level after that has more codes and stores only what the earlier levels missed. By the last level there’s enough detail to get the exact words back. This compressor is very good at its job: it rebuilds the original text exactly 98.8 to 100% of the time, depending on the task.

That’s what the “concept” in the name means. It isn’t a human idea or a sentence. It’s the information sitting in the top, coarse levels. The name sounds a little grander than the thing, and that’s fine.

The compressor: each level adds only what the levels above it missed. Image by author.

2. The writer. This is the model that generates. Like an LLM that only outputs token IDs, it only outputs codes. It writes all codes of level 1 in one go, then all codes of level 2, and so on. Inside a level nothing waits in line. The only waiting is between levels, because each level corrects the one above it.

After the last level, the compressor’s decoder turns the codes into words. That’s the first moment any text exists.

The writer on a real BBC article (my run in Step 2): one level per pass, readable text only at the end. Image by author.

So the number of passes equals the number of levels, not the number of tokens. That’s the whole source of the speed.

Passes for a 1,024-token answer. LLM and NCM numbers are from the paper (OpenWebText); the diffusion rounds are from my MDLM run. Image by author.The details that bite
  • “31x faster” is compared to diffusion models, not to ChatGPT. On XSum summarization NCM matches the strongest diffusion model’s ROUGE-L (28.0 vs 26.6) while being 31x faster. It’s one experimental fast method beating another one. There is no comparison with any production LLM.
  • A same-size LLM still writes better text. On OpenWebText the normal autoregressive model scores a generation perplexity of 35.45 against NCM’s 83.12 (lower is better). Translation too: 25.2 BLEU vs 22.6.
  • The biggest NCM trained so far is 725M parameters. Nobody knows yet whether it holds up at the size of the models we use daily.
  • No streaming. Chat apps feel fast because tokens appear as they’re written. NCM’s early levels aren’t readable words (you’ll see that below), so the user sees nothing until the last level is done.
  • Fixed depth. Even a short reply goes through every level.
What “31x faster” is actually compared against. Image by author.

Where it does look promising: it needed about 4x fewer training tokens on OpenWebText (127B vs 500B+) to get its results, and it does very well on puzzles where every part of the answer depends on every other part. More on that in Step 5.

Source: Next-Concept Modeling paper (arXiv 2610.14162), Figure 1The build

Everything below runs on Stanford’s released code and checkpoints, on an NVIDIA RTX 4060 Laptop GPU. The decoding settings are the same ones the repo’s official eval uses.

Step 0: what “cutting rounds” does to a diffusion model

Before NCM, I ran MDLM (170M parameters, trained on OpenWebText), one of the diffusion models the paper compares against. Same prompt and seed, a 1,024-token canvas, once with 48 rounds and once with only 8:

for steps in [48, 8]:
    print(f"{steps} rounds, {res['secs']} s:  {text}\n")
48 rounds, 5.38 s:  Scientists have found that Paris is receiving support from around the world in this regard.  The numbers see many lines in the fight against pollution. To see these improvements other industrial solutions will be limited
8 rounds, 1.38 s:  Scientists have found that the grasp is of, is not innate. Humans function like adults, except of the many lines, the liver sense a leak and see essential closing to get released and be gone

Neither is great writing; it’s a small model. But 48 rounds gives sentences, 8 rounds gives word salad. That’s the trade-off NCM is trying to escape: fewer rounds without falling apart.

Step 1: load the summarizer

The XSum checkpoint is trained on BBC news: give it an article, it writes a one-line summary. Loading it means loading both halves:

tk = VQVAETokenizer.from_config(cfg.tokenizer)          # the compressor (text <-> codes)
net = NextConceptTransformer(vqvae_local=tk.vqvae, config=cfg.model).cuda()  # the writer
levels = list(tk.vqvae.vq.levels)
print("codes per level:", levels)
print("passes:", len(levels), "| summary length in codes:", levels[-1])
codes per level: [4, 6, 10, 14, 20, 26, 32, 40, 48]
passes: 9 | summary length in codes: 48
writer: 88M params

Nine levels, so nine passes for the whole summary. Level 1 has 4 codes, the last level has 48.

Step 2: watch one summary sharpen, level by level

Normally you only see the final line. Here I asked the decoder to turn every level into words. The input is a BBC article about a fasting-style diet that helped the pancreas heal itself (in mice):

codes = net.generate(None, x, temperature=1.0, top_k=1, top_p=0.0, cfg_scale=0.0, cfg_null_eos=EOS)
_, z_levels = tk.vqvae.vq.idx_to_zhats(codes, return_zlevels=True)
texts = [to_text(pick_tokens(tk.vqvae.decoder(z))[0].tolist()) for z in zs]
level 1 ( 4 codes)  decades - eurozone
level 2 ( 6 codes)  habits - cancer
level 3 (10 codes)  discovered containing - cause.
level 4 (14 codes)  have that iodinere - type.
level 5 (20 codes)  have diet iodine emits theas - cause type.
level 6 (26 codes)  Scientists discovered diet that causes pancreas possibly root causes 2.
level 7 (32 codes)  Scientists discovered vegan diet reduces causes the pancre - possibly root of type diabetes.
level 8 (40 codes)  Scientists discovered a vegan diet reduces causes in the pancre - possibly cause root causes type 2 diabetes.
level 9 (48 codes)  Scientists have discovered a vegan diet that causes in the pancreas - possibly cause the causes of type 2 diabetes.

passes: 9  time: 0.30 s  article tokens: 479

Three things stand out.

Level 1 has nothing to do with the article. “Decades, eurozone” is what four coarse codes look like when you force them into words. That’s exactly why streaming doesn’t work: the early levels are not a short, rough version of the answer you could show a user.

By level 6 the topic is there: scientists, diet, pancreas, type 2. The words are still broken, but the model clearly knows what the article is about.

The final line has the gist, and the details are off. The article describes a fasting-mimicking diet that resembles a vegan diet and helped regenerate pancreas cells. NCM says “a vegan diet that causes… type 2 diabetes”. Right neighbourhood, wrong claim.

The whole thing took 9 passes and well under half a second: 0.30 s in this notebook run, and between 0.18 and 0.39 s across my other runs on the same laptop. I didn’t run an LLM on the same article, so I’m not putting a speed ratio next to that number.

Step 3: ten more articles, against BBC’s own summaries

One article is an anecdote. So I took the first ten articles of the XSum test set and printed NCM’s line next to the summary BBC actually wrote. A few of them:

[1] NCM: A man has been arrested in connection with a number of firearms ammunition and ammunition were seized in Edinburgh.
    BBC: A man has appeared in court after firearms, ammunition and cash were seized by police in Edinburgh.
[6] NCM: British declining Houvenaghel has been sacked by the British Cycling for its "systematic failings" in the sport.
    BBC: A "medal at any cost" approach created a "culture of fear" at British Cycling, says former rider Wendy Houvenaghel.
[7] NCM: A coffee coffee coach at a restaurant in the US to sell a coffee shop he owns to sell or buy off a sum.
    BBC: Have you heard the one about the computer programmer who bought a failing comedy club in Texas and turned it into a million dollar a year business?
[9] NCM: Celtic manager Brendan Rodgers says he is excited to fans to his fans as he prepare to face Queens Park Rangers on Sunday.
    BBC: Manager Brendan Rodgers is sure Celtic can exploit the wide open spaces of Hampden when they meet Rangers in Sunday's League Cup semi-final.
time per summary: 0.32-0.36 s, 9 passes each

Counting all ten by hand: 8 of 10 got the topic right (the right people, place and event). 2 of 10 were garbled (article 5, about the Essilor and Luxottica merger, came out as invented brand names; article 7 became a coffee shop). Even the good ones bend facts: Houvenaghel wasn’t sacked, and Celtic were playing Rangers, not Queens Park Rangers.

For an 88M research model that’s decent. It’s nowhere near what an LLM gives you, and the paper doesn’t claim it is.

Step 4: give it something that isn’t BBC news

Two inputs from outside its training world: a short article about Voyager 1 and the NCM paper itself.

for name in ["voyager-1-one-light-day.pdf", "ncm-paper-2610.14162.pdf"]:
voyager-1-one-light-day.pdf  (574 tokens, reads 512)
  NCM: The latest launch of space Nasa agency - Nasa's astronaut spacecraft mission - has launched its launch launch from the Nasa space astronauts astronaut - and an unmanned space mission.
ncm-paper-2610.14162.pdf  (30810 tokens, reads 512)
  NCM: acy-acy--Quible and analyticalocrographed, test, unique scenery, digital technology and tablets.

Two lessons here. It’s a specialist: a space article becomes “launch launch… astronaut astronaut”, and a research paper becomes nonsense. And it only reads the first 512 tokens. The paper is 30,810 tokens long, so the model saw the title page and part of the abstract. Easy to miss if you only look at the output.

Step 5: where it actually shines, Sudoku

In Sudoku you can’t fill row 1 and move on. Every number depends on numbers elsewhere on the board, which is bad news for a model that writes left to right. NCM looks at the whole board at every level.

I ran the released 25M Sudoku checkpoint on all 2,000 hard test boards:

merged 1 shards -> 2000 sudoku-hard outputs
 solved %  solved  cell %  valid %
    86.15 1723/2000   98.35    86.15

1,723 of 2,000 hard boards solved, 86.15%, which matches the paper’s 86.1%. A same-size autoregressive model solves about 1% in the paper’s table, and the strongest non-autoregressive baseline in the table 81.3%.

Source: Next-Concept Modeling paper (arXiv 2610.14162), Table 3What to do with this today

1. Keep building on LLMs. NCM is a research model, not a product. The checkpoints are small, task-specific and clearly behind same-size LLMs on open text and translation.

2. Read speed claims with “faster than what?” The 31x is against diffusion models, on one task, on one H100. Speed headlines in this space almost always need that question.

3. Watch it for “whole answer at once” problems. Puzzles, constraint-style outputs and tasks where every part depends on every other part are where coarse-to-fine already wins.

4. Watch the training-cost angle. Getting results with about 4x fewer training tokens matters as good data gets more expensive.

The short version
  • NCM compresses text into levels of codes, writes each level in one parallel pass, and decodes words only at the end.
  • Passes = levels, so 1,024 tokens take 32 passes instead of 1,024.
  • “31x faster” is vs diffusion models, not vs ChatGPT or any production LLM.
  • On my laptop: 9 passes, under half a second per BBC summary; the gist was right in 8 of 10, details often wrong.
  • No streaming: early levels aren’t readable text.
  • It shines on Sudoku (86% of hard boards) and trails same-size LLMs on open text.

Diffusion language models showed that writing doesn’t have to happen in a queue. NCM borrows its level-by-level idea from VAR, which did coarse-to-fine for images, and brings it to text. It isn’t the model you ship next sprint, but it’s a clear sign that not every piece of writing has to happen one token at a time. Credit to the Hazy Research and Scaling Intelligence teams at Stanford, with Together AI, for releasing the code and checkpoints so anyone can check these numbers on their own GPU.

Video version: watch the NCM video on YouTube

The full code

Everything above comes from one notebook. Here is all of it, so you can run it on your own GPU. It needs a CUDA GPU; the XSum summarizer fits easily in 8 GB.

Setup, once. Clone the repo, install it, and download the released checkpoints and test data:

git clone https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm.git repo
pip install -r repo/requirements.txt pypdf
cd repo
hf download hazyresearch/ncm-checkpoints --local-dir artifacts
hf download hazyresearch/ncm-datasets --repo-type dataset --local-dir data
python evaluate.py --config config/eval/sudoku-hard.yaml --checkpoint-dir artifacts/sudoku/hard --data-dir data/sudoku/hard --out eval/sudoku-hard-full

The last command runs the Sudoku checkpoint on all 2,000 hard boards and saves the generations; the notebook only re-scores them. Then point NCM_HOME at the folder that holds repo/, and put any PDFs you want summarized in demo/docs/ (I saved a BBC article as bbc-article.pdf).

Settings and paths

import os, sys, time, json, pickle, re, contextlib, io, warnings, subprocess
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
PROJ = os.environ["NCM_HOME"]   # folder with repo/ (git clone of HazyResearch/ncm), hf-cache/ and demo/docs/
os.environ["HF_HOME"] = os.path.join(PROJ, "hf-cache")
os.environ["TRANSFORMERS_VERBOSITY"] = "error"
REPO = os.path.join(PROJ, "repo")
sys.path.insert(0, REPO); os.chdir(REPO)

Load the XSum summarizer

import torch
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
from omegaconf import OmegaConf
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from models.next_concept import NextConceptTransformer
from tokenization.vqvae_tokenizer import VQVAETokenizer
 
cfg = OmegaConf.load("config/eval/xsum.yaml")
cfg.tokenizer.vqvae.checkpoint_path = "artifacts/xsum/tokenizer.pt"
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    tk = VQVAETokenizer.from_config(cfg.tokenizer)          # the compressor (text <-> codes)
    tk.vqvae = tk.vqvae.cuda().eval()
    net = NextConceptTransformer(vqvae_local=tk.vqvae, config=cfg.model).cuda()  # the writer
sd = torch.load("artifacts/xsum/generator.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
net.load_state_dict(sd["model"], strict=True); net.eval()
 
levels = list(tk.vqvae.vq.levels)
print("codes per level:", levels)
print("passes:", len(levels), "| summary length in codes:", levels[-1])
print(f"writer: {sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters())/1e6:.0f}M params")

Decoding helpers (same settings as the repo’s official eval)

# helpers: the same decoding settings as the repo's official eval (scripts/eval_shard.py)
G = cfg.generation
P = int(cfg.model.prefix_len)
EOS, PAD = tk.pre_tokenizer.eos_token_id, tk.pre_tokenizer.pad_token_id
src_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")   # only to tokenize the article
ALLOW = sd["inference"]["token_unigram"].double().cuda()
freq, mu = float(G.frequency_penalty), float(G.frequency_deficit)
ADJ = [float(v) for v in str(G.adjacency_penalty).split(",")]
 
def pick_tokens(logits):
    B, T, V = logits.shape
    lg = logits.double(); allow = (ALLOW[:V] * T)[None, :]
    al, aw, ad = ADJ[0], int(ADJ[1]), ADJ[2]
    cnt = torch.zeros(B, V, dtype=torch.float64, device=lg.device)
    out = torch.empty(B, T, dtype=torch.long, device=lg.device); hist = []
    for t in range(T):
        step = lg[:, t, :].clone()
        step -= freq * (cnt - allow).clamp_min(0.0)
        step += mu * ((T - t) / T) * (allow - cnt).clamp_min(0.0)
        for j, h in enumerate(reversed(hist[-aw:])):
            step.scatter_add_(1, h[:, None], torch.full((B, 1), -al * ad ** j, dtype=torch.float64, device=lg.device))
        p = step.argmax(-1); out[:, t] = p; hist.append(p)
        cnt.scatter_add_(1, p[:, None], torch.ones(B, 1, dtype=torch.float64, device=lg.device))
    return out
 
def to_text(ids):
    ids = list(ids)
    if EOS in ids: ids = ids[:ids.index(EOS)]
    return tk.pre_tokenizer.decode([t for t in ids if t not in (EOS, PAD)], skip_special_tokens=True).strip()

Summarize a PDF and decode every level

@torch.no_grad()
def summarize(article, every_level=False):
    ids = src_tok(article)["input_ids"]
    x = torch.tensor([(ids[:P] + [PAD] * P)[:P]], device="cuda")   # the model reads the first 512 tokens
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); t0 = time.perf_counter()
    codes = net.generate(None, x, temperature=1.0, top_k=1, top_p=0.0, cfg_scale=0.0, cfg_null_eos=EOS)
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); secs = time.perf_counter() - t0
    _, z_levels = tk.vqvae.vq.idx_to_zhats(codes, return_zlevels=True)
    zs = z_levels if every_level else z_levels[-1:]
    texts = [to_text(pick_tokens(tk.vqvae.decoder(z))[0].tolist()) for z in zs]
    return texts, secs, len(ids)
 
from pypdf import PdfReader
def read_pdf(path):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", " ".join(p.extract_text() or "" for p in PdfReader(path).pages)).strip()
 
article = read_pdf(os.path.join(PROJ, "demo", "docs", "bbc-article.pdf"))
summarize(article)  # warm-up
texts, secs, n_tok = summarize(article, every_level=True)
for k, (n, t) in enumerate(zip(levels, texts), 1):
    print(f"level {k} ({n:2d} codes)  {t}")
print(f"\npasses: {len(levels)}  time: {secs:.2f} s  article tokens: {n_tok}")

Ten XSum test articles against BBC’s own summaries

passages = pickle.load(open("data/xsum/passages.pickle", "rb"))
refs = pickle.load(open("data/xsum/reference_summaries.pickle", "rb"))
 
def article_text(item):
    if isinstance(item, str): return item
    art = list(item[:P]); art = art[:art.index(PAD)] if PAD in art else art
    return src_tok.decode(art)
 
def ref_text(r):
    return r if isinstance(r, str) else to_text(r)
 
times = []
for i in range(10):
    (s,), secs, _ = summarize(article_text(passages[i])); times.append(secs)
    print(f"[{i}] NCM: {s}\n    BBC: {ref_text(refs[i])}\n")
print(f"time per summary: {min(times):.2f}-{max(times):.2f} s, {len(levels)} passes each")

Inputs that aren’t BBC news

for name in ["voyager-1-one-light-day.pdf", "ncm-paper-2610.14162.pdf"]:
    (s,), secs, n_tok = summarize(read_pdf(os.path.join(PROJ, "demo", "docs", name)))
    print(f"{name}  ({n_tok} tokens, reads {min(n_tok, P)})\n  NCM: {s}\n")

Score the Sudoku run

r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "scripts/eval_merge.py", "--config", "config/eval/sudoku-hard.yaml",
                    "--glob", "eval/sudoku-hard-full/shard_*.pkl"], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", env={**os.environ, "PYTHONIOENCODING": "utf-8"})
print(r.stdout.strip()[-600:])

The diffusion comparison in Step 0 uses the sampler from the MDLM repo with the kuleshov-group/mdlm-owt weights, so it isn’t repeated here.

items.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
items.summary: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair . Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder . Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years. Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff? Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way. In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close. There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective. I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.” With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day. I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning? They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for. In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?” We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions. [Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight. They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology. The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.” Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with. It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined. There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate? A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey. I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do. There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events. You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well. This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means. It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well. Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?” The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app. I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that. That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do. That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding. For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.” It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster. A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up. At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people. How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference. Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now . Have a good time.” And he ended the call. Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed? I actually wrote something about this . I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI. There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.” That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things. So we’ve reached some definitions of AGI. We’re far from other definitions. Some people will say AGI is when it awakens and is sentient and can do every single thing that any human ever can do. I think we’re pretty far from that. At this point you can have arguments, and people do have arguments, of “well, Astra is AGI,” or “was [OpenAI’s] o3 with tools AGI” or “was ChatGPT AGI,” whatever. If that’s the argument we’re having, we just need to set aside that term and come up with different, more-specific things we mean by that.” The president wants to call it “Super Intelligence.” I don’t know if you’ve heard. [Laughs] I have heard. The thing I find saddest about that is just that it was an existing term that is becoming increasingly relevant. I have a lot of feelings about words and terminology. Are you AGI-pilled? Do you think we’re going to get there in the current run of technology? I think it is obviously possible enough that we need to think seriously about it, which is my stance on a lot of this weird stuff. I’m not like, “This is definitely happening, it’s definitely happening in two years.” But I’m like, “Look, I think this is very solidly plausible and very solidly in the realm of real things that could happen that we should prepare for.” I work in the national security space. There’s things like, “Will China launch a full-scale amphibious invasion of Taiwan?” where most analysts in the space will say “probably not,” and “probably they would lose.” Also, “We would see signs of them preparing and whatever, but we should take that seriously.” We should not just laugh anyone out of the room and call that science fiction. We should be ready for a range of different contingencies and scenarios. Do you think Claude is conscious? I have no idea. That’s an answer. I mean, that is legitimately an answer. It is scientifically such an unsolved problem. What do we mean by consciousness? And is that a thing or is it actually 10 different things that we’re lumping together or what? I have no idea. What do you think? No. I seem to be the person in this ecosystem who gets asked questions like that and I’m like, “No.” Because the thing that I struggle with is, there are lots of other things where we’re already confused about whether they’re conscious. That’s why I do the work that I do, because I think we need to have different structures and many more people involved with many more perspectives being represented. You have some hindsight now. You knew it was going to suck going into it. You definitely know it sucked coming out of it. What would you have done differently about that time? It’s kind of hard to give the full answer to that because it would take unpicking all this stuff and all these legal restrictions and blah, blah, blah, blah. For sure a thing would have been building stronger relationships with executives on the team. The way that the company related to the board could have been different if more board members had had that. I knew some of the folks pretty well, but that’s one thing. I don’t know. I think we could have… Yeah, no, I think beyond that, it just gets hard to… You have to go in and say, “What were all the different micro decisions and why do we make those decisions and which ones could be—” What is the show? It’s a show about decisions. I’ve got another hour. [Laughs] Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, and then my answers would all get annoying and legal. Fair enough. I’m curious about it because as they go public, there will be market forces acting on them in a totally new way. There will be an investor class. There’ll be an entire CNBC machine that wakes up every day and is like, “Is Anthropic winning or is OpenAI winning?” That is a race dynamic that might be really healthy. It might keep them from trying to kill everyone in the world because they have a bunch of investors looking for their next quarterly earnings, or it might push them further into an unhealthy kind of race. How do you see that playing out, given what you know of these people? It’s going to be really interesting to see if going public is good or bad for their governance. A lot of people are like, “Oh no, going public, there’s going to be so much pressure to make a profit that they’re not going to be able to consider other things.” But at the same time, the corporate governance of public companies is much more structured, much more regulated, and subject to much more external scrutiny than for private companies. I think even things like getting to see Anthropic’s S-1 and thinking, “Okay, what are they doing and why are they doing it? And how do they think about the risks they’re facing, and how do they communicate about those with investors?” Or even things like the Trump administration putting in place this kind of accord , they call it “Super Intelligence,” that several of the leading companies signed. That was structured around, for example, having certain types of things being reported to an independent committee of the board. That idea of an independent committee of the board is kind of toothless if it’s a private company that is deciding on its own. I thought about you when I read that. I was like, “Boy, some independent boards have gotten in a lot of trouble before.” But if it’s a public company, then an independent committee of the board has a pretty strong legal meaning. So I don’t know. It’s something that I’m watching with great interest. The other race dynamic here is China. You mentioned China before. Inside of our country, a bunch of labs are going to go public. They’re going to become some of the richest companies in the history of the world, and they’re going to fight for every dollar that capitalism can generate, and hopefully that restrains them. The market forces will restrain them, and hopefully your work with legislators in this country does something. And then there’s a whole other country that doesn’t listen to us or have anything to do with us, and they’re just going to distill our models and do whatever they want. That is the other argument for not placing any restrictions on these companies that everyone hears all the time. What should I make of that? I’m of two minds about it. How should I think about it? Yeah. I think of this as the ”But China!” argument, which is like, “Well, yeah, we should do this, we should do that, ‘But China!’” I think the way to engage with it is an actual genuine problem that we have to grapple with, and we should be strategic and thoughtful about it and do our best to try and solve it as a problem as opposed to using it as a throwaway excuse. Like, “Oh yeah, sure, sure, sure. All that stuff would be so nice, ‘But China!’, so we’re stuck. There’s nothing we can do.” So what does that look like in practice? If you’re serious about wanting the US to have stronger AI than China, then you need to think really hard about how much US AI development is helping Chinese AI progress. So the one that people talk about all the time, as you mentioned, is distillation, which is, “Are they using US models to generate massive amounts of training data for their own models and therefore progressing faster than they would otherwise?” So certainly I think it makes sense to try and crack down on that and prevent it from happening. But another one, for example, is security and how easy would it be for Chinese actors or other actors, frankly, to steal algorithmic secrets, to steal wholesale model weights. If they can steal the weights of your Astra or your Mythos model and just take them back to their own servers, your lead has vanished. You now have a lead of zero. Right now these companies, especially the smaller ones, but even OpenAI and Anthropic, do not have very good security. We’ve seen both of them over the last few months have external teams manage to hack into spaces that have large amounts of algorithmic secrets. In OpenAI’s case, it was their monorepo and GitHub, which had all of their code. And in Anthropic’s case, I think — and actually maybe the OpenAI case also involved this — the hackers got access to Slack . You’re just going to have so insanely much rich information about how to build better AI if you can get that access. So when our AI gets better, are we actually lengthening our lead or are we just pulling China along with us in these different ways? The other aspect of this is just seriously treating China as an actor in this space and trying to think seriously about their motivations and their likely actions and responses. In my mind, a huge reason that a lot of things are not happening right now is most people are not convinced about this threat model that AI will become the machine god and will take over and humans will all die or will be subservient or whatever. I think it’s fair for people to not be convinced of that, because the evidence is sort of conflicting and unclear, but if that is actually what we think could seriously happen, then China doesn’t want that either. So then it becomes a question of, “Okay, how do we try and get them on the same page of, ‘this threat that we’re worried about is a real threat to worry about?’ Because then they will be making their own decisions in their own self-interest.” I think an approach of, “Well, the US has to force China to do something using some kind of leverage,” is never ever going to work. But an approach of, “Well, look, if we think this is a serious problem that’s going to affect us as humans, and the people in China are also humans, and also if we think this is a problem around who has control, the Chinese Communist Party really, really wants to have control, and so they’re going to have their own incentives and their own decision-making around how to fix that.” Well, let me put it on a spectrum for you. This is very dumb and you’re going to laugh, but just go with me on this. On the one end, it is nuclear weapons and the Chinese government wants a nuclear weapon and they’re going to do whatever they can to control that weapon and they will run their industries differently. If they get out of line, the CEO of Alibaba goes. He just disappears for a while and then comes back — Chinese government stuff. We need a nuclear weapon, too. If we don’t get there first, then we’ll never get the nonproliferation treaty that we need to keep us all safe for mutually assured destruction. That’s one framework. Way on the other end, I spent five years of my life listening to telecom executives tell me that if we didn’t build 5G networks first, China would get them, and then something . No one could ever tell me what the “something” was. Where on that spectrum between 5G and nuclear weapons is the US-China AI race? I think we need another dimension because in that example, your dimension is significance. But I think the controllability is a huge question as well. So it’s like, what are the examples that people use? Is it a nuclear weapon or is it dragons from House of the Dragon ? Casey Newton had a great Platformer post where he explained he was watching House of the Dragon and thought, “This is what the AI companies are doing. They’re trying to build these things that they think will help them, but actually it’s just going to rain down destruction.” [Laughs] Casey told me he was buying an iPhone Duo so he could watch more TV. He’s a dear friend, but okay. But I think that’s really important because if we think this is a technology we can control, then obviously we want to have the best technology. Obviously, we want to go foot to the floor, get there as fast as we can, and the same is true for China. The question is, if we are not sure if we can control it, then what do we do? Maybe we want to be more cautious and then maybe we want to try and figure out a way to not have China just be overtaking us. But if we’re correct we should be worried about— So that’s nuclear weapons. Well, no, but if it’s dragons, if we’re correct that we need to be worried about whether we can control this, then that’s also something that should be interesting to China. I remember this Casey post, but let me just try to pull this apart so I understand it. The difference between dragons and nuclear weapons is the dragons have some agency, right? They can go away and do bad things on their own. Yes. The dragons might just decide to burn down your whole city. Obviously these are machines — they’re just math, they’re not magical. So instead of dragons, you could think of it as nuclear weapons with faulty control settings, where you build nuclear weapons, but it’s impossible to be sure that it’s not just going to go off and fly to a city and fly to one of your own cities and wipe you out. That’s a very different technology than real nuclear weapons that exist. It is true. No one ever said that about 5G. I’ll be clear about that. The reason I’m asking about this is because those problems do align nation-states, right? We do have nuclear nonproliferation agreements. As you mentioned, there are all kinds of incentives for nation-states to not do cyberattacks willy-nilly because those have real-world consequences. Is there any evidence that these governments have started to align on these problems? Or is it still the pure “But China!” race dynamic? I actually think there is starting to be some early evidence. One way I think about what happened this year in AI from a policy perspective, less than a product or economic perspective, is we saw these two big demonstrations of the two major concerns people have. So the two major concerns are misuse and misalignment, meaning misuse is bad people using AI for bad things and misalignment is AI going rogue or doing things we didn’t want. So this year we had Mythos and we had the Hugging Face attack. Both of those are just really vivid, crisp real-world demonstrations of what these misuse and misalignment concerns could look like. The US and Chinese governments are starting from very different places on AI regulation. They’re both starting from where they started, and what they did with, internet regulation. So the US is starting from a “hands off, laissez-faire, absolutely nothing, do whatever you want” approach. China is starting from a massively locked-down internet with tons of censorship and the Great Firewall. So those are two very different starting points. I’m not a China expert, but I operate a lot in China circles and I’ve lived in China and so on. But it seems like just over the past even one to three months, starting from those two very different points, they are seeing more in common around threats from major cyberattacks and also threats of loss of control. I’m a language nerd and it’s really interesting tracking the different language China uses about AI. So they’re now talking about loss of control as a thing, but they probably usually don’t mean the same thing that Westerners mean where “loss of control” is like “AI takeover.” They probably mean something more prosaic, but then sometimes they talk about “extreme loss of control,” which maybe is the thing we mean. I do think that there are starting to be some signs of convergence. I think it’ll be a long road. The state of the US-China relationship is such that there’s going to be very, very, very little trust on either side. So I am not optimistic that they’ll just get to sit down in a room and hash out a deal and everything will be great. But I think there is enough space. Basically, if there’s enough shared threat perception, then it might be possible at some point in the future to do something about that. Helen, you’ve given me so much time. As you can tell, I’m just delighted with this conversation. It’s been very fun. We are on the cusp of a new Congress. There are a bunch of new governors. The data center referendums passed overwhelmingly in this country. There’s a new set of regulators in town, right? They’re going to do some stuff. What are some signs people should look for to indicate we’re going to be on the right path and what are some signs that we’re just chasing our tail? Set AI aside, forget about AI. Congress in general is very bad at passing things right now. This is not a this administration thing, this is not an AI thing. So one sign is like, can Congress pass anything? That will be a good sign. It’s also really interesting to look at what state legislatures have been doing in AI. There’s been a lot of concern about the possibility of a state patchwork on AI, with different states passing conflicting things. With the issues that we’ve been talking about today, which I think of as frontier AI risks or the risks from the most advanced systems, there’s actually been a pretty coordinated push in different states. California passed this one bill and then New York passed almost the same bill with just a little more added to it. And then Illinois passed almost the same bill with a little more added to it. I think there’s going to be a lot of momentum over the next year or two to keep building on that at the state level. So that is something that I’ll be watching. Even just specifically California is already looking at how they can strengthen things. So that is something I’ll be looking for. I think honestly, with such a Democratic Congress, I am also concerned that they will overstep here, that they will try and do something that is too sweeping. You had this huge mess in Colorado where they passed this giant AI bill that then was a terrible idea. And so then they had all these committees and follow-up and it was awful. A lot of what we need right now is focused on these frontier systems and the possibility that we have really, really advanced systems in a short amount of time and having much more transparency around that and much clearer standards for how they manage risk. I would not be that excited about an attempt to do a really comprehensive AI regulatory push that covers AI all across the economy and all different kinds of AI systems that are less advanced. There are negative signals that are like “nothing’s going to happen,” and there are negative signals like, “oh, maybe too much is going to happen,” but it’ll be interesting to see where they get to. I suspect we’re going to want to have you back as this Congress starts to get to work and we see some of these ideas. I would love to. I’m eager for your take on it. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thanks so much. This was really fun. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
