items.title: I was flying when the FAA grounded all flights. Everything was chaos, and I got stuck on the tarmac for hours.
items.summary: I got stuck in Miami airport amid the FAA grounding chaos. Gentry Hale I was at 35,000 feet when my captain said an air traffic control issue grounded flights. Several passengers and I were worried it was related to cybersecurity or AI. We landed in Miami but couldn't deplane for hours, and I ended up paying $600 for a hotel room. I spend a huge portion of my life on airplanes as a frequent traveler and journalist, so I'm used to the usual delays , missed connections, and last-minute flight changes that come with commercial air travel. But I have never experienced anything like the crippling air traffic control outage on Friday, November 13, that displaced thousands of passengers and crews and canceled over 12,500 flights. I had been at cruising altitude, flying back from a vacation in the Caribbean island of Curaçao toward my home in Salt Lake City, when the Federal Aviation Administration halted departing flights across the entire US. Before Friday, the FAA had only ordered a nationwide ground stop twice in modern history: once in January 2023, following a failure of a key pilot-alert system , and after the September 11 terrorist attacks. Given the rare track record, I wasn't thrilled to find myself midair when I heard the news. What should have been a quick two-hour layover in Miami unraveled into a chaotic overnight delay, with hours spent on a gridlocked tarmac as passengers raced for vanishing hotel rooms and flight inventory. We learned about the nationwide shutdown at 35,000 feet Before boarding in Curaçao, my flight had already been delayed by about 30 minutes, and I jokingly texted a friend that it better not be delayed any further because I refused to spend the night in Miami. I should have knocked on wood, because about 40 minutes out from landing, the cabin speakers crackled to life. The captain said he was sure some of us had WiFi and had seen messages about a nationwide ground stop , then confirmed it was true. Trying to keep chill while we sat on the plane for hours and sparred over hotels and new flights. Gentry Hale Hushed conversations throughout the cabin ensued, and I looked to my neighbor to check the news since I didn't have WiFi myself. This was the first time in a long time I was nervous on a plane. I read that officials said a telecommunications issue was affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the regional facilities responsible for directing and guiding aircraft at higher altitudes between airports. I also read that officials did not believe the disruption was the result of AI or a cyberattack — something that I'd been wondering about. For some reason, that scared me even more. What was it, then? My next thought: If air traffic control has a communications failure, how are we going to land? I was relieved when the captain informed us that planes already in the sky, including mine, were cleared to land at their destinations, and that the order had frozen departures. Although I didn't know it at the time, officials later said that pilots, air traffic controllers , and dispatchers have various backup methods and digital tools for communication, and pilots are trained to navigate and land without comms. Still, the timing of the halt was unnerving, coming after the widespread Microsoft cloud disruptions the day before and the National Weather Service data hiccups earlier Friday. Landing in Miami was only the beginning of the chaos When our wheels finally touched down at Miami International Airport, I checked my phone and saw that the captain had kept us informed to the best of his knowledge; no further news had been released, but at least we had been able to land. But now we were stuck on the plane. Because inbound flights were still arriving while outbound planes sat at their gates, the airport's ramp space was gridlocked. With nowhere to park and unload passengers, our plane sat idling on the tarmac for the next two hours. There were too many planes for the number of gates at Miami airport during Friday's FAA outage. Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images Around 7:30 p.m., about an hour after landing, passengers around me began murmuring that rebooking options were finally appearing in the American Airlines app. When I refreshed my screen, every option required flying out the following evening on grueling 12- to 14-hour itineraries with multiple layovers. Unwilling to spend a half-day hopping around the US from Florida to Utah, I accepted that I would spend the full weekend in Miami. But before I booked something for Sunday or Monday, I refreshed the list one more time. Buried at the very bottom was a single direct flight departing at 7:45 p.m. on Saturday night. I booked it immediately, snagging one of the final three open seats — and crossed my fingers that the snowball effect would slow by then and my flight would actually take off. Hotel rooms disappeared almost as quickly as flights were canceled Still trapped on the tarmac, another problem emerged: finding a place to sleep. Around me, passengers were frantically refreshing booking apps as airport hotels sold out in real time. I barely managed to book a room at the Hyde Hotel in Midtown Miami, about 15 minutes away. It wasn't cheap — $621 for the night, to be exact. The airline wasn't required to help me out in the uncontrollable flight disruption, and I'm not sure my travel insurance will reimburse me, so I've accepted I may eat that money. The passenger pick-up area was swarming with cars as people dispersed to their hotels. Gentry Hale When I finally deplaned around 8 p.m., cleared customs, and arrived at the lobby, the front desk agent told me the hotel had surged from about 40% full at 5 p.m. local time to sold out by 9 p.m. — filled to capacity by displaced flyers in under four hours. Even in a major hospitality hub like Miami, inventory evaporates quickly when thousands of stranded travelers are competing for the same beds. Despite the pain in my wallet, knowing I wasn't spending the night on an airport terminal floor felt like I had won the lottery. I was reminded that no matter how much I prepare, I'm at the whim of the air system Once I reached my hotel, I refreshed my news app to see that the FAA had lifted the nationwide ground stop, allowing departures to slowly resume, but the effects had already disrupted the whole country. Air travel is notorious for its snowball effect: a single thunderstorm in Dallas or Atlanta can trigger cascading delays thousands of miles away as planes and crews get displaced . A simultaneous shutdown of the entire US airspace system was a whole other beast. A friend scheduled to fly to Las Vegas had his trip canceled before he had even left for the airport. But another friend flying from Panama to Denver ended up stranded in Houston — her second overnight stall in 48 hours after weather disruptions the day before. I'm lucky I got a hotel; rooms were getting scarce by the time I booked. Joe Raedle/Getty Images For someone who flies regularly, the unexpected chaos was a reality check. I can build buffer time into my schedule, book early-morning departures and pack carry-on only, but none of that will protect me when a backbone of the national airspace system goes offline. Lying in my hotel room in Miami, I'll admit I felt a flicker of hesitation about stepping back onto a plane Saturday evening. The thought of pilots losing clear communication with the ground is terrifying. But that fear is merely one of the trade-offs we accept every time we board a flight to see the world — and I know the pilots are highly trained to deal with emergencies like lost comms. Read the original article on Business Insider

  • Several passengers and I were worried it was related to cybersecurity or AI.
  • We landed in Miami but couldn't deplane for hours, and I ended up paying $600 for a hotel room.

For someone who flies regularly, the unexpected chaos was a reality check. I can build buffer time into my schedule, book early-morning departures and pack carry-on only, but none of that will protect me when a backbone of the national airspace system goes offline.

Lying in my hotel room in Miami, I'll admit I felt a flicker of hesitation about stepping back onto a plane Saturday evening. The thought of pilots losing clear communication with the ground is terrifying.

But that fear is merely one of the trade-offs we accept every time we board a flight to see the world — and I know the pilots are highly trained to deal with emergencies like lost comms.

items.summary_html:
A font store, a local Noto install, and why reuse is the real test of a coding agent.

I’m building smallsymbols, a visual emoji atlas that compares four emoji renderers. In the authoring tools behind it, I work with Cursor. When I asked it to build a feature that generates derived images, it didn’t use the font store I had already written for the project. It used the Noto font installed locally on my machine. I noticed because I still had an older version installed, and some of the derived graphics looked visibly different: Noto draws a few emojis differently in the newer version than in the one on my system.

This article was drafted with AI assistance from my notes and ideas. The projects, experiences and opinions are my own.

The font store exists to prevent exactly that kind of mismatch. It manages emoji fonts in multiple versions and formats — Noto as SVG and PNG, for example — and makes sure everything uses one consistent font version. The feature still ran on my machine. It was also architecturally wrong. A design decision had been bypassed. And it wasn’t a one-off. The agent has gone around the font store more than once, with the same pattern: a path that worked locally and never went through the place that was supposed to own the fonts.

The font store is a decision, not leftover architecture

The font store is one place that knows which font versions and formats exist, and that every renderer and every derived graphic should use the same one. That sounds like bookkeeping. It is actually a product decision: if you’re comparing renderers, or generating graphics from the same emoji, they have to start from the same font version. Otherwise you aren’t looking at a renderer difference, or at a stable derived image. You’re looking at an accidental mix of versions.

Renderers and derived graphics share one font version through the store. The agent’s shortcut used the older local Noto, so a few emojis looked different.

This is not a workaround I introduced because opening a font file directly is too hard for humans. It bundles a responsibility so that different parts of the software don’t make contradictory assumptions. When Cursor ignored it and reached for whatever Noto happened to be on my system, it solved the immediate problem — generate the images — and quietly violated the decision that was supposed to apply to all of them. Generating code is not the same as building software. The first can succeed while the second comes out inconsistent.

That is a quality failure, not a step toward more autonomy. The code can look fine. The feature can even produce output. It is still wrong in the same family of ways I wrote about in My Coding Agent Passed Every Test. The Code Was Wrong., just under a different test. Last time, the tests were green and the logic was wrong. This time, the problem wasn’t a hard-coded example. It was a design decision the agent didn’t reuse.

The claim that we won’t need abstractions

There’s a popular argument that as models get better, we won’t need programming languages at all. AI will skip source code and emit machine code, even optimized binaries, directly from a description of the outcome.

Elon Musk put a version of this at a public xAI all-hands in February 2026. He said things may move, by the end of the year, “to where you don’t even bother doing coding,” because “the AI just creates the binary directly,” and that traditional coding is “an intermediate step that actually will not be needed.”

I don’t think the interesting question is the timeline. Programming languages are abstractions. Compilers already produce binaries. The hard part of software is not the last translation step. It is keeping a decision in one place so the next change does not contradict the last one. Abstractions do that work for agents at least as much as they do for humans. My font store is already that problem, at the application layer. No need to wait for machine code.

More code, less reuse

What happened in my repo is a small case of a larger pattern: agents are very good at producing new code, and much less reliable at using what is already there.

GitClear’s 2026 report The Maintainability Gap, based on 623 million analyzed changes from 2023 to 2026, found that cross-file function calls — a signal of reuse — are down 35 percent. Refactoring, measured as “moved” code, fell from 21 percent of changed lines in 2022 to 3.8 percent in 2026, while copy-and-paste rose from 9.4 percent to 15.7 percent. The report’s own framing is not that AI writes bad code, but that the default workflow is incentivized to deliver “atomic code — a happy-path, a passing test, a closed ticket” and to tax the reuse that makes a codebase cheaper to own later.

GitClear sells code-quality tools, and this is a correlation with the AI era, not a controlled experiment. I still recognize the shape. New code that stands alone, instead of calling the function you already have, is exactly what the local Noto font was.

What I do now

Better AI should not mean the agent writes more. It should mean the agent is better at seeing what it does not need to write. Software engineering is the art of not having to solve the same problem again. An abstraction is how that decision stays in force.

I don’t assume Cursor will find the font store on its own. I use targeted search and review prompts that look specifically for the wrong usage: did this go through the font store, or did it open a font some other way? The habit is close to the second-agent reviews I described in the earlier article, only the questions here are about architecture, not about whether the tests were hard-coded.

When I plan a new feature, wiring up the font store is part of the plan, not an afterthought. And I search the repo for font files that have newly appeared. A new font file is a concrete smell that something bypassed the store. None of this is glamorous, and I do it because the failure does not always announce itself. I only caught this case because my local font was out of date, and a few emojis looked wrong.

This is also why files like AGENTS.md have caught on: a “README for agents,” now an open standard used by tens of thousands of projects and stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation. The industry is betting that agents write better software when you tell them about the architecture that already exists, not when you delete the layers. Instructions alone are not a guarantee, though. I still search and review, because an agent that can write the code can also walk around the rule.

The agent that writes less

We still tend to picture a smarter coding agent as one that produces more code, faster. I think that’s the wrong picture. The agent that spends an hour reading the repository and then changes five lines to call a function that already exists is doing the better job, not the slower one.

In AI Won’t Rewrite Photoshop, I argued that agents make shared software more valuable, not less. The same idea applies one level down, inside your own repo. And in Building Got Cheaper. Madness Became Affordable. I wrote that cheaper building raises your ambition. It also makes it cheap to rebuild a problem you already solved. That’s the kind of madness not to afford.

The better AI gets at coding, the less new code it should need to write.

items.title: What is MCP and How It Gives AI One Standard Way to Plug Into Your Tools
items.summary: The Model Context Protocol is often called “USB-C for AI.” Here is what it actually is, how the pieces fit together, what a tiny MCP server looks like in Python, and what to watch out for before you connect one. Think about the drawer of old phone chargers most of us have at home. One cable for this phone, a different one for that tablet, another for the headphones. Every device had its own plug. Then USB-C came along, and slowly one cable started working with almost everything. AI apps had a similar problem with tools. Every time you wanted a chatbot or agent to read your files, query a database, or check a ticket in some system, someone had to write a custom connector for that exact app and that exact tool. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an attempt to fix that with one shared plug. The problem MCP solves In the article on AI agents, we saw that a language model becomes much more useful when it can use tools. But the model doesn’t run tools by itself. The app around it does. And each app used to wire up each tool in its own way. Here’s the engineering problem in numbers. Say there are 5 AI apps and 10 tools people want to connect. If every app builds its own connector for every tool, that’s 5 × 10 = 50 separate integrations to write and maintain. With a shared standard, each app implements the protocol once and each tool implements it once. That’s 5 + 10 = 15 pieces of work, and any app can talk to any tool. When Anthropic open-sourced MCP in November 2024, this is exactly how they described it: AI models were “trapped behind information silos,” and every new data source needed “its own custom implementation” [1]. MCP replaces those one-off integrations with a single protocol. What MCP actually is MCP is an open standard for how AI applications talk to external tools and data. It’s not a model, and it’s not a product. It’s a set of rules, like HTTP is for websites. It also doesn’t decide how the AI uses what it gets. The official docs are clear that MCP only covers the exchange of context. How the app uses the model is up to the app [2]. The three main pieces MCP uses a client-server setup with three roles [2]: Host. The AI application the user actually works in, like Claude Desktop, VS Code, or ChatGPT. Client. A small connector inside the host. The host creates one client for each server it connects to. Server. A program that offers capabilities to the AI. For example, a GitHub server, a Postgres server, or a server for your company’s internal order system. Going back to the charger drawer: the host is your laptop, each client is a USB-C port, and each server is a device you plug in. A server can run locally on your machine, talking to the host through standard input and output (called stdio), or remotely over the internet using a transport called Streamable HTTP [2]. Either way, the messages themselves use JSON-RPC 2.0, a simple, well-known format for “call this method with these inputs, get this result back.” What a server can offer An MCP server can expose three main kinds of things, called primitives [2]: Tools. Actions the AI can take, like “search tickets,” “run this SQL query,” or “create a calendar event.” Resources. Data the AI can read for context, like a file’s contents or a database schema. Prompts. Reusable templates, like a ready-made “summarize this bug report” instruction. The flow is simple. The client asks the server what it offers (for tools, that’s a tools/list request). The server replies with each tool’s name, a description, and a schema for its inputs. The host passes that list to the model. When the model decides to use a tool, the host sends a tools/call request to the right server and hands the result back to the model [2]. Same pattern as tool calling in any agent. The model decides. The code does. MCP just standardizes the “code does” part. A tiny MCP server in Python This is where it gets practical. With the official Python SDK [3], a working server is a few lines. Here’s a toy server for a small online shop: from mcp.server import MCPServer mcp = MCPServer("Shop") ORDERS = {"4512": "Held at Lahore warehouse since Monday"} @mcp.tool() def order_status(order_id: str) -> str: """Look up the delivery status of an order by its ID.""" return ORDERS.get(order_id, "Order not found") That’s the whole thing. The function’s type hints become the input schema, and the docstring becomes the description the model reads. No hand-written JSON, no protocol code. You can test it in the MCP Inspector with uv run mcp dev server.py, which comes with the SDK’s cli extra [3]. Once it’s running, any MCP-compatible host can discover order_status and let the model call it. In a real project, you’d replace the dictionary with a call to your actual database or API. The point is that you write this connector once, and it works with every host that speaks MCP. Who uses it MCP spread fast. In December 2025, about a year after launch, Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a new fund under the Linux Foundation co-founded by Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI, with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg [4][5]. The Linux Foundation is the same neutral home behind projects like Kubernetes and Node.js. At that time, the MCP team reported over 10,000 active servers and client support in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, VS Code, and more [4]. So it’s no longer one company’s experiment. It’s shared infrastructure. What to watch out for MCP makes connecting tools easy. That’s also the risk. Tool descriptions are instructions too. The model reads each tool’s description to decide how to use it. In April 2025, security researchers at Invariant Labs showed “tool poisoning” attacks, where a malicious server hides instructions inside a tool description. In their demo, an innocent-looking “add two numbers” tool told the agent to read private config files and quietly pass them along [6]. It’s a form of prompt injection, aimed at the tool list instead of the chat. Descriptions can change later. The same researchers showed a server can look harmless when you approve it and change its tool descriptions afterward, which they called a “rug pull” [6]. More tools, more power. A server that can send email or edit records gives the AI that power too. A mistake now becomes an action. A few habits help, in line with the official security guidance [7]: Security practices Only install servers from sources you trust, the same way you’d treat any package you run. Give each server the smallest permissions it needs. Read-only where possible. Keep a human approval step for risky actions like sending, deleting, or paying. Treat everything a tool returns as untrusted data, not as instructions. The short version MCP is an open standard that gives AI apps one common way to connect to tools and data. Instead of writing a custom connector for every app and every tool, you build an MCP server once, and any MCP-compatible host can use it. It has three roles (host, client, server) and three main things a server can offer (tools, resources, prompts). Under the hood, it’s JSON-RPC messages over stdio or HTTP. It’s genuinely useful for anyone building agents. Just remember that every server you plug in is new code your AI will trust, so choose and limit them carefully. So the next time someone says “we added MCP support,” a good follow-up question is: “Which servers, and what are they allowed to do?” References [1] Anthropic, “Introducing the Model Context Protocol,” Nov 25, 2024. https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol [2] Model Context Protocol docs, “Architecture overview.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture [3] MCP Python SDK, official GitHub repository. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk [4] MCP Blog, “MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation,” Dec 9, 2025. https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025–12–09-mcp-joins-agentic-ai-foundation/ [5] The Linux Foundation, “Linux Foundation Announces the Formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF),” Dec 9, 2025. https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation [6] Invariant Labs, “MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks,” Apr 2025. https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks [7] Model Context Protocol, “Security Best Practices.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices I write one simple AI explainer every week. Follow if you want the next one. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an attempt to fix that with one shared plug.

What MCP actually is

MCP is an open standard for how AI applications talk to external tools and data. It’s not a model, and it’s not a product. It’s a set of rules, like HTTP is for websites.

It also doesn’t decide how the AI uses what it gets. The official docs are clear that MCP only covers the exchange of context. How the app uses the model is up to the app [2].

Going back to the charger drawer: the host is your laptop, each client is a USB-C port, and each server is a device you plug in.

from mcp.server import MCPServer

mcp = MCPServer("Shop")

ORDERS = {"4512": "Held at Lahore warehouse since Monday"}

In April 2025, security researchers at Invariant Labs showed “tool poisoning” attacks, where a malicious server hides instructions inside a tool description. It’s a form of prompt injection, aimed at the tool list instead of the chat.

Descriptions can change later. The same researchers showed a server can look harmless when you approve it and change its tool descriptions afterward, which they called a “rug pull” [6].

More tools, more power. A server that can send email or edit records gives the AI that power too. A mistake now becomes an action.

A few habits help, in line with the official security guidance [7]:

Security practices

Only install servers from sources you trust, the same way you’d treat any package you run.

Give each server the smallest permissions it needs. Read-only where possible.

Keep a human approval step for risky actions like sending, deleting, or paying.

Treat everything a tool returns as untrusted data, not as instructions.

The short version

MCP is an open standard that gives AI apps one common way to connect to tools and data. Instead of writing a custom connector for every app and every tool, you build an MCP server once, and any MCP-compatible host can use it.

It has three roles (host, client, server) and three main things a server can offer (tools, resources, prompts). Under the hood, it’s JSON-RPC messages over stdio or HTTP.

It’s genuinely useful for anyone building agents. Just remember that every server you plug in is new code your AI will trust, so choose and limit them carefully.

So the next time someone says “we added MCP support,” a good follow-up question is: “Which servers, and what are they allowed to do?”

References

[1] Anthropic, “Introducing the Model Context Protocol,” Nov 25, 2024. https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol

[2] Model Context Protocol docs, “Architecture overview.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture

[3] MCP Python SDK, official GitHub repository. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk

[4] MCP Blog, “MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation,” Dec 9, 2025. https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025–12–09-mcp-joins-agentic-ai-foundation/

[5] The Linux Foundation, “Linux Foundation Announces the Formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF),” Dec 9, 2025. https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation

[6] Invariant Labs, “MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks,” Apr 2025. https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks

items.title: Everything That Led to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Fall
items.summary: Jensen Huang is gone from Nvidia, the chipmaker he co-founded 33 years ago. The origins of that downfall go back to the 2010s—to when Alice Huang, one of the women with whom he allegedly had an affair, was setting herself up to become a major Nvidia customer. Their relationship went unnoticed for a long time, but then it became just one element in a growing array of scandals around Jensen that eventually led to his resignation on Wednesday. As the drama widened, it came to include two more alleged affairs, a confrontation at Jensen’s home and a fateful board meeting. Below, you’ll find a curated timeline of what happened.

items.title: I watched Jensen Huang speak 9 days before his resignation. Two things stand out now.
items.summary: Jensen Huang in San Francisco on Nov. 3 without his famous leather jacket. Alistair Barr/Business Insider A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Nine days before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, I sat near the front row at a San Francisco conference and watched him discuss the future of AI. Two things struck me that day. Both seem more significant now. First, Huang wasn't wearing his famous black leather jacket . Instead, as you can see in the photo I took, he wore a dark fabric zip-up. At the time, I thought it was funny. His jacket had become such a recognizable part of his image that seeing him without it was a bit jarring. Now, with revelations about his extramarital affairs and allegations involving a possible Chinese spy , I wonder whether the wardrobe change meant something. The initial allegations were already public by November 3. Of course, that's hindsight talking. Maybe a jacket is just a jacket. The second thing was more consequential. Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao (left) interviewing Jensen Huang at the startup's conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026. Alistair Barr/Business Insider Near the end of the conversation, Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao asked Huang about his unusual management style. He had 60 executives reporting directly to him . Huang explained that he'd designed this structure more than 30 years ago, when personal computers and email were transforming business. Rather than a traditional hierarchy, he wanted information flowing freely among executives empowered to make decisions. Then came the obvious question: What should a company's leadership structure look like in the AI age? "I don't know the answer to that," Huang replied. At the time, I thought that was a bit odd. Nvidia is leading the AI revolution and Jensen leads Nvidia. Wouldn't he be thinking of how best to run this company in the future? Today, that exchange seems especially relevant. With Huang gone, Nvidia faces an extraordinary succession challenge . Sixty direct reports may have worked brilliantly under its founder. But it also means there isn't an obvious deputy to take the reins. If he'd had two or three direct reports, those people would have had more experience with more responsibility. But 60 direct reports, by definition, means that each one of those execs only had a small piece of Nvidia to oversee. Does this mean Nvidia is doomed? I'm not sure. The way Jensen described Nvidia's structure back on Nov. 3 provides some hope. Huang said he gave executives considerable freedom to make decisions and work together, rather than taking orders from the top. Instead of a rigid management hierarchy, Nvidia organized itself around projects, with teams forming and changing as needed. "Irrespective of whatever internal or external threats and opportunities, the company will naturally adapt itself, it should adapt itself to new opportunities," he said. "That was the organization I created." The talk ended on a poignant note. Again, with hindsight, I can't help thinking he knew something was coming. "I'm super proud of you," he told Fireworks' Qiao. "Don't forget us little people someday." Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

Nine days before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, I sat near the front row at a San Francisco conference and watched him discuss the future of AI.

Two things struck me that day. Both seem more significant now.

First, Huang wasn't wearing his famous black leather jacket. Instead, as you can see in the photo I took, he wore a dark fabric zip-up. At the time, I thought it was funny. His jacket had become such a recognizable part of his image that seeing him without it was a bit jarring.

Now, with revelations about his extramarital affairs and allegations involving a possible Chinese spy, I wonder whether the wardrobe change meant something. The initial allegations were already public by November 3.

Of course, that's hindsight talking. Maybe a jacket is just a jacket.

The second thing was more consequential.

Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao (left) interviewing Jensen Huang at the startup's conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026.

Alistair Barr/Business Insider

Near the end of the conversation, Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao asked Huang about his unusual management style. He had 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang explained that he'd designed this structure more than 30 years ago, when personal computers and email were transforming business. Rather than a traditional hierarchy, he wanted information flowing freely among executives empowered to make decisions.

Then came the obvious question: What should a company's leadership structure look like in the AI age?

"I don't know the answer to that," Huang replied.

At the time, I thought that was a bit odd. Nvidia is leading the AI revolution and Jensen leads Nvidia. Wouldn't he be thinking of how best to run this company in the future?

Today, that exchange seems especially relevant.

With Huang gone, Nvidia faces an extraordinary succession challenge. Sixty direct reports may have worked brilliantly under its founder. But it also means there isn't an obvious deputy to take the reins.

If he'd had two or three direct reports, those people would have had more experience with more responsibility. But 60 direct reports, by definition, means that each one of those execs only had a small piece of Nvidia to oversee.

The talk ended on a poignant note. Again, with hindsight, I can't help thinking he knew something was coming.

"I'm super proud of you," he told Fireworks' Qiao. "Don't forget us little people someday."

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill
items.summary: Anthropic is positioning its new model , Claude Fable 5.2 , for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates. Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API , it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work. The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input . In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work. The tests I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests: Bug fix : I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed. Code review : I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points. Code writing : The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates. Bug fix Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me). The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s. Astra : 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s. Code review This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table. Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s. Astra : 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s. Code writing Both models scored 50 of 50. Each one wrote working checks for 27 countries’ VAT IDs and 34 countries’ IBANs with no libraries to lean on. Neither model had trouble here. Both passed all the checks in one run. Astra took 23 turns, almost as many as Fable 5.2’s 24. Fable 5.2 still cost 2.3 times as much and took 1.7 times as long for the same score. In this run, the extra tokens didn’t raise the score. The numbers: Fable 5.2: 24 turns, 1,495,712 in, 87,542 out (47,458 reasoning), $4.83, 838 s. Astra: 23 turns, 460,271 in, 24,007 out (9,328 reasoning), $2.06, 483 s. Results Test Claude Fable 5.2 GPT-6 Astra Bug fix (of 50) 50 50 Code review (of 50) 49 45 Code writing (out of 50) 50 50 Total tokens in / out 4,400,139 / 226,917 884,143 / 39,494 Estimated cost $13.39 $3.99 Total time 2,157 s 832 s Fable 5.2 led on code review and tied Astra on the other two tasks. Across the two tied tasks, its estimated API cost was 2.4 times Astra’s ($7.34 vs. $3.04), and it took 1.9 times as long (1,164 vs. 605 seconds). What do I think? For tasks like these, I’d start with Astra. It matched Fable 5.2’s scores on bug fixing and code writing at about 41% of the estimated cost, and it finished all three tasks faster. I’d consider Fable 5.2 for a careful code review, where it found three more defects in this test. Both models missed defects. Fable 5.2’s standard token rates are lower, but it used about five times as many tokens as Astra across these three runs. Brockman’s point about price per task held up here.

items.title: The Pentagon is testing war robots that can hunt in packs without GPS and find battlefield targets on their own. Humans still call the shots.
items.summary: The uncrewed ground vehicles mapped out the area as they drove, not relying on GPS to navigate. DARPA The Pentagon research arm DARPA tested autonomous ground robots in GPS-denied environments. The robots mapped out the area and located enemy targets. Once the targets were identified, the human operator overseeing the process decided next steps. The Pentagon's research arm tested how ground drones could be sent out in groups to look for and hunt down targets while keeping a human operator in the loop to make decisions. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency , or DARPA, program examined how uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, could quickly drive, map out terrain, and gather information on their own in contested environments. Lessons will inform ongoing developments in uncrewed technologies across the US military, officials said. Last month, DARPA experimented with four autonomous UGVs at an exercise at Fort Knox, Kentucky, as part of its Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER, program. During the exercise, the ground robots conducted surveillance of the surrounding area, independently searching for enemy forces for an operator located away from the action. Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA, told Business Insider that "we're moving sensors and effectors forward to the tactical edge while keeping the operator in safety out of harm's way," but humans still "maintained control and custody and situational awareness at all times." Once launched, the UGVs went off on their missions. Gregory said they could work together or independently depending on the scenario. Meanwhile, the human operator supervised the UGVs, assigned them tasks, checked their findings, and then decided how best to engage enemy targets. At the Fort Knox demonstration, the operator used satellite imagery to task the robots. One UGV stopped in place once it spotted a potential target — a closed box holding a drone inside — and then the human operator decided to launch a simulated rocket at the target. An important part of the recent RACER robotic testing program was ensuring that the UGVs could perform their tasks without GPS. Instead, the robots built the map as they moved. The US military has said it needs to be prepared to fight through contested or denied environments where GPS isn't readily available, and is looking into alternative precision navigation and timing solutions, as well as more traditional tactics. Once a potential enemy target has been identified, a human operator decides the next steps. DARPA The military is also considering other possible disruptions, such as terrain interference or loss of signal. "We developed this new software so that ground vehicles could use only their onboard sensors to make decisions to move as fast as possible," Gregory said. The software was tested on four-wheel, all-terrain UGVs as well as tracked UGVs to ensure it could be deployed on different hardware. While teams worked to build systems using commercial technologies, the RACER program also involved five years of research to better understand the scientific and technical challenges of autonomy, artificial intelligence algorithms, and ground mobility. DARPA's work also relied on observations from Russia's war in Ukraine on the distinct role of ground robots and how operators employ them in different situations. Autonomous UGVs face distinct challenges depending on the terrain, environment, and climate. In the desert, for example, robots might need to navigate sand, rocks, and other obstacles, while extreme heat might strain the batteries and communications systems. Swamplands, forests, muddy fields, and snow can also make operations more difficult, requiring robots to be able to adapt to very different conditions. RACER's demonstration offers lessons for the broader US military. While some are specific to autonomous ground robots , others — including operating without GPS, teaming humans with machines, and maintaining human oversight in robotic operations — could apply to uncrewed systems across the military. It's also sharing the lessons with industry. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Post-training Stages and Preference Data — It is much easier to judge than to generate
items.summary: Goal: understand the stages of LLM post-training, then what preferences are, why post-training needs them, and how preference data is collected. Part 1: Post-training Stages 1. Pre-training builds knowledge, post-training builds behavior • Pre-training: the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next word, which gives it knowledge but no manners. • Post-training: it takes far less compute, yet largely decides how well a model follows instructions, how safe it is and how it reasons (Developers Digest, n.d.). • Recipe: the sequence of post-training steps a lab follows; a canonical recipe is the standard version of its time. The recipe changed more in the last year than in the three years before (Lambert & Timbers, 2026). Note. Era summary as in Lambert and Timbers (2026). 2. Stage 1: SFT, learning from example answers • Abbreviation: SFT is supervised fine-tuning, training a model on example prompts paired with ideal answers. • Main difference from pre-training: pre-training learns from raw text, so the model continues text; SFT learns from prompt-and-answer pairs, so it learns to answer. It teaches format and tone quickly, but the model can only imitate what it has been shown. • Analogy: an apprentice cook learning from a head chef’s recipe book. The apprentice picks up the house style fast, but only knows the dishes in the book, and a surprise ingredient leaves them guessing. 3. Stage 2: preference tuning, learning which answer people prefer • Abbreviations: – RL: reinforcement learning, learning from scores on the model’s own attempts. – RLHF: RL from human feedback, where the scores come from a judge trained on human preferences. – PPO: proximal policy optimization, an RL algorithm that keeps each update small. – DPO: direct preference optimization, which trains directly on pairs of answers marked better and worse, with no separate reward model and no RL loop (Rafailov et al., 2023). • Main difference from SFT: SFT copies one ideal answer; preference tuning learns from rankings of several answers, so it can tell which of two good answers is better. The rankings train a reward model (a separate judge model) and the main model adjusts to earn higher scores. The weakness is reward hacking: the model learns to please the judge instead of being right. DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop. • Analogy: the cook makes four versions of a dish and a tasting panel ranks them. A critic learns to score like the panel, and the cook adjusts toward what the critic likes. DPO skips the critic and learns from pairs. Rejection sampling keeps only the critic’s best of ten versions for practice. Reward hacking is fancy plating that wins over the critic without better food. • DPO vs RL: DPO trains offline on a fixed dataset, so it is simpler, more stable and fast to iterate on, but limited by the dataset’s coverage, a slightly lower performance ceiling. Online RL such as PPO generates fresh completions and can explore new regions, often reaching higher peak performance, at the cost of more compute and more moving parts (Ivison et al., 2024; Tajwar et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024). • DPO data: it needs feedback data, not necessarily human feedback. UltraFeedback was the first prominent open synthetic preference dataset and helped kickstart the DPO era (Cui et al., 2023), and Tülu 3 followed with larger synthetic-feedback recipes (Lambert et al., 2024). 4. Stage 3: RLVR, learning from answers that can be checked • Abbreviations: – RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards, where a program checks whether the answer is correct. – GRPO: group relative policy optimization, which scores a group of answers and reinforces the above-average ones. – AI2: the Allen Institute for AI, which introduced the RLVR term (Lambert et al., 2024). • Main difference from preference tuning: a learned judge can be fooled; a program that checks the math result, the code tests or a numeric range is cheap, objective and hard to game, but only works where an answer can be checked. This is also how models learn to think: careful attempts win more often, so they get reinforced. • Analogy: swap the tasting panel for a thermometer and a timer. A rushed, raw dish fails the reading and earns nothing; a cook who checks the oven and adjusts earns the reward. After thousands of dishes, checking as you go becomes the habit, and that habit is what learning to think looks like. 5. Stage 4: specialists first, then distillation • Abbreviations: – MOPD: multi-teacher on-policy distillation; several specialist teachers train one student on the student’s own answers. – KL: Kullback-Leibler divergence, a score for how different two models’ next-word probabilities are; reverse KL penalizes the student for saying things the teacher would never say (Gu et al., 2024). • Main difference from RLVR: one RLVR run on every domain got expensive and conflict-prone, because mixing math, code and agentic RL trades capabilities off against each other. Specialists are cheap and parallelizable, and on-policy distillation matured. So one specialist is trained per domain, then a general student writes its own answers and the relevant teacher marks it token by token (Lambert & Timbers, 2026; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Distillation means a student learns from a teacher’s outputs (Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy means it learns from its own attempts, including its own mistakes (Agarwal et al., 2024). • Analogy: a kitchen with a pastry, a grill and a sauce chef, each trained separately. A trainee cooks whole dishes alone and the matching chef tastes every spoonful as it cooks, so the correction lands at the exact step. Training one trainee on all three at once is how habits clash, such as high heat that suits a grill but ruins a custard. Note. Summary of Stages 1 to 4 above; stage order as in Lambert and Timbers (2026). 6. Where human experts fit • SFT: expert-written answers. • Preference tuning: expert rankings. • RLVR: rubrics, for example in finance and law. A good rubric accepts more than one valid method, and in a MOPD pipeline the finance teacher is only as good as the tasks and rubrics behind it. Rubrics are already delivering gains beyond verifiable domains (Gunjal et al., 2025). • Hard-to-verify tasks: the DeepSeek-V4 report describes rubric-guided RL data scored by a generative reward model, which works with only a small set of diverse human annotations (DeepSeek-AI, 2026). Part 2: Preference Data 1. Preferences are what we reach for when there is no right answer • Why it works: it is far easier to judge than to generate, so people can tell which answer is better even when they could not write it themselves (Lambert, n.d.). Note. Examples and framing as in Lambert (n.d.). 2. Three branches converge into RLHF • Optimal control: a framework for optimization with dynamic programming and mathematical underpinnings, which led to reinforcement learning and then deep RL (Lambert et al., 2023). • Deep learning: neural networks and the scaling of data and problem complexity, which led to large language models (Lambert et al., 2023). • Economics and decision theory: individual preferences, decision theory and methods for comparing preferences (Lambert et al., 2023). Note. Figure from Lambert et al. (2023), shown with the original attribution. 3. Utility: from logic to number • Port-Royal Logic: it supports the idea that decision quality is an outcome weighted by its probability (Arnauld, 1662). 4. Reward: giving the model a direction • Value function: gives directions toward preferred behavior (Singh et al., 2009). • Decisions: are made to transition to higher-valued states (Singh et al., 2009). 5. Interface of preference data • Likert score: the rater gives a response a score on a fixed scale, as in early Claude’s preference interface (Bai et al., 2022). • A/B test: the rater chooses between two responses (Lambert, n.d.). • Pairwise with ties: the rater chooses between two responses or marks a tie, as in the Chatbot Arena public evaluation (Chiang et al., 2024). • A single bit: thumbs up or thumbs down on one response (Lambert, n.d.). • Pick from many: the rater picks the best from several responses, the default in image models (Lambert, n.d.). 6. Ratings and rankings • Ratings: a score on one completion in isolation (Lambert, n.d.). • Rankings: relative comparisons between responses, often on a Likert scale (Bai et al., 2022). 7. The unaudited gap • Chain: Spec → Data → Behaviour; the Spec is the documented intended behavior, for example the Model Spec (OpenAI, 2024). • Unaudited link: the step from Data to Behaviour is not checked, meaning nobody verifies whether the values written down by the annotators are actually reflected in the final model (Lambert, n.d.). Appendix • A1. Origin of weights – They are the billions of numbers inside a model, starting as small random values. Pre-training nudges them until they encode grammar, facts and reasoning patterns; post-training makes comparatively small adjustments. • A2. Token, vector, embedding table – A token is a chunk of text with a fixed ID, a label with no meaning of its own. A vector is a list of numbers that represents meaning. The embedding table turns each token ID into its starting vector. Only the embedding table and the layers that transform vectors are weights; tokens and vectors are the data flowing through them. • A3. RL vs SFT – Studying a book of grandmaster games (SFT) versus playing thousands of games and learning only whether you won (RL). SFT is capped near the quality of its examples; RL can go beyond them. • A4. Two reward models in Llama 2 – Helpfulness and safety can pull against each other, like a taste critic and a health inspector: the tastiest dish can break the health rules, and a kitchen that plays it too safe serves nothing. For risky prompts the safety score takes priority. • A5. R1-Zero vs R1, and cold start – R1-Zero was the experiment, pure RL with strong reasoning but messy output; R1 was the product. A cold start gives the model a small SFT warm-up so it already writes in a clean, consistent format, and RL then spends its effort on correctness instead of readability. • A6. Rubrics and rubric weights – A rubric is a judging checklist of yes-or-no items any judge can run on any answer, like “the middle is fully cooked” at a baking contest. Rubric weights, from 1 to 10, set how many points each item is worth. They are not model weights: the weighted score becomes the reward that adjusts the model’s weights. • A7. Teacher marking vs golden answer and reward model – No. The student writes its own answer and only the relevant teacher marks it at every token. A golden answer is one fixed text and a reward model gives one score at the end, while a teacher gives an opinion on every word. • A8. Conflicting skills in the student – Much less than in one mixed RL run, because each question gets feedback from one teacher only. The conflict does not vanish, since the student has finite capacity and the mix of questions still has to be tuned. • A9. KL divergence and reverse KL – Zero means two distributions are identical. Reverse KL punishes the student for putting probability on words the teacher thinks are unlikely, so it avoids mistakes the expert would never make and commits to good answers. • A10. Trace distillation SFT vs the final climb in MAI-Thinking-1 – A trace is written step-by-step reasoning, and a climb is Microsoft AI’s word for a long RL run that keeps improving a score. In trace distillation SFT, traces from three specialists (SWE and agentic; STEM; helpfulness and safety) are collected and one model is fine-tuned on them. The final climb is one more RL run on that consolidated model. Like three tutors writing binders of worked solutions that one student studies, then sits mock exams with a grader. Goal: understand the stages of LLM post-training, then what preferences are, why post-training needs them, and how preference data is collected.Part 1: Post-training Stages1. Pre-training builds knowledge, post-training builds behavior

• Pre-training: the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next word, which gives it knowledge but no manners.

• Post-training: it takes far less compute, yet largely decides how well a model follows instructions, how safe it is and how it reasons (Developers Digest, n.d.).

• Recipe: the sequence of post-training steps a lab follows; a canonical recipe is the standard version of its time. The recipe changed more in the last year than in the three years before (Lambert & Timbers, 2026).

Note. Era summary as in Lambert and Timbers (2026).

2. Stage 1: SFT, learning from example answers

• Abbreviation: SFT is supervised fine-tuning, training a model on example prompts paired with ideal answers.

• Main difference from pre-training: pre-training learns from raw text, so the model continues text; SFT learns from prompt-and-answer pairs, so it learns to answer. It teaches format and tone quickly, but the model can only imitate what it has been shown.

• Analogy: an apprentice cook learning from a head chef’s recipe book. The apprentice picks up the house style fast, but only knows the dishes in the book, and a surprise ingredient leaves them guessing.

3. Stage 2: preference tuning, learning which answer people prefer

• Abbreviations:

– RL: reinforcement learning, learning from scores on the model’s own attempts.

– RLHF: RL from human feedback, where the scores come from a judge trained on human preferences.

– PPO: proximal policy optimization, an RL algorithm that keeps each update small.

– DPO: direct preference optimization, which trains directly on pairs of answers marked better and worse, with no separate reward model and no RL loop (Rafailov et al., 2023).

• Main difference from SFT: SFT copies one ideal answer; preference tuning learns from rankings of several answers, so it can tell which of two good answers is better. The rankings train a reward model (a separate judge model) and the main model adjusts to earn higher scores. The weakness is reward hacking: the model learns to please the judge instead of being right. DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop.

• Analogy: the cook makes four versions of a dish and a tasting panel ranks them. A critic learns to score like the panel, and the cook adjusts toward what the critic likes. DPO skips the critic and learns from pairs. Rejection sampling keeps only the critic’s best of ten versions for practice. Reward hacking is fancy plating that wins over the critic without better food.

• DPO vs RL: DPO trains offline on a fixed dataset, so it is simpler, more stable and fast to iterate on, but limited by the dataset’s coverage, a slightly lower performance ceiling. Online RL such as PPO generates fresh completions and can explore new regions, often reaching higher peak performance, at the cost of more compute and more moving parts (Ivison et al., 2024; Tajwar et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024).

• DPO data: it needs feedback data, not necessarily human feedback. UltraFeedback was the first prominent open synthetic preference dataset and helped kickstart the DPO era (Cui et al., 2023), and Tülu 3 followed with larger synthetic-feedback recipes (Lambert et al., 2024).

4. Stage 3: RLVR, learning from answers that can be checked

• Abbreviations:

– RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards, where a program checks whether the answer is correct.

– GRPO: group relative policy optimization, which scores a group of answers and reinforces the above-average ones.

– AI2: the Allen Institute for AI, which introduced the RLVR term (Lambert et al., 2024).

• Main difference from preference tuning: a learned judge can be fooled; a program that checks the math result, the code tests or a numeric range is cheap, objective and hard to game, but only works where an answer can be checked. This is also how models learn to think: careful attempts win more often, so they get reinforced.

• Analogy: swap the tasting panel for a thermometer and a timer. A rushed, raw dish fails the reading and earns nothing; a cook who checks the oven and adjusts earns the reward. After thousands of dishes, checking as you go becomes the habit, and that habit is what learning to think looks like.

5. Stage 4: specialists first, then distillation

• Abbreviations:

– MOPD: multi-teacher on-policy distillation; several specialist teachers train one student on the student’s own answers.

– KL: Kullback-Leibler divergence, a score for how different two models’ next-word probabilities are; reverse KL penalizes the student for saying things the teacher would never say (Gu et al., 2024).

• Main difference from RLVR: one RLVR run on every domain got expensive and conflict-prone, because mixing math, code and agentic RL trades capabilities off against each other. Specialists are cheap and parallelizable, and on-policy distillation matured. So one specialist is trained per domain, then a general student writes its own answers and the relevant teacher marks it token by token (Lambert & Timbers, 2026; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Distillation means a student learns from a teacher’s outputs (Hinton et al., 2015), and on-policy means it learns from its own attempts, including its own mistakes (Agarwal et al., 2024).

• Analogy: a kitchen with a pastry, a grill and a sauce chef, each trained separately. A trainee cooks whole dishes alone and the matching chef tastes every spoonful as it cooks, so the correction lands at the exact step. Training one trainee on all three at once is how habits clash, such as high heat that suits a grill but ruins a custard.

Note. Summary of Stages 1 to 4 above; stage order as in Lambert and Timbers (2026).

6. Where human experts fit

• SFT: expert-written answers.

• Preference tuning: expert rankings.

• RLVR: rubrics, for example in finance and law. A good rubric accepts more than one valid method, and in a MOPD pipeline the finance teacher is only as good as the tasks and rubrics behind it. Rubrics are already delivering gains beyond verifiable domains (Gunjal et al., 2025).

• Hard-to-verify tasks: the DeepSeek-V4 report describes rubric-guided RL data scored by a generative reward model, which works with only a small set of diverse human annotations (DeepSeek-AI, 2026).

Part 2: Preference Data1. Preferences are what we reach for when there is no right answer

• Why it works: it is far easier to judge than to generate, so people can tell which answer is better even when they could not write it themselves (Lambert, n.d.).

Note. Examples and framing as in Lambert (n.d.).

2. Three branches converge into RLHF

• Optimal control: a framework for optimization with dynamic programming and mathematical underpinnings, which led to reinforcement learning and then deep RL (Lambert et al., 2023).

• Deep learning: neural networks and the scaling of data and problem complexity, which led to large language models (Lambert et al., 2023).

• Economics and decision theory: individual preferences, decision theory and methods for comparing preferences (Lambert et al., 2023).

Note. Figure from Lambert et al. (2023), shown with the original attribution.

3. Utility: from logic to number

• Port-Royal Logic: it supports the idea that decision quality is an outcome weighted by its probability (Arnauld, 1662).

4. Reward: giving the model a direction

• Value function: gives directions toward preferred behavior (Singh et al., 2009).

• Decisions: are made to transition to higher-valued states (Singh et al., 2009).

5. Interface of preference data

• Likert score: the rater gives a response a score on a fixed scale, as in early Claude’s preference interface (Bai et al., 2022).

• A/B test: the rater chooses between two responses (Lambert, n.d.).

• Pairwise with ties: the rater chooses between two responses or marks a tie, as in the Chatbot Arena public evaluation (Chiang et al., 2024).

• A single bit: thumbs up or thumbs down on one response (Lambert, n.d.).

• Pick from many: the rater picks the best from several responses, the default in image models (Lambert, n.d.).

6. Ratings and rankings

• Ratings: a score on one completion in isolation (Lambert, n.d.).

• Rankings: relative comparisons between responses, often on a Likert scale (Bai et al., 2022).

7. The unaudited gap

• Chain: Spec → Data → Behaviour; the Spec is the documented intended behavior, for example the Model Spec (OpenAI, 2024).

• Unaudited link: the step from Data to Behaviour is not checked, meaning nobody verifies whether the values written down by the annotators are actually reflected in the final model (Lambert, n.d.).

Appendix

• A1. Origin of weights

– They are the billions of numbers inside a model, starting as small random values. Pre-training nudges them until they encode grammar, facts and reasoning patterns; post-training makes comparatively small adjustments.

• A2. Token, vector, embedding table

– A token is a chunk of text with a fixed ID, a label with no meaning of its own. A vector is a list of numbers that represents meaning. The embedding table turns each token ID into its starting vector. Only the embedding table and the layers that transform vectors are weights; tokens and vectors are the data flowing through them.

• A3. RL vs SFT

– Studying a book of grandmaster games (SFT) versus playing thousands of games and learning only whether you won (RL). SFT is capped near the quality of its examples; RL can go beyond them.

• A4. Two reward models in Llama 2

– Helpfulness and safety can pull against each other, like a taste critic and a health inspector: the tastiest dish can break the health rules, and a kitchen that plays it too safe serves nothing. For risky prompts the safety score takes priority.

• A5. R1-Zero vs R1, and cold start

– R1-Zero was the experiment, pure RL with strong reasoning but messy output; R1 was the product. A cold start gives the model a small SFT warm-up so it already writes in a clean, consistent format, and RL then spends its effort on correctness instead of readability.

• A6. Rubrics and rubric weights

– A rubric is a judging checklist of yes-or-no items any judge can run on any answer, like “the middle is fully cooked” at a baking contest. Rubric weights, from 1 to 10, set how many points each item is worth. They are not model weights: the weighted score becomes the reward that adjusts the model’s weights.

• A7. Teacher marking vs golden answer and reward model

– No. The student writes its own answer and only the relevant teacher marks it at every token. A golden answer is one fixed text and a reward model gives one score at the end, while a teacher gives an opinion on every word.

• A8. Conflicting skills in the student

– Much less than in one mixed RL run, because each question gets feedback from one teacher only. The conflict does not vanish, since the student has finite capacity and the mix of questions still has to be tuned.

• A9. KL divergence and reverse KL

– Zero means two distributions are identical. Reverse KL punishes the student for putting probability on words the teacher thinks are unlikely, so it avoids mistakes the expert would never make and commits to good answers.

• A10. Trace distillation SFT vs the final climb in MAI-Thinking-1

– A trace is written step-by-step reasoning, and a climb is Microsoft AI’s word for a long RL run that keeps improving a score. In trace distillation SFT, traces from three specialists (SWE and agentic; STEM; helpfulness and safety) are collected and one model is fine-tuned on them. The final climb is one more RL run on that consolidated model. Like three tutors writing binders of worked solutions that one student studies, then sits mock exams with a grader. That is why it is closer to R1 than to V4 (Microsoft AI, 2026).

items.title: Even San Francisco Is Turning Against AI
items.summary: For years, San Francisco has been a haven for AI optimists, leaving many of them baffled when they travel beyond the Bay Area and encounter people outside their industry who despise the tech. Increasingly, though, not even the City by the Bay is managing to keep AI hatred at, well, bay — at least if its dating scene is any indication. According to on the ground reporting by The Verge , AI has become a dealbreaker among the lovelorn on dating apps, despite the city being the intellectual heart of the AI boom. “Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if.” Sometimes people will be like, ‘F*ck AI,'” a 25-year-old analyst told the outlet. It only took her a few minutes of swiping to pull up a profile that said: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.” Even local voters are swiping left on the tech. Several Bay Area cities, including San Francisco, Oakland, and Richmond, have passed short-term moratoriums on data center construction over the past few months. Other intrusions of tech into daily life have caused friction among locals, including the proliferation of AI food slop posters and self-driving robotaxis . Some consider AI a central concern in their search for a partner for altogether different reasons. Another lonely heart The Verge talked to works at an AI safety nonprofit and can’t help but factor in how AI might soon destroy the world when he considers his future love life and considerations like having kids. “A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” he told the outlet. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future.” So would he date someone who works in AI? He’s not quite sure. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he added. Of course, this is San Francisco we’re talking about. So naturally people consider AI important to dating because they use the tech to optimize their love escapades. One 21-year-old software engineer explained to the Verge how he used AI to automate his dating life since he’s too busy running a startup. He lets an AI agent control his Hinge account where it mimics how he texts and acts while automatically messaging women, gauges if a woman makes a good match, and automatically marks down a date on his calendar “If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” he told the site, claiming that he goes on two dates a week. His AI dating scheme, he boasted, has lowered his “CPN” — or, with all apologies in advance, “cost per nut.” Only in San Francisco. You take the AI luddites with the AI lunatics. More on AI: Wealthy Tech Guys Can’t Get Dates Because They’re So Widely Hated That Not Even Money Is Making Women Grimace and Deal With Them
