items.title: Agentic RAG vs. Plain Hybrid RAG: What My Hydropower Benchmark Revealed
items.summary:
Most RAG applications follow a simple path: Retrieve a few documents → send them to an LLM → generate an answer. That works for straightforward lookup questions. But it becomes fragile when the question spans multiple manuals, needs numerical reasoning, contains tables, or asks for an engineering recommendation grounded in plant documentation. I built an Agentic RAG system for Small Hydropower Plant (SHP) engineering to explore a harder question: Can a multi-agent retrieval workflow improve the quality of answers from private technical documents without depending on paid inference APIs? The answer, based on my evaluation so far, is nuanced: it improves retrieval precision, but comes with a substantial latency cost and does not automatically outperform a well-designed plain RAG pipeline on faithfulness. The complete implementation is available here: Agentic RAG for Small Hydropower . Built for learners: no paid inference APIs required One of my goals was to make this project accessible to students and independent learners who cannot afford recurring API bills. The core RAG pipeline runs locally using Ollama and open-weight models. Document processing, embeddings, retrieval, answer generation, and runtime quality checks do not require paid cloud inference APIs. Once the required models and dependencies are downloaded, you can experiment on compatible hardware without paying per question or per token. For offline benchmarking, I used Gemini and Groq through their available free tiers to evaluate answers against the golden dataset. Those services are optional: evaluation can also use a local Ollama judge. Free-tier quotas and availability may change, so they should not be treated as an unlimited resource. This does not mean running the system has zero cost — hardware, electricity, and inference time still matter. But if you already have a suitable computer, it removes a major barrier to learning: a recurring inference bill. For me, that makes the project useful beyond hydropower. It provides a practical starting point for learning document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, agent orchestration, tool use, and evaluation within a limited budget. The problem: engineering knowledge is not a single-document lookup task Small hydropower projects involve a mix of technical manuals, regulatory guidelines, turbine-selection references, hydrology documents, financial policies, scanned reports, tables, and drawings. A typical question may require several kinds of evidence at once: Which turbine is suitable for a particular head and discharge? What are the applicable regulatory requirements? Which maintenance practices reduce silt erosion? Can the system calculate power output from provided values? Is the answer actually supported by the retrieved documents? A traditional RAG pipeline may retrieve relevant passages, but it usually has no mechanism to decide whether the retrieved context is sufficient, whether a calculation should use a tool, or whether the generated answer contains unsupported claims. That is where the agentic approach becomes useful. Before retrieval: turning engineering documents into usable evidence The first challenge was preparing the documents. Hydropower knowledge arrives in different formats: digital PDFs, scanned reports, Word documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and images. Each format needs a different extraction approach. I built a multi-tier parsing pipeline that converts these files into Markdown before chunking and embedding. Tier 1: Dedicated parsers for Office documents and text For formats with accessible document structure, the pipeline uses dedicated libraries: This avoids sending every file through a more expensive OCR process. Tier 2: Markdown extraction for digital PDFs For PDFs, the pipeline first uses pymupdf4llm to extract text into Markdown, aiming to retain headings and table structure. If the extracted output contains at least 80 characters, the current implementation accepts it. If the output is shorter — or extraction fails — the document moves to the Docling fallback. This is a practical routing heuristic, but it has a limitation: a PDF containing both digital text and scanned pages may pass the threshold even when some pages need OCR. Page-level quality checks would improve this approach. Tier 3: OCR and layout recovery Scanned PDFs and failed PDF extractions are processed with Docling, with OCR and table-structure recovery enabled when the required backend is available. Images also enter the Docling conversion path. The PDF OCR configuration prefers EasyOCR, with RapidOCR as an alternative. It uses CUDA acceleration when available and otherwise falls back to CPU execution. The aim is to recover readable text and useful table structure. Complex drawings, dense tables, and formulas remain difficult, so extracted Markdown should not be assumed to reproduce every detail correctly. Keeping the source traceable Alongside the Markdown, the parser records source information such as the filename, file type, content hash, parsing duration, and page count where available. Parsing failures are recorded explicitly. The content hash also supports caching: an unchanged document can reuse its existing Markdown output, avoiding unnecessary processing. The resulting flow is: Raw documents → format-specific parsing or OCR → Markdown and metadata → chunking → embeddings and indexing This stage directly affects everything that follows. If a table loses its units or OCR misreads a formula, the retrieval and generation stages may work with incorrect evidence. Improving parsing is therefore part of improving answer quality. Binary SHA-256 deduplication is an efficient first line of defense to prevent wasting heavy parsing and OCR compute on identical files, but for the same converted file, Binary deduplication will NOT be applicable — the system will treat them as two completely separate files An actual record saved in data/parsed/metadata.json { "source_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\raw\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf", "file_name": "AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf", "file_type": "PDF", "file_hash": "127653ce9e3151fd6732fd83bfc66e570ab762bdafb22d568fcef524ce0d19bc", "page_count": 0, "parsed_at": 1793168584.5575593, "parse_duration_s": 0.0, "parsed_md_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\parsed\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment__127653ce.md", "error": null } Chunking methodology: preserving structure and source context After parsing, the documents are available as Markdown. The next challenge is dividing them into passages that are useful for retrieval without losing their context. I implemented a Markdown-aware hierarchical chunker. It uses document structure and text length for boundaries, rather than an LLM or embedding-based semantic segmentation model. The chunker uses a 4-pass rule-based pipeline rather than an LLM or arbitrary character slicing: [Raw Markdown Document] │ ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 1 │ Scan whole document → Divide into Structural Sections └─────────┘ │ Output: `sections` list ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 2 │ Process all sections → Split into Target-Sized Chunks (1,800 chars) └─────────┘ │ Output: `raw_chunks` list ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 3 │ Scan all raw chunks → Merge Tiny Leftover Fragments (< 150 chars) └─────────┘ │ Output: `merged_chunks` list ▼ ┌─────────┐ │ Pass 4 │ Enrich all chunks → Inject Citation Banners & Compute Token Counts └─────────┘ │ Output: `final_chunks` list (Written to `chunks.jsonl`) ▼ [Final Output] 1. Split by document structure (Pass 1) Instead of chopping text blindly every NNN characters, the chunker walks through the document line-by-line, tracking markdown headings (#, ##, ###, ####) like a tree or outline. Whenever a heading or a horizontal divider (---) appears, it finishes the current section. It also checks if the heading mentions a slide or page number. When a heading includes a label such as “Slide 12” or “Page 8,” that location is captured as metadata. Page references therefore depend on what the parsing stage preserves; they are not automatically available for every chunk. 2. Split long narrative sections at natural boundaries (Pass 2) Within a section, long text is divided at paragraph boundaries. Oversized paragraphs are further split at sentence boundaries. In simple words: If a text section is too long (>1,800 characters): It first splits cleanly at double newlines (

) to preserve whole paragraphs. If a single paragraph is still too massive, it splits at sentence boundaries (., !, ?). Conditional Overlap: Traditional RAG blindly copies the last N characters (often cutting words in half). Here, the previous paragraph is only carried over if its length is ≤150 characters. The default settings are: The overlap is conditional, rather than a fixed sliding window: the previous paragraph is repeated only when it fits within the overlap allowance. The 1,800-character setting is a target, not a strict maximum. Long individual sentences, table rows, fragment merging, and added source metadata can produce larger chunks. max_chars = 1800 overlap_chars = 150 Imagine a document section with four paragraphs: Paragraph 1 (900 chars): Details about Francis turbine runner design. Paragraph 2 (800 chars): Details about guide vanes and water flow. Paragraph 3 (85 chars): "Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure." Paragraph 4 (600 chars): Explaining preventative coatings and blade maintenance. What happens: 1. Building Chunk 1: Adds Para 1 (900 chars) + Para 2 (800 chars) + Para 3 (85 chars) = 1,785 chars. Current chunk is full (≈1800). 2. Along comes Paragraph 4 (600 chars): 1,785+600=2,385 chars (exceeds 1,800!). So Chunk 1 is saved containing: [Para 1 + Para 2 + Para 3]. 3. Now, how should Chunk 2 start? The code looks at the last paragraph of Chunk 1 (Paragraph 3). Paragraph 3 is 85 chars long. Is 85≤150 (overlap_chars)? YES! Because Paragraph 3 is a short, complete sentence, the code carries it over as a natural bridge into Chunk 2: Chunk 2 begins with: "Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure. [Paragraph 4 text about coatings and blade maintenance...]" Result: Chunk 2 now has immediate context on why coatings are needed, without cutting any words or sentences in half! What if Paragraph 3 had been huge (e.g. 600 chars)? If Paragraph 3 had been 600 chars, len(current_chunk[-1]) <= 150 would be False. Repeating a massive 600-character block would waste one-third of Chunk 2's capacity. The condition fails, so Chunk 2 starts cleanly with Paragraph 4 alone. 3. Preserve table headers and rows (Pass 2) Tables need different handling from narrative text. In standard chunkers, a long table gets sliced across arbitrary character limits, leaving half the data rows orphaned without column names. This chunker: If a table has 40 rows and exceeds 1,800 characters, it slices it into smaller tables, repeating the top column headers on every slice: Detects Markdown tables (| col1 | col2 |). Slices large tables row-by-row . Repeats the table header and divider row at the top of every chunk slice so the numbers always retain their meaning. Tags the chunk with is_table = True so the agent can run table-specific filtered searches. 4. Attach breadcrumbs and citation metadata (Pass 3) When an embedding model or LLM sees an isolated chunk like “The operating head is 45 meters” , it doesn’t know which plant or turbine that applies to. To fix this, the chunker injects a context banner directly at the top of the chunk’s text: [Source: Turbine_Manual.pdf | Location: Slide/Page 12 | Section: Turbine Manual > Selection Guidelines > Francis Turbines] The operating head is 45 meters... In Pass 2: The chunker fills Chunk 1 up to the target limit (∼1,800 characters). There are 50 characters left over at the end of the section: example:"Refer to Figure 4 for full assembly diagrams." (49 chars) Pass 2 splits this leftover into Chunk 2. The Problem: If left alone, Chunk 2 would be indexed into Qdrant as its own chunk with only 49 characters! If a user searches for something, retrieving that tiny chunk alone is useless. Pass 3 to the rescue: Pass 3 looks at Chunk 2: Size = 49 characters. Is 49<150 (min_chars)? Yes! It appends that 49-character sentence back into Chunk 1. Result: Chunk 1 becomes 1,849 characters (which is completely fine because 1,800 is a soft target), and the tiny orphan chunk is eliminated! Both the raw content and the banner-enriched content are saved. 5. Save chunks for embedding and retrieval (pass 4) Chunks are saved to data/chunks/chunks.jsonl (streaming format for easy reading line-by-line). A high-level statistics file (data/chunks/chunk_summary.json) records total chunks, average tokens, and table counts. tiktoken (cl100k_base) is used for fast token size estimation: These counts help inspect chunk sizes, but they are not exact token counts for the Qwen embedding model because the tokenizers differ. The goal is to create passages that remain understandable after retrieval: a paragraph carries its section context, a table slice retains its headers, and each result can be traced back to its source. # 1. Build the citation context banner banner_parts = [ f"Source: {source_file}", # "HDP_AHN511.ppt" f"Location: Slide/Page {page_or_slide}", # "Location: Slide/Page 1" f"Section: {breadcrumb}" # "Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing..." ] banner = f"[{' | '.join(banner_parts)}]

" # 2. Prepend banner to the raw text enriched_content = banner + raw_text # 3. Generate structured chunk ID chunk_id = f"{file_stem}__{file_hash[:8]}__c{idx:04d}" # Output -> "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002" The chunk is written as a single-line JSON record: { "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002", "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt", "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)", "document_title": "HDP_AHN511", "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power", "section_hierarchy": [ "HDP_AHN511", "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power" ], "page_or_slide": 1, "chunk_index": 2, "total_chunks": 37, "is_table": false, "char_count": 531, "token_count": 121, "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power]

> **[Slide 1 Image/Diagram OCR]**: HETT", "raw_content": "## Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power
Based On UI Mechanism..." } Vector indexing: storing embeddings and evidence in Qdrant After chunking, each passage is embedded locally using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. The indexer expects a 1,024-dimensional vector and stores it in a Qdrant collection named shp_knowledge. Every chunk is represented by a list of 1,024 numbers. Each stored point has three parts: A unique identifier for the chunk: Qdrant requires point IDs to be valid numbers or UUIDs.Instead of generating a random UUID (like uuid4()), it uses uuid5 , which turns the string chunk_id (e.g. Turbine__127653ce__c0001) into the exact same UUID every single time. If you run indexing twice, Qdrant will simply overwrite/update the existing point instead of creating duplicate entries. point_uuid = manager.chunk_id_to_uuid("HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002") # Returns deterministic UUID5: "877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a" An embedding vector for similarity search. Each chunk is converted into a vector using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. Typical chunks are small relative to the configured input limit. However, the chunk-size target is not a strict maximum: long sentences, table rows, merged fragments, and source banners can produce larger inputs. Oversized chunks should therefore be checked using the embedding model’s tokenizer and the input limit configured in the serving runtime. The chunker’s tiktoken counts are estimates, not exact counts for the Qwen model. { "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002", "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt", ... "embedding": [ 0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, -0.025804, 0.025764, ... 1024 float numbers total ... ] } A metadata payload containing the text and its source context point = models.PointStruct( # 1. Unique deterministic ID id="877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a", # 2. The 1024-dim vector for Cosine similarity search vector=[0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, ...], # 3. Payload: Metadata + Context text for LLM retrieval and filtering payload={ "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002", "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt", "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)", "is_table": "false", "page_or_slide": 1, "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power", "section_hierarchy": ["HDP_AHN511", "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power"], "token_count": 121, "char_count": 531, "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ...", "text": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ..." } ) The embedding helps locate passages with similar meaning. The payload lets the application read the evidence, apply filters, and identify where it came from. How metadata is generated Metadata is assembled during parsing and chunking, then carried into the index. It is derived from filenames, document structure, extracted location labels, and chunk statistics rather than generated by an LLM. This metadata helps the agents retrieve more selectively. A request for a discharge table can use a table filter, while a document-specific question can constrain retrieval to a source file. How indexing works The indexer reads embedded chunks from JSONL, checks that each vector has the expected dimensions, and uploads points in batches of 128 by default. It converts each chunk ID into a deterministic UUID5 identifier. Re-indexing the same chunk updates the corresponding point instead of creating another copy. That handles repeated indexing of unchanged chunks. Updating a document is a separate concern: changed content can produce new chunk IDs, so removing obsolete document versions requires an explicit cleanup strategy. The collection uses cosine similarity to compare query vectors with stored chunk vectors. Its configuration requests on-disk vectors and payloads, and the indexer creates payload indexes for source_file, file_type, is_table, and page_or_slide. Why I chose Qdrant Qdrant fits three requirements of this project. Local deployment. The application can connect to a Qdrant server inside the organization’s infrastructure. The index manager also supports embedded local disk storage for development, reducing setup requirements for learners. Similarity search with metadata filters. Engineering questions often need both semantic matching and precise constraints. Keeping vectors and source metadata together allows the retriever to combine those requirements. A straightforward indexing workflow. Collections, payloads, deterministic point IDs, and batch upserts map naturally to the project’s document-and-chunk model. These were practical reasons for choosing Qdrant; ChromaDB was also a viable option for local development and metadata-based retrieval. I chose Qdrant for its dedicated vector-search service and configurable payload indexes, which fit my document-filtering requirements. This was an architectural choice, rather than a claim that Qdrant universally outperforms ChromaDB. The project does not benchmark it against other vector databases. Qdrant’s role in hybrid retrieval Qdrant provides the dense retrieval component. A separate local BM25 retriever handles keyword matching, and the application combines their rankings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Dense retrieval helps with conceptual similarity. BM25 helps with exact terminology, project names, and document identifiers. Combining the two gives the system complementary ways to find evidence before synthesis and answer generation. The architecture I built The system is designed to run locally with Ollama and Qdrant, making it suitable for document sets that should remain inside an organization. The high-level workflow is: Here is Deatailed archietcture: User Query │ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ │ Planner Agent │◄──────────────────────────────────┐ └────────┬────────┘ │ ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐ │ (direct_answer) (out_of_scope) (rag_retrieval) │ │ │ │ │ END │ ▼ │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Orchestrator Agent │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ │ │ Send() API │ │ ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ │ │ [Narrative] [Tabular] [MCP] │ │ (Manuals) (Tables) (Formulas) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └────────────────┼────────────────┘ │ │ ▼ │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Aggregate Results │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ │ ▼ │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Synthesizer Agent │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ │ ▼ │ │ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Retrieval Grader │ │ │ │ (Gate 1: Pre-Gen) │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ (Insufficient │ │ │ & retry < max) │ (Sufficient or | | |Insufficient&retry>=max| │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ Generator Agent │ │ │ │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ │ │Generation Guardail│ │ │ │ │(Gate 2: Post-Gen) │ │ │ │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ (Grounded) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────┴─────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ │ │ │ │ END │ │ │ │ (Ungrounded | | │ │ & retry < max)| | │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌───────────────────────────────────────┴┐ │ │ Feedback Agent │ │ │ (Diagnoses query gaps & missing terms)│ │ └────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ (Ungrounded & retry >= max) ▼ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ Fallback Agent │ │ (Circuit Breaker) │ │ - Out-of-scope refusal │ │ - Partial answer + warning │ └─────────────┬──────────────┘ ▼ END Each stage has a focused responsibility. 1. Planner Agent The Planner Agent first classifies the request into one of three routes: Direct answer : Conversational greetings or general questions that do not need documentation. Out-of-scope query : Questions outside small hydropower engineering (e.g. general politics, unrelated code), routed to a polite domain-boundary refusal. RAG-required technical query : Technical questions that proceed to retrieval. For engineering questions, it elaborates domain terms and decomposes broad queries into focused sub-queries with targeted metadata filters (e.g., tagging a discharge inquiry with is_table: true). 2. Orchestrator and specialized workers The Orchestrator dispatches sub-queries to specialized workers using LangGraph’s dynamic Send() API: Narrative retriever : Dense and keyword retrieval over technical principles, manuals, and descriptive text (filter: is_table=false). Tabular retriever : Targeted retrieval over head-flow matrices, turbine efficiency curves, and cost tables (filter: is_table=true). MCP tool worker : Deterministic engineering calculations (power equations P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns, penstock sizing) and plant telemetry via a dedicated FastAPI Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. You can add multiple workers as you want. For document retrieval, the system combines dense semantic search (Qdrant) and sparse keyword search (BM25) using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) . Exact equipment designations, Indian Standards (IS codes), and plant names receive exact-match boosting. 3. Synthesizer Agent The Synthesizer performs deterministic evidence assembly without an additional LLM call. It gathers worker outputs, removes duplicate chunks, balances evidence across sub-queries, and constructs a context dossier with source references for the generator. This stage still takes processing time, but avoids the inference overhead of another model call. 4. Dual Quality Gates & Self-Correction Loop To improve answer reliability, the system implements two independent verification gates: Gate 1: Pre-Generation Retrieval Sufficiency (Corrective RAG) Before invoking the generator, a retrieval grader checks whether the retrieved evidence actually contains the required formulas, numbers, or parameters. If critical evidence is missing and retry budget remains, the workflow requests another retrieval attempt. The Generator Agent The generator drafts an answer when evidence passes Gate 1, or makes a best-effort attempt using available evidence when the retry budget is exhausted.qwen3.5:9b Drafts an engineering response strictly constrained to the synthesized dossier with bracketed source citations. Gate 2: Post-Generation Grounding & Numerical Guardrail A local guardrail checks numerical claims against the available evidence. Structure-aware preprocessing reduces false positives from formatting elements such as Markdown headings, list numbers, and citation markers. The Diagnostic Feedback Agent (Self-Correction) If either Gate 1 (insufficient context) or Gate 2 (hallucination) fails and retry budget remains, the workflow routes to a Feedback Agent . It analyzes the gap, suggests missing technical synonyms or filters, and loops back to the Planner for a targeted re-retrieval attempt (guarded by a circuit breaker to prevent infinite loops). Circuit Breaker Fallback If the post-generation check fails after the retry budget is exhausted, the system returns a fallback response: partial findings, a data-unavailable notice, or a best-effort answer explicitly marked as unverified. Local-first technology choices Core Framework : Python, LangGraph (stateful graph with MemorySaver thread checkpoints), and LangChain. Local Inference : Ollama running qwen3.5:9b (reasoning/generator) and qwen3-embedding:0.6b (1,024-dim dense vectors). Vector & Keyword Stores : Qdrant (dual-mode: Docker network server or embedded local disk) and custom in-memory BM25 with disk serialization. Deterministic Computation : FastAPI-based MCP tool server for exact formula execution. Document Ingestion : Multi-tier smart parser (pymupdf4llm, Docling GPU vision OCR, RapidOCR, openpyxl, python-docx). User Interface and FastAPI Backend Architecture To make the system practical for plant engineers and operators, the user-facing interface is completely decoupled from the underlying agent execution engine. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Streamlit Web Frontend (Port 8601) │ │ [Engineering Chat] [Hydro Calculator] [Citations] │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ JSON REST HTTP Requests (session_id, query, health probes, uploads) │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ FastAPI Server (Port 8600) │ │ - Pre-compiles LangGraph Singleton at startup │ │ - Manages session threads & MemorySaver checkpointing│ │ - Probes Ollama, Qdrant, and LangSmith health │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ [Compiled LangGraph Multi-Agent Engine] 1. Decoupled Client-Server Design The system decouples the presentation layer from the agent execution engine and calculation services across three dedicated, non-conflicting service ports (8600–8602): Streamlit Web Portal (Port 8601) : The interactive engineering interface (ui/app.py). It provides a multi-turn chat window, an evidence citations inspector (revealing source files, section breadcrumbs, and similarity scores), an interactive hydro sizing calculator, and a real-time system health diagnostics sidebar. FastAPI Agent Backend (Port 8600) : The FastAPI backend (src/api/app.py)compiles the LangGraph workflow once at startup. It exposes POST /api/v1/chat for agent execution, GET /api/v1/health for diagnostics, and POST /api/v1/documents/upload for saving uploaded documents. Uploaded files require a separate ingestion run before they become searchable. FastAPI MCP Tool Server (Port 8602) : A dedicated Model Context Protocol service (src/mcp_server/server.py) exposing deterministic formulas (P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns​, Sarkaria penstock economic diameter) and SCADA telemetry simulation via JSON-RPC 2.0 and OpenAPI Swagger endpoints (http://localhost:8602/docs). 2. items.summary_html:
Most RAG applications follow a simple path:

Retrieve a few documents → send them to an LLM → generate an answer.

That works for straightforward lookup questions. But it becomes fragile when the question spans multiple manuals, needs numerical reasoning, contains tables, or asks for an engineering recommendation grounded in plant documentation.

I built an Agentic RAG system for Small Hydropower Plant (SHP) engineering to explore a harder question:

Can a multi-agent retrieval workflow improve the quality of answers from private technical documents without depending on paid inference APIs?

The answer, based on my evaluation so far, is nuanced: it improves retrieval precision, but comes with a substantial latency cost and does not automatically outperform a well-designed plain RAG pipeline on faithfulness.

The complete implementation is available here: Agentic RAG for Small Hydropower.
Built for learners: no paid inference APIs required

One of my goals was to make this project accessible to students and independent learners who cannot afford recurring API bills.

The core RAG pipeline runs locally using Ollama and open-weight models. Document processing, embeddings, retrieval, answer generation, and runtime quality checks do not require paid cloud inference APIs. Once the required models and dependencies are downloaded, you can experiment on compatible hardware without paying per question or per token.

For offline benchmarking, I used Gemini and Groq through their available free tiers to evaluate answers against the golden dataset. Those services are optional: evaluation can also use a local Ollama judge. Free-tier quotas and availability may change, so they should not be treated as an unlimited resource.

This does not mean running the system has zero cost — hardware, electricity, and inference time still matter. But if you already have a suitable computer, it removes a major barrier to learning: a recurring inference bill.

For me, that makes the project useful beyond hydropower. It provides a practical starting point for learning document ingestion, hybrid retrieval, agent orchestration, tool use, and evaluation within a limited budget.

The problem: engineering knowledge is not a single-document lookup task

Small hydropower projects involve a mix of technical manuals, regulatory guidelines, turbine-selection references, hydrology documents, financial policies, scanned reports, tables, and drawings.

A typical question may require several kinds of evidence at once:

  • Which turbine is suitable for a particular head and discharge?
  • What are the applicable regulatory requirements?
  • Which maintenance practices reduce silt erosion?
  • Can the system calculate power output from provided values?
  • Is the answer actually supported by the retrieved documents?

A traditional RAG pipeline may retrieve relevant passages, but it usually has no mechanism to decide whether the retrieved context is sufficient, whether a calculation should use a tool, or whether the generated answer contains unsupported claims.

That is where the agentic approach becomes useful.

Before retrieval: turning engineering documents into usable evidence

The first challenge was preparing the documents. Hydropower knowledge arrives in different formats: digital PDFs, scanned reports, Word documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and images. Each format needs a different extraction approach.

I built a multi-tier parsing pipeline that converts these files into Markdown before chunking and embedding.

Tier 1: Dedicated parsers for Office documents and text

For formats with accessible document structure, the pipeline uses dedicated libraries:

This avoids sending every file through a more expensive OCR process.

Tier 2: Markdown extraction for digital PDFs

For PDFs, the pipeline first uses pymupdf4llm to extract text into Markdown, aiming to retain headings and table structure.

If the extracted output contains at least 80 characters, the current implementation accepts it. If the output is shorter — or extraction fails — the document moves to the Docling fallback.

This is a practical routing heuristic, but it has a limitation: a PDF containing both digital text and scanned pages may pass the threshold even when some pages need OCR. Page-level quality checks would improve this approach.

Tier 3: OCR and layout recovery

Scanned PDFs and failed PDF extractions are processed with Docling, with OCR and table-structure recovery enabled when the required backend is available. Images also enter the Docling conversion path.

The PDF OCR configuration prefers EasyOCR, with RapidOCR as an alternative. It uses CUDA acceleration when available and otherwise falls back to CPU execution.

The aim is to recover readable text and useful table structure. Complex drawings, dense tables, and formulas remain difficult, so extracted Markdown should not be assumed to reproduce every detail correctly.

Keeping the source traceable

Alongside the Markdown, the parser records source information such as the filename, file type, content hash, parsing duration, and page count where available. Parsing failures are recorded explicitly.

The content hash also supports caching: an unchanged document can reuse its existing Markdown output, avoiding unnecessary processing.

The resulting flow is:

Raw documents → format-specific parsing or OCR → Markdown and metadata → chunking → embeddings and indexing

This stage directly affects everything that follows. If a table loses its units or OCR misreads a formula, the retrieval and generation stages may work with incorrect evidence. Improving parsing is therefore part of improving answer quality.

Binary SHA-256 deduplication is an efficient first line of defense to prevent wasting heavy parsing and OCR compute on identical files, but for the same converted file, Binary deduplication will NOT be applicable — the system will treat them as two completely separate files

An actual record saved in data/parsed/metadata.json
{
  "source_path": "D:\GenAi_Code\Agentic_RAG\data\raw\AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf",
  "file_name": "AK - Hydrology of Ungauged Catchment.pdf",
  "file_type": "PDF",
  "file_hash": "127653ce9e3151fd6732fd83bfc66e570ab762bdafb22d568fcef524ce0d19bc",
  "page_count": 0,

  "parse_duration_s": 0.0,

Chunking methodology: preserving structure and source context

After parsing, the documents are available as Markdown. The next challenge is dividing them into passages that are useful for retrieval without losing their context. I implemented a Markdown-aware hierarchical chunker. It uses document structure and text length for boundaries, rather than an LLM or embedding-based semantic segmentation model.

The chunker uses a 4-pass rule-based pipeline rather than an LLM or arbitrary character slicing:

[Raw Markdown Document]
       │
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 1  │  Scan whole document → Divide into Structural Sections
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `sections` list
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 2  │  Process all sections → Split into Target-Sized Chunks (1,800 chars)
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `raw_chunks` list
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 3  │  Scan all raw chunks → Merge Tiny Leftover Fragments (< 150 chars)
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `merged_chunks` list
       ▼
   ┌─────────┐
   │ Pass 4  │  Enrich all chunks → Inject Citation Banners & Compute Token Counts
   └─────────┘
       │  Output: `final_chunks` list (Written to `chunks.jsonl`)
       ▼
[Final Output]
1. Split by document structure (Pass 1)

Instead of chopping text blindly every NNN characters, the chunker walks through the document line-by-line, tracking markdown headings (#, ##, ###, ####) like a tree or outline. Whenever a heading or a horizontal divider (---) appears, it finishes the current section. It also checks if the heading mentions a slide or page number.

When a heading includes a label such as “Slide 12” or “Page 8,” that location is captured as metadata. Page references therefore depend on what the parsing stage preserves; they are not automatically available for every chunk.

2. Split long narrative sections at natural boundaries (Pass 2)

Within a section, long text is divided at paragraph boundaries. Oversized paragraphs are further split at sentence boundaries.

In simple words: If a text section is too long (>1,800 characters):

  1. It first splits cleanly at double newlines ( ) to preserve whole paragraphs.
  2. If a single paragraph is still too massive, it splits at sentence boundaries (., !, ?).
  3. Conditional Overlap: Traditional RAG blindly copies the last N characters (often cutting words in half). Here, the previous paragraph is only carried over if its length is ≤150 characters.

The default settings are:

The overlap is conditional, rather than a fixed sliding window: the previous paragraph is repeated only when it fits within the overlap allowance.

The 1,800-character setting is a target, not a strict maximum. Long individual sentences, table rows, fragment merging, and added source metadata can produce larger chunks.

max_chars = 1800
overlap_chars = 150

Imagine a document section with four paragraphs:

Paragraph 1 (900 chars): Details about Francis turbine runner design.
Paragraph 2 (800 chars): Details about guide vanes and water flow.
Paragraph 3 (85 chars): "Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure."
Paragraph 4 (600 chars): Explaining preventative coatings and blade maintenance.
What happens:

1. Building Chunk 1:
  Adds Para 1 (900 chars) + Para 2 (800 chars) + Para 3 (85 chars) = 1,785 chars.
  Current chunk is full (≈1800).
2. Along comes Paragraph 4 (600 chars):
  1,785+600=2,385 chars (exceeds 1,800!).
  So Chunk 1 is saved containing: [Para 1 + Para 2 + Para 3].
3. Now, how should Chunk 2 start?
  The code looks at the last paragraph of Chunk 1 (Paragraph 3).
  Paragraph 3 is 85 chars long.
  Is 85≤150 (overlap_chars)? YES!
  Because Paragraph 3 is a short, complete sentence, the code carries it over as a natural bridge into Chunk 2:

Chunk 2 begins with:
"Cavitation occurs when local water pressure drops below vapor pressure.
[Paragraph 4 text about coatings and blade maintenance...]"

  Result: Chunk 2 now has immediate context on why coatings are needed, without cutting any words or sentences in half!

What if Paragraph 3 had been huge (e.g. 600 chars)?
  If Paragraph 3 had been 600 chars, len(current_chunk[-1]) <= 150 would be False.
  Repeating a massive 600-character block would waste one-third of Chunk 2's capacity.
  The condition fails, so Chunk 2 starts cleanly with Paragraph 4 alone.
3. Preserve table headers and rows (Pass 2)

Tables need different handling from narrative text. In standard chunkers, a long table gets sliced across arbitrary character limits, leaving half the data rows orphaned without column names. This chunker: If a table has 40 rows and exceeds 1,800 characters, it slices it into smaller tables, repeating the top column headers on every slice:

  1. Detects Markdown tables (| col1 | col2 |).
  2. Slices large tables row-by-row.
  3. Repeats the table header and divider row at the top of every chunk slice so the numbers always retain their meaning.
  4. Tags the chunk with is_table = True so the agent can run table-specific filtered searches.
4. Attach breadcrumbs and citation metadata (Pass 3)

When an embedding model or LLM sees an isolated chunk like “The operating head is 45 meters”, it doesn’t know which plant or turbine that applies to. To fix this, the chunker injects a context banner directly at the top of the chunk’s text:

[Source: Turbine_Manual.pdf | Location: Slide/Page 12 | Section: Turbine Manual > Selection Guidelines > Francis Turbines]
The operating head is 45 meters...
In Pass 2:
The chunker fills Chunk 1 up to the target limit (∼1,800 characters).
There are 50 characters left over at the end of the section:
 example:"Refer to Figure 4 for full assembly diagrams." (49 chars)
Pass 2 splits this leftover into Chunk 2.

The Problem:
If left alone, Chunk 2 would be indexed into Qdrant as its own chunk with only 49 characters! If a user searches for something, retrieving that tiny chunk alone is useless.

Pass 3 to the rescue:
Pass 3 looks at Chunk 2:
  Size = 49 characters.
  Is 49<150 (min_chars)? Yes!
  It appends that 49-character sentence back into Chunk 1.

Result: Chunk 1 becomes 1,849 characters (which is completely fine because 1,800 is a soft target), and the tiny orphan chunk is eliminated!

Both the raw content and the banner-enriched content are saved.

5. Save chunks for embedding and retrieval (pass 4)
  • Chunks are saved to data/chunks/chunks.jsonl (streaming format for easy reading line-by-line).
  • A high-level statistics file (data/chunks/chunk_summary.json) records total chunks, average tokens, and table counts.
  • tiktoken (cl100k_base) is used for fast token size estimation:

These counts help inspect chunk sizes, but they are not exact token counts for the Qwen embedding model because the tokenizers differ.

The goal is to create passages that remain understandable after retrieval: a paragraph carries its section context, a table slice retains its headers, and each result can be traced back to its source.

# 1. Build the citation context banner
banner_parts = [
    f"Source: {source_file}",                    # "HDP_AHN511.ppt"
    f"Location: Slide/Page {page_or_slide}",     # "Location: Slide/Page 1"
    f"Section: {breadcrumb}"                     # "Section: HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing..."
]
banner = f"[{' | '.join(banner_parts)}]

"

# 2. Prepend banner to the raw text
enriched_content = banner + raw_text

# 3. Generate structured chunk ID
chunk_id = f"{file_stem}__{file_hash[:8]}__c{idx:04d}"

# Output -> "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002"

The chunk is written as a single-line JSON record:

Vector indexing: storing embeddings and evidence in Qdrant

After chunking, each passage is embedded locally using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. The indexer expects a 1,024-dimensional vector and stores it in a Qdrant collection named shp_knowledge. Every chunk is represented by a list of 1,024 numbers.

Each stored point has three parts:

  • A unique identifier for the chunk: Qdrant requires point IDs to be valid numbers or UUIDs.Instead of generating a random UUID (like uuid4()), it uses uuid5, which turns the string chunk_id (e.g. Turbine__127653ce__c0001) into the exact same UUID every single time. If you run indexing twice, Qdrant will simply overwrite/update the existing point instead of creating duplicate entries.
point_uuid = manager.chunk_id_to_uuid("HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002")
# Returns deterministic UUID5: "877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a"
  • An embedding vector for similarity search. Each chunk is converted into a vector using qwen3-embedding:0.6b. Typical chunks are small relative to the configured input limit. However, the chunk-size target is not a strict maximum: long sentences, table rows, merged fragments, and source banners can produce larger inputs. Oversized chunks should therefore be checked using the embedding model’s tokenizer and the input limit configured in the serving runtime. The chunker’s tiktoken counts are estimates, not exact counts for the Qwen model.
{
  "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002",
  "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt",
  ...
  "embedding": [
    0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, -0.025804, 0.025764, 
    ... 1024 float numbers total ...
  ]
}
  • A metadata payload containing the text and its source context
point = models.PointStruct(
    # 1. Unique deterministic ID
    id="877250c9-fe3a-55c0-96a9-89d7d65a689a",

    # 2. The 1024-dim vector for Cosine similarity search
    vector=[0.002478, 0.005229, -0.005374, ...],

    # 3. Payload: Metadata + Context text for LLM retrieval and filtering
    payload={
        "chunk_id": "HDP_AHN511__9fe0f668__c0002",
        "source_file": "HDP_AHN511.ppt",
        "file_type": "PowerPoint (legacy)",
        "is_table": "false",
        "page_or_slide": 1,
        "breadcrumb": "HDP_AHN511 > Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power",
        "section_hierarchy": ["HDP_AHN511", "Slide 1: Dynamic Pricing of electrical power"],
        "token_count": 121,
        "char_count": 531,
        "content": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ...",
        "text": "[Source: HDP_AHN511.ppt | Location: Slide/Page 1 | Section: ...]

## Slide 1: ..."
    }
)

The embedding helps locate passages with similar meaning. The payload lets the application read the evidence, apply filters, and identify where it came from.

How metadata is generated

Metadata is assembled during parsing and chunking, then carried into the index. It is derived from filenames, document structure, extracted location labels, and chunk statistics rather than generated by an LLM.

This metadata helps the agents retrieve more selectively. A request for a discharge table can use a table filter, while a document-specific question can constrain retrieval to a source file.

How indexing works

The indexer reads embedded chunks from JSONL, checks that each vector has the expected dimensions, and uploads points in batches of 128 by default.

It converts each chunk ID into a deterministic UUID5 identifier. Re-indexing the same chunk updates the corresponding point instead of creating another copy.

That handles repeated indexing of unchanged chunks. Updating a document is a separate concern: changed content can produce new chunk IDs, so removing obsolete document versions requires an explicit cleanup strategy.

The collection uses cosine similarity to compare query vectors with stored chunk vectors. Its configuration requests on-disk vectors and payloads, and the indexer creates payload indexes for source_file, file_type, is_table, and page_or_slide.

Why I chose Qdrant

Qdrant fits three requirements of this project.

Local deployment. The application can connect to a Qdrant server inside the organization’s infrastructure. The index manager also supports embedded local disk storage for development, reducing setup requirements for learners.

Similarity search with metadata filters. Engineering questions often need both semantic matching and precise constraints. Keeping vectors and source metadata together allows the retriever to combine those requirements.

A straightforward indexing workflow. Collections, payloads, deterministic point IDs, and batch upserts map naturally to the project’s document-and-chunk model.

These were practical reasons for choosing Qdrant; ChromaDB was also a viable option for local development and metadata-based retrieval. I chose Qdrant for its dedicated vector-search service and configurable payload indexes, which fit my document-filtering requirements. This was an architectural choice, rather than a claim that Qdrant universally outperforms ChromaDB. The project does not benchmark it against other vector databases.

Qdrant’s role in hybrid retrieval

Qdrant provides the dense retrieval component. A separate local BM25 retriever handles keyword matching, and the application combines their rankings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

Dense retrieval helps with conceptual similarity. BM25 helps with exact terminology, project names, and document identifiers. Combining the two gives the system complementary ways to find evidence before synthesis and answer generation.

The architecture I built

The system is designed to run locally with Ollama and Qdrant, making it suitable for document sets that should remain inside an organization.

Each stage has a focused responsibility.

1. Planner Agent

The Planner Agent first classifies the request into one of three routes:

  • Direct answer: Conversational greetings or general questions that do not need documentation.
  • Out-of-scope query: Questions outside small hydropower engineering (e.g. general politics, unrelated code), routed to a polite domain-boundary refusal.
  • RAG-required technical query: Technical questions that proceed to retrieval.

For engineering questions, it elaborates domain terms and decomposes broad queries into focused sub-queries with targeted metadata filters (e.g., tagging a discharge inquiry with is_table: true).

2. Orchestrator and specialized workers

The Orchestrator dispatches sub-queries to specialized workers using LangGraph’s dynamic Send() API:

  • Narrative retriever: Dense and keyword retrieval over technical principles, manuals, and descriptive text (filter: is_table=false).
  • Tabular retriever: Targeted retrieval over head-flow matrices, turbine efficiency curves, and cost tables (filter: is_table=true).
  • MCP tool worker: Deterministic engineering calculations (power equations P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns, penstock sizing) and plant telemetry via a dedicated FastAPI Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

You can add multiple workers as you want. For document retrieval, the system combines dense semantic search (Qdrant) and sparse keyword search (BM25) using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Exact equipment designations, Indian Standards (IS codes), and plant names receive exact-match boosting.

3. Synthesizer Agent

The Synthesizer performs deterministic evidence assembly without an additional LLM call. It gathers worker outputs, removes duplicate chunks, balances evidence across sub-queries, and constructs a context dossier with source references for the generator. This stage still takes processing time, but avoids the inference overhead of another model call.

4. Dual Quality Gates & Self-Correction Loop

To improve answer reliability, the system implements two independent verification gates:

  • Gate 1: Pre-Generation Retrieval Sufficiency (Corrective RAG)
    Before invoking the generator, a retrieval grader checks whether the retrieved evidence actually contains the required formulas, numbers, or parameters. If critical evidence is missing and retry budget remains, the workflow requests another retrieval attempt.
  • The Generator Agent
    The generator drafts an answer when evidence passes Gate 1, or makes a best-effort attempt using available evidence when the retry budget is exhausted.qwen3.5:9b Drafts an engineering response strictly constrained to the synthesized dossier with bracketed source citations.
  • Gate 2: Post-Generation Grounding & Numerical Guardrail
    A local guardrail checks numerical claims against the available evidence. Structure-aware preprocessing reduces false positives from formatting elements such as Markdown headings, list numbers, and citation markers.
  • The Diagnostic Feedback Agent (Self-Correction)
    If either Gate 1 (insufficient context) or Gate 2 (hallucination) fails and retry budget remains, the workflow routes to a Feedback Agent. It analyzes the gap, suggests missing technical synonyms or filters, and loops back to the Planner for a targeted re-retrieval attempt (guarded by a circuit breaker to prevent infinite loops).
  • Circuit Breaker Fallback
    If the post-generation check fails after the retry budget is exhausted, the system returns a fallback response: partial findings, a data-unavailable notice, or a best-effort answer explicitly marked as unverified.
Local-first technology choices
  • Core Framework: Python, LangGraph (stateful graph with MemorySaver thread checkpoints), and LangChain.
  • Local Inference: Ollama running qwen3.5:9b (reasoning/generator) and qwen3-embedding:0.6b (1,024-dim dense vectors).
  • Vector & Keyword Stores: Qdrant (dual-mode: Docker network server or embedded local disk) and custom in-memory BM25 with disk serialization.
  • Deterministic Computation: FastAPI-based MCP tool server for exact formula execution.
  • Document Ingestion: Multi-tier smart parser (pymupdf4llm, Docling GPU vision OCR, RapidOCR, openpyxl, python-docx).
User Interface and FastAPI Backend Architecture

To make the system practical for plant engineers and operators, the user-facing interface is completely decoupled from the underlying agent execution engine.

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              Streamlit Web Frontend (Port 8601)        │
  │  [Engineering Chat]  [Hydro Calculator]  [Citations]   │
  └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                    JSON REST HTTP Requests
           (session_id, query, health probes, uploads)
                              │
                              ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 FastAPI Server (Port 8600)             │
  │   - Pre-compiles LangGraph Singleton at startup        │
  │   - Manages session threads & MemorySaver checkpointing│
  │   - Probes Ollama, Qdrant, and LangSmith health        │
  └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                [Compiled LangGraph Multi-Agent Engine]
1. Decoupled Client-Server Design

The system decouples the presentation layer from the agent execution engine and calculation services across three dedicated, non-conflicting service ports (8600–8602):

  1. Streamlit Web Portal (Port 8601):
    The interactive engineering interface (ui/app.py). It provides a multi-turn chat window, an evidence citations inspector (revealing source files, section breadcrumbs, and similarity scores), an interactive hydro sizing calculator, and a real-time system health diagnostics sidebar.
  2. FastAPI Agent Backend (Port 8600):
    The FastAPI backend (src/api/app.py)compiles the LangGraph workflow once at startup. It exposes POST /api/v1/chat for agent execution, GET /api/v1/health for diagnostics, and POST /api/v1/documents/upload for saving uploaded documents. Uploaded files require a separate ingestion run before they become searchable.
  3. FastAPI MCP Tool Server (Port 8602):
    A dedicated Model Context Protocol service (src/mcp_server/server.py) exposing deterministic formulas (P=ηρgQH, specific speed Ns​, Sarkaria penstock economic diameter) and SCADA telemetry simulation via JSON-RPC 2.0 and OpenAPI Swagger endpoints (http://localhost:8602/docs).
2. Core API Endpoints

The frontend interacts with the agent engine across three primary endpoints:

  • POST /api/v1/documents/upload: Accepts an uploaded document and saves it to the application’s data directory. The current endpoint does not automatically parse, chunk, embed, or index the file. Those steps run separately.
  • GET /api/v1/health: Real-time diagnostic heartbeat that verifies whether the local Ollama LLM, Qdrant vector database (including indexed point counts), and LangSmith tracing are online.
  • POST /api/v1/upload: Ingestion endpoint that accepts new plant documents (.pdf, .docx, .pptx), immediately passing them through the multi-tier parser and chunker for live vector indexing into Qdrant.
3. Key UI Components

The Streamlit interface organizes engineering workflows into focused tabs:

  • Engineering Assistant: Chat window rendering markdown responses, equations, and active warnings if the fallback circuit breaker was tripped.
  • Citations Inspector: An evidence inspection pane displaying the exact source documents, section breadcrumbs, similarity scores, and text excerpts used to ground each response.
  • Hydro Sizing Calculator: Computes power output and estimated annual energy directly in the Streamlit application using Python. It also provides a rule-based turbine-selection suggestion. This UI calculator operates independently of the MCP tool server used by the agent workflow.
  • System Diagnostics Sidebar: Live status pills displaying the connection health of Ollama and Qdrant, active latency telemetry, and the session ID.
Fully on-prem at runtime

A core design goal of this project is that the RAG system can run fully on-premises without depending on external inference APIs.

At runtime, the architecture uses local components:

  • Ollama for LLM inference and embeddings
  • Qdrant for vector storage and semantic retrieval
  • Local BM25 for keyword retrieval
  • Local document parsing, chunking, indexing, orchestration, and guardrails
  • FastAPI and Streamlit for the application layer

This means that plant manuals, DPRs, maintenance reports, drawings, and operational documents can remain within the organization’s own infrastructure.

External APIs such as Gemini and Groq were used only in the offline evaluation workflow as LLM-as-a-judge providers for scoring the golden dataset. They are not required for the runtime RAG pipeline.

For environments with stricter data policies, the evaluation layer can also be replaced with a local Ollama-based judge. The trade-off is that external judge models can provide an additional independent perspective during benchmarking, while a fully local evaluation setup preserves complete data isolation.

Evaluation: runtime checks and offline benchmarking

I used two evaluation layers: checks inside the running agent workflow, and an offline benchmark against a golden dataset. They answer different questions.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Runtime In-Flight Evaluation (Zero External APIs)                   │
│    - Gate 1: Retrieval Sufficiency Grader (qwen3.5:9b)                 │
│    - Gate 2: Faithfulness & Numerical Guardrail (qwen3.5:9b, ≥ 0.90)   │
│    - Feedback Loop & Circuit Breaker (Bounded retry budget)            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. Offline Benchmark: Agentic RAG vs. Plain Hybrid-RAG                 │
│    - 10 Head-to-Head Policy & Licensing Benchmark Cases                │
│    - Multi-provider LLM-as-a-Judge (Google Gemini 2.5 Flash & Groq)    │
│    - Evaluates: Faithfulness, Precision, Recall, Relevancy, Latency    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Runtime evaluation (In-Flight Quality Gates): checking each response

During execution, the system uses the local qwen3.5:9b model as a judge at two stages.

  1. Retrieval Sufficiency Check (Pre-Gen): The retrieval sufficiency check evaluates whether the assembled context contains the information required to answer the question. When evidence is missing, it identifies the gaps and can trigger feedback and another retrieval attempt. The Pre-Gen Retrieval Sufficiency check (Gate 1) does NOT use a numerical threshold like 0.90. Instead, it uses a semantic boolean decision (is_sufficient: True / False) based on engineering completeness criteria.
  2. Faithfulness & Grounding Check (Post-Gen): The faithfulness check evaluates the generated answer against the available evidence. It returns a groundedness verdict, a faithfulness score, and any statements it considers unsupported. The configured faithfulness threshold is 0.90.

Both checks share a bounded retry budget (cycle_count < MAX_CYCLES). When the budget is exhausted, insufficient retrieval proceeds to best-effort generation; a failed faithfulness check then routes to a fallback response with a warning.

These checks do not require a golden answer or an external inference API. However, an LLM judge is still fallible: passing the check is a probabilistic model assessment, not a mathematical proof of factual truth

Offline evaluation: testing against the golden dataset

For empirical benchmarking, I evaluated the updated Agentic RAG workflow against a standard Plain Hybrid-RAG baseline (single dense vector search + BM25 keyword search without agents or decomposition) across 10 complex Small Hydropower policy and licensing questions from the golden dataset.

Here, “offline” means evaluation outside the live request workflow — not disconnected from the internet. API-based judging sends the evaluation content to those providers. A fully local evaluation setup can instead use an Ollama-based judge. Evaluations were performed using automated LLM-as-a-Judge scoring via Google Gemini 2.5 Flash with automated failover to Groq (openai/gpt-oss-120b).

Metrics used

The first four metrics are LLM-assigned scores on a 0–1 scale in this benchmark. They should be interpreted as judge estimates, rather than exact measurements of factual accuracy.

Hallucination rate is reported separately from average faithfulness; it is not calculated as 1 − faithfulness. Latency is measured from execution, with mean and median used to compare the two pipelines.

Together, these measures help distinguish a grounded but incomplete answer from a comprehensive answer containing unsupported claims — and show how much processing time each architecture requires.

Interpreting the results fairly

The updated head-to-head comparison covers the same ten policy/licensing questions for both systems. It does not establish performance across all engineering tasks.

The benchmark also uses multiple judge models through provider fallback, which can introduce scoring variation. A stronger follow-up would use a fixed judge configuration, repeated runs, and human review of difficult cases, especially calculations, tables, and conflicting evidence.

What the evaluation showed

I compared the updated Agentic RAG workflow with a plain hybrid-RAG baseline across 10 policy and licensing questions.

The result surprised me in a useful way.

  • A Massive Jump in Context Precision (+15.2%):
    Agentic RAG improved context precision from 57.8% to 73.0%. In Plain RAG, a broad query dumps irrelevant chunks into the prompt. In Agentic RAG, the Planner’s sub-query decomposition, the Orchestrator’s targeted worker dispatch (is_table=true/false), and the Synthesizer's deduplication successfully filtered out noise, ensuring the LLM received clearer evidence.
  • Faithfulness Did Not Improve Beyond Baseline (90.0%):
    For straightforward single-hop policy queries, once Plain RAG finds the correct paragraph, a strong generator model (qwen3.5:9b) is already capable of writing an accurate response. Adding multiple agents did not increase factual grounding for these questions.
  • The 3.1× Latency Penalty:
    Running multiple agents on local hardware compounds inference latency. Passing queries sequentially through Planner → Orchestrator → Multiple Workers→ Synthesizer → Grader→ Generator → Guardrail increased average response time from∼2.2 minutes to ∼6.8 minutes.

That is the central lesson from this project:

More agents do not automatically mean more reliable answers.

They add value when they improve retrieval quality, tool selection, and safe failure behavior. But every extra reasoning step adds latency, complexity, and more opportunities for error.

What did not work perfectly?

This project also taught me where Agentic RAG remains difficult.

Guardrails can fail for the wrong reasons

An earlier version of the numerical guardrail incorrectly flagged heading labels such as 3.1 and 4.3 as unsupported engineering claims. That created false failures and unnecessary fallback responses. The fix was not simply “use another LLM.” It required better structure-aware preprocessing before evaluating numbers.

Multi-agent workflows are expensive

Multiple LLM calls, retrieval operations, validation checks, and correction loops add processing overhead. In my local benchmark, this made the agentic workflow substantially slower than a single retrieval-and-generation pipeline.

This latency is not necessarily a fixed limitation. More capable GPUs — either on-premises or cloud-hosted — and an optimized inference engine such as vLLM could reduce model-serving overhead. Prefix caching can avoid reprocessing shared prompt prefixes, while efficient batching can improve throughput when serving concurrent requests. However, higher throughput does not automatically mean a faster answer for an individual user. vLLM optimization documentation

Faithful answers can still be incomplete.

In one benchmark question, the generated answer was grounded in the retrieved content, but the context lacked the expected preference criteria. The system was faithful, but incomplete. This distinction is important:

  • Faithfulness asks: “Did the answer invent claims?”
  • Recall asks: “Did retrieval find the evidence needed to answer fully?”

A trustworthy system needs both.

Future Recommendations: Moving from Prototype to Production

Future improvements should focus on practical reliability, speed, and testing, rather than merely adding more agents.

1. Hardware & Inference Optimization (Tackling the Latency Bottleneck)

The 3.1× latency penalty observed during local testing is a solvable engineering challenge:

  • Hardware upgrades: Higher-memory-bandwidth GPUs, either on-premises or cloud-hosted, could reduce decoding latency when memory access is the limiting factor. Actual gains depend on the model, quantization, context length, available VRAM, and serving configuration. Greater hardware bandwidth does not translate directly into an equivalent end-to-end speedup.
  • Optimized inference engines: Evaluate compatible model configurations with vLLM or TensorRT-LLM to determine whether they improve response latency, throughput, or memory efficiency.
  • Continuous batching: An inference server can batch independent LLM requests that arrive concurrently, improving GPU utilization and serving throughput. This does not automatically parallelize the agent graph or remove dependencies between stages. Deterministic MCP calculations are separate tool operations, not LLM inference requests.
  • Prefix caching: Reusing cached computation for matching prompt prefixes can reduce repeated prompt-processing work. Reuse requires compatible model and cache settings; placing the same evidence after different agent instructions does not necessarily produce a matching prefix. Prefix caching also does not eliminate the time needed to generate new tokens.
  • Smaller models for selected tasks: Test lightweight, quantized models for narrowly defined tasks such as intent classification. Retain a more capable model where evaluation shows it is needed. Retrieval sufficiency checks require particular care because an incorrect verdict can affect the entire answer.
2. Adaptive Query Routing (Plain RAG by Default)

Not every question wants a multi-agent swarm:

  • Simple, single-hop factual questions should route through a fast, low-latency Plain Hybrid-RAG path.
  • The full agentic pipeline (decomposition, tabular workers, and verification loops) should only be activated when a router identifies multi-part questions, table-heavy requests, mathematical calculations, or when initial retrieval confidence is low.
3. Production Ingestion & Asynchronous Jobs
  • Currently, the upload endpoint saves the document without triggering ingestion. A future improvement would connect uploading to an asynchronous job that performs parsing, chunking, embedding, and indexing, with visible progress and failure reporting.
4. Automated Regression Testing & Benchmark Expansion
  • Automated CI/CD Regression Suites: Comprehensive unit and integration assertions testing graph edge routing, circuit breaker trips, regex guardrail numerical filters, citation formatting, and MCP tool parameter validation.
  • Expanded Evaluation Corpus: The current 10-case comparison is a solid pilot, but a comprehensive benchmark should include 50+ diverse engineering scenarios: complex nested tables, OCR-heavy historical plant scans, multi-step hydraulic calculations, and adversarial edge cases.
Final takeaway

Building Agentic RAG is not about making a chatbot appear more intelligent.

It is about deciding when to retrieve, when to calculate, when to retry, when to abstain, and how to show the user what evidence supports an answer.

My current system is not a finished production engineering advisor. It is an evaluated local-first prototype that demonstrates both the promise and the trade-offs of Agentic RAG for domain-specific technical knowledge.

The biggest result was not that Agentic RAG “beat” plain RAG.

It was learning exactly where it helped: retrieval precision and structured workflows — and where it still needs work: latency, recall, testing, and reliable engineering-grade verification.

Agentic RAG vs. Plain Hybrid RAG: What My Hydropower Benchmark Revealed was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Scientists Made Monkeys Watch Minions to Study Their Brains
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards. First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me . Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files . Humans watching monkeys watching Minions Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci. Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips. To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos. “Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said. Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick , The Peanut Butter Falcon , Whiplash , Room , Me and Earl and the Dying Girl , The Tomorrow Man , Dom Hemingway , Life After Beth , Woodshock , and The Comedian. “Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said. A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present , and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques. Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes. “These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded. In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe. In other news… Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE. These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites. The Lambayeque Valley Complex, its location in Peru, and the sites with human skeletal remains studied in this work. Image: Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study. The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University. Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot? Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One. The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study. Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. A Natufian figurine depicting a stylised human body modelled in clay 15,000 years ago, bearing adult and child fingerprints. Image: © Laurent Davin Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.” It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination. The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence. Western harvester ant queen. Image: Blaine J. Cole. Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant ( Pogonomyrmex occidentalis ) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study. “We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.” This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum. Thanks for reading! See you next week.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files. 

Humans watching monkeys watching Minions

Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said. 

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present, and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques.
