In other news…

Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice

Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE. 

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.  

The Lambayeque Valley Complex, its location in Peru, and the sites with human skeletal remains studied in this work. Image: Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen.

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633  individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.

Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?

Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh

Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One.

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

A Natufian figurine depicting a stylised human body modelled in clay 15,000 years ago, bearing adult and child fingerprints. Image: © Laurent Davin

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.

The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning

Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Western harvester ant queen. Image: Blaine J. Cole.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study. 

“We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.  

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Ukraine's naval drones made their name attacking Russian warships. Now they're taking the fight onto land.
items.summary: Ukraine uses the Magura drone to hit Russia's navy, and it's increasingly finding new targets in the air and helping operations on land. Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA Ukraine's naval drones have been hammering Russian warships. Now, the drones, including UFORCE's Magura, are threatening Russian ground targets. The naval drones "pose a threat to the Russian occupiers on land as well," a commander said. Ukrainian naval drones that have hammered Russia's navy are now coming for Russian targets on land. Magura drones made by Ukrainian-founded defense company UFORCE played an important role in Ukraine becoming a formidable force at sea even without a conventional fleet of warships. Naval drones have damaged and destroyed numerous Russian vessels, pushing Moscow to move much of its Black Sea Fleet away from occupied Crimea. Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate, the GUR, revealed in August that it had used Maguras as FPV drone carriers to strike Russian targets on land, leveraging a control vehicle equipped with the "Podlyot" radar complex, which detects aircraft, missiles, and drones, and a Parol-4 IFF interrogator, used to distinguish between friendly and hostile aircraft. The Maguras "pose a threat to the Russian occupiers on land as well," the commander of the GUR's "Group 13" said. "This marks a fundamental shift in the nature of the conflict," said the commander, who uses the call sign "Thirteen." Oleg Rogynskyy, the founder and CEO of UFORCE, told Business Insider that he couldn't comment on the operational specifics, but he said that "it's not hard to imagine" a Magura launching something like the company's heavy Nemesis drone, which could then fly inland to target Russian air defense systems. The Russian air defense systems, he said, were built to take out missiles, not incoming heavy bomber drones flying low at night. In other August wins, the GUR said that drones launched from Maguras destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, and then later that month, they hit two S-400 launchers and a ground-based antenna used to control Orion drones. A month earlier, a naval drone used by the 123rd Territorial Defense Brigade dropped a ground robot off on the Kinburn Spit for an unusual combat mission. And Ukraine is training for more operations like these. Rogynskyy said that Maguras were used in a September exercise to launch drones, drop off amphibious ground drones for a beach assault, and deliver supplies. He said he expects to see more creative uses as time goes on. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spotlighted the growing capabilities of Ukraine's naval drones in an address to the UK Parliament. "We started with simple kamikaze sea drones. Then we built drones with turrets that can shoot down helicopters," he said. "Now we have drones that can shoot down Russian fighter jets from the sea. We have developed boats that carry other drones. We also have boats that strike targets on land from the sea." The GUR said in October that after destroying ships in Russia's Black Sea Fleet , "the Magura drone was significantly improved." It explained that now "it is a multifunctional platform capable not only of sinking surface objects, but also of carrying missile weapons, as well as aerial drones for striking ground targets." Before they became drone carriers, Magura drones were armed with alternative weaponry for engaging non-naval targets. In 2024, for instance, one shot down a helicopter with a missile. Last year, the GUR said that Maguras had been used to shoot down Russian fighter jets. Rogynskyy said some of these uses were a surprise to the company. "I didn't expect it. It's the ingenuity of Ukrainian engineers and Ukrainian soldiers that really drives this," he said. UFORCE, which also makes ground drones, AI software, and command-and-control systems, is one of Ukraine's biggest defense companies. Founded in Ukraine and headquartered in London, with major hubs in Kyiv and Washington, DC, it has also attracted significant international interest. The company's Magura drones have been involved in multiple multinational military exercises. UFORCE has also developed a new MV7 model for UK waters and is partnering with RECONCRAFT , an American special-operations boat maker, though no new production runs, customers, or contracts have yet been announced. UFORCE announced on Thursday that it raised $700 million in a Series A funding round from investors, including the UK government and Silicon Valley-based venture capital firms, bringing the company's total valuation to $6 billion. The company wants to scale its manufacturing both in Ukraine and in partner countries to strengthen their defense. Talking about this round of investment, Rogynskyy told Business Insider that "it's time to scale." He said that the future of naval warfare "is all about fully unmanned navies and autonomous patrol presence, et cetera, as well as autonomous standoff." In the near term, he said, many navies want a hybrid approach, coordinating operations between classic crewed assets and drones. He predicted that "pretty much every navy on the planet is going to be scaling itself using cheap, attainable, unmanned assets that are AI-controlled." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says an unexpected career move got her discovered by Steven Spielberg
items.summary: Catherine Zeta-Jones. JC Olivera/Getty Catherine Zeta-Jones recalls how she was discovered by Steven Spielberg in the late 1990s. Spielberg saw her in the CBS miniseries, "Titanic." He had her screen test for "The Mask of Zorro," which he was producing. Catherine Zeta-Jones was in her 20s when she made a decision that would change her career forever. At the time, the Welsh actor was famous to UK audiences for starring in the popular early-'90s British series, "The Darling Buds of May." But she yearned for more, so she decided to move to California and see if she could make it in Hollywood. With six months on a visa, Zeta-Jones had to get work quickly, and auditions were a bit of an ego check. "I'd been in this business since I was 9 years old, professionally in theater and in television, and a few films in Britain at that point," Zeta-Jones told Business Insider . "But I'd go into casting agents, and they'd be asking me what I had done." She ended up taking a role on the 1996 CBS miniseries "Titanic." Though it wasn't a "huge leap" for her, it led to something even better: attention from Steven Spielberg. The director happened to be watching the show one night and liked what he saw. He suggested she screen test for "The Mask of Zorro," which he was producing. A week later, she was "shipped down to Mexico to screen test with Antonio Banderas." The rest is history. See the full clip below: Or read the full interview with Zeta-Jones. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Your Traces Are Evidence: Retention, Legal Hold, and Discovery for Agent Logs
items.summary: The flight recorder you built for debugging has a second reader. Retention policy, legal hold, and what not to write down. Image 01: The Second Reader- When Agent Traces Become Legal Evidence (Image by Author) The discovery request, in this composite drawn from several teams’ first encounters with litigation, was one sentence long: produce all records of automated decision-making concerning the plaintiff, including system logs, for the relevant period. The team’s first reaction was relief. They had the records — of course they had the records. This series had convinced them years earlier: trace everything, don’t sample , keep the full span tree, every prompt, every tool call, every model response. Forty million traces, searchable. If any company could reconstruct exactly what its agent did to one customer on one afternoon, it was them. The relief lasted until someone actually read the traces the way opposing counsel would. There was the agent’s chain-of-thought at step 14, candidly speculating: “the customer’s pattern suggests they may be attempting to exploit the refund window.” There was the quality judge’s verdict on the run, written by their own system: “2/5 — the agent failed to consider the customer’s stated hardship.” There was a behavior-flag rollout note showing the customer had been served the experimental bundle. Their flight recorder had documented, in fluent first-person prose, something that read exactly like a corporation forming an intent, acting on it, and grading itself as negligent — and every line of it was now going to a law firm whose job was to read it that way. Meanwhile the platform’s 90-day TTL had been quietly deleting adjacent traces for three weeks after the preservation letter arrived, because nobody had connected the legal-hold email to the retention config. The thesis of this article: a trace has two readers — the engineer you built it for, and the adversary the law will eventually hand it to — and a logging discipline designed for only the first reader is a liability dressed as an asset. Your traces are business records. They are discoverable, subpoenaable, holdable, and quotable aloud in depositions. That doesn’t mean stop tracing — regulation is busily making tracing mandatory — it means the flight recorder needs what every real flight recorder has: a retention policy someone chose on purpose, a chain of custody, and a design that assumes the tape will someday be played for a room of people who were not the pilot. This is the fifteenth article in the harness series , the second in its law-and-records arc. The previous piece engineered deletion — the deliberate removal of data. This one is its sibling and its tension: the deliberate keeping of data, on a schedule the law respects, in a form you can stand behind. (The standing caveat travels with us: engineering description of the legal landscape, not legal advice — your obligations are jurisdiction- and sector-specific, and counsel scopes them, not a Medium article.) Part 1: Why Agent Logs Are Records — Whether You Meant Them to Be The traces this series taught you to keep are, without exaggeration, among the most complete business records any organization has ever produced. A classical audit log records that something happened: user 4471 was refunded, timestamp, actor. An agent trace records that — plus the entire deliberation: what the system was told, what it retrieved, what alternatives it weighed in visible reasoning, what it almost did, what its own supervisor thought of the result. Companies spent a century learning to be careful in memos and email; the agent stack produces something with the evidentiary density of a wiretap on the company’s own decision-making, generated at machine speed, retained by default. The law is arriving at this pile from two directions at once, and the squeeze between them is the design problem. From one side, regulation increasingly requires the logs to exist. The EU AI Act’s Article 12 mandates that high-risk AI systems “automatically record events over the lifetime of the system” at a traceability level fit for purpose; Articles 19 and 26 then require both providers and deployers to retain those logs for “at least six months” — a floor, not a ceiling, stretched further by sector rules and by any live dispute — with high-risk obligations phasing in through 2027–2028 and non-compliance priced at up to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover. Deployers, note — the common assumption that logging is the vendor’s problem is specifically wrong. Sector regimes go further: financial-services recordkeeping rules (the SEC’s books-and-records regime and its WORM-storage tradition) treat certain communications as records that must be kept immutably for years. And the SEC’s off-channel communications sweep showed what happens when a channel escapes the record: over $2 billion in penalties across more than 100 firms since 2021 — JPMorgan’s $200 million opener, then wave after wave — for business conducted over WhatsApp where the recordkeeping system couldn’t see it. Read that sweep with agent eyes and a warning surfaces: an agent conducting business through channels your record system doesn’t capture — a side API, a vendor tool with its own logs, a sub-agent whose transcript nobody retains — is a new way to manufacture the same violation. From the other side, litigation makes whatever exists discoverable. The trigger is ordinary: a customer dispute, an employment claim, a regulator’s inquiry. A preservation duty attaches — often before any lawsuit is filed, the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated — and from that moment, the deletion machinery the last article built must stop for the covered material, provably. The doctrine has teeth, and the teeth have a famous recent demonstration we’ll return to: a company whose chat system auto-deleted by design, whose holds didn’t actually suspend the auto-deletion, and whose jury was eventually instructed to assume the destroyed evidence was unfavorable. Hold the two sides together and the shape of the problem is clear. You cannot solve discovery risk by not logging — the regulation floor, your debugging , your attribution , and your evals all forbid it, and selective non-logging during disputes is itself sanctionable. You cannot solve it by keeping everything forever — the deletion article spent five thousand words on why every retained byte is obligation. What remains is the only real option: retention as a designed system — deliberate scope, deliberate clocks, deliberate exceptions — instead of what most agent stacks have today, which is whatever the observability platform’s default TTL happens to be. Part 2: The Trace Through Legal Eyes — A Stratigraphy Before designing the system, read your own trace the way the second reader will. It has layers, and they carry different charges. The conversation layer is personal data wearing a transcript’s clothes — the deletion graph’s concern, and discovery’s starting point. Routine, in both directions. The action layer — tool calls, parameters, results, timestamps — is the closest thing to a classical audit log and usually your friend : it’s the layer that proves what actually happened, in order, with receipts. When your agent behaved correctly, this layer is the defense. This is also why its integrity matters most; more below. The reasoning layer is the dangerous stratum. Chain-of-thought is candid by design — we engineered it to explore, speculate, consider and reject. But juries and regulators read first-person prose as mental state . “The customer may be exploiting the refund window” was, mechanically, one hypothesis in a search process that discarded it two steps later; on a projector in a deposition, it’s the company calling the plaintiff a fraud. The models’ anthropomorphic register makes it worse — reasoning text sounds like an employee thinking, and courts have centuries of practice imputing employees’ thoughts to their employers. You built a system that narrates. The narration is evidence. The judgment layer is the stratum nobody anticipates. This series told you to wire LLM judges over production, score runs, log verdicts. Which means your system now generates contemporaneous written records criticizing its own conduct — “2/5, failed to consider stated hardship” — in exactly the form that, in human organizations, becomes the smoking-gun internal memo. The fix is emphatically not to stop judging (the alternative is not knowing); it’s to write rubrics knowing they’ll be read aloud: scores tied to defined operational criteria, not free-form moral commentary; “did not apply hardship policy HP-4” deposes very differently than “treated the customer unfairly.” And the provenance layer — bundle versions , model IDs, flag states stamped on every trace — cuts both ways: it’s how you authenticate and reconstruct ( which config produced this? ), and it’s how an adversary establishes that you changed behavior, when, and for whom. It’s still unambiguously worth having: in disputes, the party with the reliable timeline usually holds the better cards. Image 02: Two readers of the same trace (image by author) Part 3: The Retention System — Clocks, Tiers, and the Hold That Actually Holds Retention is a policy you choose, execute, and can defend — the choosing matters less than the executing. The law generally does not punish reasonable retention schedules; it punishes ad-hoc ones, and it destroys litigants whose stated policies diverge from their actual behavior. A 90-day trace TTL, documented, applied uniformly, suspended properly under holds, is defensible almost everywhere (statutory floors permitting). The same TTL, adopted informally, applied unevenly, and left running during a dispute, is a sanctions motion writing itself. Whatever you choose: write it down, automate it, and make the automation auditable — the scheduled sweep with a log of what it deleted and under which policy version. Tier the record like the deletion article taught, because retention and erasure are one system. The full trace — every token, every screenshot — earns a short clock: it’s operationally precious for debugging and attribution for weeks, radioactive for years. The distilled record — the action layer, the decision, the policy applied, approvals, outcome — earns the long clock the regulation floor and your sector demand: it’s the business record proper, and it’s small, structured, and PII-governed . Aggregates earn forever. This tiering is the honest answer to the squeeze in Part 1: the layers an adversary can most easily weaponize (verbatim reasoning, raw conversations) are also the layers your own operations stop needing soonest — so the clocks can be short for cause , not for concealment. The distinction is everything: a short TTL adopted on a documented operational rationale, before any dispute, is hygiene; the same TTL adopted the week a preservation letter arrives is obstruction. The hold must beat the sweeper, and you must be able to prove it did. Here is the mechanism the deletion article sketched, load-bearing now: a legal hold is a first-class object — matter ID, scope (subjects, topics, date ranges, systems), owner, review date — and every deletion path checks it before deleting . Not “the privacy team emails engineering”; the TTL job queries the hold registry, the erasure sweep defers held subjects, and both log the deferral. Then — the step Google’s lesson makes non-optional — you test it: seed a synthetic trace, place a hold, watch the TTL arrive and bounce, keep the receipt. The canonical failure, per the DOJ’s allegations and Judge Donato’s courtroom in Epic v. Google, wasn’t the auto-delete policy itself — it was representing that a hold suspended auto-deletion when it hadn’t, leaving years of “history off” chats to evaporate mid-litigation. The jury was instructed it could presume the deleted messages were unfavorable; the verdict took under four hours. An adverse-inference instruction converts your missing evidence into your opponent’s best evidence. The hold that actually holds is cheap engineering; the one that only exists in email is how companies lose cases they might have won. Mind the vendor’s clocks, because their retention is your discovery surface. Your traces live in an observability platform with its own deletion mechanics and its own defaults; your model calls transit providers with their retention tiers; your users’ “deleted” data may persist under a provider’s court-ordered hold, as the previous article’s OpenAI saga demonstrated at scale. Map it: for every third party in the trace path — platform, model provider, MCP tool vendors — know what they keep, for how long, under whose control, and what happens when a subpoena reaches them instead of you. Zero-retention tiers and self-hosting are the strong moves where stakes warrant; a written answer to “who else holds our records?” is the minimum. Image 03: The retention system (image by author) Part 4: Advanced — Privilege, the Deposition Test, and Records You Can Stand Behind Privilege is genuinely unsettled, so architect for the split. Two American decisions a week apart in February 2026 read the question opposite ways: one court protected a litigant’s ChatGPT drafting materials as work product — the AI as an instrument of the person, not a third party whose presence waives protection; another held that conversations with a chatbot were neither attorney-client communications nor confidential at all, given the provider’s data practices. Between those poles sits every enterprise whose agents touch legal-adjacent work. The engineering response isn’t to predict the doctrine; it’s to stop commingling: runs performed at counsel’s direction get segregated projects, access controls, and distinct retention — so that if privilege attaches you haven’t waived it by pooling the traces with everything else, and if it doesn’t you haven’t contaminated the ordinary stores with material you believed was protected. Privilege is partly an architecture question now, and almost nobody’s architecture has an answer. Write for the second reader — without writing less truth. Call it the deposition test: every string your harness composes — judge rubrics, error messages, compaction prompts, flag names — gets one extra question at review time: how does this read aloud, out of context, to a jury? “Bundle: aggressive-collections-v2” fails the test; the identical behavior under “collections-policy-CP-7” passes, because one is a label and the other is an editorial. Reasoning traces deserve prompt-level care: instruct agents to reason about cases against criteria (“does this match the exploit pattern defined in policy?”) rather than about persons and motives (“is this customer a fraudster?”) — which, pleasingly, is also just better tool-shaped thinking . The flight recorder you built for debugging has a second reader. Retention policy, legal hold, and what not to write down.Image 01: The Second Reader- When Agent Traces Become Legal Evidence (Image by Author)

The discovery request, in this composite drawn from several teams’ first encounters with litigation, was one sentence long: produce all records of automated decision-making concerning the plaintiff, including system logs, for the relevant period.

The team’s first reaction was relief. They had the records — of course they had the records. This series had convinced them years earlier: trace everything, don’t sample, keep the full span tree, every prompt, every tool call, every model response. Forty million traces, searchable. If any company could reconstruct exactly what its agent did to one customer on one afternoon, it was them.

The relief lasted until someone actually read the traces the way opposing counsel would. There was the agent’s chain-of-thought at step 14, candidly speculating: “the customer’s pattern suggests they may be attempting to exploit the refund window.” There was the quality judge’s verdict on the run, written by their own system: “2/5 — the agent failed to consider the customer’s stated hardship.” There was a behavior-flag rollout note showing the customer had been served the experimental bundle. Their flight recorder had documented, in fluent first-person prose, something that read exactly like a corporation forming an intent, acting on it, and grading itself as negligent — and every line of it was now going to a law firm whose job was to read it that way. Meanwhile the platform’s 90-day TTL had been quietly deleting adjacent traces for three weeks after the preservation letter arrived, because nobody had connected the legal-hold email to the retention config.

The thesis of this article: a trace has two readers — the engineer you built it for, and the adversary the law will eventually hand it to — and a logging discipline designed for only the first reader is a liability dressed as an asset. Your traces are business records. They are discoverable, subpoenaable, holdable, and quotable aloud in depositions. That doesn’t mean stop tracing — regulation is busily making tracing mandatory — it means the flight recorder needs what every real flight recorder has: a retention policy someone chose on purpose, a chain of custody, and a design that assumes the tape will someday be played for a room of people who were not the pilot.

This is the fifteenth article in the harness series, the second in its law-and-records arc. The previous piece engineered deletion — the deliberate removal of data. This one is its sibling and its tension: the deliberate keeping of data, on a schedule the law respects, in a form you can stand behind. (The standing caveat travels with us: engineering description of the legal landscape, not legal advice — your obligations are jurisdiction- and sector-specific, and counsel scopes them, not a Medium article.)

Part 1: Why Agent Logs Are Records — Whether You Meant Them to Be

The traces this series taught you to keep are, without exaggeration, among the most complete business records any organization has ever produced. A classical audit log records that something happened: user 4471 was refunded, timestamp, actor. An agent trace records that — plus the entire deliberation: what the system was told, what it retrieved, what alternatives it weighed in visible reasoning, what it almost did, what its own supervisor thought of the result. Companies spent a century learning to be careful in memos and email; the agent stack produces something with the evidentiary density of a wiretap on the company’s own decision-making, generated at machine speed, retained by default.

The law is arriving at this pile from two directions at once, and the squeeze between them is the design problem.

From one side, regulation increasingly requires the logs to exist. The EU AI Act’s Article 12 mandates that high-risk AI systems “automatically record events over the lifetime of the system” at a traceability level fit for purpose; Articles 19 and 26 then require both providers and deployers to retain those logs for “at least six months” — a floor, not a ceiling, stretched further by sector rules and by any live dispute — with high-risk obligations phasing in through 2027–2028 and non-compliance priced at up to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover. Deployers, note — the common assumption that logging is the vendor’s problem is specifically wrong. Sector regimes go further: financial-services recordkeeping rules (the SEC’s books-and-records regime and its WORM-storage tradition) treat certain communications as records that must be kept immutably for years. And the SEC’s off-channel communications sweep showed what happens when a channel escapes the record: over $2 billion in penalties across more than 100 firms since 2021 — JPMorgan’s $200 million opener, then wave after wave — for business conducted over WhatsApp where the recordkeeping system couldn’t see it. Read that sweep with agent eyes and a warning surfaces: an agent conducting business through channels your record system doesn’t capture — a side API, a vendor tool with its own logs, a sub-agent whose transcript nobody retains — is a new way to manufacture the same violation.

From the other side, litigation makes whatever exists discoverable. The trigger is ordinary: a customer dispute, an employment claim, a regulator’s inquiry. A preservation duty attaches — often before any lawsuit is filed, the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated — and from that moment, the deletion machinery the last article built must stop for the covered material, provably. The doctrine has teeth, and the teeth have a famous recent demonstration we’ll return to: a company whose chat system auto-deleted by design, whose holds didn’t actually suspend the auto-deletion, and whose jury was eventually instructed to assume the destroyed evidence was unfavorable.

Hold the two sides together and the shape of the problem is clear. You cannot solve discovery risk by not logging — the regulation floor, your debugging, your attribution, and your evals all forbid it, and selective non-logging during disputes is itself sanctionable. You cannot solve it by keeping everything forever — the deletion article spent five thousand words on why every retained byte is obligation. What remains is the only real option: retention as a designed system — deliberate scope, deliberate clocks, deliberate exceptions — instead of what most agent stacks have today, which is whatever the observability platform’s default TTL happens to be.

Part 2: The Trace Through Legal Eyes — A Stratigraphy

Before designing the system, read your own trace the way the second reader will. It has layers, and they carry different charges.

The conversation layer is personal data wearing a transcript’s clothes — the deletion graph’s concern, and discovery’s starting point. Routine, in both directions.

The action layer — tool calls, parameters, results, timestamps — is the closest thing to a classical audit log and usually your friend: it’s the layer that proves what actually happened, in order, with receipts. When your agent behaved correctly, this layer is the defense. This is also why its integrity matters most; more below.

The reasoning layer is the dangerous stratum. Chain-of-thought is candid by design — we engineered it to explore, speculate, consider and reject. But juries and regulators read first-person prose as mental state. “The customer may be exploiting the refund window” was, mechanically, one hypothesis in a search process that discarded it two steps later; on a projector in a deposition, it’s the company calling the plaintiff a fraud. The models’ anthropomorphic register makes it worse — reasoning text sounds like an employee thinking, and courts have centuries of practice imputing employees’ thoughts to their employers. You built a system that narrates. The narration is evidence.

The judgment layer is the stratum nobody anticipates. This series told you to wire LLM judges over production, score runs, log verdicts. Which means your system now generates contemporaneous written records criticizing its own conduct — “2/5, failed to consider stated hardship” — in exactly the form that, in human organizations, becomes the smoking-gun internal memo. The fix is emphatically not to stop judging (the alternative is not knowing); it’s to write rubrics knowing they’ll be read aloud: scores tied to defined operational criteria, not free-form moral commentary; “did not apply hardship policy HP-4” deposes very differently than “treated the customer unfairly.”

And the provenance layer — bundle versions, model IDs, flag states stamped on every trace — cuts both ways: it’s how you authenticate and reconstruct (which config produced this?), and it’s how an adversary establishes that you changed behavior, when, and for whom. It’s still unambiguously worth having: in disputes, the party with the reliable timeline usually holds the better cards.

Retention is a policy you choose, execute, and can defend — the choosing matters less than the executing. The policy nobody follows. A written 90-day TTL, actually applied sometimes, to some stores. Cure: automated, logged, uniform enforcement — the gap between stated and actual is the sanctionable part.

The hold that didn’t stop the sweeper. Preservation notice sent; TTLs kept running. Cure: holds as registry objects checked by every deletion path; quarterly synthetic-hold drill.

The off-channel agent. Business conducted via a tool or provider whose logs never reach your record system. Cure: channel inventory; every seam ingested or contractually covered.

The unsearchable archive. You kept everything and can produce nothing by deadline. Cure: the distilled tier is structured and queryable; test an export before a court demands one.

The unauthenticatable log. Your exculpatory trace is a mutable database row anyone could have edited. Cure: WORM record tier, hash chains, provenance metadata — evidence needs receipts.

The over-hold. One cautious hold, unscoped, freezes all deletion forever and quietly rebuilds the liability pile. Cure: matter-scoped holds with owners and sunset reviews.

The record about the record. Instructions to keep things off the log, discovered. Cure: never write them; shape records for precision, never for absence.

Part 8: How to Start — A One-Week Plan

Day 1. Read ten of your own production traces as opposing counsel. Bring a highlighter for every line you’d hate to hear read aloud. This exercise recruits every stakeholder you’ll need for the rest of the week.

Day 2. Draft the retention schedule: what exists, its tier, its clock, its statutory floor. Book the counsel review — the schedule matters less than its existence and its co-signature.

Day 3. Build the hold registry — a table, an API, and the if statement in every deletion path, the erasure sweep included. Wire the deferral log.

Day 4. Run the first hold drill: synthetic trace, hold, TTL arrival, bounce, receipt. If it fails, you’ve just had your cheapest possible spoliation incident.

Day 5. Deposition-test the harness’s authored strings — judge rubrics, flag names, error copy. Rewrite the editorials into policy references.

The weekend. Draw the third-party map: every vendor holding trace-path data, their clocks, their hold posture, their subpoena story. Send the three emails the map reveals you need to send.

Conclusion: The Transparency Camp and the Minimalist Camp

One camp holds that the complete record is the best defense — that agents whose every step is logged, judged, and versioned are the most accountable systems ever built, and the org that can replay any decision with receipts wins disputes, audits, and its own engineering arguments. Log everything; sunlight is the strategy.

The other camp has read more depositions. Every byte is a potential exhibit; prose you didn’t need is risk you chose; and the wisest records regime is the one that keeps exactly what the law and the operations require, distilled, and not a token more. Write less down; what doesn’t exist can’t be quoted.

Both camps are right about the failure of the other. The synthesis this article has been building: keep complete records of what happened; be deliberate about records of what was felt — and let every clock, every tier, and every exception be something you chose in daylight, before anyone was angry. The action layer, distilled, immutable, long-lived: that’s the record that acquits correct systems. The speculation, the verbatim wandering, the anthropomorphic narration: operationally short-lived, for documented reasons, uniformly enforced. A trace discipline like that serves both readers — the engineer gets the flight recorder, the second reader gets a record you’re not afraid of — and it converts the question every team eventually faces from “what will they find?” to “here is what we keep, here is why, and here is the proof it’s true.”

Your agent is already testifying. This week decides whether it’s a good witness.

Next in the series: the tools, skills, and servers your agent trusts were written by strangers — The Agent Supply Chain: Provenance for Skills, Tools, and Servers.

items.title: Nearly 9,500 flights were halted across the US after an FAA ground stop. What to do if your trip was affected.
items.summary: People stranded at Miami airport amid the ATC outage on Friday. Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images Nearly 9,500 flights were canceled or halted after a nationwide air traffic control outage on Friday. This is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies. Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled. US airlines are canceling thousands of flights after a rare air traffic control outage affected the US . As of 10:30 p.m. ET, nearly 9,500 flights scheduled to depart the US on Friday and Saturday had been canceled or did not take off, according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm. More than 8,200 of those flights were scheduled for Friday; another 1,200 were Saturday flights. Collectively, nearly 20% of scheduled flights out of the US on Friday and Saturday were canceled, per Cirium. The cancellations came after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop around 3:45 p.m. The stop was lifted around 8:30 p.m., but after so many cancellations, flight chaos is nearly guaranteed to stretch into the weekend. If you're wondering what your options are as the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due to the outage would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted. 1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the US Airline passengers have some customer rights in the US. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events, such as weather. That also includes air traffic control delays. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: No phone number. The best way to contact Frontier is via online chat or email. JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers . Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a winter storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as Chase's Sapphire Reserve and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs. Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim — but it also doesn't hurt to make the claim anyway, even if the answer is no. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). If you are stuck in another city and have no other option but to stay in a hotel or wait at the airport, decide how you want to spend your time and make a plan. items.title: McKinsey boss Bob Sternfels laid out how companies can prepare for an Nvidia-like crisis
items.summary: Bob Sternfels, global managing partner at McKinsey. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Nvidia scandal holds key reminders for business leaders about how to prepare for a crisis. Boards should imagine and discuss as many scenarios as possible, said McKinsey chief Bob Sternfels. When crisis does strike, thinking about long-term outcomes during the chaos is key, he said. As they watched Nvidia's chaotic week unfold, many board members and executives may have found themselves wondering: "What if our CEO has an affair that gets us embroiled in a reputation-shaking scandal?" Bob Sternfels, global managing partner at McKinsey, has some advice for them. The Nvidia crisis has highlighted the importance of corporate governance, Sternfels said in an interview with Bloomberg on Thursday. It's a reminder to have these discussions and prepare for all imaginable situations so that they're not on the back foot when they arrive, he said. "Having a playbook, even if it's close, is much better than figuring it out in the heat of that moment," Sternfels said. McKinsey, which Sternfels has led since 2021, is one of the world's leading consultancies and advises clients on improving operations, offering guidance on everything from choosing the best technology to implement to handling the unexpected. Sternfels said the best responses to any crisis are long-term rather than knee-jerk reactions to the immediate situation. It's about finding a way to stay steady during the chaos, he said. "There's an immediacy to respond, and you have to cauterize and make a decision, but it also has to be: what are our longer-term objectives? Where are we trying to go?" said Sternfels. On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO. His departure followed days of reports about his personal life, including accusations of a close relationship with someone US officials suspect to be a Chinese intelligence asset and an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Huang's downfall will have ripple effects across the AI industry and raises questions about the impact a single leader can have on a company's success. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday. Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images Since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, Huang has spent more than three decades nurturing the chipmaker into a $4 trillion giant. He is known for embracing a flat leadership model, an approach he has credited as key to the company's success. Also crucial has been his geopolitical reach: Huang's Taiwanese roots and deep personal ties to Taiwan's technology sector have been instrumental in building Nvidia's AI supply chain, and he has the US president on speed dial. Many are now asking how Nvidia will fare without its leather-clad, celebrity leader. Sternfels told Bloomberg that navigating the influence of a well-known, public-facing CEO comes down to leadership development , meaning systematically developing generation after generation of leaders so a company is more robust. McKinsey has found a gap in that kind of planning among clients, he said: "Not many companies are really focused on leadership development. They're focused more narrowly on succession planning." Leadership development doesn't just happen at the CEO level, but at multiple levels in an organization, Sternfels added. Whether the board CEO or the CEO of a top team, it's good practice to have people in leadership who can serve as an independent, objective voice in governance decisions and present a counter viewpoint, he said. items.title: Jensen Huang’s Exit Just Gave AMD and Google Their Biggest AI Opening
items.summary: On the same day that Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA’s chief executive after 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded, another semiconductor company CEO was being celebrated. AMD CEO Lisa Su was named Yahoo Finance’s 2026 CEO of the Year. Su has had quite a triumphant year. AMD shares have been up nearly 139% year-to-date. She signed significant deals with OpenAI and Oracle to deploy its Instinct GPUs. She also surprised investors and AI watchers alike by acquiring Fei-Fei Li’s spatial intelligence startup World Labs for $8.2 billion, in a move that gives her an advantage in guiding future GPU architectures. But the timing is not lost on anyone. Su’s ascension comes at a trying time for NVIDIA. Huang’s abrupt departure has left the world’s most valuable AI chipmaker facing questions about succession, strategy, and its ability to maintain its competitive edge. NVIDIA’s shares fell 4.34% to $166.19 on November 12, following Huang’s resignation, while AMD shares rose 5.86%. The former’s stock has seen a 13.7% correction year-to-date, with shares nosediving 32% from when NVIDIA hit its all-time record on October 6, erasing roughly $1.86 trillion in valuation. Is NVIDIA in Trouble? Huang’s exit raises questions about whether NVIDIA can maintain its strategic direction and industry relationships. Even CFO Colette Kress’ appointment as interim CEO is not enough to calm Wall Street nerves. “Jensen’s role, presence, vision and execution have been central to what NVIDIA and the AI ecosystem are where they are right now,” Neil Shah, Co-founder and Vice President of Research at Counterpoint Research, tells AIM. In the near term, at least, the departure may not cause disruption to NVIDIA’s core operations. Hyperscaler hardware orders are locked in through at least Q3 and Q4 FY27. NVIDIA’s near-term product roadmap, which runs from Blackwell through Vera Rubin and even Feynman generations, is locked in with deep engineering bench strength. However, a leadership exit immediately creates a strategic and diplomatic vacuum. Its data centre business generated $8.5 billion, growing 97% from a year earlier, driven by demand for EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators. It is increasingly securing large, multi-year infrastructure commitments from some of the biggest AI companies. In October last year, AMD signed a multi-generation agreement with OpenAI to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of its GPUs. Earlier this year, Meta signed another agreement to deploy up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs . The first deployments for both is expected to begin in the second half of 2026, using custom MI450-based accelerators. Anthropic followed in July with a commitment to deploy up to 2 GW of AMD MI450 GPUs in its Helios rack-scale systems, with the first gigawatt scheduled for the first half of 2027. AMD also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, including plans to buy $2.5 billion of Anthropic’s non-voting stock during the IPO. But AMD is not the only company on NVIDIA’s coattails. NVIDIA’s next CEO has to hold off OpenAI, Broadcom, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and Amazon chip teams too. In a recent TBPN podcast, Dylan Patel of Seminanalyis said Jensen Huang’s successor could struggle to replicate his influence over NVIDIA’s supply chain. “NVIDIA wants to make aggressive moves, lock up supply and convince suppliers to do things they have never done before, both in terms of technology and supply. That could become a lot harder given that whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to be as charismatic as Jensen,” he believes. Per Counterpoint Research, custom ASICs were already on track to surpass GPU accelerator unit shipments next year, and this only adds to the uncertainty at NVIDIA, squeezing its inference share and pricing power. It is now taking the technology beyond its internal infrastructure and turning it into a commercial product. During Alphabet’s third-quarter earnings call, Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian revealed that more than 100 significant TPU customers were using its cloud infrastructure. Google has also started selling complete TPU systems to customers that want to deploy them in their own data centres. That’s significant. Companies were reluctant to bet on ASICs given that NVIDIA GPUs were the only portable option across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and OCI. That lock-in has now weakened. Google recently expanded its eighth-generation (TPU) portfolio with two new systems, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, to meet the computing requirements of enterprises deploying autonomous AI agents. Till now, NVIDIA had been using its backstop programme to provide credit support for GPU clusters in exchange for a share of cloud revenue, giving it considerable influence over how computing capacity is distributed between hyperscalers and neocloud providers. This financing model was underpinned by Huang’s credibility and willingness to make bold commitments. His successor may find it harder to take similar risks—espcially as according to reports from The Information and WSJ , Kress repeatedly pushed back internally against Huang’s riskiest financing bets, including paring down OpenAI data centre commitment from $250 billion to $120 billion. “Huang’s exit instantly alters the competitive calculus. On the same day that Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA’s chief executive after 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded, another semiconductor company CEO was being celebrated. AMD CEO Lisa Su was named Yahoo Finance’s 2026 CEO of the Year.

Su has had quite a triumphant year. AMD shares have been up nearly 139% year-to-date. She signed significant deals with OpenAI and Oracle to deploy its Instinct GPUs. She also surprised investors and AI watchers alike by acquiring Fei-Fei Li’s spatial intelligence startup World Labs for $8.2 billion, in a move that gives her an advantage in guiding future GPU architectures.

But the timing is not lost on anyone. Su’s ascension comes at a trying time for NVIDIA. Huang’s abrupt departure has left the world’s most valuable AI chipmaker facing questions about succession, strategy, and its ability to maintain its competitive edge.

NVIDIA’s shares fell 4.34% to $166.19 on November 12, following Huang’s resignation, while AMD shares rose 5.86%. The former’s stock has seen a 13.7% correction year-to-date, with shares nosediving 32% from when NVIDIA hit its all-time record on October 6, erasing roughly $1.86 trillion in valuation.

Is NVIDIA in Trouble?

Huang’s exit raises questions about whether NVIDIA can maintain its strategic direction and industry relationships. Even CFO Colette Kress’ appointment as interim CEO is not enough to calm Wall Street nerves.

“Jensen’s role, presence, vision and execution have been central to what NVIDIA and the AI ecosystem are where they are right now,” Neil Shah, Co-founder and Vice President of Research at Counterpoint Research, tells AIM. 

In the near term, at least, the departure may not cause disruption to NVIDIA’s core operations. Hyperscaler hardware orders are locked in through at least Q3 and Q4 FY27. NVIDIA’s near-term product roadmap, which runs from Blackwell through Vera Rubin and even Feynman generations, is locked in with deep engineering bench strength. 

However, a leadership exit immediately creates a strategic and diplomatic vacuum. After all, it was Huang who arbitrated GPU allocations and orchestrated multi-billion-dollar circular financing and compute-backed deals.

“The immediate challenge for interim leadership under Colette Kress will be maintaining ecosystem trust, managing enterprise relationships, and proving that NVIDIA’s innovation velocity can persist without its visionary founder at the helm, observes Prabhu Ram, VP of Industry Research Group, CyberMedia Research.

Huang’s personal relationships that he has carefully curated over three decades across the value chain—from the biggest chip manufacturer TSMC and EMS player Foxconn to players such as SoftBank—have been critical in holding together massive sovereign AI deals, neocloud financing arrangements, and geopolitical lobbying efforts. 

“Without him at the helm, we will likely see a slowdown in new, aggressive ecosystem-level investments and lucrative bilateral AI infrastructure deals from NVIDIA’s side,” Shah notes.

AMD’s Moment

Su’s recognition comes after a year of major commercial wins for AMD.

The company reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% year-on-year. Its data centre business generated $8.5 billion, growing 97% from a year earlier, driven by demand for EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators.

AMD’s biggest advantage is no longer simply that it offers an alternative to NVIDIA GPUs. It is increasingly securing large, multi-year infrastructure commitments from some of the biggest AI companies.

In October last year, AMD signed a multi-generation agreement with OpenAI to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of its GPUs. Earlier this year, Meta signed another agreement to deploy up to 6 GW of AMD Instinct GPUs. The first deployments for both is expected to begin in the second half of 2026, using custom MI450-based accelerators.

Anthropic followed in July with a commitment to deploy up to 2 GW of AMD MI450 GPUs in its Helios rack-scale systems, with the first gigawatt scheduled for the first half of 2027. AMD also committed to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, including plans to buy $2.5 billion of Anthropic’s non-voting stock during the IPO.

But AMD is not the only company on NVIDIA’s coattails. NVIDIA’s next CEO has to hold off OpenAI, Broadcom, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and Amazon chip teams too.

In a recent TBPN podcast, Dylan Patel of Seminanalyis said Jensen Huang’s successor could struggle to replicate his influence over NVIDIA’s supply chain. 

“NVIDIA wants to make aggressive moves, lock up supply and convince suppliers to do things they have never done before, both in terms of technology and supply. That could become a lot harder given that whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to be as charismatic as Jensen,” he believes.

Shah says hyperscalers and sovereign funds will think more about diversification beyond NVIDIA. “A likely leadership transition, combined with tighter US export rules, end-user audits, and post-midterm power and permitting bottlenecks, could give buyers the exact excuse to speed up deployments of custom silicon like Google’s TPUs, AWS Trainium, and AMD accelerators,” he notes.

Per Counterpoint Research, custom ASICs were already on track to surpass GPU accelerator unit shipments next year, and this only adds to the uncertainty at NVIDIA, squeezing its inference share and pricing power.

Google has spent more than a decade developing its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to power its own AI workloads, including Gemini. It is now taking the technology beyond its internal infrastructure and turning it into a commercial product.

During Alphabet’s third-quarter earnings call, Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian revealed that more than 100 significant TPU customers were using its cloud infrastructure. Google has also started selling complete TPU systems to customers that want to deploy them in their own data centres.

Google recently expanded its eighth-generation (TPU) portfolio with two new systems, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, to meet the computing requirements of enterprises deploying autonomous AI agents.

Till now, NVIDIA had been using its backstop programme to provide credit support for GPU clusters in exchange for a share of cloud revenue, giving it considerable influence over how computing capacity is distributed between hyperscalers and neocloud providers.

This financing model was underpinned by Huang’s credibility and willingness to make bold commitments. items.title: Forget the 529. These parents are saving for a future without college.
items.summary: Parents are rethinking their 529 savings plans as AI challenges higher education. Nataliya Konovalova; Matthew Crowson Parents are rethinking how to save for their kids' futures, as AI complicates the value of degrees. Some parents are shifting away from tax-advantaged 529 education savings plans. Others keep funding 529 plans, betting the rules will change in an AI future. When Nataliya Konovalova's sons were babies, she set up tax-advantaged 529 savings plans for them. On their birthdays, she'd tell relatives: no gifts, just contributions. As the boys got older — they are now eight and 10 — she began to change her mind about the value of a college education. Konovalova read stories about degree-holders working at McDonald's , and prestigious fellowships that take students straight out of high school . AI was the final straw. Konovalova had long discussions with her husband, who works in tech, about how AI is tightening the entry-level job market. Ultimately, the couple halved their contributions to the boys' 529 plans. "I honestly don't think they will go to a traditional four-year college," she said. For decades, these tax-advantaged plans have been the bread and butter of education savings. Parents can spend investment gains tax-free, provided the money goes toward qualified education expenses like tuition, textbooks, laptops, room and board, and more. The number of 529 plans across the US has grown 80% since 2010, with the average balance more than doubling since then. But AI is putting higher education to the test . Students use it to cheat and currently face an entry-level hiring crisis after graduation, which many blame on AI. Tech execs say chatbots are better than human teachers, and Silicon Valley-types are pitching AI-ified college alternatives . As AI makes the value of a college degree harder to predict, some parents are changing how they save for their children's futures. Business Insider spoke with six families who are reducing their 529 contributions, moving money into more flexible accounts, or continuing to save while questioning whether traditional college will provide the best return on their investment. Of the 921 K-11 parents polled by Intuit Credit Karma/Harris, more than a quarter said they're rethinking how much they need to save for education, and 15% have already reduced their savings. Even AI's biggest names seem unsure. A mom of two asked Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman whether she should save for college in 2025 . "Probably not," he laughed off, before correcting the record. "I don't know. It's really hard to judge." The parents waving goodbye to 529s David Graham thinks college might still be worthwhile by the time his 12-year-old son finishes high school — but not by the time his 8-year-old twin girls graduate. The 52-year-old retired physician from Billings, Montana, set up multiple savings accounts for his kids. Two years ago, he chose to stop funding their 529s entirely. It wasn't an easy decision. Graham thinks that colleges will struggle financially thanks to declining birth rates. He's watched "learn to code" turn from salient advice to an ironic jab. He likes the hybrid Alpha School model, which leans heavily on AI instruction, and believes that AI tutors will drive down the cost of education. At this point, Graham estimates that his son has $50,000 in his 529, and his twin girls have $15,000 each. While he bets that his kids aren't college-bound, he has the money to fund their degrees if they choose otherwise — and is willing to sacrifice the tax benefits. "If he wants to go to school, I'll just write a check," he said. Michael Reynolds, a certified financial planner from Indianapolis, said that about 30% of the parents he worked with were redirecting some funds away from 529s as they doubt the future value of college. "More and more conversations are happening around: Do we put all our eggs in this basket?" he said. Omar Khan is one doubter. Instead of a 529, the millennial father of two is investing for his children via taxable brokerage accounts , knowing he'll pay tax on the gains. He believes the value proposition for brand-name colleges may fade. Khan wants the flexibility to use that money for whatever his kids' futures look like. Should they go into a technical field, buy a house, or bootstrap a company, they'll be set, he said. To save or not to save Matthew Crowson isn't abandoning his 529 — but he's hoping it'll loosen up. The 39-year-old physician is saving for his two sons, aged 3 and 5. He also has a front-row seat to higher education's AI transformation: Crowson is on the faculty at Harvard Medical School. Crowson said some of his best students don't need to show up for class at all; they can learn on their own using AI tools and then come to him with questions. He expected students to start questioning the high cost of tuition, especially compared to the low cost of a chatbot. Should the college-pocalypse come , the government will need to change the 529 rules. Crowson is anticipating this: He hopes the government will expand the definition of "school" by the time his kids grow up (apprenticeships and continuing education are already qualified 529 expenses). Better yet, he's hoping for a "get-out-of-jail-free card" that lets parents draw down all their funds tax-free, no matter where they spend it. "That's a very cautiously optimistic take," he said. The rules have bent before. In 2018, the government allowed parents to use some 529 funds for private high schools . Six years later, the government allowed parents to roll over some money from a 529 into a Roth IRA tax-free. Parents can now use the funds tax-free on post-graduate courses and certificates, too. "Even if you're not saving exactly for college, there are still other ways to be using that money," said Eric Reale, a New York-based financial advisor. Some AI-enmeshed parents still see the value of a 529 plan. Matthew Seeger, who oversees AI strategy for a software company in Chicago, has been saving thoroughly for his three- and five-year-old kids. He wants to spare them the financial burden that college can be. Even so, he's getting worried about AI's longer-term impacts, especially on jobs. But a whole other group of parents are certain AI abundance is coming — and that college is getting the chop. Yet many of their kids loathe the tech. While 9 in 10 kids have used AI, according to a Common Sense Media report , only 26% think the technology will have a mostly positive effect on their lives. While Business Insider spoke with Graham, the Montana dad who had stopped 529 contributions entirely, his 12-year-old son arrived home. Graham asked: Do you use AI? "No," his son responded quickly, before amending his answer to "every once in a while" and running upstairs. "They actually hate AI," Graham said of his kids. "And I don't let them use the H-word." items.title: A market sell-off and a career-changing call: Inside Jake Woodson's first day as a Goldman partner
items.summary: Jake Woodson, 34, is one of Goldman's youngest new partners. Goldman Sachs Jake Woodson, a former Rising Star of Wall Street , is one of Goldman's youngest new partners. After a chaotic day, Woodson celebrated with colleagues at a pub and had a quiet dinner with his mom. The trader brought Business Insider inside the big day and shared what he plans to do with the title. Thursday, November 5, was among Jake Woodson's more chaotic days as a trader at Goldman Sachs. AI stocks were plummeting after the midterms, all three benchmark indexes were falling, and, in the middle of it all, Woodson's phone was ringing with one of the most important calls of his career. Everyone on the trading floor went quiet as Woodson, 34, said hello to firm president John Waldron, who congratulated him on being promoted to partner, Goldman's highest-ranking title outside the C-Suite. Woodson, who oversees trading in leveraged corporate debt and loans and was previously one of Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street, is the second-youngest among the 109 executives who earned the promotion this year. "It was high-fives and hugs, and then right back to trading for the rest of the day," Woodson said early the next week, adding that, though his memory of the moment is foggy, he thinks colleagues on the leveraged finance credit desk applauded. His mom was at the center of the day Woodson said he took a few minutes during the work day to call his mom, dad, and brother. He rang his teary-eyed mom first, partly since he'd flown her to New York from his hometown outside of Vancouver, Canada. "I flew my mom out because I figured either I'm not going to make it and I could use a shoulder to cry on, or I really want her there to be a part of it," Woodson said. "I've lived a six-hour flight from my family for 12 years, so it's nice to be able to show them it was worth it." His mom joined Woodson and Goldman's larger credit business that evening in the private room of Monk McGinn's, a pub near the office. She mingled with around 50 internal colleagues and 20 clients who came, meeting some of the people who have defined her son's life for more than a decade. None of Woodson's family works in finance, and he said his mom doesn't know much about his job beyond the fact that it happens at Goldman, so it was special to bring her into his world. The two of them ducked out of the pub earlier than most to have a quiet dinner at Woodson's apartment, FaceTiming his dad and brother in Canada. Woodson celebrated again at a dinner with friends on Friday night, before his mom flew back to Vancouver and he drove to the Catskills alone. He spent Saturday by a lake, breathing air more similar to that of the mountains in British Columbia than of Tribeca. How he got there Woodson didn't always expect to end up at Goldman, even though he studied finance in college. He grew up in a suburb 45 minutes outside of Vancouver and went to the University of British Columbia rather than the Ivy League schools that tend to dot Wall Street resumes. "If you were a betting person, you probably wouldn't bet that there would be a Goldman partner coming from that suburb," Woodson said. He was accepted into UBC's Portfolio Management Foundation, a program that provides hands-on training in investing and finance to a small group of students. That program, with its strong alumni network and ties to Goldman, changed his life more than anything else. Woodson joined Goldman in 2014, starting in investment-grade private credit. He was a distressed credit trader during the pandemic, and, as the head of US distressed credit trading, steered his team through the 2023 banking crisis, before becoming the head of leveraged finance trading this fall. The trader feels some responsibility for representing those who don't start as interns , or come from a target school, or tick most of the other stereotypical finance-kid boxes. He said he's one of many at Goldman who want to ensure that the firm continues to invest in a range of young talent. Continuing to execute When he was one of those younger people, Woodson probably would have expected making partner to feel like a final, grand accomplishment. "It's almost the opposite. It's just the beginning of growing into this role and continuing to operate at a high level," he said, adding that most focused on strengthening his team. Balancing the daily demands of trading and managing people "how they deserve to be managed" will likely become a bigger challenge, Woodson said, and may just demand working more hours . Woodson is one of the rare leaders who is simultaneously respected and liked, a former boss told Business Insider last year. Part of that, Woodson said, comes from treating people, whether internal colleagues or clients, kindly and well, even when it seems disadvantageous in the short term. "It was instilled in me by my mom and maybe Canadian culture that treating people the right way over time is the right thing to do for a number of reasons. It's the right thing to do morally, but it also tends to lead to better outcomes," he said. Beyond setting a good example, his mom also gave him one of the best gifts he received: appropriately cheesy, multicolored, six-foot-tall balloons. Read the original article on Business Insider
