items.summary_html:
AI can reduce the work involved in acquiring customers, although the value of each growth tactic depends on which customer problem it addresses and whether the resulting activity produces worthwhile additional business.

Ten ways to acquire, convert and retain customers, ranked for a small team’s first experiment, with separate assessments of AI contribution, creative freedom, execution effort and commercial evidence.

A visitor reaches a software company’s pricing page, spends several minutes trying to establish whether the product supports an important integration, and eventually leaves because the answer is buried in documentation. The marketing team could spend another thousand dollars attracting similar visitors, although a more useful experiment might be to answer that particular question before the next potential customer disappears.

This is the kind of distinction I want to make when evaluating AI marketing tools. Generating more content, finding more prospects and operating more campaigns are valuable capabilities when they remove a real obstacle, but additional activity is a poor substitute for understanding why an interested person does not become a suitable customer.

The timing is interesting because AI is expanding beyond generating marketing material into handling customer conversations and operating commercial systems. On November 11, Tano announced a $4 million seed round for its creator-campaign business, which combines AI agents with human strategists. Meanwhile, Digging Beagle has examined both hidden commercial objectives inside simulated shopping assistants and newly available write operations in Google’s advertising integration.

Those developments cover different parts of the same relationship: attracting attention, influencing decisions and changing the systems that spend money on reaching customers.

The question for Fryday #13 is therefore fairly practical: which AI-backed growth mechanism deserves a limited budget, and what evidence would justify spending more?

How the ranking works

I ranked ten mechanisms for a small team that already has a working product and some means of observing customer behavior. These are editorial priorities for choosing a first pilot, rather than a comparison of ten vendors tested under identical conditions.

Each entry has six four-square assessments, separated into two groups.

TECH / BUILD covers how much substantive work AI performs, how much room exists for original creative execution, and how difficult the mechanism is to deploy and maintain.

APPLICATION / MARKET covers how readily the mechanism transfers between businesses, the strength of its published commercial evidence, and how well its use can be bounded and inspected.

Higher is better for AI backing, creative range, reuse, sales evidence and trust controls. Setup burden runs in the opposite direction: green indicates light effort, while orange or red indicates a more demanding implementation.

The bars are judgments about the mechanism in the stated context, not measured ROI, vendor security ratings or probabilities of success.

Randomly comparing eligible visitors with and without an AI adviser helps distinguish additional purchases from customers who would have bought anyway, while refunds, delivery costs and unsupported claims reveal whether the improvement remains commercially useful.#1. Product-grounded presale advice

Best first pilot when customers reach the product but cannot establish whether it suits them.

An assistant that can explain compatibility, delivery conditions, plan restrictions and alternatives has a narrower job than an agent instructed to maximize sales. It can help a customer understand the offer without deciding that every conversation should end in an upsell.

There is unusually useful evidence here. Randomized retail experiments conducted in 2023–2024 found a 16.3% sales increase for an AI presale chatbot against its tested baseline. A newer Javo study randomized visitors across 100 participating websites and reported 10.0% higher revenue per visitor relative to no agent in the direct-selling evaluation. That latter paper was written by the product’s founder, and its reported results have not been independently replicated.

The studies differ in design and environment, so their percentages cannot be combined into a general expected uplift. They do, however, make product advice a more defensible first experiment than simply assuming that greater content volume will produce greater demand.

The commercial objective needs limits. Digging Beagle’s November analysis of hidden seller goals describes simulated assistants steering customers toward undisclosed operator objectives, including cases involving disclosed customer vulnerability. Those were research scenarios, not documented predatory sales, but they provide a good test for a presale assistant: can it admit that the product is unsuitable or recommend a cheaper option when the evidence supports that answer?

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟩🟩🟩🟩        Cross-market reuse  🟨🟨🟨⬜
Creative range  🟨🟨🟨⬜        Sales evidence      🟨🟨🟨⬜
Setup burden    🟧🟧🟧⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

I would test the assistant against the existing product-page experience using revenue per eligible visitor, completed purchases, returns and unsupported claims. Measuring only visitors who chose to chat would bias the comparison toward people who were already unusually interested.

Sources: Retail field experiments · Javo field evaluation · Digging Beagle: hidden seller objectives

#2. Selective lifecycle messaging

Use customer behavior to send fewer, more relevant messages.

A customer who purchases gifts twice a year does not need the same reminders as somebody replenishing supplies every month. Treating both as equally active subscribers can inflate sending volume while making the messages less useful.

Klaviyo’s October 14 account of Criquet Shirts describes a change from broad customer segments toward more individualized targeting using Orita’s machine-learning scoring. According to the vendor-published case, the retailer sent approximately 40% fewer messages while increasing revenue 30% during the first three months.

The result followed segmentation experiments, better customer data and continuing human editorial decisions. It should not be presented as a controlled measurement of how much an LLM alone contributed.

That limitation does not undermine the practical idea. A company with an existing customer base can investigate whether restraint improves the relationship, particularly when customers purchase seasonally or have already shown that particular messages are irrelevant.

For SaaS, a comparable intervention might identify a customer struggling to activate an important feature and offer appropriate help rather than another generic upgrade campaign.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟨🟨🟨⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟨🟨🟨⬜
Creative range  🟧🟧⬜⬜        Sales evidence      🟧🟧⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟨🟨⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

The experiment should retain a group that receives the existing communication treatment, then compare purchases, renewals, unsubscribes and discounts over an appropriate period. Attribution inside the messaging platform can be helpful, although it does not automatically establish how much revenue would have arrived without the messages.

Source: Klaviyo: Criquet Shirts and AI segmentation

#3. A genuinely useful free diagnostic

Demonstrate expertise through a result the visitor can inspect.

A compatibility checker, migration estimator or technical diagnostic can introduce a product more effectively than another promise that the company understands its customers.

The visitor arrives with a question and leaves with an assessment, even if they choose not to buy anything. AI may help interpret unusual inputs or explain the result, while calculations and rules that can be specified reliably should remain deterministic.

HubSpot’s AI Search Grader is an existing example of an assessment offered as an entry point to a broader product relationship. It establishes that the mechanism is already commercially available, although HubSpot’s product description does not provide an independent estimate of incremental customer acquisition caused by the grader.

The attraction for small teams is that the free experience can be narrowly bounded. A security company might test one configuration weakness; a developer platform might examine compatibility with a selected environment; a financial application might explain a fee calculation using publicly documented rules.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟧🟧⬜⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟩🟩🟩🟩
Creative range  🟩🟩🟩🟩        Sales evidence      🟥⬜⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟨🟨⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

A first pilot should measure completed diagnostics, qualified follow-on actions and the cost of delivering each result. If the tool can be used repeatedly without limits, inference and retrieval costs may turn an effective introduction into an expensive public utility.

The value proposition is stronger when the diagnostic remains useful even for somebody who never supplies an email address.

Source: HubSpot AI Search Grader

#4. Outreach triggered by a meaningful business signal

Contact the customer because something relevant happened, rather than because their address appeared in a database.

Sales teams frequently possess better information than they can use. Product telemetry, customer history and CRM records may contain useful signals, although those systems are often disconnected from the people responsible for acting on them.

Clay’s case study involving Recharge reports a 20% increase in opportunity conversion and 12% higher meeting conversion after the company connected product, transaction and CRM signals to automated growth campaigns.

Those results come from a vendor-published customer case, while the intervention combined data integration, audience selection, AI-supported messaging and campaign operations. The reported uplift cannot be assigned exclusively to AI.

The mechanism is nevertheless attractive for a business whose existing customers or prospects have demonstrated a relevant need. Someone repeatedly exploring migration instructions may benefit from a specific implementation offer, whereas a guessed personal compliment or invented familiarity provides no comparable justification for contact.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟨🟨🟨⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟧🟧⬜⬜
Creative range  🟨🟨🟨⬜        Sales evidence      🟧🟧⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟧🟧🟧⬜        Trust controls      🟧🟧⬜⬜

The first useful metric is accepted opportunities that later become suitable customers, with negative responses and opt-outs retained in the analysis. More replies are not inherently better if they come from people who never wanted the conversation.

This approach also requires greater engineering and governance effort than generating personalized emails, because its usefulness depends on accurate, permissioned and current customer signals.

Source: Clay: Recharge growth operations

#5. Making product information usable by buying agents

Help automated shoppers understand the actual offer instead of trying to manufacture flattering recommendations.

A buying assistant cannot compare a merchant’s products reliably when compatibility requirements, stock information, delivery conditions and prices contradict one another across different pages.

Improving structured product data therefore has a practical commercial purpose, even when the work itself involves more data discipline than generative AI.

Shopify’s Q1 2026 commerce analysis found that AI-referred sessions beginning on product detail pages converted at nearly 50% higher rates than comparable organic-search sessions. It also reported 14% higher average order values for orders attributed to AI-powered search.

These are observational differences between traffic sources, not proof that adding agent-readable product information causes a similar improvement. Buyers arriving from AI systems may already have completed much of their evaluation before visiting the merchant.

The opportunity is consequently to make genuine offers easier to interpret and verify, rather than to infer that any mention in an AI answer is valuable customer acquisition.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟧🟧⬜⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟧🟧⬜⬜
Creative range  🟧🟧⬜⬜        Sales evidence      🟧🟧⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟨🟨⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

I would inspect which AI-referred visitors reach accurate, available products and how their orders perform after cancellations and returns. The mechanism is strongest for businesses with complex catalogs or substantial compatibility questions, and less compelling when the product is already simple and well described.

Source: Shopify: AI-referred shopper behavior

#6. Paid search that adapts to intent

Explore useful search demand beyond a manually maintained keyword list.

Google’s AI Max for Search combines broader search-term matching, generated assets and landing-page selection. These capabilities can help an advertiser discover queries that its existing campaign structure misses, although they can also spend money pursuing demand that never becomes commercially useful.

At launch in May 2025, Google reported a typical 14% increase in conversions or conversion value at similar acquisition cost or return on ad spend for participating advertisers. That is platform-reported launch evidence rather than an independently measured November 2026 outcome.

The important distinction for a small business is between conversions counted by the advertising system and customers who justify the cost of acquiring them.

An automation that becomes better at generating form submissions may look successful while producing a weaker sales pipeline, particularly if the definition of a conversion was too broad at the start.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟩🟩🟩🟩        Cross-market reuse  🟨🟨🟨⬜
Creative range  🟨🟨🟨⬜        Sales evidence      🟧🟧⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟨🟨⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟧🟧⬜⬜

Before increasing spend, I would retain a suitable campaign comparison, inspect the generated claims and evaluate downstream customer quality against acquisition costs.

That is a more useful application of AI than making budget allocation entirely autonomous before the business has agreed on what a worthwhile conversion means.

Source: Google: Introducing AI Max for Search

#7. Scaling creator partnerships without automating the creator

Use agents for coordination while keeping genuine creative relationships central.

Creator marketing involves unusually large amounts of repetitive work: discovering suitable partners, checking audience fit, negotiating deliverables, arranging payments, reviewing material and recording results.

AI can reduce that administrative burden without requiring the creative work itself to become synthetic.

On November 11, Tano announced a $4 million seed round, bringing its total funding to $5 million. Its platform combines AI agents with creator strategists to coordinate campaigns and evaluate their outcomes.

The company reports that HelloFresh saw a 93% increase in conversion rate, while other clients experienced improvements in campaign metrics. These are company-reported customer outcomes without a complete public experimental comparison, so they cannot establish the causal contribution of the agents alone.

That does not make the operating model uninteresting. Reducing the cost of coordinating smaller creators could make partnerships feasible that previously required more staff time than their potential commercial value justified.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟨🟨🟨⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟧🟧⬜⬜
Creative range  🟩🟩🟩🟩        Sales evidence      🟧🟧⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟧🟧🟧⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

For a small pilot, creator fees, usage rights, production costs and paid amplification belong in the calculation alongside purchases or qualified customers. Disclosure and genuine editorial control also matter because an audience’s trust can be damaged by a campaign that is successful at generating posts but careless about the relationship behind them.

The opportunity is to make worthwhile partnerships easier to manage, rather than increase the number of people sending nearly identical promotional messages.

Sources: Tano funding announcement · Cherry Ventures: investment analysis

#8. An invited conversation that reaches the next useful step

Respond to expressed interest without treating permission to answer as permission to sell indefinitely.

A visitor asking for a comparison guide or compatibility checklist has created an opportunity for an appropriate response. A conversational system can deliver the resource, clarify a specific requirement and route an unusual question to the right person.

Manychat’s AI Step documentation describes goals, business context and bounded conversational tasks, while its AI Goals feature supports actions such as sharing links and capturing leads in supported channels.

The documentation establishes available functionality, but it does not provide a controlled commercial uplift for this acquisition design. A comment trigger or automatic reply is also not inherently an AI contribution merely because it appears in a product that offers AI elsewhere.

The useful application begins where natural-language interpretation improves the response beyond what a straightforward automation rule could achieve.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟧🟧⬜⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟧🟧⬜⬜
Creative range  🟨🟨🟨⬜        Sales evidence      🟥⬜⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟨🟨⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

I would measure whether the requested resource was delivered, whether a relevant next step occurred and whether recipients opted out or complained.

A message can be perfectly personalized and still be unwelcome when the person expected one answer rather than an extended sales conversation.

Source: Manychat AI Step

#9. Creative variants treated as controlled experiments

Use faster production to test genuinely different propositions, not to manufacture content volume.

Generating alternative titles, images, scripts and localizations is an obvious application of AI. The marginal production cost can fall dramatically, but reduced effort does not guarantee that a particular variation will persuade anybody.

The randomized retail research discussed earlier provides a useful warning. Its AI-generated marketing-message and Google advertising-title experiments did not establish statistically significant sales improvements over their tested baselines.

Those experiments used particular workflows and models in 2023–2024, so they should not be interpreted as evidence that modern AI creative is universally ineffective.

They do show why the ability to produce many variations must be separated from evidence that those variations improve the business.

A useful experiment would compare genuinely different explanations of the same approved offer, maintaining factual consistency while changing a meaningful creative choice.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟨🟨🟨⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟩🟩🟩🟩
Creative range  🟩🟩🟩🟩        Sales evidence      🟥⬜⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟩⬜⬜⬜        Trust controls      🟧🟧⬜⬜

The relevant measures are qualified customer actions, production cost and downstream conversion, with the original creative retained as a comparison.

This ranks ninth because a team can become very efficient at creating material that does not remove the obstacle preventing somebody from buying. The tactic becomes much more attractive when the team already knows which customer question or objection the experiment should address.

Source: Generative AI and Sales Productivity: retail field experiments

#10. An agent operating the advertising account

Automate approved changes only after the business knows which changes are worth making.

An assistant that reads advertising performance reports may require relatively limited authority. An assistant that can create or modify advertising assets operates across a different boundary, even when the surrounding interface looks almost identical.

Digging Beagle’s November 11 assessment documents a concrete example. Google Ads MCP version 0.0.6, released on November 2, introduced default-listed write-capable tools for advertising assets, video-related operations and labels.

Google’s implementation describes a validate-first proposal followed by explicit confirmation before a mutation is committed. Existing OAuth permissions still apply, and the documented tools do not allow the agent to change campaign budgets or bids.

This was a capability change, not a confirmed attack or an observed unauthorized advertising modification.

The review question is whether an agent host rechecks its permissions when a familiar integration acquires new tools. A server that was previously used for reading reports should not automatically receive broad approval for every future write operation.

TECH / BUILD                    APPLICATION / MARKET
AI backing      🟨🟨🟨⬜        Cross-market reuse  🟧🟧⬜⬜
Creative range  🟧🟧⬜⬜        Sales evidence      🟥⬜⬜⬜
Setup burden    🟧🟧🟧⬜        Trust controls      🟨🟨🟨⬜

For an initial pilot, the agent can identify an issue, prepare an exact proposed change and present it for review, while the operator confirms the intended account, asset and effect.

The account’s resulting audit history should establish what changed. That is stronger evidence than a conversational statement claiming that the agent completed the requested operation.

This ranks last for a small team’s first growth experiment, rather than as a judgment that operating automation has little value. It becomes attractive when the team already possesses reliable customer data, campaign objectives and authorization rules.

Sources: Digging Beagle: Google Ads MCP · Google Ads MCP documentation

What would justify increasing the budget?

These ten mechanisms are not substitutes for one another, which is why the ranking follows the obstacles a small business is likely to encounter rather than simply rewarding the largest amount of automation.

Acquisition, evaluation, conversion and retention present different obstacles, so a business should select its automation according to the customer decision it needs to improve rather than add more activity to an unrelated stage.

Product-grounded advice takes first place because its effect on a purchase decision can be tested against an existing experience, and it has relevant experimental evidence. A useful diagnostic ranks highly despite limited published sales evidence because a team can constrain its scope and cost while learning whether the result attracts suitable prospects.

An agent operating an advertising account, meanwhile, may be technically impressive without establishing why the account deserves additional spending. Its value becomes easier to demonstrate once the company has defined the commercial outcome and can inspect each consequential change.

For the first experiment, I would preserve a comparable group of customers, measure the resulting purchases or qualified opportunities, and follow those outcomes far enough to observe cancellations, poor fit and service costs.

The customer-level comparison matters because a campaign can generate attributed revenue without creating the same amount of additional business. Customers may have purchased anyway, and platform activity metrics rarely settle that question on their own.

A suitable first pilot therefore has three properties: it addresses an identified obstacle, produces an observable commercial result, and can be stopped or corrected when the evidence does not support expansion.

For a crypto or financial product, the same reasoning would favor accurate explanations, compatibility checks and transparent costs over invented returns, artificial community activity or hidden pressure applied through an assistant.

The next improvement in AI growth may come from better models, but a small team should be able to justify the mechanism it purchases without first believing the model’s promises about its own usefulness.

Before funding the next automation, I would ask which customer decision it improves, how that improvement will be measured, and what the business would have earned without it.

items.title: Semantic Models: What They Are, the Types Available, and When to Use Which
items.summary: The same question, three different queries Ask “What was net revenue last quarter?” through three consumers that share one warehouse, and you can get three answers. A finance report filters on ship_date, excludes tax and subtracts refunds. A BI dashboard filters on created_at and sums amount. An LLM-generated query joins orders to refunds and sums amount again, so any order with two refunds is counted twice and cancelled orders stay in. All three queries run without errors, and each is internally consistent. They disagree because the definition of net revenue lives in each consumer’s own query logic, not in one shared place. A semantic model moves it out of the queries and into a single governed object. The metric, its filters, its time dimension, the join path and the grain are declared once, and every consumer compiles its SQL from that declaration. On the left, each consumer carries its own logic. On the right, all three request the metric from one model. The rest of this article covers what a semantic model contains, why raw schemas break LLM-generated SQL, the main types of semantic model, how each is consumed, and how to choose among them. The short rule is to pick the one that lives where your data and your queries already live, and to define every metric once. What a semantic model is A semantic model is a governed description of your data in business terms: entities, metrics, dimensions, relationships and rules. People write it once, and both humans and software read it. Think of it as the glossary and rulebook that sits between raw tables and everyone who asks questions of them. The term has a second meaning in AI work: an embedding model that maps text to vectors so that similar meanings land close together. That powers semantic search over documents and is a separate topic. This article covers the analytics meaning. What a semantic model encodes A semantic model turns database structure into business meaning. It typically defines six kinds of things. The examples are illustrative. The important property is that each definition exists once and every consumer shares it. A dashboard, a notebook and an LLM agent all compute net revenue the same way, because none of them redefines it. Why raw schemas fail LLMs The most dangerous failure of text-to-SQL is not an error message. It is a query that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number. The model may join tables incorrectly or misread a column’s meaning, and nothing sits between the question and the generated SQL to catch it. Five causes recur in practice. Ambiguous columns. status, amount and date mean different things in different tables. Which date is the order date, and which is the ship date? Undefined metrics. “Revenue”, “active user” and “churn” each have several defensible definitions, and the schema holds none of them. Hidden join paths. Several routes may connect two tables, and only one is correct for the question asked. Fan-out and grain errors. Joining a one-to-many table before aggregating duplicates rows and inflates totals without any warning. Implicit filters. Test accounts, cancelled orders and soft-deleted rows are excluded by convention, not by structure. Better models help but cannot fully fix these, because the missing information is not in the schema. It lives in people’s heads and in old dashboards. Types of semantic models Semantic models differ mainly in where they live, because that decides who can use them and how portable they are. Six types cover most of what you will meet. Read the picture from the bottom. Tables sit in the data platform, a semantic model of one of four kinds sits above them, and consumers ask for metrics by name. Three notes on the table. Warehouse-native objects are structured definitions. A Snowflake semantic view describes logical tables, relationships, facts, dimensions and metrics, and it can also carry verified queries and instructions for AI-generated SQL. A Databricks metric view separates measure definitions from dimensions, so the engine computes the right aggregation for whatever grouping a user asks for, and it can carry synonyms for AI accuracy. OSI is about portability. It is a vendor-neutral, open-source format for datasets, metrics, dimensions and relationships, backed by several data and analytics vendors. Treat it as something to watch rather than something to depend on today. Verification scope. The Snowflake, Databricks, Microsoft and OSI details were checked against current vendor documentation. The Looker, Cube, AtScale, code-defined and ontology rows describe the general design and were not benchmarked here. Product names and features change quickly, so confirm against current docs before choosing. How semantic models are consumed A semantic model is only useful when something reads it. Five consumption patterns are common, and one model can serve several of them at once. All five patterns read the same model, and the model generates the SQL that the warehouse runs. The fourth and fifth patterns are where semantic models matter most for AI. Fabric IQ, for example, answers questions over governed models while respecting role-based access and row-level security, so the assistant cannot see more than the user could. A later section walks through how an LLM consumes a model step by step. Which semantic model to use when Start from where your data lives and where your people already ask questions. The table maps common situations to a starting point. Read the path from the top and stop at the first yes. It is a starting point, not a rule, because many teams combine types. Four questions settle most choices. Where does the data live? Prefer a model that sits next to it. Where do people already ask questions? Prefer the tool they already use. Who owns the definitions? Prefer a home where that team can review and version them. What must be portable? If the answer is “everything”, favor an independent layer or an open format. These types are not exclusive. A common arrangement is one metric layer for numbers plus an ontology for relationships between concepts. Deep dive: consuming a semantic model from an LLM The semantic model shrinks the LLM’s job from writing SQL to choosing from a menu of defined terms. Questions the model describes flow left to right. Anything it does not describe stops at the semantic layer with an explicit refusal. In a typical design, the LLM decomposes a question into the right combination of metrics and dimensions, and the semantic engine generates the SQL deterministically. If the model picks the right metric and dimensions, the query is correct, and it cannot return numbers that differ subtly from run to run. The trade-off is coverage: only questions the model describes can be answered. A grounded pipeline has five stages. Interpret. The LLM maps the question to metrics, dimensions, filters and a time range, using the names, descriptions and synonyms in the model. Validate. The request is checked against the model. An unknown metric or an invalid combination is rejected. Compile. The semantic engine generates SQL using the defined joins, filters and grain. Execute and explain. The warehouse runs the query, and the answer comes back with the definitions that produced it. Fall back. If the question is not modeled, the system says so clearly and routes it to a guarded alternative or a person. Worked example: one question, two routes This example is illustrative. The tables, columns and definitions are invented. The question is “What was net revenue by region last quarter?”, asked in October 2026. Route 1: raw schema. Given tables orders, refunds and customers, a model might plausibly write this. SELECT c.region, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.id WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-07-01' AND o.created_at < '2026-10-01' GROUP BY c.region;s It runs and returns numbers, and it is wrong in four ways: it counts cancelled orders, includes tax, filters on creation date instead of ship date, and the join to refunds duplicates any order with more than one refund. It never subtracts a refund at all. Route 2: semantic layer. The model defines net_revenue once: order amount excluding tax and cancelled orders, minus refunds, recognized on ship date. The LLM then only has to produce a structured request. { "metrics": ["net_revenue"], "group_by": ["customer__region"], "time": { "grain": "quarter", "range": "2026-Q3" } } The engine compiles the correct SQL from the definition. The LLM had no opportunity to get the logic wrong, and every consumer of net_revenue gets the same number. How to measure the impact on your own data Accuracy depends on the dataset, the question set and the model, so measure the effect on your own data instead of borrowing someone else’s figure. A repeatable evaluation needs five things: Write a golden set of real questions with verified answers. Run each question several times, since consistency is part of trust. Score three outcomes separately: correct, wrong but plausible, and correctly declined. Track coverage, meaning the share of real questions the semantic model can answer. Record cost and latency alongside accuracy. Pitfalls and design guidance Coverage is the price of determinism. A semantic layer answers only what it models. Grow it from the questions people actually ask, using query logs and declined requests as the backlog. Start small. Model the dozen metrics people argue about first. Keep a fallback, and label it. For exploratory questions, guarded text-to-SQL is reasonable, but mark its answers as unverified. Prefer the semantic layer first and text-to-SQL second for ad hoc work. Give every metric an owner. A definition nobody owns drifts, and drift brings back the inconsistency you built the layer to remove. Version it. Metric changes alter historical numbers, so record when and why a definition changed. Write good descriptions and synonyms. The LLM selects terms by reading them. Vague names produce wrong selections. Do not model everything. An oversized model slows interpretation and invites the same ambiguity you are removing. Takeaways A semantic model states what your data means once, in business terms, so people and LLMs share one definition instead of guessing. Six types exist: warehouse-native, BI-platform, code-defined, independent, ontology-based and interchange formats. They differ mainly in where they live. Choose by where your data lives and where your people already ask questions, then check who owns the definitions and what must be portable. Dashboards, SQL, APIs, built-in assistants and your own LLM agent can all consume the same model. For LLMs, a semantic layer fails loudly with a clear refusal, while raw-schema text-to-SQL can fail quietly with a plausible wrong number. Start with the dozen contested metrics, give each an owner, version every change, and measure on your own questions. items.summary_html:
The same question, three different queries

Ask “What was net revenue last quarter?” through three consumers that share one warehouse, and you can get three answers. A finance report filters on ship_date, excludes tax and subtracts refunds. A BI dashboard filters on created_at and sums amount. An LLM-generated query joins orders to refunds and sums amount again, so any order with two refunds is counted twice and cancelled orders stay in. All three queries run without errors, and each is internally consistent.

They disagree because the definition of net revenue lives in each consumer’s own query logic, not in one shared place. A semantic model moves it out of the queries and into a single governed object. The metric, its filters, its time dimension, the join path and the grain are declared once, and every consumer compiles its SQL from that declaration.

On the left, each consumer carries its own logic. On the right, all three request the metric from one model.

The rest of this article covers what a semantic model contains, why raw schemas break LLM-generated SQL, the main types of semantic model, how each is consumed, and how to choose among them. The short rule is to pick the one that lives where your data and your queries already live, and to define every metric once.

What a semantic model is

A semantic model is a governed description of your data in business terms: entities, metrics, dimensions, relationships and rules. People write it once, and both humans and software read it. Think of it as the glossary and rulebook that sits between raw tables and everyone who asks questions of them.

The term has a second meaning in AI work: an embedding model that maps text to vectors so that similar meanings land close together. That powers semantic search over documents and is a separate topic. This article covers the analytics meaning.

What a semantic model encodes

A semantic model turns database structure into business meaning. It typically defines six kinds of things. The examples are illustrative.

The important property is that each definition exists once and every consumer shares it. A dashboard, a notebook and an LLM agent all compute net revenue the same way, because none of them redefines it.

Why raw schemas fail LLMs

The most dangerous failure of text-to-SQL is not an error message. It is a query that runs and returns a plausible, wrong number. The model may join tables incorrectly or misread a column’s meaning, and nothing sits between the question and the generated SQL to catch it.

Five causes recur in practice.

  • Ambiguous columns. status, amount and date mean different things in different tables. Which date is the order date, and which is the ship date?
  • Undefined metrics. “Revenue”, “active user” and “churn” each have several defensible definitions, and the schema holds none of them.
  • Hidden join paths. Several routes may connect two tables, and only one is correct for the question asked.
  • Fan-out and grain errors. Joining a one-to-many table before aggregating duplicates rows and inflates totals without any warning.
  • Implicit filters. Test accounts, cancelled orders and soft-deleted rows are excluded by convention, not by structure.

Better models help but cannot fully fix these, because the missing information is not in the schema. It lives in people’s heads and in old dashboards.

Types of semantic models

Semantic models differ mainly in where they live, because that decides who can use them and how portable they are. Six types cover most of what you will meet.

Read the picture from the bottom. Tables sit in the data platform, a semantic model of one of four kinds sits above them, and consumers ask for metrics by name.

Three notes on the table.

  • Warehouse-native objects are structured definitions. A Snowflake semantic view describes logical tables, relationships, facts, dimensions and metrics, and it can also carry verified queries and instructions for AI-generated SQL. A Databricks metric view separates measure definitions from dimensions, so the engine computes the right aggregation for whatever grouping a user asks for, and it can carry synonyms for AI accuracy.
  • OSI is about portability. It is a vendor-neutral, open-source format for datasets, metrics, dimensions and relationships, backed by several data and analytics vendors. Treat it as something to watch rather than something to depend on today.
  • Verification scope. The Snowflake, Databricks, Microsoft and OSI details were checked against current vendor documentation. The Looker, Cube, AtScale, code-defined and ontology rows describe the general design and were not benchmarked here. Product names and features change quickly, so confirm against current docs before choosing.
How semantic models are consumed

A semantic model is only useful when something reads it. Five consumption patterns are common, and one model can serve several of them at once.

All five patterns read the same model, and the model generates the SQL that the warehouse runs.

The fourth and fifth patterns are where semantic models matter most for AI. Fabric IQ, for example, answers questions over governed models while respecting role-based access and row-level security, so the assistant cannot see more than the user could. A later section walks through how an LLM consumes a model step by step.

Which semantic model to use when

Start from where your data lives and where your people already ask questions. The table maps common situations to a starting point.

Read the path from the top and stop at the first yes. It is a starting point, not a rule, because many teams combine types.

Four questions settle most choices.

  1. Where does the data live? Prefer a model that sits next to it.
  2. Where do people already ask questions? Prefer the tool they already use.
  3. Who owns the definitions? Prefer a home where that team can review and version them.
  4. What must be portable? If the answer is “everything”, favor an independent layer or an open format.

These types are not exclusive. A common arrangement is one metric layer for numbers plus an ontology for relationships between concepts.

Deep dive: consuming a semantic model from an LLM

The semantic model shrinks the LLM’s job from writing SQL to choosing from a menu of defined terms.

Questions the model describes flow left to right. Anything it does not describe stops at the semantic layer with an explicit refusal.

In a typical design, the LLM decomposes a question into the right combination of metrics and dimensions, and the semantic engine generates the SQL deterministically. If the model picks the right metric and dimensions, the query is correct, and it cannot return numbers that differ subtly from run to run. The trade-off is coverage: only questions the model describes can be answered.

A grounded pipeline has five stages.

  1. Interpret. The LLM maps the question to metrics, dimensions, filters and a time range, using the names, descriptions and synonyms in the model.
  2. Validate. The request is checked against the model. An unknown metric or an invalid combination is rejected.
  3. Compile. The semantic engine generates SQL using the defined joins, filters and grain.
  4. Execute and explain. The warehouse runs the query, and the answer comes back with the definitions that produced it.
  5. Fall back. If the question is not modeled, the system says so clearly and routes it to a guarded alternative or a person.
Worked example: one question, two routes

This example is illustrative. The tables, columns and definitions are invented. The question is “What was net revenue by region last quarter?”, asked in October 2026.

Route 1: raw schema. Given tables orders, refunds and customers, a model might plausibly write this.

SELECT c.region, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-07-01' AND o.created_at < '2026-10-01'
GROUP BY c.region;s

It runs and returns numbers, and it is wrong in four ways: it counts cancelled orders, includes tax, filters on creation date instead of ship date, and the join to refunds duplicates any order with more than one refund. It never subtracts a refund at all.

Route 2: semantic layer. The model defines net_revenue once: order amount excluding tax and cancelled orders, minus refunds, recognized on ship date. The LLM then only has to produce a structured request.

{
  "metrics": ["net_revenue"],
  "group_by": ["customer__region"],
  "time": { "grain": "quarter", "range": "2026-Q3" }
}

The engine compiles the correct SQL from the definition. The LLM had no opportunity to get the logic wrong, and every consumer of net_revenue gets the same number.

How to measure the impact on your own data

Accuracy depends on the dataset, the question set and the model, so measure the effect on your own data instead of borrowing someone else’s figure. A repeatable evaluation needs five things:

  1. Write a golden set of real questions with verified answers.
  2. Run each question several times, since consistency is part of trust.
  3. Score three outcomes separately: correct, wrong but plausible, and correctly declined.
  4. Track coverage, meaning the share of real questions the semantic model can answer.
  5. Record cost and latency alongside accuracy.
Pitfalls and design guidance
  • Coverage is the price of determinism. A semantic layer answers only what it models. Grow it from the questions people actually ask, using query logs and declined requests as the backlog.
  • Start small. Model the dozen metrics people argue about first.
  • Keep a fallback, and label it. For exploratory questions, guarded text-to-SQL is reasonable, but mark its answers as unverified. Prefer the semantic layer first and text-to-SQL second for ad hoc work.
  • Give every metric an owner. A definition nobody owns drifts, and drift brings back the inconsistency you built the layer to remove.
  • Version it. Metric changes alter historical numbers, so record when and why a definition changed.
  • Write good descriptions and synonyms. The LLM selects terms by reading them. Vague names produce wrong selections.
  • Do not model everything. An oversized model slows interpretation and invites the same ambiguity you are removing.
Takeaways
  1. A semantic model states what your data means once, in business terms, so people and LLMs share one definition instead of guessing.
  2. Six types exist: warehouse-native, BI-platform, code-defined, independent, ontology-based and interchange formats. They differ mainly in where they live.
  3. Choose by where your data lives and where your people already ask questions, then check who owns the definitions and what must be portable.
  4. Dashboards, SQL, APIs, built-in assistants and your own LLM agent can all consume the same model.
  5. For LLMs, a semantic layer fails loudly with a clear refusal, while raw-schema text-to-SQL can fail quietly with a plausible wrong number.
  6. Start with the dozen contested metrics, give each an owner, version every change, and measure on your own questions.

In the layered architecture described later in this series, the semantic model grounds what the system knows, and a decision model governs what it does next.

items.title: How Modern Web Guidance Helps Coding Agents Choose Browser APIs
items.summary: Illustration generated with AI. How to give an agent current browser guidance, with a Codex dialog refactor that uncovered a focus regression in WebKit. Modern Web Guidance is a skill from the Chrome team that gives coding agents a searchable library of web-platform guides and browser compatibility data. The team built it because agents can fall back on familiar JavaScript patterns even when HTML or CSS can handle the same job. The guides help an agent choose an API based on the browsers a project actually supports. Chrome announced the stable 1.0 release on November 10, 2026, with Firefox and Edge joining the project. Chrome’s release announcement To use it with a compatible agent such as Codex or Claude Code, run npx modern-web-guidance@latest install from your project directory. Record your browser requirements in the project’s agent instructions, such as AGENTS.md in Codex. You can name minimum browser versions or set a target like Baseline 2025, which covers features that became interoperable across major browsers by the end of that year. Installation and browser targets Then give the agent a concrete task, such as simplifying a settings dialog while preserving its keyboard behavior. The skill tells the agent to search for the relevant UI pattern and retrieve a guide before editing. The guide supplies implementation advice and helps the agent decide whether a feature needs a fallback for older browsers. How the guide library works Eight rewrites of one dialog Browser capture of the first guided version for current browsers, Playwright WebKit 27.2, November 12, 2026. What does access to those guides change in a refactor? The test started with a small notification-settings page. Its custom dialog used 46 nonblank lines of JavaScript to open and close the overlay, keep the background inactive, manage keyboard focus, and apply or discard a change. The task was to simplify the code while preserving those behaviors. Within each pair, two fresh Codex sessions got the same prompt, starting files, and browser requirements. Both ran GPT-5.6 Terra at low reasoning effort. One had Modern Web Guidance 1.0 installed. Two pairs targeted Safari 26.2 and newer and set a Baseline 2025 target. The other two required support back to Safari 18.4 and asked for a fallback or a supported alternative when an API was too new. The finished pages went through six scenarios in Chrome 157, Firefox 159, and Playwright WebKit 27.2. The older-target pages also had to pass in Playwright WebKit 18.4. These are specific test environments. The Safari versions describe project requirements, while the WebKit versions describe the test builds. Two guided sessions reached the outer time limit after writing their changes. Their saved pages went through the same checks. Every run chose a native . Codex reached for that element even with no guidance installed. The change showed up one step later, in how the button opened it. The browser takes over opening the dialog All four unguided versions called showModal() from JavaScript. The two guided versions for current browsers handed the opening action to the button itself. The button from the first guided run shows both attributes. commandfor="delivery-editor" command="show-modal">Edit delivery commandfor names the dialog by ID. command="show-modal" tells the browser what to do when the button is activated. The app still uses JavaScript to restore the saved form value on opening and apply a change on Save. The browser now handles the act of opening the modal. MDN’s Invoker Commands reference Author-created chart from the November 12, 2026 experiment. “Passed” means all six scenarios passed in the test environments for that pair. The focus regressions were observed in WebKit after opening by mouse. In the current-browser pairs, the guided code came in at 15 nonblank JavaScript lines each, compared with 20 and 21 without the guides. Those counts cover the entire rewrite, including changes to focus and form handling. Under the older-browser requirement, both guided versions kept showModal(). The difference shrank to one line in each pair. In an extra check outside the current-browser target, the buttons that relied on the HTML command did nothing in WebKit 18.4. Safari added support for those commands in 26.2. Browser support for Invoker Commands The opener and the previously focused element All four unguided versions passed all six scenarios in their test environments. One of the four guided versions did. All eight passed in Chrome and Firefox. In WebKit, three guided versions left focus off Edit delivery after a mouse opening followed by Escape, Cancel, or Save. One of those versions still used showModal(). The same symptom appeared with either way of opening the dialog. The effect was easy to reproduce in the first pair. Click Edit delivery , press Escape, then press Enter. In WebKit 27.2, both dialogs closed on Escape. Enter reopened the unguided version, where focus had returned to the button. The guided version stayed closed. Focus had landed on the page’s body. The dialog guide in version 1.0.0 advises against writing focus restoration code and says, “The browser returns it to the invoker.” The logs show all four guided sessions retrieved that guide. The reason Codex kept or removed any particular line remains unknown. Version 1.0.0 dialog guide The HTML Standard describes a more precise rule. When a modal opens, the browser records the element that was focused immediately beforehand and attempts to restore that focus when the modal closes. In Safari, clicking a button generally leaves it unfocused. The element that opened the dialog and the element that previously held focus can therefore be different. HTML Standard · MDN on clicking and focus The same generated page makes that difference visible. In the WebKit 27.2 probe, opening with Enter from the focused button and closing with Escape returned focus to the button. Opening with a mouse click and closing with Escape left body as the active element in the three affected versions. The passing guided version for the older target kept editSettings.focus() in its close handler. It gave the application an explicit destination for focus, as all four unguided versions did. For a pull request like this, make the expected behavior explicit. Open the modal with a click and with the keyboard. After Escape, Cancel, and Save, check that focus lands back on the opener in a browser the project supports. The button should still be ready for the user’s next Enter, even when HTML handled the opening. You can name minimum browser versions or set a target like Baseline 2025, which covers features that became interoperable across major browsers by the end of that year. Installation and browser targets

Then give the agent a concrete task, such as simplifying a settings dialog while preserving its keyboard behavior. The skill tells the agent to search for the relevant UI pattern and retrieve a guide before editing. The guide supplies implementation advice and helps the agent decide whether a feature needs a fallback for older browsers. How the guide library works

Eight rewrites of one dialogBrowser capture of the first guided version for current browsers, Playwright WebKit 27.2, November 12, 2026.

What does access to those guides change in a refactor? The test started with a small notification-settings page. Its custom dialog used 46 nonblank lines of JavaScript to open and close the overlay, keep the background inactive, manage keyboard focus, and apply or discard a change. The task was to simplify the code while preserving those behaviors.

Within each pair, two fresh Codex sessions got the same prompt, starting files, and browser requirements. Both ran GPT-5.6 Terra at low reasoning effort. One had Modern Web Guidance 1.0 installed. Two pairs targeted Safari 26.2 and newer and set a Baseline 2025 target. The other two required support back to Safari 18.4 and asked for a fallback or a supported alternative when an API was too new.

The finished pages went through six scenarios in Chrome 157, Firefox 159, and Playwright WebKit 27.2. The older-target pages also had to pass in Playwright WebKit 18.4. These are specific test environments. The Safari versions describe project requirements, while the WebKit versions describe the test builds. Two guided sessions reached the outer time limit after writing their changes. Their saved pages went through the same checks.

Every run chose a native . Codex reached for that element even with no guidance installed. The change showed up one step later, in how the button opened it.

The browser takes over opening the dialog

All four unguided versions called showModal() from JavaScript. The two guided versions for current browsers handed the opening action to the button itself. The button from the first guided run shows both attributes.

        commandfor="delivery-editor" command="show-modal">Edit delivery

commandfor names the dialog by ID. command="show-modal" tells the browser what to do when the button is activated. The app still uses JavaScript to restore the saved form value on opening and apply a change on Save. The browser now handles the act of opening the modal. MDN’s Invoker Commands reference

Author-created chart from the November 12, 2026 experiment. “Passed” means all six scenarios passed in the test environments for that pair. The focus regressions were observed in WebKit after opening by mouse.

In the current-browser pairs, the guided code came in at 15 nonblank JavaScript lines each, compared with 20 and 21 without the guides. Those counts cover the entire rewrite, including changes to focus and form handling. Under the older-browser requirement, both guided versions kept showModal(). The difference shrank to one line in each pair. In an extra check outside the current-browser target, the buttons that relied on the HTML command did nothing in WebKit 18.4. Safari added support for those commands in 26.2. Browser support for Invoker Commands

The opener and the previously focused element

All four unguided versions passed all six scenarios in their test environments. One of the four guided versions did. All eight passed in Chrome and Firefox. In WebKit, three guided versions left focus off Edit delivery after a mouse opening followed by Escape, Cancel, or Save. One of those versions still used showModal(). The same symptom appeared with either way of opening the dialog.

The effect was easy to reproduce in the first pair. Click Edit delivery, press Escape, then press Enter. In WebKit 27.2, both dialogs closed on Escape. Enter reopened the unguided version, where focus had returned to the button. The guided version stayed closed. Focus had landed on the page’s body.

The dialog guide in version 1.0.0 advises against writing focus restoration code and says, “The browser returns it to the invoker.” The logs show all four guided sessions retrieved that guide. The reason Codex kept or removed any particular line remains unknown. Version 1.0.0 dialog guide

The HTML Standard describes a more precise rule. When a modal opens, the browser records the element that was focused immediately beforehand and attempts to restore that focus when the modal closes. In Safari, clicking a button generally leaves it unfocused. The element that opened the dialog and the element that previously held focus can therefore be different. HTML Standard · MDN on clicking and focus

The same generated page makes that difference visible. In the WebKit 27.2 probe, opening with Enter from the focused button and closing with Escape returned focus to the button. Opening with a mouse click and closing with Escape left body as the active element in the three affected versions. The passing guided version for the older target kept editSettings.focus() in its close handler. It gave the application an explicit destination for focus, as all four unguided versions did.

For a pull request like this, make the expected behavior explicit. Open the modal with a click and with the keyboard. After Escape, Cancel, and Save, check that focus lands back on the opener in a browser the project supports. The button should still be ready for the user’s next Enter, even when HTML handled the opening.

items.title: Trump's transportation chief demands $50 billion to prevent another huge FAA fiasco
items.summary: US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said that Congress needs to Homeland Security $50 billion to fix the matter at the root. Alex Wong/Getty Images Trump's transportation chief wants $50 billion to replace aging tech blamed for Friday ground stop. Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy cited old routers overloading for the repeated failures. Nationwide FAA halt delayed about 10,000 flights, and led to over 6,000 cancellations. The Department of Transportation says it wants $50 billion to replace aging technology that led to Friday's ground stop . In a press conference on Friday evening, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the US has "old switches, old routers" that became overloaded with data and failed, disrupting communications at multiple air-route traffic-control centers. "We should talk to our senators and our members of Congress to say 'we don't deserve this, America,'" Duffy said. "This is the greatest country — by the way, with the greatest president — let's give the money to fix this very real problem." "How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?" Duffy added. During the press conference, Duffy repeatedly said the administration needs $50 billion to replace the hardware and software that has been around since the 1980s. He added that the system can no longer handle the volume of data moving through it. "We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it — nickel-and-diming it together — does not work. This is what happens when that takes place, " Mullin said. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the US as a safety precaution, while aircraft already in the air continued toward their destinations or were diverted as needed. The ground stop was lifted around 8:15 pm ET on Friday, but the disruption left airlines scrambling to reposition planes and crews. Roughly 10,000 flights were delayed and nearly 5,000 canceled, according to Business Insider's count. The officials said they have seen no evidence that the failure was caused by a cyberattack or system failures linked to artificial intelligence, but added that they are still investigating the precise cause of the outage. items.title: FAA SMART AI system vendor and Microsoft both say ground stop isn't their fault
items.summary: Passengers wait inside Dulles International Airport in Virginia after the FAA grounded flights nationwide. Daniel Heuer/Reuters Authorities are investigating the cause of the major FAA outage. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind the FAA's new SMART system, said it wasn't their fault Microsoft wrote that its products weren't involved either, which the Trump administration confirmed. What caused the nationwide plane chaos? Microsoft and the company behind the FAA's new AI-powered SMART system have something to say: It wasn't us. On Friday afternoon, thousands of flights were delayed after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all planes grounded nationwide because of communications issues. At a press conference at the White House Friday night, Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or attack caused by "SI" — the administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence. Some online had speculated that the problem was related to the SMART system, a tool from Air Space Intelligence that uses AI to monitor air traffic and prevent delays. In September, POLITICO reported that airline industry veterans were initially nervous about the new system because of the FAA's vague description. The SMART system began rolling out to wider use this week. But on Friday, ASI wrote in an X post that their system wasn't connected to the massive FAA outage. "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.," the company said . Microsoft had its own problems this week, as a worldwide outage knocked out services like email for hours, snarling the workweek at major companies and inspiring memes from office workers. Some wondered online if Microsoft was connected. It quickly shot those suspicions down. "We have no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company wrote on X . At the press conference Friday night, Mullin confirmed Microsoft was not to blame. Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed antiquated equipment that was "overwhelmed" for the outage. Duffy, at the same press conference, demanded $50 billion from Congress to update FAA equipment. The FAA outage is nearly unprecedented, with only one other nationwide ground stop since federal aviation officials famously froze US airspace during the 9/11 terrorist attacks. The ground stop was lifted on Friday night, but not before more than 5,000 flights were canceled, according to FlightAware.com . Photos from airports across the country showed crowds forming as passengers were taken off flights and planes lining up on the tarmac. Read the original article on Business Insider

Daniel Heuer/Reuters

  • Authorities are investigating the cause of the major FAA outage.
  • Air Space Intelligence, the company behind the FAA's new SMART system, said it wasn't their fault
  • Microsoft wrote that its products weren't involved either, which the Trump administration confirmed.

What caused the nationwide plane chaos?

Microsoft and the company behind the FAA's new AI-powered SMART system have something to say: It wasn't us.

On Friday afternoon, thousands of flights were delayed after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all planes grounded nationwide because of communications issues.

At a press conference at the White House Friday night, Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or attack caused by "SI" — the administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence.

Some online had speculated that the problem was related to the SMART system, a tool from Air Space Intelligence that uses AI to monitor air traffic and prevent delays. In September, POLITICO reported that airline industry veterans were initially nervous about the new system because of the FAA's vague description.

The SMART system began rolling out to wider use this week.

But on Friday, ASI wrote in an X post that their system wasn't connected to the massive FAA outage.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.," the company said.

Microsoft had its own problems this week, as a worldwide outage knocked out services like email for hours, snarling the workweek at major companies and inspiring memes from office workers. Some wondered online if Microsoft was connected.

It quickly shot those suspicions down.

"We have no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company wrote on X.

At the press conference Friday night, Mullin confirmed Microsoft was not to blame. Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed antiquated equipment that was "overwhelmed" for the outage.

Duffy, at the same press conference, demanded $50 billion from Congress to update FAA equipment.

The FAA outage is nearly unprecedented, with only one other nationwide ground stop since federal aviation officials famously froze US airspace during the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

The ground stop was lifted on Friday night, but not before more than 5,000 flights were canceled, according to FlightAware.com.

Photos from airports across the country showed crowds forming as passengers were taken off flights and planes lining up on the tarmac.

items.title: Photos show trouble at airports nationwide as FAA grounds all flights
items.summary: A passenger walks past a board displaying delayed flights at JFK International in New York City after the FAA issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" on Friday. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters Passengers are being taken off planes nationwide. The FAA ordered all planes grounded. The Transportation Secretary cited a "communications" issue at all air-traffic control centers. It's a bad night to be traveling. Passengers are being deplaned, and flights are delayed after the FAA grounded every flight nationwide because of what it called "extraordinary circumstances." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was ordered because of a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Officials have not yet said what caused the communication issue. As the ground stop became a multi-hour ordeal, passengers have begun to crowd boarding areas, have been asked to leave flights, and are scrambling to find their luggage. 'All flights have been halted' Passengers wait at McGhee Tyson Airport after the FAA issued a ground stop for all flights across the U.S. on Nov. 13. Adam Sparks/News Sentinel/Reuters Boarding areas began to fill up at airports across the country. On Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a temporary telecommunications outage. "Out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted," said the FAA. "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis." The exact cause remains unclear A person stands in front of a departures board at Logan international airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." Brian Snyder/Reuters Flight boards are flashing red and orange across all major airports. Transportation officials have not yet said why they issued the ground stop. The FAA is prepared to make a system update Passengers wait inside the main terminal after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Dulles International Airport, in Dulles, Virginia, US, November 13, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Heuer Daniel Heuer/Reuters In some airports, stranded passengers are congregating in terminals as security check lines grow longer. The outage occurred the same day the FAA rolled out SMART , a new AI-powered tool designed to help manage air traffic. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, said Friday's disruption was not "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Lines are growing in many airports Queues are forming at the Salt Lake City airport after passengers were told to disembark a flight to Chicago. Jon Lett Jon Lett, a passenger who was traveling from the Salt Lake City Airport to Kansas City, told Business Insider that everyone on his flight has been told to disembark and wait. Lett said that, though the mood among passengers remains "chill," there is no telling whether his flight will be able to depart anytime soon. Planes are parked on the tarmac Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI / AFP via Getty Images Photos show planes parked back-to-back at Chicago O'Hare International Airport. National ground stops are historically rare for the FAA. In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of an outage involving its pilot alert system. Before that, nationwide air traffic was halted following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Traffic outside the airports also began to pile up Traffic piles up outside a terminal at Dulles International in Virginia after the FAA issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" on Friday. Daniel Heuer/Reuters Passengers are stranded Air travelers wait inside the Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026. Chris Day / The Commercial Appeal/Reuters Some passengers are settling in and preparing for a night spent at the airport. Air travelers could be seen camping out on the floor and napping. Luggage is slow to appear People line up to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. Adam Gray/Getty Images Lines to collect luggage are also growing in some airports. It is unclear whether they are arriving passengers or travelers giving up on their flight for the day. Travelers are left sitting in the plane People wait whilst onboard a plane at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington, DC Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images Not everyone has been ordered to disembark. Photos showed some passengers sitting in unmoving planes. The FAA has not issued any updates Emmanuel Romero, relaxes on the ground as his daughters Arianne Romero, left, Hannah Romero, right, and wife, Alejandra Para, wait in the terminal at St. Louis Lambert International Airport to hear if their flight to California will be cancelled on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. The family's flight is affected by the nationwide ground stop the FAA issued to all flights Friday afternoon. The family was in Missouri to see Hannah graduate from her Advanced Individual Training (AIT) with the Army at Fort Leonard Wood. (Photo by David Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images) David Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images As of 8 p.m., the FAA has not issued any new updates on when the ground stop will end. Some exhausted passengers with canceled flights are lying down on the floor to rest. Read the original article on Business Insider
